abstract: The learning dynamics of the back-propagation algorithm are in(cid:173) vestigated when complexity constraints are added to the standard Least Mean Square (LMS) cost function. It is shown that loss of generalization performance due to overtraining can be avoided when using such complexity constraints. Furthermore, "energy," hidden representations and weight distributions are observed and compared during learning. An attempt is made at explaining the results in terms of linear and non-linear effects in relation to the gradient descent learning algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how backpropagation behaves when the learning objective includes constraints on network complexity. The starting point is the standard least mean square cost, which measures prediction error. Adding complexity constraints changes what learning is asked to achieve by making the complexity of the resulting network relevant to optimization.

The motivating problem is overtraining: continued training can reduce performance on examples beyond the training set. The authors show that the loss of generalization associated with overtraining can be avoided with these constraints. This makes the objective's design important to the relationship between fitting training data and retaining useful behavior on other inputs.

The investigation also follows the network during learning by observing its energy, hidden representations, and weight distributions. These views examine how the internal system changes alongside performance. The authors attempt to explain their observations through linear and nonlinear effects in gradient descent. The paper thus links a practical generalization result with a study of the learning dynamics that accompany it.
summary.tldr: Adding complexity constraints to backpropagation's error objective can prevent the loss of generalization caused by overtraining.

title: Dynamic Behavior of Constained Back-Propagation Networks

abstract: A nonlinear neural framework, called the Generalized Hopfield network, is proposed, which is able to solve in a parallel distributed manner systems of nonlinear equations. The method is applied to the general nonlinear optimization problem. We demonstrate GHNs implementing the three most important optimization algorithms, namely the Augmented Lagrangian, Generalized Reduced Gradient and Successive Quadratic Programming methods. Unfortunately such problems can not be solved with guaranteed quality, (Bruck, 1987), getting trapped in locally optimal solutions. paragraphs: The paper proposes Generalized Hopfield Networks as a framework for solving systems of nonlinear equations through parallel, distributed computation. It then applies this framework to nonlinear optimization. The approach treats an optimization calculation as the evolving behavior of interconnected processing elements, giving the problem a dynamical network representation.

The authors demonstrate implementations of three optimization methods: Augmented Lagrangian, Generalized Reduced Gradient, and Successive Quadratic Programming. These implementations connect the proposed neural framework to established procedures for optimization. The contribution is therefore an organization of optimization computations within a network, extending the types of calculations that such networks can express.

This organization offers a direct model for parallelizing the work. The authors argue that it broadens the practical range of problems that can benefit from nonlinear optimization, including pattern recognition, supervised learning, and content-addressable memory design. The significance lies in combining nonlinear problem structure with distributed execution, so that the network's dynamics serve as a computational mechanism for carrying out optimization.
summary.tldr: Generalized Hopfield Networks implement nonlinear equation solving and established optimization methods as parallel network dynamics.

title: Generalized Hopfield Networks and Nonlinear Optimization

paragraphs: This paper applies a neural network trained by backpropagation to commodity trading decisions. The intended output is a long or short market position, expressing which direction the system expects to be profitable. The learning problem is therefore framed around a trading decision rather than simply producing a numerical price forecast.

The network uses fundamental and technical variables as inputs and learns their relationship to the desired trading position. The supplied abstract identifies 18 fundamental variables and gives the technical-variable count as 6 or 18. Training uses one year of historical data. The approach treats these different sources of market information as inputs to a single learned decision rule.

The abstract reports that the predicted positions would have produced $10,301 in profit from an investment below $1,000. Its wording describes a calculated trading outcome, rather than establishing that the profit was realized in live trading. The contribution is an application of supervised neural learning to connecting market indicators with directional commodity positions.
summary.tldr: A backpropagation network learns commodity trading positions from market variables and reports a profitable calculated trading outcome.

title: A B-P ANN Commodity Trader

paragraphs: The paper studies face recognition under sharply changing lighting conditions. It compares images from a contrast-sensitive silicon retina with those from a conventional gain-controlled camera. The question is whether processing built into the sensor can preserve useful facial information as illumination changes.

Both inputs feed a recognition system using wavelet-based features and elastic matching. To examine the effect of the retina's analog preprocessing, the authors also digitally bandpass-filter the conventional camera images to adjust their power spectrum. This comparison considers whether sensor-level processing offers useful properties beyond that particular digital adjustment.

The authors report recognition-rate increases of up to 50 percent with the silicon retina and attribute the benefit to its adjustable sensitivity. They interpret the experiments as showing that analog on-chip preprocessing produces image data richer in features that stay associated with the object across lighting changes. The contribution therefore concerns the acquisition stage as well as recognition: changing how the image is sensed can improve the stability of the information supplied to the classifier.
summary.tldr: A contrast-sensitive silicon retina improves face recognition under changing illumination, with reported recognition-rate increases of up to 50 percent.

title: Illumination-Invariant Face Recognition with a Contrast Sensitive Silicon Retina

paragraphs: Parti-game addresses reinforcement learning with delayed rewards in continuous, multidimensional state spaces. The difficulty is that uniformly exploring or planning across such a space becomes increasingly expensive as dimensions are added. The algorithm instead changes the resolution of its representation, concentrating detail in regions that are critical to finding a solution.

It maintains a decision-tree partition of the state space and uses ideas from game theory and computational geometry to refine that partition efficiently and reactively. The representation can therefore distinguish important local situations without assigning the same fine detail everywhere. This makes the allocation of planning and learning effort part of the algorithm's response to the problem.

The authors report simulations with two to nine state dimensions, including mazes, path planning, nonlinear dynamics, and uncurling snake robots in constrained spaces. In every reported case, a good solution was found in fewer than twenty trials and within a few minutes. These results support variable resolution as a practical way to address the state-space growth encountered in the tested control problems.
summary.tldr: Parti-game learns efficiently by refining only critical regions of a continuous state space.

title: The Parti-Game Algorithm for Variable Resolution Reinforcement Learning in Multidimensional State-Spaces

abstract: We develop a principled strategy to sample a function optimally for function approximation tasks within a Bayesian framework. Using ideas from optimal experiment design, we introduce an objective function (incorporating both bias and variance) to measure the degree of approximation, and the potential utility of the data points towards optimizing this objective. We show how the general strategy can be used to derive precise algorithms to select data for two cases: learning unit step functions and polynomial functions. In particular, we investigate whether such active algorithms can learn the target with fewer examples. We obtain theoretical and empirical results to suggest that this is the case.

Using ideas from optimal experiment design, we introduce an objective function (incorporating both bias and variance) to measure the degree of approximation, and the potential utility of the data points towards optimizing this objective. We show how the general strategy can be used to derive precise algorithms to select data for two cases: learning unit step functions and polynomial functions. In particular, we investigate whether such active algorithms can learn the target with fewer examples. We obtain theoretical and empirical results to suggest that this is the case.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a learner should choose where to sample a function when its goal is to approximate that function accurately. It develops a Bayesian strategy for selecting observations according to their expected usefulness. The sampling decision becomes part of learning, with the objective of obtaining an accurate approximation from fewer examples.

The strategy draws on optimal experiment design and measures approximation quality using an objective that includes both bias and variance. Bias concerns systematic approximation error, while variance concerns how much the learned result can vary. Candidate observations are assessed by their potential contribution to improving this combined objective, connecting data selection directly to the quality of the eventual approximation.

The authors turn the general framework into explicit selection algorithms for unit step functions and polynomial functions. They then investigate whether these active choices reduce the number of examples needed to learn the target. Both theoretical and empirical results suggest that they can. The contribution combines a general principle for choosing informative samples with concrete applications to two specified function-learning problems.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian sampling strategy accounts for bias and variance to choose useful observations and potentially learn functions with fewer examples.

title: Active Learning for Function Approximation

We show that if the number of layers is fixed, then the VC dimension grows as W log W, where W is the number of parameters in the network. paragraphs: This paper studies the expressive capacity of feedforward neural networks whose activation functions consist of polynomial pieces. It measures that capacity through VC dimension, which concerns how flexibly a model can assign binary labels to collections of inputs. The central question is how this capacity changes with the number of adjustable parameters.

The authors derive both upper and lower bounds. When the number of layers is fixed, the bounds establish growth proportional to W log W, where W counts the network parameters. Having bounds in both directions identifies the growth rate rather than merely placing a ceiling on what these networks can express.

The fixed-depth condition is essential to the comparison presented in the abstract. When the number of layers is unrestricted, the stated growth becomes quadratic in W. Thus, parameter count alone does not describe the capacity scaling: the permitted depth also matters. The result provides a theoretical distinction between increasing the size of a fixed-depth network and allowing depth to grow.
summary.tldr: For piecewise-polynomial networks, VC dimension grows as W log W at fixed depth, compared with quadratic growth when depth is unrestricted.

title: Almost Linear VC Dimension Bounds for Piecewise Polynomial Networks

abstract: Boosting algorithms and successful applications thereof abound for clas- siﬁcation and regression learning problems, but not for unsupervised learning. We propose a sequential approach to adding features to a ran- dom ﬁeld model by training them to improve classiﬁcation performance between the data and an equal-sized sample of “negative examples” gen- erated from the model’s current estimate of the data density. Training in each boosting round proceeds in three stages: ﬁrst we sample negative examples from the model’s current Boltzmann distribution. Next, a fea- ture is trained to improve classiﬁcation performance between data and negative examples. Finally, a coefﬁcient is learned which determines the importance of this feature relative to ones already in the pool. Negative examples only need to be generated once to learn each new feature. The validity of the approach is demonstrated on binary digits and continuous synthetic data.
originalAbstract: Boosting algorithms and successful applications thereof abound for clas- siﬁcation and regression learning problems, but not for unsupervised learning. We propose a sequential approach to adding features to a ran- dom ﬁeld model by training them to improve classiﬁcation performance between the data and an equal-sized sample of “negative examples” gen- erated from the model’s current estimate of the data density. Training in each boosting round proceeds in three stages: ﬁrst we sample negative examples from the model’s current Boltzmann distribution. Next, a fea- ture is trained to improve classiﬁcation performance between data and negative examples. Finally, a coefﬁcient is learned which determines the importance of this feature relative to ones already in the pool. Negative examples only need to be generated once to learn each new feature. The validity of the approach is demonstrated on binary digits and continuous synthetic data.

paragraphs: The paper adapts boosting to unsupervised learning by turning density estimation into a sequence of classification problems. It builds a random field model one feature at a time. Each new feature is trained to distinguish observed data from an equally sized set of negative examples generated by the current model.

Every round has three stages. The method first samples negative examples from the model's Boltzmann distribution. It then trains a feature to improve discrimination between those samples and the data. Finally, it learns a coefficient controlling the feature's importance relative to those already included. Negative examples need to be generated only once for each new feature.

This creates its own classification signal without requiring externally supplied class labels: the distinction is between actual observations and the model's current samples. The authors demonstrate the approach on binary digits and continuous synthetic data. These demonstrations support using sequential discriminative feature learning to construct an unsupervised density model, extending the boosting idea beyond its more established classification and regression settings.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised boosting builds a density model by repeatedly learning features that distinguish observed data from samples generated by the current model.

title: Self Supervised Boosting

abstract: The relative depth of objects causes small shifts in the left and right ret- inal positions of these objects, called binocular disparity. Here, we describe a neuromorphic implementation of a disparity selective com- plex cell using the binocular energy model, which has been proposed to model the response of disparity selective cells in the visual cortex. Our system consists of two silicon chips containing spiking neurons with monocular Gabor-type spatial receptive fields (RF) and circuits that combine the spike outputs to compute a disparity selective complex cell response. The disparity selectivity of the cell can be adjusted by both position and phase shifts between the monocular RF profiles, which are both used in biology. Our neuromorphic system performs better with phase encoding, because the relative responses of neurons tuned to dif- ferent disparities by phase shifts are better matched than the responses of neurons tuned by position shifts.
originalAbstract: The relative depth of objects causes small shifts in the left and right ret- inal positions of these objects, called binocular disparity. Here, we describe a neuromorphic implementation of a disparity selective com- plex cell using the binocular energy model, which has been proposed to model the response of disparity selective cells in the visual cortex. Our system consists of two silicon chips containing spiking neurons with monocular Gabor-type spatial receptive fields (RF) and circuits that combine the spike outputs to compute a disparity selective complex cell response. The disparity selectivity of the cell can be adjusted by both position and phase shifts between the monocular RF profiles, which are both used in biology. Our neuromorphic system performs better with phase encoding, because the relative responses of neurons tuned to dif- ferent disparities by phase shifts are better matched than the responses of neurons tuned by position shifts.

paragraphs: Objects at different depths appear at slightly different positions in the two eyes. This binocular disparity provides the signal studied here. The paper implements a model of a visual cortical complex cell that responds selectively to disparity, translating the binocular energy model into a system built from silicon circuits and spiking neurons.

Two chips contain neurons with Gabor-type spatial receptive fields, which describe how each neuron responds to patterns seen by one eye. Additional circuits combine their spike outputs to produce a disparity-selective response. The preferred disparity can be changed by shifting either the positions or the phases of the two eyes’ receptive-field profiles, matching two mechanisms used in biology.

The implemented system performs better when disparity is encoded through phase shifts. The stated reason is that responses across neurons tuned to different disparities are better matched with phase tuning than with position tuning. This result identifies a practical difference between two biologically motivated implementations within this hardware system, rather than establishing a universal preference for phase encoding.
summary.tldr: A two-chip spiking-neuron system implements disparity-selective vision and performs better with phase-based than position-based tuning.

title: A Neuromorphic Multi-chip Model of a Disparity Selective Complex Cell

abstract: Recent research has demonstrated that useful POMDP solutions do not require consideration of the entire belief space. We extend this idea with the notion of temporal abstraction. We present and explore a new reinforcement learning algorithm over grid-points in belief space, which uses macro-actions and Monte Carlo updates of the Q-values. We apply the algorithm to a large scale robot navigation task and demonstrate that with temporal abstraction we can consider an even smaller part of the belief space, we can learn POMDP policies faster, and we can do information gathering more efficiently.
originalAbstract: Recent research has demonstrated that useful POMDP solutions do not require consideration of the entire belief space. We extend this idea with the notion of temporal abstraction. We present and explore a new reinforcement learning algorithm over grid-points in belief space, which uses macro-actions and Monte Carlo updates of the Q-values. We apply the algorithm to a large scale robot navigation task and demonstrate that with temporal abstraction we can consider an even smaller part of the belief space, we can learn POMDP policies faster, and we can do information gathering more efficiently.

paragraphs: Planning with partial observability requires reasoning about uncertainty over the current state. A POMDP represents that uncertainty through beliefs, and its belief space contains the possibilities a planner might consider. This paper builds on the observation that useful solutions can be found without examining that entire space.

The proposed algorithm adds temporal abstraction through macro-actions, allowing planning to operate over extended actions. It learns over grid points in belief space and uses Monte Carlo updates to estimate Q-values, which express the value of available choices. The approach therefore combines selective coverage of uncertainty with a coarser treatment of action over time.

On a large-scale robot navigation task, the authors demonstrate that temporal abstraction lets the algorithm consider an even smaller portion of belief space. They also report faster policy learning and more efficient information gathering. These findings connect the planning representation to practical behavior: macro-actions reduce the belief-space coverage needed in the demonstrated task while supporting decisions that help resolve uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Macro-actions let a POMDP learner cover less belief space while learning faster and gathering information more efficiently in robot navigation.

title: Approximate Planning in POMDPs with Macro-Actions

abstract: This paper presents a non-asymptotic statistical analysis of Kernel-PCA with a focus different from the one proposed in previous work on this topic. Here instead of considering the reconstruction error of KPCA we are interested in approximation error bounds for the eigenspaces themselves. We prove an upper bound depending on the spacing between eigenvalues but not on the dimensionality of the eigenspace. As a consequence this allows to infer stability results for these estimated spaces.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a non-asymptotic statistical analysis of Kernel-PCA with a focus different from the one proposed in previous work on this topic. Here instead of considering the reconstruction error of KPCA we are interested in approximation error bounds for the eigenspaces themselves. We prove an upper bound depending on the spacing between eigenvalues but not on the dimensionality of the eigenspace. As a consequence this allows to infer stability results for these estimated spaces.

paragraphs: Kernel principal component analysis estimates spaces that capture structure in a kernel representation of data. This paper asks how accurately those spaces themselves are estimated. That focus differs from assessing reconstruction error, which concerns how well a representation reproduces data rather than how close the estimated eigenspaces are to their underlying targets.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic statistical analysis, so their result concerns finite amounts of data rather than only a limiting regime. They prove an upper bound on eigenspace approximation error. The bound depends on the spacing between eigenvalues, making spectral separation an explicit part of the accuracy analysis.

A notable feature is that the bound does not depend on the dimensionality of the eigenspace. From this result, the authors infer stability properties for the estimated spaces. The contribution is a direct theoretical account of the reliability of kernel-PCA eigenspaces, complementing analyses that judge the method through the reconstruction quality of its output.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds kernel-PCA eigenspace estimation error using eigenvalue spacing without dependence on eigenspace dimensionality.

title: On the Convergence of Eigenspaces in Kernel Principal Component Analysis

abstract: Given a redundant dictionary of basis vectors (or atoms), our goal is to ﬁnd maximally sparse representations of signals. Previously, we have argued that a sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) framework is particularly well-suited for this task, showing that it has far fewer local minima than other Bayesian-inspired strategies. In this paper, we provide further evi- dence for this claim by proving a restricted equivalence condition, based on the distribution of the nonzero generating model weights, whereby the SBL solution will equal the maximally sparse representation. We also prove that if these nonzero weights are drawn from an approximate Jef- freys prior, then with probability approaching one, our equivalence con- dition is satisﬁed. Finally, we motivate the worst-case scenario for SBL and demonstrate that it is still better than the most widely used sparse rep- resentation algorithms. These include Basis Pursuit (BP), which is based on a convex relaxation of the ℓ0 (quasi)-norm, and Orthogonal Match- ing Pursuit (OMP), a simple greedy strategy that iteratively selects basis vectors most aligned with the current residual.

Previously, we have argued that a sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) framework is particularly well-suited for this task, showing that it has far fewer local minima than other Bayesian-inspired strategies. In this paper, we provide further evi- dence for this claim by proving a restricted equivalence condition, based on the distribution of the nonzero generating model weights, whereby the SBL solution will equal the maximally sparse representation. We also prove that if these nonzero weights are drawn from an approximate Jef- freys prior, then with probability approaching one, our equivalence con- dition is satisﬁed. Finally, we motivate the worst-case scenario for SBL and demonstrate that it is still better than the most widely used sparse rep- resentation algorithms. These include Basis Pursuit (BP), which is based on a convex relaxation of the ℓ0 (quasi)-norm, and Orthogonal Match- ing Pursuit (OMP), a simple greedy strategy that iteratively selects basis vectors most aligned with the current residual.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent a signal using as few elements as possible from a redundant dictionary. Because the dictionary offers overlapping ways to express the signal, finding a valid representation does not by itself establish that it is maximally sparse. The authors investigate when sparse Bayesian learning, or SBL, recovers that sparsest representation.

Their main theoretical result gives a restricted equivalence condition determined by the distribution of the nonzero weights generating the signal. When that condition holds, the SBL solution equals the maximally sparse representation. They also prove that drawing those weights from an approximate Jeffreys prior satisfies the condition with probability approaching one. This connects recovery behavior to assumptions about the generating weights.

The authors additionally motivate a worst-case scenario for SBL and demonstrate better performance there than Basis Pursuit and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit. These results strengthen their argument for SBL while retaining a distinction between conditional recovery guarantees and the comparative performance demonstrated in the paper.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes weight-distribution conditions under which sparse Bayesian learning recovers a maximally sparse signal representation.

title: Comparing the Effects of Different Weight Distributions on Finding Sparse Representations

abstract: We describe a novel method for learning templates for recognition and localization of objects drawn from categories. A generative model repre- sents the conﬁguration of multiple object parts with respect to an object coordinate system; these parts in turn generate image features. The com- plexity of the model in the number of features is low, meaning our model is much more efﬁcient to train than comparative methods. Moreover, a variational approximation is introduced that allows learning to be or- ders of magnitude faster than previous approaches while incorporating many more features. This results in both accuracy and localization im- provements. Our model has been carefully tested on standard datasets; we compare with a number of recent template models. In particular, we demonstrate state-of-the-art results for detection and localization.

A generative model repre- sents the conﬁguration of multiple object parts with respect to an object coordinate system; these parts in turn generate image features. The com- plexity of the model in the number of features is low, meaning our model is much more efﬁcient to train than comparative methods. paragraphs: This paper develops a method for learning object-category templates that support both recognition and localization. Recognizing a category means identifying the kind of object present; localization additionally identifies where it appears. The method connects these goals through a model of how an object's parts are arranged and how those parts produce image features.

The generative model describes multiple parts relative to an object coordinate system. Its computational complexity grows slowly enough with the number of features to make training substantially more efficient than the compared methods. A variational approximation further accelerates learning, allowing the model to incorporate many more features while reducing training time by orders of magnitude relative to previous approaches.

The authors report that these computational changes also improve accuracy and localization. Tests on standard datasets compare the approach with recent template models and demonstrate results described as state of the art for detection and localization. The contribution links efficient learning with a richer feature representation and reported improvements in both recognition tasks.
summary.tldr: An efficient generative model of object parts enables faster learning with more features and improves reported detection and localization results.

title: Efficient Unsupervised Learning for Localization and Detection in Object Categories

abstract: In this paper, we show that the hinge loss can be interpreted as the neg-log-likelihood of a semi-parametric model of posterior probabilities. From this point of view, SVMs represent the parametric component of a semi-parametric model ﬁtted by a maximum a posteriori estimation pro- cedure. This connection enables to derive a mapping from SVM scores to estimated posterior probabilities. Unlike previous proposals, the sug- gested mapping is interval-valued, providing a set of posterior probabil- ities compatible with each SVM score. This framework offers a new way to adapt the SVM optimization problem to unbalanced classiﬁca- tion, when decisions result in unequal (asymmetric) losses. Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art procedures.

paragraphs: This paper gives support vector machines a probabilistic interpretation by connecting their hinge loss to a model of posterior class probabilities. Specifically, the loss can be understood as a negative log-likelihood within a semiparametric model. In this interpretation, the SVM supplies the parametric part, fitted through maximum a posteriori estimation.

That connection produces a way to translate an SVM score into probability information. The result is an interval of compatible posterior probabilities, rather than a single probability assigned to each score. This distinction matters because the proposed interpretation retains a range of probability values consistent with the score instead of forcing a unique estimate.

The authors use the framework to modify SVM optimization for unbalanced classification when different mistakes carry different losses. Probability information is therefore connected directly to the consequences of classification decisions. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art procedures. The contribution combines a new interpretation of the training objective, an interval-valued probability mapping, and a practical adaptation for asymmetric decision costs.
summary.tldr: A semiparametric interpretation of SVMs yields probability intervals and a way to train classifiers for unequal error costs.

title: A Probabilistic Interpretation of SVMs with an Application to Unbalanced Classification

abstract: A new algorithm for on-line learning linear-threshold functions is proposed which efficiently combines second-order statistics about the data with the logarithmic behavior" of multiplicative/dual-norm algorithms. An initial theoretical analysis is provided suggesting that our algorithm might be viewed as a standard Perceptron algorithm operating on a transformed sequence of examples with improved margin properties. We also report on experiments carried out on datasets from diverse domains, with the goal of comparing to known Perceptron algorithms (first-order, second-order, additive, multiplicative). Our learning procedure seems to generalize quite well, and converges faster than the corresponding multiplicative baseline algorithms."

We also report on experiments carried out on datasets from diverse domains, with the goal of comparing to known Perceptron algorithms (first-order, second-order, additive, multiplicative). Our learning procedure seems to generalize quite well, and converges faster than the corresponding multiplicative baseline algorithms."

paragraphs: This paper proposes an online algorithm for learning linear-threshold functions, which classify examples according to which side of a linear boundary they occupy. The algorithm combines second-order information about the data with the logarithmic behavior associated with multiplicative and dual-norm learning algorithms. The goal is to bring these properties together efficiently.

An initial theoretical analysis suggests an interpretation in terms of an ordinary Perceptron operating on transformed examples. Under that interpretation, the transformation improves margin properties, meaning the examples have a more favorable relationship to the separating boundary. The authors present this as a suggested view of the algorithm, rather than a fully established general explanation.

Experiments across diverse domains compare the procedure with first-order, second-order, additive, and multiplicative Perceptron methods. The authors report that it appears to generalize well and converges faster than the corresponding multiplicative baselines. The contribution is thus an algorithmic combination supported by preliminary theoretical insight and empirical comparisons, with the stated speed finding specifically referring to those multiplicative baseline algorithms.
summary.tldr: A new online Perceptron variant combines second-order statistics with multiplicative-style behavior and converges faster than corresponding multiplicative baselines in experiments.

title: On higher-order perceptron algorithms

abstract: Contours have been established in the biological and computer vision literatures as a compact yet descriptive representation of object shape. While individual contours provide structure, they lack the large spatial support of region segments (which lack internal structure). We present a method for further grouping of contours in an image using their relationship to the contours of a second, related image. Stereo, motion, and similarity all provide cues that can aid this task; contours that have similar transformations relating them to their matching contours in the second image likely belong to a single group. To find matches for contours, we rely only on shape, which applies directly to all three modalities without modification, in constrant to the specialized approaches developed for each independently. Visually salient contours are extracted in each image, along with a set of candidate transformations for aligning subsets of them. For each transformation, groups of contours with matching shape across the two images are identified to provide a context for evaluating matches of individual contour points across the images. The resulting contexts of contours are used to perform a final grouping on contours in the original image while simultaneously finding matches in the related image, again by shape matching. We demonstrate grouping results on image pairs consisting of stereo, motion, and similar images. Our method also produces qualitatively better results against a baseline method that does not use the inferred contexts.

paragraphs: Contours describe object shape compactly, but individual contours cover less spatial extent than region segments. This paper uses a second, related image to help determine which contours in the first image belong together. The guiding idea is that contours linked to their counterparts by similar transformations are likely to form a common group.

The method extracts visually salient contours and proposes transformations that align subsets across the images. For each transformation, shape matches identify groups that supply context for evaluating matches between individual contour points. Those contexts then support a final step that jointly groups contours in the original image and finds their counterparts in the related one.

Because matching relies on shape, the same approach applies to stereo pairs, motion pairs, and similar images without separate matching procedures for each setting. The authors demonstrate all three types of grouping and report qualitatively better results than a baseline without the inferred contexts. The findings support using cross-image relationships to enrich the evidence available for grouping individual contours.
summary.tldr: Shape correspondences with a related image provide context that improves contour grouping across stereo, motion, and similarity settings.

title: Grouping Contours Via a Related Image

abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) use brain signals to convey a user's intent. Some BCI approaches begin by decoding kinematic parameters of movements from brain signals, and then proceed to using these signals, in absence of movements, to allow a user to control an output. Recent results have shown that electrocorticographic (ECoG) recordings from the surface of the brain in humans can give information about kinematic parameters (e.g., hand velocity or finger flexion). The decoding approaches in these demonstrations usually employed classical classification/regression algorithms that derive a linear mapping between brain signals and outputs. However, they typically only incorporate little prior information about the target kinematic parameter. In this paper, we show that different types of anatomical constraints that govern finger flexion can be exploited in this context. Specifically, we incorporate these constraints in the construction, structure, and the probabilistic functions of a switched non-parametric dynamic system (SNDS) model. We then apply the resulting SNDS decoder to infer the flexion of individual fingers from the same ECoG dataset used in a recent study. Our results show that the application of the proposed model, which incorporates anatomical constraints, improves decoding performance compared to the results in the previous work. Thus, the results presented in this paper may ultimately lead to neurally controlled hand prostheses with full fine-grained finger articulation.

paragraphs: Decoding finger movements from brain activity is one route toward brain-controlled devices. Earlier demonstrations used signals recorded from the brain's surface to estimate movement parameters, often through linear classification or regression. These approaches incorporated relatively little prior information about the anatomical rules governing the movements being predicted.

This paper incorporates anatomical constraints on finger flexion into a switched non-parametric dynamic system model. The constraints influence the model's construction, structure, and probability functions. This makes knowledge about the target movement part of the decoding process, rather than asking the relationship between brain signals and finger flexion to emerge entirely from a generic mapping.

The authors evaluate their decoder on the same electrocorticographic dataset used in an earlier study and report improved decoding of individual finger flexion. The result supports using anatomical information in movement decoding. Fine-grained neural control of hand prostheses is presented as a possible eventual application, rather than an outcome demonstrated by this evaluation.
summary.tldr: Incorporating anatomical constraints into a dynamic model improves finger-flexion decoding on a previously studied ECoG dataset.

title: Anatomically Constrained Decoding of Finger Flexion from Electrocorticographic Signals

abstract: Crowdsourcing systems, in which tasks are electronically distributed to numerous ``information piece-workers'', have emerged as an effective paradigm for human-powered solving of large scale problems in domains such as image classification, data entry, optical character recognition, recommendation, and proofreading. Because these low-paid workers can be unreliable, nearly all crowdsourcers must devise schemes to increase confidence in their answers, typically by assigning each task multiple times and combining the answers in some way such as majority voting. In this paper, we consider a general model of such rowdsourcing tasks, and pose the problem of minimizing the total price (i.e., number of task assignments) that must be paid to achieve a target overall reliability. We give new algorithms for deciding which tasks to assign to which workers and for inferring correct answers from the workers’ answers. We show that our algorithm significantly outperforms majority voting and, in fact, are asymptotically optimal through comparison to an oracle that knows the reliability of every worker.

paragraphs: Crowdsourcing systems often repeat assignments because individual workers can provide unreliable answers. Repetition improves confidence but also increases cost. This paper formulates the design problem as achieving a target overall reliability while minimizing the number of task assignments, treating that count as the price paid for reliable results.

The authors address both sides of the process: deciding which workers receive which tasks and inferring the correct answers from their responses. These are connected decisions because the information available for answer inference depends on how assignments were distributed. Majority voting supplies a familiar comparison for combining repeated answers.

The proposed algorithm significantly outperforms majority voting and is shown to be asymptotically optimal through comparison with an oracle that knows every worker's reliability. That oracle provides an informed reference point for judging assignment cost. The asymptotic qualification matters: the result describes optimality in the relevant limiting regime, rather than asserting that every finite crowdsourcing instance matches an all-knowing procedure.
summary.tldr: Joint task-assignment and answer-inference algorithms reduce crowdsourcing cost and achieve asymptotic optimality against a reliability-aware oracle.

title: Iterative Learning for Reliable Crowdsourcing Systems

abstract: We consider feature selection and weighting for nearest neighbor classifiers. A technical challenge in this scenario is how to cope with the discrete update of nearest neighbors when the feature space metric is changed during the learning process. This issue, called the target neighbor change, was not properly addressed in the existing feature weighting and metric learning literature. In this paper, we propose a novel feature weighting algorithm that can exactly and efficiently keep track of the correct target neighbors via sequential quadratic programming. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that guarantees the consistency between target neighbors and the feature space metric. We further show that the proposed algorithm can be naturally combined with regularization path tracking, allowing computationally efficient selection of the regularization parameter. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through experiments.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that guarantees the consistency between target neighbors and the feature space metric. paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification depends on which examples are closest under the chosen distance metric. Learning feature weights changes that metric and can abruptly change the identities of the nearest neighbors. The paper addresses this target-neighbor change, which creates a consistency problem when an optimization method continues using neighbors selected under an earlier metric.

The authors propose a feature-weighting algorithm based on sequential quadratic programming that tracks the correct target neighbors exactly and efficiently. This keeps the neighbor choices consistent with the feature-space metric as learning proceeds. They describe it, to their knowledge, as the first algorithm to guarantee this consistency, addressing a difficulty they identify in previous feature-weighting and metric-learning work.

The method also combines naturally with regularization path tracking. Following how solutions change with regularization allows computationally efficient selection of the regularization parameter. Experiments demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution thus connects two practical aspects of learning a distance metric: maintaining valid neighbor relationships during optimization and efficiently choosing the amount of regularization.
summary.tldr: A sequential quadratic programming method keeps target neighbors exactly consistent with learned feature weights and supports efficient regularization selection.

title: Target Neighbor Consistent Feature Weighting for Nearest Neighbor Classification

abstract: We present a new approach to sample from generic binary distributions, based on an exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm applied to a piecewise continuous augmentation of the binary distribution of interest. An extension of this idea to distributions over mixtures of binary and continuous variables allows us to sample from posteriors of linear and probit regression models with spike-and-slab priors and truncated parameters. We illustrate the advantages of these algorithms in several examples in which they outperform the Metropolis or Gibbs samplers.
originalAbstract: We present a new approach to sample from generic binary distributions, based on an exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm applied to a piecewise continuous augmentation of the binary distribution of interest. An extension of this idea to distributions over mixtures of binary and continuous variables allows us to sample from posteriors of linear and probit regression models with spike-and-slab priors and truncated parameters. We illustrate the advantages of these algorithms in several examples in which they outperform the Metropolis or Gibbs samplers.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to draw samples from distributions over binary variables. Such variables have discrete alternatives, while Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is a method built around movement through a continuous representation. The central idea is to augment the binary distribution with auxiliary variables so that an exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm can be applied to a piecewise continuous representation.

The augmentation supplies the connection between the binary sampling problem and the continuous algorithm. The authors also extend the approach to distributions containing both binary and continuous variables. This makes the framework applicable to posterior sampling in linear and probit regression with spike-and-slab priors and truncated parameters, combining discrete choices with continuous quantities.

Several examples illustrate advantages over Metropolis or Gibbs sampling. These comparisons support the usefulness of the proposed samplers in the examples studied. The broader methodological contribution is a construction that makes exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo available for binary distributions and extends the same idea to mixed-variable inference problems.
summary.tldr: Auxiliary variables enable exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling for binary and mixed-variable distributions, outperforming Metropolis or Gibbs samplers in several examples.

title: Auxiliary-variable Exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Samplers for Binary Distributions

abstract: Fitting high-dimensional statistical models often requires the use of non-linear parameter estimation procedures. As a consequence, it is generally impossible to obtain an exact characterization of the probability distribution of the parameter estimates. This in turn implies that it is extremely challenging to quantify the uncertainty' associated with a certain parameter estimate. Concretely, no commonly accepted procedure exists for computing classical measures of uncertainty and statistical significance as confidence intervals or p-values. We consider here a broad class of regression problems, and propose an efficient algorithm for constructing confidence intervals and p-values. The resulting confidence intervals have nearly optimal size. When testing for the null hypothesis that a certain parameter is vanishing, our method has nearly optimal power. Our approach is based on constructing a de-biased' version of regularized M-estimators. The new construction improves over recent work in the field in that it does not assume a special structure on the design matrix. Furthermore, proofs are remarkably simple. We test our method on a diabetes prediction problem.

paragraphs: Estimating many regression parameters is only part of a statistical analysis; researchers also need to know how uncertain those estimates are. In high-dimensional problems, nonlinear estimation procedures make the distribution of an estimate difficult to characterize exactly. This complicates the construction of confidence intervals and significance tests.

The paper proposes an efficient method for a broad class of regression problems by constructing a de-biased version of regularized M-estimators. Regularization supports estimation, while the correction creates a basis for uncertainty calculations. The resulting algorithm produces confidence intervals and p-values, connecting fitted parameter values to classical tools for assessing statistical evidence.

The authors establish nearly optimal interval sizes and nearly optimal power for testing whether a parameter is zero. These claims concern both precision of uncertainty statements and ability to detect nonzero parameters. Their construction improves on recent work by avoiding a special structural assumption on the design matrix. They also report simple proofs and test the method on a diabetes prediction problem, illustrating its use in an applied regression setting.
summary.tldr: De-biasing regularized regression estimates enables efficient confidence intervals and hypothesis tests with nearly optimal statistical properties.

title: Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing for High-Dimensional Statistical Models

abstract: We present a novel MCMC sampler for Dirichlet process mixture models that can be used for conjugate or non-conjugate prior distributions. The proposed sampler can be massively parallelized to achieve significant computational gains. A non-ergodic restricted Gibbs iteration is mixed with split/merge proposals to produce a valid sampler. Each regular cluster is augmented with two sub-clusters to construct likely split moves. Unlike many previous parallel samplers, the proposed sampler accurately enforces the correct stationary distribution of the Markov chain without the need for approximate models. Empirical results illustrate that the new sampler exhibits better convergence properties than current methods.

Each regular cluster is augmented with two sub-clusters to construct likely split moves. Unlike many previous parallel samplers, the proposed sampler accurately enforces the correct stationary distribution of the Markov chain without the need for approximate models. Empirical results illustrate that the new sampler exhibits better convergence properties than current methods.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an MCMC sampler for Dirichlet process mixture models that supports both conjugate and nonconjugate priors. Its aim is to obtain substantial computational gains through parallel execution while preserving the correct stationary distribution. This matters because faster sampling should still target the distribution specified by the original model.

The sampler combines a restricted Gibbs iteration with proposals to split or merge clusters. The restricted iteration is non-ergodic on its own; the combined procedure produces a valid sampler. Each ordinary cluster carries two additional sub-clusters, which are used to construct plausible split proposals and guide changes to the clustering.

The authors emphasize that the method enforces the correct stationary distribution without substituting an approximate model. Empirical comparisons show better convergence behavior than the methods considered. The contribution therefore combines a highly parallel computational structure with a mechanism for moving between cluster configurations, providing reported speed and convergence benefits while retaining the intended probabilistic target.
summary.tldr: A parallel Dirichlet process mixture sampler uses sub-cluster split proposals while preserving the correct stationary distribution.

title: Parallel Sampling of DP Mixture Models using Sub-Cluster Splits

abstract: Particle colliders enable us to probe the fundamental nature of matter by observing exotic particles produced by high-energy collisions. Because the experimental measurements from these collisions are necessarily incomplete and imprecise, machine learning algorithms play a major role in the analysis of experimental data. The high-energy physics community typically relies on standardized machine learning software packages for this analysis, and devotes substantial effort towards improving statistical power by hand crafting high-level features derived from the raw collider measurements. In this paper, we train artificial neural networks to detect the decay of the Higgs boson to tau leptons on a dataset of 82 million simulated collision events. We demonstrate that deep neural network architectures are particularly well-suited for this task with the ability to automatically discover high-level features from the data and increase discovery significance.

paragraphs: Particle-collision measurements are incomplete and imprecise, making statistical analysis essential to identifying rare physical processes. This paper studies neural networks for detecting Higgs boson decays to tau leptons. The authors train their models using a dataset containing 82 million simulated collision events.

The approach addresses a feature-design problem in high-energy physics. Analysts commonly devote substantial effort to constructing high-level variables from raw collider measurements to improve statistical power. The paper investigates deep neural networks' ability to discover useful high-level features automatically, making representation learning part of the detection procedure.

The reported findings indicate that deep architectures are particularly well suited to this task and can increase discovery significance. Their value lies in learning informative structure from the data for distinguishing the decay process of interest. The evidence comes from the simulated-event study described in the abstract, so the result concerns improved analysis for this search task rather than a reported experimental discovery. It supports learned features as a way to strengthen the statistical use of collider measurements.
summary.tldr: Deep networks learn useful features from simulated collider events and improve significance for detecting Higgs decays to tau leptons.

title: Searching for Higgs Boson Decay Modes with Deep Learning

abstract: In this paper, we consider sparse networks consisting of a finite number of non-overlapping communities, i.e. disjoint clusters, so that there is higher density within clusters than across clusters. Both the intra- and inter-cluster edge densities vanish when the size of the graph grows large, making the cluster reconstruction problem nosier and hence difficult to solve. We are interested in scenarios where the network size is very large, so that the adjacency matrix of the graph is hard to manipulate and store. The data stream model in which columns of the adjacency matrix are revealed sequentially constitutes a natural framework in this setting. For this model, we develop two novel clustering algorithms that extract the clusters asymptotically accurately. The first algorithm is {\it offline}, as it needs to store and keep the assignments of nodes to clusters, and requires a memory that scales linearly with the network size. The second algorithm is {\it online}, as it may classify a node when the corresponding column is revealed and then discard this information. This algorithm requires a memory growing sub-linearly with the network size. To construct these efficient streaming memory-limited clustering algorithms, we first address the problem of clustering with partial information, where only a small proportion of the columns of the adjacency matrix is observed and develop, for this setting, a new spectral algorithm which is of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper studies community recovery in large sparse networks with a finite number of disjoint clusters. Connections are denser within communities than between them, but both densities vanish as the graph grows. This makes recovery increasingly noisy while the adjacency matrix becomes difficult to store. The authors consider a stream in which its columns arrive sequentially.

They develop two algorithms with asymptotically accurate cluster recovery. The offline version retains node assignments and uses memory proportional to network size. The online version can classify a node when its column arrives and then discard that information, requiring memory that grows sublinearly. The distinction directly links the retained output information to the memory requirement.

To construct these methods, the authors first study clustering when only a small fraction of adjacency-matrix columns is available. They develop a spectral algorithm for that partial-information problem, which also has independent interest. The overall result shows how limited observations and sequential access can support asymptotically accurate recovery under the paper's sparse, non-overlapping community setting.
summary.tldr: Two streaming algorithms recover communities asymptotically accurately in the studied sparse networks, with linear or sublinear memory depending on retained assignments.

title: Streaming, Memory Limited Algorithms for Community Detection

abstract: Many modern data analysis problems involve inferences from streaming data. However, streaming data is not easily amenable to the standard probabilistic modeling approaches, which assume that we condition on finite data. We develop population variational Bayes, a new approach for using Bayesian modeling to analyze streams of data. It approximates a new type of distribution, the population posterior, which combines the notion of a population distribution of the data with Bayesian inference in a probabilistic model. We study our method with latent Dirichlet allocation and Dirichlet process mixtures on several large-scale data sets.
originalAbstract: Many modern data analysis problems involve inferences from streaming data. However, streaming data is not easily amenable to the standard probabilistic modeling approaches, which assume that we condition on finite data. We develop population variational Bayes, a new approach for using Bayesian modeling to analyze streams of data. It approximates a new type of distribution, the population posterior, which combines the notion of a population distribution of the data with Bayesian inference in a probabilistic model. We study our method with latent Dirichlet allocation and Dirichlet process mixtures on several large-scale data sets.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a mismatch between streaming data and standard Bayesian modeling. Conventional probabilistic inference conditions on a finite collection of observations, whereas a stream presents data as an ongoing source. The authors develop an approach that connects Bayesian inference to a population-level view of the data.

Their central object is the population posterior, a distribution that combines the notion of a data population with inference in a probabilistic model. They introduce population variational Bayes to approximate this target. The contribution therefore includes both a new distribution to reason about and an approximation method designed around it, making the population perspective part of the inference formulation.

The authors study the approach using latent Dirichlet allocation and Dirichlet process mixtures on several large-scale datasets. These studies place the method in two different probabilistic modeling settings. The stated contribution is a framework for applying Bayesian models to streams, supported by these applications; the abstract does not claim a particular quantitative improvement. Its significance lies in adapting the inference target itself to the streaming setting.
summary.tldr: Population variational Bayes supports Bayesian modeling of streams by approximating a posterior defined through a data-population perspective.

title: The Population Posterior and Bayesian Modeling on Streams

abstract: Multidimensional recurrent neural networks (MDRNNs) have shown a remarkable performance in the area of speech and handwriting recognition. The performance of an MDRNN is improved by further increasing its depth, and the difficulty of learning the deeper network is overcome by using Hessian-free (HF) optimization. Given that connectionist temporal classification (CTC) is utilized as an objective of learning an MDRNN for sequence labeling, the non-convexity of CTC poses a problem when applying HF to the network. As a solution, a convex approximation of CTC is formulated and its relationship with the EM algorithm and the Fisher information matrix is discussed. This paper investigates Hessian-free optimization as a way to overcome that learning difficulty and make deeper multidimensional recurrent networks usable.

Its non-convexity creates a problem when applying Hessian-free optimization. The authors formulate a convex approximation to CTC and discuss how this approximation relates to the expectation-maximization algorithm and the Fisher information matrix.

Using the resulting approach, they successfully train a multidimensional recurrent network with up to 15 layers and report improved sequence-labeling performance. The contribution links greater model depth to an optimization method adapted to the particular training objective. The convex approximation addresses the identified obstacle in applying Hessian-free learning; the reported training result demonstrates that the combined approach can support substantially deeper networks.
summary.tldr: A convex approximation to CTC enables Hessian-free training of multidimensional recurrent networks up to 15 layers, improving sequence labeling.

title: Hessian-free Optimization for Learning Deep Multidimensional Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Accuracy and interpretability are two dominant features of successful predictive models. Typically, a choice must be made in favor of complex black box models such as recurrent neural networks (RNN) for accuracy versus less accurate but more interpretable traditional models such as logistic regression. This tradeoff poses challenges in medicine where both accuracy and interpretability are important. We addressed this challenge by developing the REverse Time AttentIoN model (RETAIN) for application to Electronic Health Records (EHR) data. RETAIN achieves high accuracy while remaining clinically interpretable and is based on a two-level neural attention model that detects influential past visits and significant clinical variables within those visits (e.g. key diagnoses). RETAIN mimics physician practice by attending the EHR data in a reverse time order so that recent clinical visits are likely to receive higher attention. RETAIN was tested on a large health system EHR dataset with 14 million visits completed by 263K patients over an 8 year period and demonstrated predictive accuracy and computational scalability comparable to state-of-the-art methods such as RNN, and ease of interpretability comparable to traditional models.

The model uses two levels of neural attention to identify influential past visits and significant clinical variables within those visits. This gives the prediction an interpretation at both the encounter level and the level of information such as diagnoses.

The model processes attention in reverse chronological order, taking inspiration from how physicians review a patient's history. The mechanism connects the temporal organization of the record with the model's assessment of which visits and variables are influential for its prediction.

They report predictive accuracy and computational scalability comparable to state-of-the-art methods such as recurrent neural networks, with ease of interpretation comparable to traditional models. The findings support the possibility of combining strong predictive performance with accessible explanations of influential information in electronic health records.
summary.tldr: RETAIN uses reverse-time, two-level attention to make health-record predictions interpretable while achieving accuracy comparable to recurrent networks.

title: RETAIN: An Interpretable Predictive Model for Healthcare using Reverse Time Attention Mechanism

abstract: This paper presents Generalized Correspondence-LDA (GC-LDA), a generalization of the Correspondence-LDA model that allows for variable spatial representations to be associated with topics, and increased flexibility in terms of the strength of the correspondence between data types induced by the model. We present three variants of GC-LDA, each of which associates topics with a different spatial representation, and apply them to a corpus of neuroimaging data. In the context of this dataset, each topic corresponds to a functional brain region, where the region's spatial extent is captured by a probability distribution over neural activity, and the region's cognitive function is captured by a probability distribution over linguistic terms. We illustrate the qualitative improvements offered by GC-LDA in terms of the types of topics extracted with alternative spatial representations, as well as the model's ability to incorporate a-priori knowledge from the neuroimaging literature. We furthermore demonstrate that the novel features of GC-LDA improve predictions for missing data.

paragraphs: This paper develops a topic model that connects spatial brain activity with language describing cognitive function. In its neuroimaging application, a topic represents a functional brain region through two linked probability distributions: one describes the region’s spatial extent, and the other describes associated linguistic terms. This provides a joint representation of where activity occurs and what function it is associated with.

Generalized Correspondence-LDA extends the earlier correspondence model in two ways. It permits different spatial representations for topics and allows more flexibility in how strongly the data types correspond. The authors present three variants, each with a different spatial representation, and apply them to a corpus of neuroimaging data.

The reported findings include qualitative improvements in the kinds of topics recovered when alternative spatial representations are used. The model can also incorporate prior knowledge from neuroimaging research. Its new features improve predictions of missing data, giving a predictive result alongside the qualitative evidence that more flexible spatial and cross-data modeling produces useful representations.
summary.tldr: GC-LDA links brain-activity locations with cognitive language using flexible spatial topics and improves missing-data prediction.

title: Generalized Correspondence-LDA Models (GC-LDA) for Identifying Functional Regions in the Brain

abstract: We propose a framework for Semi-Supervised Active Clustering framework (SSAC), where the learner is allowed to interact with a domain expert, asking whether two given instances belong to the same cluster or not. We study the query and computational complexity of clustering in this framework. We consider a setting where the expert conforms to a center-based clustering with a notion of margin. We show that there is a trade off between computational complexity and query complexity; We prove that for the case of $k$-means clustering (i.e., when the expert conforms to a solution of $k$-means), having access to relatively few such queries allows efficient solutions to otherwise NP hard problems. In particular, we provide a probabilistic polynomial-time (BPP) algorithm for clustering in this setting that asks $O\big(k^2\log k + k\log n)$ same-cluster queries and runs with time complexity $O\big(kn\log n)$ (where $k$ is the number of clusters and $n$ is the number of instances). The success of the algorithm is guaranteed for data satisfying the margin condition under which, without queries, we show that the problem is NP hard. We also prove a lower bound on the number of queries needed to have a computationally efficient clustering algorithm in this setting.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much easier clustering becomes when a learner can consult a domain expert. The permitted question is simple: do these two instances belong to the same cluster? The proposed semi-supervised active clustering framework studies both the number of expert questions and the computation required to produce a clustering.

The analysis assumes that the expert follows a center-based clustering with a specified margin condition. For the k-means case, the authors give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm using O(k² log k + k log n) queries and O(kn log n) time, where k counts clusters and n counts instances. Its success guarantee depends on the stated margin condition.

The striking comparison is that clustering remains NP-hard without queries even under that margin condition. A relatively small amount of expert interaction can therefore make an otherwise computationally hard problem efficiently solvable in this setting. A lower bound on the required queries also shows that expert input has a quantifiable computational value, rather than being an unrestricted source of help.
summary.tldr: Under a margin condition, a small number of same-cluster queries enables efficient clustering where computation alone remains NP-hard.

title: Clustering with Same-Cluster Queries

abstract: Commonly used in many applications, robust PCA represents an algorithmic attempt to reduce the sensitivity of classical PCA to outliers. The basic idea is to learn a decomposition of some data matrix of interest into low rank and sparse components, the latter representing unwanted outliers. Although the resulting problem is typically NP-hard, convex relaxations provide a computationally-expedient alternative with theoretical support. However, in practical regimes performance guarantees break down and a variety of non-convex alternatives, including Bayesian-inspired models, have been proposed to boost estimation quality. Unfortunately though, without additional a priori knowledge none of these methods can significantly expand the critical operational range such that exact principal subspace recovery is possible. Into this mix we propose a novel pseudo-Bayesian algorithm that explicitly compensates for design weaknesses in many existing non-convex approaches leading to state-of-the-art performance with a sound analytical foundation.

paragraphs: Robust PCA seeks to separate a data matrix into a low-rank component and a sparse component representing outliers. The goal is to recover the underlying principal structure without letting a relatively small collection of corruptions dominate it. Directly solving this decomposition is typically computationally hard, motivating tractable alternatives.

Convex relaxations offer useful theory and practical computation, but their recovery guarantees can fail in regimes encountered in practice. Nonconvex methods, including approaches inspired by Bayesian modeling, try to improve estimation there. The authors identify a persistent obstacle: without additional prior knowledge, existing alternatives do not substantially widen the range in which exact principal-subspace recovery is possible.

The proposed pseudo-Bayesian algorithm is designed to compensate explicitly for weaknesses in those nonconvex approaches. The authors report state-of-the-art performance supported by an analytical foundation. Its contribution is therefore both an algorithmic redesign and a theoretical justification for that redesign. The stated result concerns improved robust recovery performance, rather than a universal guarantee that every low-rank and sparse decomposition can be recovered exactly.
summary.tldr: A pseudo-Bayesian robust PCA algorithm addresses weaknesses in existing nonconvex methods and reports state-of-the-art recovery performance with analytical support.

title: A Pseudo-Bayesian Algorithm for Robust PCA

abstract: Social media and social networking sites have become a global pinboard for exposition and discussion of news, topics, and ideas, where social media users often update their opinions about a particular topic by learning from the opinions shared by their friends. In this context, can we learn a data-driven model of opinion dynamics that is able to accurately forecast users' opinions? In this paper, we introduce SLANT, a probabilistic modeling framework of opinion dynamics, which represents users' opinions over time by means of marked jump diffusion stochastic differential equations, and allows for efficient model simulation and parameter estimation from historical fine grained event data. We then leverage our framework to derive a set of efficient predictive formulas for opinion forecasting and identify conditions under which opinions converge to a steady state. Experiments on data gathered from Twitter show that our model provides a good fit to the data and our formulas achieve more accurate forecasting than alternatives.

paragraphs: Opinions expressed on social networks can change as people encounter views shared by their friends. This paper asks whether detailed records of those events can support a model that forecasts users' future opinions. The goal is to learn how opinions evolve over time rather than describe only a static distribution of views.

The proposed framework, SLANT, represents opinions with marked jump-diffusion stochastic differential equations. This supplies a probabilistic description of change that includes event-related jumps. The framework supports efficient simulation and parameter estimation from historical event data. The authors then derive efficient formulas for forecasting opinions and identify conditions under which the modeled opinions settle into a steady state.

Experiments using Twitter data show that SLANT fits the observations well and that its forecasting formulas are more accurate than the alternatives examined. The contribution combines a model that can be learned from detailed social activity with practical prediction formulas and a theoretical account of convergence. The steady-state result is conditional, while the forecasting advantage is demonstrated empirically on the reported data.
summary.tldr: SLANT learns probabilistic opinion dynamics from social-network events and provides efficient forecasts that outperform evaluated alternatives on Twitter data.

title: Learning and Forecasting Opinion Dynamics in Social Networks

abstract: We present a novel extension of multi-output Gaussian processes for handling heterogeneous outputs. We assume that each output has its own likelihood function and use a vector-valued Gaussian process prior to jointly model the parameters in all likelihoods as latent functions. Our multi-output Gaussian process uses a covariance function with a linear model of coregionalisation form. Assuming conditional independence across the underlying latent functions together with an inducing variable framework, we are able to obtain tractable variational bounds amenable to stochastic variational inference. We illustrate the performance of the model on synthetic data and two real datasets: a human behavioral study and a demographic high-dimensional dataset.
