paragraphs: Predicting several outputs together becomes more complicated when those outputs require different probabilistic descriptions. This paper extends multi-output Gaussian processes to that heterogeneous setting. Each output receives its own likelihood function, allowing the model to preserve differences between outputs while still learning their relationships within a shared probabilistic framework.

The parameters of all these likelihoods are represented as latent functions governed jointly by a vector-valued Gaussian process. A covariance construction called a linear model of coregionalisation specifies how those functions relate. This provides the mechanism for connecting predictions across outputs without requiring them all to use the same observation model.

For computation, the authors combine an inducing-variable framework with a conditional-independence assumption across underlying latent functions. These choices yield tractable variational bounds suitable for stochastic variational inference. Performance is illustrated using synthetic data, a human behavioral study, and a high-dimensional demographic dataset. The contribution is a model and workable inference procedure for jointly predicting heterogeneous outcomes, with applications demonstrating how that formulation can be used.
summary.tldr: A multi-output Gaussian process jointly models outputs with different likelihoods using shared latent functions and tractable variational inference.

title: Heterogeneous Multi-output Gaussian Process Prediction

abstract: In this paper, we study the multi-armed bandit problem in the batched setting where the employed policy must split data into a small number of batches. While the minimax regret for the two-armed stochastic bandits has been completely characterized in \cite{perchet2016batched}, the effect of the number of arms on the regret for the multi-armed case is still open. Moreover, the question whether adaptively chosen batch sizes will help to reduce the regret also remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose the BaSE (batched successive elimination) policy to achieve the rate-optimal regrets (within logarithmic factors) for batched multi-armed bandits, with matching lower bounds even if the batch sizes are determined in an adaptive manner.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study the multi-armed bandit problem in the batched setting where the employed policy must split data into a small number of batches. While the minimax regret for the two-armed stochastic bandits has been completely characterized in \cite{perchet2016batched}, the effect of the number of arms on the regret for the multi-armed case is still open. Moreover, the question whether adaptively chosen batch sizes will help to reduce the regret also remains underexplored. paragraphs: The paper studies multi-armed bandits under a restriction that decisions must be organized into a small number of batches. A bandit policy must learn which options are rewarding while choosing among them. Batching constrains that learning process, making the relationship between available options, feedback opportunities, and regret an important theoretical question.

Earlier work had characterized minimax regret for the two-option stochastic problem. This paper addresses the multi-option case and asks whether choosing batch sizes adaptively can reduce regret. The authors introduce BaSE, a batched successive elimination policy, and prove regret guarantees that are rate-optimal up to logarithmic factors.

The accompanying lower bounds match those guarantees at that level of precision, even when batch sizes may be chosen adaptively. Consequently, adaptive batching does not bypass the fundamental regret limits established by the analysis. The contribution combines an achievable policy with a characterization of what any policy can accomplish, clarifying the statistical cost of learning through a limited number of batches.
summary.tldr: BaSE achieves optimal batched multi-armed bandit regret rates up to logarithmic factors, with lower bounds that also cover adaptive batch sizes.

title: Batched Multi-armed Bandits Problem

abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) are powerful probabilistic models, but suffer from intractable sampling and density evaluation due to the partition function. As a result, inference in EBMs relies on approximate sampling algorithms, leading to a mismatch between the model and inference. Motivated by this, we consider the sampler-induced distribution as the model of interest and maximize the likelihood of this model. This yields a class of energy-inspired models (EIMs) that incorporate learned energy functions while still providing exact samples and tractable log-likelihood lower bounds. We describe and evaluate three instantiations of such models based on truncated rejection sampling, self-normalized importance sampling, and Hamiltonian importance sampling. These models out-perform or perform comparably to the recently proposed Learned Accept/RejectSampling algorithm and provide new insights on ranking Noise Contrastive Estimation and Contrastive Predictive Coding. Moreover, EIMs allow us to generalize a recent connection between multi-sample variational lower bounds and auxiliary variable variational inference. We show how recent variational bounds can be unified with EIMs as the variational family.

paragraphs: Energy-based models can describe flexible probability distributions, but their normalization makes sampling and density evaluation difficult. Approximate sampling then creates a gap between the intended distribution and the samples actually produced. This paper changes the modeling target: it treats the distribution produced by the sampler itself as the model to learn.

The resulting energy-inspired models retain learned energy functions while providing exact samples from their own sampler-defined distributions and tractable lower bounds on log likelihood. The authors develop three versions using truncated rejection sampling, self-normalized importance sampling, and Hamiltonian importance sampling. Exact sampling here refers to the chosen sampler-induced model, which is the central shift in the formulation.

The evaluated models perform comparably to or better than Learned Accept/Reject Sampling. The framework also yields insights into ranking Noise Contrastive Estimation and Contrastive Predictive Coding. Beyond those comparisons, the authors connect energy-inspired models to auxiliary-variable variational inference and unify recent multi-sample variational bounds by using these models as the variational family. Thus, the sampler becomes both a practical modeling tool and a way to relate inference objectives.
summary.tldr: Energy-inspired models learn the distributions their samplers actually produce, enabling exact samples and tractable log-likelihood lower bounds.

title: Energy-Inspired Models: Learning with Sampler-Induced Distributions

abstract: Expected improvement and other acquisition functions widely used in Bayesian optimization use a "one-step" assumption: they value objective function evaluations assuming no future evaluations will be performed. Because we usually evaluate over multiple steps, this assumption may leave substantial room for improvement. Existing theory gives acquisition functions looking multiple steps in the future but calculating them requires solving a high-dimensional continuous-state continuous-action Markov decision process (MDP). Fast exact solutions of this MDP remain out of reach of today's methods. As a result, previous two- and multi-step lookahead Bayesian optimization algorithms are either too expensive to implement in most practical settings or resort to heuristics that may fail to fully realize the promise of two-step lookahead. This paper proposes a computationally efficient algorithm that provides an accurate solution to the two-step lookahead Bayesian optimization problem in seconds to at most several minutes of computation per batch of evaluations. The resulting acquisition function provides increased query efficiency and robustness compared with previous two- and multi-step lookahead methods in both single-threaded and batch experiments. This unlocks the value of two-step lookahead in practice. We demonstrate the value of our algorithm with extensive experiments on synthetic test functions and real-world problems.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses where to evaluate an objective using an acquisition function. Common choices, including expected improvement, value the next evaluation as though no later evaluations will occur. When several evaluations remain, this can overlook the usefulness of information that helps choose a subsequent query.

Two-step lookahead accounts for that next decision, but calculating it requires solving a difficult continuous-state, continuous-action decision problem. The paper proposes a computationally efficient algorithm that accurately solves the two-step lookahead problem in seconds to, at most, several minutes per batch of evaluations. Its contribution is making this form of planning practical despite the difficulty of fast exact solutions.

Experiments on synthetic functions and real-world problems show increased query efficiency and robustness compared with previous two-step and multi-step lookahead methods. The improvements appear in both single-threaded and batch settings. These results indicate that spending computation on a more accurate two-step acquisition decision can improve the use of objective evaluations, which is the central resource Bayesian optimization aims to allocate well.
summary.tldr: An efficient two-step lookahead algorithm improves Bayesian optimization's reported query efficiency and robustness while keeping acquisition computation practical.

title: Practical Two-Step Lookahead Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) is the problem of finding a reward function that generates a given optimal policy for a given Markov Decision Process. This paper looks at an algorithmic-independent geometric analysis of the IRL problem with finite states and actions. A L1-regularized Support Vector Machine formulation of the IRL problem motivated by the geometric analysis is then proposed with the basic objective of the inverse reinforcement problem in mind: to find a reward function that generates a specified optimal policy. The paper further analyzes the proposed formulation of inverse reinforcement learning with $n$ states and $k$ actions, and shows a sample complexity of $O(d^2 \log (nk))$ for transition probability matrices with at most $d$ non-zeros per row, for recovering a reward function that generates a policy that satisfies Bellman's optimality condition with respect to the true transition probabilities.
originalAbstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) is the problem of finding a reward function that generates a given optimal policy for a given Markov Decision Process. This paper looks at an algorithmic-independent geometric analysis of the IRL problem with finite states and actions. A L1-regularized Support Vector Machine formulation of the IRL problem motivated by the geometric analysis is then proposed with the basic objective of the inverse reinforcement problem in mind: to find a reward function that generates a specified optimal policy. The paper further analyzes the proposed formulation of inverse reinforcement learning with $n$ states and $k$ actions, and shows a sample complexity of $O(d^2 \log (nk))$ for transition probability matrices with at most $d$ non-zeros per row, for recovering a reward function that generates a policy that satisfies Bellman's optimality condition with respect to the true transition probabilities.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning asks for a reward function under which a specified policy is optimal in a given Markov decision process. This paper studies that question for finite state and action spaces through a geometric analysis that does not depend on a particular algorithm. The focus is whether the recovered reward actually supports the desired optimal behavior.

The geometric analysis motivates an L1-regularized support vector machine formulation. Its objective remains the defining inverse-learning requirement: recover a reward that generates the specified optimal policy. This ties the proposed optimization formulation to policy optimality, rather than treating reward estimation as a separate prediction problem.

The authors also analyze the samples needed when transition probabilities must be estimated. With n states, k actions, and at most d nonzero entries in each transition-matrix row, they give a sample complexity of O(d² log(nk)). The guarantee concerns recovering a reward whose generated policy satisfies Bellman's optimality condition under the true transition probabilities. The sparsity condition therefore directly shapes the stated dependence on problem size.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis yields an L1-regularized SVM formulation of inverse reinforcement learning with a sparse-transition sample-complexity guarantee.

title: On the Correctness and Sample Complexity of Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modern CNN-based object detectors assign anchors for ground-truth objects under the restriction of object-anchor Intersection-over-Unit (IoU). In this study, we propose a learning-to-match approach to break IoU restriction, allowing objects to match anchors in a flexible manner. Our approach, referred to as FreeAnchor, updates hand-crafted anchor assignment to "free" anchor matching by formulating detector training as a maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) procedure. FreeAnchor targets at learning features which best explain a class of objects in terms of both classification and localization. FreeAnchor is implemented by optimizing detection customized likelihood and can be fused with CNN-based detectors in a plug-and-play manner. Experiments on MS-COCO demonstrate that FreeAnchor consistently outperforms the counterparts with significant margins.

In this study, we propose a learning-to-match approach to break IoU restriction, allowing objects to match anchors in a flexible manner. paragraphs: Anchor-based object detectors must decide which candidate anchors should be responsible for each labeled object during training. Common assignment rules restrict those matches using geometric overlap between an anchor and the object's box. FreeAnchor replaces this hand-designed assignment with a learned matching approach that permits more flexible object-anchor associations.

The paper formulates detector training as maximum likelihood estimation and designs a likelihood specifically for detection. This objective connects matching with the two tasks a detector must perform: identifying an object's class and locating it accurately. The intended result is to learn features that explain objects well on both dimensions, rather than letting overlap rules alone determine their training assignments.

FreeAnchor can be incorporated into convolutional object detectors as a plug-in training approach. Experiments on MS-COCO report consistent improvements over the compared counterparts, with margins the authors describe as significant. The finding supports learned matching as a useful part of detector training in those experiments. Its contribution concerns how anchors acquire responsibility for objects, alongside the classification and localization behavior that responsibility encourages.
summary.tldr: FreeAnchor learns object-anchor matches through a detection likelihood and consistently improves the compared detectors on MS-COCO.

title: FreeAnchor: Learning to Match Anchors for Visual Object Detection

abstract: This paper explores the task of interactive image retrieval using natural language queries, where a user progressively provides input queries to refine a set of retrieval results. Moreover, our work explores this problem in the context of complex image scenes containing multiple objects. We propose Drill-down, an effective framework for encoding multiple queries with an efficient compact state representation that significantly extends current methods for single-round image retrieval. We show that using multiple rounds of natural language queries as input can be surprisingly effective to find arbitrarily specific images of complex scenes. Furthermore, we find that existing image datasets with textual captions can provide a surprisingly effective form of weak supervision for this task. We compare our method with existing sequential encoding and embedding networks, demonstrating superior performance on two proposed benchmarks: automatic image retrieval on a simulated scenario that uses region captions as queries, and interactive image retrieval using real queries from human evaluators.

paragraphs: Finding a particular image of a complex scene can require several descriptions, especially when the scene contains multiple objects. This paper studies an interactive search process in which a user supplies successive natural-language queries to refine the results. Each round adds information about the image the user wants.

Drill-down encodes those multiple queries in a compact state representation, extending methods designed for a single retrieval round. The representation lets the system use the accumulated descriptions during search. The authors also find that existing image datasets with captions provide effective weak supervision, making caption information useful for learning this interactive task.

The findings show that multiple language-query rounds can be effective for locating highly specific complex scenes, and that useful training signals can come from captioned images.
summary.tldr: Drill-down combines successive language queries in a compact representation to retrieve increasingly specific images of complex scenes.

title: Drill-down: Interactive Retrieval of Complex Scenes using Natural Language Queries

abstract: In many environments, only a relatively small subset of the complete state space is necessary in order to accomplish a given task. We develop a simple technique using emergency stops (e-stops) to exploit this phenomenon. Using e-stops significantly improves sample complexity by reducing the amount of required exploration, while retaining a performance bound that efficiently trades off the rate of convergence with a small asymptotic sub-optimality gap. We analyze the regret behavior of e-stops and present empirical results in discrete and continuous settings demonstrating that our reset mechanism can provide order-of-magnitude speedups on top of existing reinforcement learning methods.

Using e-stops significantly improves sample complexity by reducing the amount of required exploration, while retaining a performance bound that efficiently trades off the rate of convergence with a small asymptotic sub-optimality gap. We analyze the regret behavior of e-stops and present empirical results in discrete and continuous settings demonstrating that our reset mechanism can provide order-of-magnitude speedups on top of existing reinforcement learning methods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents may face a much larger state space than they need to complete a particular task. Exploring that entire space can consume many learning interactions. This paper develops emergency-stop mechanisms that exploit the observation that, in many environments, successful behavior requires only a relatively small subset of possible states.

The proposed reset mechanism reduces required exploration and thereby improves sample complexity. Its analysis retains a performance bound that trades faster convergence against a small asymptotic suboptimality gap. This makes the tradeoff explicit: concentrating exploration can accelerate learning while allowing some difference between eventual performance and the optimum. The paper also analyzes the resulting regret behavior.

Experiments in both discrete and continuous settings show that emergency stops can provide order-of-magnitude speedups when added to existing reinforcement learning methods. The result presents resets as a useful addition to learning algorithms in suitable environments. Its motivation depends on task-relevant behavior occupying a small part of the state space, rather than every state being equally necessary.
summary.tldr: Emergency-stop resets can accelerate reinforcement learning by restricting exploration, with a bounded tradeoff in eventual performance.

title: Mo' States Mo' Problems: Emergency Stop Mechanisms from Observation

abstract: In the context of stochastic continuum-armed bandits, we present an algorithm that adapts to the unknown smoothness of the objective function. We exhibit and compute a polynomial cost of adaptation to the Hölder regularity for regret minimization. To do this, we first reconsider the recent lower bound of Locatelli and Carpentier, 2018, and define and characterize admissible rate functions. Our new algorithm matches any of these minimal rate functions. We provide a finite-time analysis and a thorough discussion about asymptotic optimality.

Our new algorithm matches any of these minimal rate functions. We provide a finite-time analysis and a thorough discussion about asymptotic optimality.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic bandits with a continuous space of possible actions. The objective function’s smoothness influences how effectively an algorithm can learn where to act, but that smoothness may be unknown. The central question is how much regret must be paid for adapting to this missing knowledge.

The authors focus on Hölder regularity, a way of describing smoothness, and establish a polynomial cost of adaptation for regret minimization. They revisit an existing lower bound and define admissible rate functions. These functions describe achievable patterns of regret rates across different regularity levels, making the tradeoffs involved in adaptation explicit.

They then introduce an algorithm that adapts to unknown smoothness and matches any of the characterized minimal rate functions. The analysis includes finite-time guarantees and a discussion of asymptotic optimality. The result pairs a description of the cost of adaptation with an algorithm that meets the corresponding optimal tradeoffs, clarifying what can be achieved without knowing the objective’s regularity in advance.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the polynomial regret cost of adapting to unknown smoothness in continuum-armed bandits and gives an algorithm matching optimal tradeoffs.

title: Polynomial Cost of Adaptation for X-Armed Bandits

abstract: Value-function-based methods have long played an important role in reinforcement learning. However, finding the best next action given a value function of arbitrary complexity is nontrivial when the action space is too large for enumeration. We develop a framework for value-function-based deep reinforcement learning with a combinatorial action space, in which the action selection problem is explicitly formulated as a mixed-integer optimization problem. As a motivating example, we present an application of this framework to the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), a combinatorial optimization problem in which a set of locations must be covered by a single vehicle with limited capacity. On each instance, we model an action as the construction of a single route, and consider a deterministic policy which is improved through a simple policy iteration algorithm. Our approach is competitive with other reinforcement learning methods and achieves an average gap of 1.7% with state-of-the-art OR methods on standard library instances of medium size.

paragraphs: Value-based reinforcement learning requires choosing an action using an estimate of its value. When each action is a combinatorial object, the number of possibilities can make exhaustive comparison impractical. This paper develops a framework that makes action selection an explicit mixed-integer optimization problem, connecting a learned value function to a structured optimization procedure.

The application is the capacitated vehicle routing problem, where a single vehicle with limited capacity must cover a set of locations. The authors define each action as constructing an entire route. They use a deterministic policy and improve it through a simple policy iteration algorithm, with optimization handling the search over possible route actions.

On standard library instances of medium size, the approach is competitive with other reinforcement learning methods and has an average gap of 1.7% relative to state-of-the-art operations research methods. The result demonstrates a practical way to use value-based learning when actions are too numerous to enumerate. Its reported performance concerns the tested routing instances, where route construction provides the combinatorial decision structure.
summary.tldr: Mixed-integer optimization enables value-based reinforcement learning to select whole routes from a combinatorial action space.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Combinatorial Actions: An Application to Vehicle Routing

abstract: Explaining AI systems is fundamental both to the development of high performing models and to the trust placed in them by their users. The Shapley framework for explainability has strength in its general applicability combined with its precise, rigorous foundation: it provides a common, model-agnostic language for AI explainability and uniquely satisfies a set of intuitive mathematical axioms. However, Shapley values are too restrictive in one significant regard: they ignore all causal structure in the data. We introduce a less restrictive framework, Asymmetric Shapley values (ASVs), which are rigorously founded on a set of axioms, applicable to any AI system, and can flexibly incorporate any causal structure known to be respected by the data. We demonstrate that ASVs can (i) improve model explanations by incorporating causal information, (ii) provide an unambiguous test for unfair discrimination in model predictions, (iii) enable sequentially incremental explanations in time-series models, and (iv) support feature-selection studies without the need for model retraining.

paragraphs: Shapley values provide a mathematically grounded way to explain a model's predictions by attributing contributions to its inputs. Their appeal is that the same framework can be applied across different AI systems. This paper identifies a restriction in that framework: its explanations ignore causal structure in the data, even when relevant causal relationships are already known.

The authors introduce Asymmetric Shapley values, or ASVs, as a more flexible framework with its own axiomatic foundation. ASVs can incorporate causal structure known to hold in the data while retaining applicability across model types. This makes existing causal knowledge part of the explanation process; the method is not presented as discovering that knowledge from scratch.

The paper demonstrates several uses of this flexibility. ASVs can incorporate causal information into explanations and provide an unambiguous test for unfair discrimination in predictions within the framework. They also support explanations that accumulate sequentially in time-series models and feature-selection studies that do not require retraining. Together, these applications show how changing the attribution framework can make explanations useful for questions involving relationships and ordering among inputs.
summary.tldr: Asymmetric Shapley values extend model-agnostic explanations to incorporate known causal structure.

title: Asymmetric Shapley values: incorporating causal knowledge into model-agnostic explainability

abstract: We study the low rank regression problem y = Mx + ε, where x and y are d1 and d2 dimensional vectors respectively. We consider the extreme high-dimensional setting where the number of observations n is less than d1 + d2. Existing algorithms are designed for settings where n is typically as large as rank(M)(d1+d2). This work provides an efficient algorithm which only involves two SVD, and establishes statistical guarantees on its performance. The algorithm decouples the problem by first estimating the precision matrix of the features, and then solving the matrix denoising problem. To complement the upper bound, we introduce new techniques for establishing lower bounds on the performance of any algorithm for this problem. Our preliminary experiments confirm that our algorithm often out-performs existing baseline, and is always at least competitive.

paragraphs: This paper studies regression in which both the input and output are vectors, connected by a low-rank matrix plus noise. The central challenge is a particularly data-scarce setting: the number of observations is smaller than the combined input and output dimensions. Existing algorithms generally target settings with substantially more observations, with sample sizes scaling with both the matrix rank and those dimensions.

The proposed algorithm separates estimation into two stages. It first estimates the precision matrix of the input features, then solves a matrix denoising problem. Its computational structure is simple, requiring only two singular value decompositions. The authors establish statistical guarantees for this approach and introduce techniques for proving lower bounds on what any algorithm can achieve in the same problem.

These upper and lower bounds address both achievable performance and fundamental estimation difficulty. Preliminary experiments provide additional evidence: the algorithm often beats the existing baseline and remains competitive in the reported comparisons. That empirical conclusion is explicitly preliminary, while the theoretical contribution addresses learning in the unusually small-sample regime.
summary.tldr: A two-SVD algorithm provides statistical guarantees for low-rank regression when observations are fewer than the combined input and output dimensions.

title: Adaptive Reduced Rank Regression

abstract: Defining and reliably finding a canonical orientation for 3D surfaces is key to many Computer Vision and Robotics applications. This task is commonly addressed by handcrafted algorithms exploiting geometric cues deemed as distinctive and robust by the designer. Yet, one might conjecture that humans learn the notion of the inherent orientation of 3D objects from experience and that machines may do so alike. In this work, we show the feasibility of learning a robust canonical orientation for surfaces represented as point clouds. Based on the observation that the quintessential property of a canonical orientation is equivariance to 3D rotations, we propose to employ Spherical CNNs, a recently introduced machinery that can learn equivariant representations defined on the Special Ortoghonal group SO(3). Specifically, spherical correlations compute feature maps whose elements define 3D rotations. Our method learns such feature maps from raw data by a self-supervised training procedure and robustly selects a rotation to transform the input point cloud into a learned canonical orientation. Thereby, we realize the first end-to-end learning approach to define and extract the canonical orientation of 3D shapes, which we aptly dub Compass. Experiments on several public datasets prove its effectiveness at orienting local surface patches as well as whole objects.

paragraphs: Many vision and robotics applications need a consistent orientation for a three-dimensional surface. Handcrafted approaches choose geometric cues that their designers expect to be reliable. This paper investigates whether a system can instead learn a robust canonical orientation directly from surfaces represented as point clouds, making the orientation itself a learned property.

The method, Compass, builds on rotation equivariance: its representation should respond predictably when the input is rotated. Spherical convolutional networks provide representations over SO(3), the space of three-dimensional rotations. Their spherical correlations produce feature maps whose entries correspond to rotations, giving the model a way to express candidate orientations within its representation.

A self-supervised training procedure learns these maps from raw data, and the method robustly selects a rotation that brings the point cloud into its learned canonical orientation. Experiments on several public datasets demonstrate effectiveness for both local surface patches and complete objects. The contribution establishes the feasibility of learning the definition and extraction of a canonical orientation in one end-to-end system.
summary.tldr: Compass uses self-supervised spherical networks to learn consistent canonical orientations for point-cloud surfaces.

title: Learning to Orient Surfaces by Self-supervised Spherical CNNs

abstract: In this paper, we revisit the problem of distribution-independently learning halfspaces under Massart noise with rate $\eta$. Recent work resolved a long-standing problem in this model of efficiently learning to error $\eta + \epsilon$ for any $\epsilon > 0$, by giving an improper learner that partitions space into $\text{poly}(d,1/\epsilon)$ regions. Here we give a much simpler algorithm and settle a number of outstanding open questions: (1) We give the first \emph{proper} learner for Massart halfspaces that achieves $\eta + \epsilon$. (2) Based on (1), we develop a blackbox knowledge distillation procedure to convert an arbitrarily complex classifier to an equally good proper classifier. (3) By leveraging a simple but overlooked connection to \emph{evolvability}, we show any SQ algorithm requires super-polynomially many queries to achieve $\mathsf{OPT} + \epsilon$. We then zoom out to study generalized linear models and give an efficient algorithm for learning under a challenging new corruption model generalizing Massart noise. Finally we study our algorithm for learning halfspaces under Massart noise empirically and find that it exhibits some appealing fairness properties as a byproduct of its strong provable robustness guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning linear decision boundaries, or halfspaces, under Massart label noise with rate eta. Earlier work efficiently reached error eta plus epsilon using a classifier that partitions space into many regions. The authors give a simpler proper learner: its output remains a halfspace while achieving the same error target.

They use this result to develop a black-box distillation procedure that converts a complex classifier into an equally good proper classifier in the studied setting. They also establish a limit on a stronger target. Through a connection to evolvability, they show that statistical query algorithms need super-polynomially many queries to achieve OPT plus epsilon. This separates the achievable noise-rate guarantee from the more demanding optimal-error guarantee.

The work then extends to generalized linear models under a new corruption model that generalizes Massart noise, providing an efficient learning algorithm. Empirical evaluation of the halfspace method also reveals appealing fairness properties associated with its robustness guarantees. Those fairness observations are experimental findings, while the error guarantees and statistical query lower bound are theoretical results.
summary.tldr: A proper halfspace learner achieves eta-plus-epsilon error under Massart noise, alongside distillation results and a lower bound for stronger statistical query guarantees.

title: Classification Under Misspecification: Halfspaces, Generalized Linear Models, and Evolvability

abstract: Contextual policies are used in many settings to customize system parameters and actions to the specifics of a particular setting. In some real-world settings, such as randomized controlled trials or A/B tests, it may not be possible to measure policy outcomes at the level of context—we observe only aggregate rewards across a distribution of contexts. This makes policy optimization much more difficult because we must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem over the entire space of contextual policies, for which existing optimization methods are not suitable. We develop effective models that leverage the structure of the search space to enable contextual policy optimization directly from the aggregate rewards using Bayesian optimization. We use a collection of simulation studies to characterize the performance and robustness of the models, and show that our approach of inferring a low-dimensional context embedding performs best. Finally, we show successful contextual policy optimization in a real-world video bitrate policy problem.

paragraphs: A contextual policy chooses actions or system settings according to the situation. Optimizing such a policy becomes difficult when feedback reports only an overall reward across many contexts. The learner sees whether the complete policy worked well, but cannot directly observe how well it performed in each individual context.

This paper develops Bayesian optimization models for that aggregate-feedback setting. The models use structure in the policy search space to make a high-dimensional optimization problem more manageable. Rather than requiring context-specific rewards, the approach searches over contextual policies using the aggregate outcomes that are actually available, addressing a measurement constraint that can arise in randomized trials and A/B tests.

Simulation studies compare the models' performance and robustness. Among the approaches studied, inferring a low-dimensional embedding of context performs best. The authors also demonstrate successful optimization of a real-world video bitrate policy. Together, these results support learning a compact representation of context as a useful way to optimize differentiated actions when evaluation only supplies a combined measure of success.
summary.tldr: Structured Bayesian optimization learns contextual policies from aggregate rewards, with inferred low-dimensional context embeddings performing best in the reported simulations.

title: High-Dimensional Contextual Policy Search with Unknown Context Rewards using Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Near out-of-distribution detection (OOD) is a major challenge for deep neural networks. We demonstrate that large-scale pre-trained transformers can significantly improve the state-of-the-art (SOTA) on a range of near OOD tasks across different data modalities. For instance, on CIFAR-100 vs CIFAR-10 OOD detection, we improve the AUROC from 85% (current SOTA) to more than 96% using Vision Transformers pre-trained on ImageNet21k. On a challenging genomics OOD detection benchmark, we improve the AUROC from 66% to 77% using transformer and unsupervised pre-training. To further improve performance, we explore the few-shot outlier exposure setting where a few examples from outlier classes may be available; we show that pre-trained transformers are particularly well-suited for outlier exposure, and that the AUROC of OOD detection on CIFAR-100 vs CIFAR-10 can be improved to 98.7% with just 1 image per OOD class, and 99.46% with 10 images per OOD class. For multi-modal image-text pre-trained transformers such as CLIP, we explore a new way of using just the names of outlier classes as a sole source of information without any accompanying images, and show that this outperforms previous SOTA on standard OOD benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Near out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize unfamiliar inputs that remain close to familiar data. This paper investigates whether large pretrained transformers improve that difficult distinction across data modalities. The authors report substantial gains in both image and genomics benchmarks, showing that the benefit extends beyond one type of input.

For CIFAR-100 versus CIFAR-10 detection, ImageNet21k-pretrained Vision Transformers raise AUROC from the reported previous best of 85% to over 96%. On a genomics benchmark, transformers with unsupervised pretraining increase AUROC from 66% to 77%. These results establish the paper's main empirical finding: large-scale pretraining can materially improve near-distribution detection in the evaluated settings.

The authors also study limited information about outliers. With one image per outlier class, image-detection AUROC reaches 98.7%; with ten, it reaches 99.46%. A separate approach uses image-text models such as CLIP with only outlier class names and no accompanying images. That approach also surpasses previous state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks, showing that textual descriptions can provide useful outlier information.
summary.tldr: Pretrained transformers improve near out-of-distribution detection, with further gains from a few outlier images or even outlier class names.

title: Exploring the Limits of Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: We introduce an automatic curriculum algorithm, Variational Automatic Curriculum Learning (VACL), for solving challenging goal-conditioned cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning problems. We motivate our curriculum learning paradigm through a variational perspective, where the learning objective can be decomposed into two terms: task learning on the current curriculum, and curriculum update to a new task distribution. Local optimization over the second term suggests that the curriculum should gradually expand the training tasks from easy to hard. Our VACL algorithm implements this variational paradigm with two practical components, task expansion and entity curriculum, which produces a series of training tasks over both the task configurations as well as the number of entities in the task. Experiment results show that VACL solves a collection of sparse-reward problems with a large number of agents. Particularly, using a single desktop machine, VACL achieves 98% coverage rate with 100 agents in the simple-spread benchmark and reproduces the ramp-use behavior originally shown in OpenAI’s hide-and-seek project.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement learning becomes challenging when many agents must achieve goals but receive rewards only rarely. Variational Automatic Curriculum Learning, or VACL, addresses this by automatically selecting a progression of training tasks. The aim is to make difficult cooperative problems learnable through a changing curriculum.

The authors derive their approach from a variational perspective that separates the objective into learning on the current curriculum and updating the task distribution. Local optimization of the second term suggests gradually expanding from easier tasks to harder ones. VACL implements that principle through task expansion and an entity curriculum, varying both task configurations and the number of entities involved.

Experiments show that VACL solves a collection of sparse-reward problems with many agents. Using one desktop machine, it reaches 98% coverage with 100 agents on simple-spread and reproduces ramp-use behavior previously demonstrated in OpenAI's hide-and-seek project. These findings illustrate how a curriculum spanning task structure and entity count can support learning complex cooperative behaviors in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: VACL automatically expands task difficulty and entity count, enabling reported success on sparse-reward cooperative problems with many agents.

title: Variational Automatic Curriculum Learning for Sparse-Reward Cooperative Multi-Agent Problems

abstract: Finding the minimal structural assumptions that empower sample-efficient learning is one of the most important research directions in Reinforcement Learning (RL). This paper advances our understanding of this fundamental question by introducing a new complexity measure—Bellman Eluder (BE) dimension. We show that the family of RL problems of low BE dimension is remarkably rich, which subsumes a vast majority of existing tractable RL problems including but not limited to tabular MDPs, linear MDPs, reactive POMDPs, low Bellman rank problems as well as low Eluder dimension problems. This paper further designs a new optimization-based algorithm— GOLF, and reanalyzes a hypothesis elimination-based algorithm—OLIVE (proposed in Jiang et al. (2017)). We prove that both algorithms learn the near-optimal policies of low BE dimension problems in a number of samples that is polynomial in all relevant parameters, but independent of the size of state-action space. Our regret and sample complexity results match or improve the best existing results for several well-known subclasses of low BE dimension problems.

This paper further designs a new optimization-based algorithm— GOLF, and reanalyzes a hypothesis elimination-based algorithm—OLIVE (proposed in Jiang et al. (2017)). We prove that both algorithms learn the near-optimal policies of low BE dimension problems in a number of samples that is polynomial in all relevant parameters, but independent of the size of state-action space. Our regret and sample complexity results match or improve the best existing results for several well-known subclasses of low BE dimension problems.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require enormous amounts of experience unless the problem has useful structure. This paper introduces Bellman Eluder dimension as a way to describe structure that supports learning with relatively few samples. The aim is to bring many previously tractable problem families under a shared complexity measure.

The authors show that problems with low Bellman Eluder dimension include tabular and linear Markov decision processes, reactive partially observable problems, and families characterized by low Bellman rank or low Eluder dimension. They introduce an optimization-based algorithm, GOLF, and provide a new analysis of the existing hypothesis-elimination algorithm OLIVE.

For low-dimension problems, both algorithms have guarantees for learning nearly optimal policies using a number of samples polynomial in the relevant parameters and independent of state-action-space size. For several established subclasses, the regret and sample-complexity guarantees match or improve earlier results. The significance is conditional on the structural measure being small: large state and action spaces can still permit sample-efficient learning when this form of complexity remains controlled.
summary.tldr: Bellman Eluder dimension unifies many tractable reinforcement-learning settings and supports sample-efficiency guarantees for two algorithms.

title: Bellman Eluder Dimension: New Rich Classes of RL Problems, and Sample-Efficient Algorithms

abstract: An increasingly common setting in machine learning involves multiple parties, each with their own data, who want to jointly make predictions on future test points. Agents wish to benefit from the collective expertise of the full set of agents to make better predictions than they would individually, but may not be willing to release labeled data or model parameters. In this work, we explore a decentralized mechanism to make collective predictions at test time, that is inspired by the literature in social science on human consensus-making. Building on a query model to facilitate information exchange among agents, our approach leverages each agent’s pre-trained model without relying on external validation, model retraining, or data pooling. A theoretical analysis shows that our approach recovers inverse mean-squared-error (MSE) weighting in the large-sample limit which is known to be the optimal way to combine independent, unbiased estimators. Empirically, we demonstrate that our scheme effectively combines models with differing quality across the input space: the proposed consensus prediction achieves significant gains over classical model averaging, and even outperforms weighted averaging schemes that have access to additional validation data. Finally, we propose a decentralized Jackknife procedure as a tool to evaluate the sensitivity of the collective predictions with respect to a single agent's opinion.

summary.tldr: A decentralized consensus mechanism combines pretrained models at test time and improves over evaluated averaging methods without external validation data.

title: Test-time Collective Prediction

abstract: Learning an unknown n-qubit quantum state rho is a fundamental challenge in quantum computing. Information-theoretically, it is known that tomography requires exponential in n many copies of rho to estimate its entries. Motivated by learning theory, Aaronson et al. introduced many (weaker) learning models: the PAC model of learning states (Proceedings of Royal Society A'07), shadow tomography (STOC'18) for learning ``shadows" of a state, a model that also requires learners to be differentially private (STOC'19) and the online model of learning states (NeurIPS'18). In these models it was shown that an unknown state can be learned ``approximately" using linear in n many copies of rho. But is there any relationship between these models? In this paper we prove a sequence of (information-theoretic) implications from differentially-private PAC learning to online learning and then to quantum stability.Our main result generalizes the recent work of Bun, Livni and Moran (Journal of the ACM'21) who showed that finite Littlestone dimension (of Boolean-valued concept classes) implies PAC learnability in the (approximate) differentially private (DP) setting. We first consider their work in the real-valued setting and further extend to their techniques to the setting of learning quantum states. Key to our results is our generic quantum online learner, Robust Standard Optimal Algorithm (RSOA), which is robust to adversarial imprecision. We then show information-theoretic implications between DP learning quantum states in the PAC model, learnability of quantum states in the one-way communication model, online learning of quantum states, quantum stability (which is our conceptual contribution), various combinatorial parameters and give further applications to gentle shadow tomography and noisy quantum state learning.

paragraphs: Fully estimating an unknown quantum state's entries requires exponentially many copies as the number of qubits grows. Weaker learning models can instead learn approximate information using linearly many copies. This paper asks how several such models relate, including private learning, online learning, and approaches that learn selected information about a state.

The authors prove information-theoretic implications from differentially private PAC learning to online learning and then to quantum stability, a concept introduced in the paper. They extend techniques from Boolean-valued learning to real-valued learning and quantum states. A central ingredient is the Robust Standard Optimal Algorithm, a quantum online learner designed to tolerate adversarial imprecision.

Because the stated connections are information-theoretic, their contribution concerns what learning is possible across these models.
summary.tldr: The paper proves information-theoretic connections from private quantum-state learning to online learning and quantum stability using an imprecision-robust learner.

title: Private learning implies quantum stability

abstract: Many probabilistic modeling problems in machine learning use gradient-based optimization in which the objective takes the form of an expectation. These problems can be challenging when the parameters to be optimized determine the probability distribution under which the expectation is being taken, as the na\"ive Monte Carlo procedure is not differentiable. Reparameterization gradients make it possible to efficiently perform optimization of these Monte Carlo objectives by transforming the expectation to be differentiable, but the approach is typically limited to distributions with simple forms and tractable normalization constants. Here we describe how to differentiate samples from slice sampling to compute \textit{slice sampling reparameterization gradients}, enabling a richer class of Monte Carlo objective functions to be optimized. Slice sampling is a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for simulating samples from probability distributions; it only requires a density function that can be evaluated point-wise up to a normalization constant, making it applicable to a variety of inference problems and unnormalized models. Our approach is based on the observation that when the slice endpoints are known, the sampling path is a deterministic and differentiable function of the pseudo-random variables, since the algorithm is rejection-free. We evaluate the method on synthetic examples and apply it to a variety of applications with reparameterization of unnormalized probability distributions.

paragraphs: Many probabilistic learning objectives are expectations under distributions whose parameters are themselves being optimized. Sampling estimates the expectation, but ordinary Monte Carlo procedures do not automatically provide a differentiable path through the sampling step. Reparameterization gradients solve this for many simple distributions, although their usual constructions can depend on tractable distribution forms and normalization constants.

This paper develops reparameterization gradients through slice sampling. Slice sampling needs only pointwise density evaluations up to an unknown normalization constant, making it useful for a wider range of models. The key observation is conditional on knowing the slice endpoints: the sampling path is then a deterministic, differentiable function of the random inputs, because the algorithm is rejection-free.

Differentiating this path enables optimization of richer Monte Carlo objectives, including objectives involving unnormalized distributions. The authors evaluate the method on synthetic examples and several applications using such distributions. The contribution expands the kinds of samplers through which gradients can be computed, with the known-endpoint observation providing the specific basis for the proposed differentiation approach.
summary.tldr: Differentiating slice-sampling paths provides reparameterization gradients for a broader range of objectives, including those involving unnormalized distributions.

title: Slice Sampling Reparameterization Gradients

abstract: This paper considers stochastic linear bandits with general nonlinear constraints. The objective is to maximize the expected cumulative reward over horizon $T$ subject to a set of constraints in each round $\tau\leq T$. We propose a pessimistic-optimistic algorithm for this problem, which is efficient in two aspects. First, the algorithm yields $\tilde{\cal O}\left(\left(\frac{K^{0.75}}{\delta}+d\right)\sqrt{\tau}\right)$ (pseudo) regret in round $\tau\leq T,$ where $K$ is the number of constraints, $d$ is the dimension of the reward feature space, and $\delta$ is a Slater's constant; and {\em zero} constraint violation in any round $\tau>\tau',$ where $\tau'$ is {\em independent} of horizon $T.$ Second, the algorithm is computationally efficient. Our algorithm is based on the primal-dual approach in optimization and includes two components. The primal component is similar to unconstrained stochastic linear bandits (our algorithm uses the linear upper confidence bound algorithm (LinUCB)). The computational complexity of the dual component depends on the number of constraints, but is independent of the sizes of the contextual space, the action space, and the feature space. Thus, the computational complexity of our algorithm is similar to LinUCB for unconstrained stochastic linear bandits.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions in which rewards have a linear structure but the constraints can be nonlinear. The learner seeks high cumulative expected reward while satisfying constraints at each round. The challenge is to learn which actions are rewarding while also managing the restrictions imposed on those actions.

The proposed algorithm uses a primal-dual optimization approach. Its primal component follows LinUCB, a method for stochastic linear bandits, while its dual component handles the constraints. The extra computational work depends on the number of constraints but is independent of the sizes of the context, action, and feature spaces. Overall computation therefore remains similar to that of unconstrained LinUCB.

The analysis gives a pseudo-regret bound growing roughly with the square root of elapsed rounds, with dependence on feature dimension, constraint count, and a Slater constant. It also establishes zero constraint violation after a threshold round that does not depend on the total horizon. This is an eventual guarantee: the abstract does not claim zero violations from the first round.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual linear-bandit algorithm combines efficient reward learning with zero constraint violations after a horizon-independent threshold.

title: An Efficient Pessimistic-Optimistic Algorithm for Stochastic Linear Bandits with General Constraints

abstract: The first order derivative of a data density can be estimated efficiently by denoising score matching, and has become an important component in many applications, such as image generation and audio synthesis. Higher order derivatives provide additional local information about the data distribution and enable new applications. Although they can be estimated via automatic differentiation of a learned density model, this can amplify estimation errors and is expensive in high dimensional settings. To overcome these limitations, we propose a method to directly estimate high order derivatives (scores) of a data density from samples. We first show that denoising score matching can be interpreted as a particular case of Tweedie’s formula. By leveraging Tweedie’s formula on higher order moments, we generalize denoising score matching to estimate higher order derivatives. We demonstrate empirically that models trained with the proposed method can approximate second order derivatives more efficiently and accurately than via automatic differentiation. We show that our models can be used to quantify uncertainty in denoising and to improve the mixing speed of Langevin dynamics via Ozaki discretization for sampling synthetic data and natural images.

paragraphs: Derivatives of a data distribution describe its local structure, with higher-order derivatives providing information beyond the first-order score used in denoising methods. One way to obtain them is to repeatedly differentiate a learned density model. The paper identifies two difficulties with that route: it can magnify estimation errors and become computationally expensive in high-dimensional settings.

The authors instead learn higher-order derivatives directly from samples. They first connect ordinary denoising score matching to Tweedie's formula, then apply that relationship to higher-order moments. This extends the denoising learning principle to quantities that would otherwise be obtained through automatic differentiation. The approach makes those quantities explicit learning targets rather than indirect consequences of another fitted model.

Empirically, the proposed models estimate second-order derivatives more accurately and efficiently than the automatic-differentiation approach. The authors also demonstrate two uses for the learned information: quantifying uncertainty in denoising and improving the mixing speed of Langevin sampling through Ozaki discretization. Sampling experiments include synthetic data and natural images, showing how richer local distributional information can support downstream computations.
summary.tldr: A generalization of denoising score matching learns higher-order distribution derivatives directly, improving second-order estimation and supporting uncertainty estimation and sampling.

title: Estimating High Order Gradients of the Data Distribution by Denoising

abstract: We propose ACProp (Asynchronous-centering-Prop), an adaptive optimizer which combines centering of second momentum and asynchronous update (e.g. for $t$-th update, denominator uses information up to step $t-1$, while numerator uses gradient at $t$-th step). ACProp has both strong theoretical properties and empirical performance. With the example by Reddi et al. (2018), we show that asynchronous optimizers (e.g. AdaShift, ACProp) have weaker convergence condition than synchronous optimizers (e.g. Adam, RMSProp, AdaBelief); within asynchronous optimizers, we show that centering of second momentum further weakens the convergence condition. We demonstrate that ACProp has a convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ for the stochastic non-convex case, which matches the oracle rate and outperforms the $O(\frac{logT}{\sqrt{T}})$ rate of RMSProp and Adam. We validate ACProp in extensive empirical studies: ACProp outperforms both SGD and other adaptive optimizers in image classification with CNN, and outperforms well-tuned adaptive optimizers in the training of various GAN models, reinforcement learning and transformers. To sum up, ACProp has good theoretical properties including weak convergence condition and optimal convergence rate, and strong empirical performance including good generalization like SGD and training stability like Adam. We provide the implementation at \url{ https://github.com/juntang-zhuang/ACProp-Optimizer}.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers use gradient history to adjust their updates. This paper proposes ACProp, which combines centering of the second momentum with an asynchronous update rule. At step t, the numerator uses the current gradient, while the denominator uses information only through step t−1. The two parts of the update therefore draw on different information horizons.

Using a previously established example, the authors show that asynchronous optimizers have weaker convergence conditions than synchronous alternatives. Within asynchronous methods, centering further weakens the condition. They also prove an O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate for stochastic nonconvex optimization, matching the oracle rate and improving on the stated O(log(T)/sqrt(T)) rates for Adam and RMSProp.

ACProp outperforms SGD and other adaptive methods in the reported classification experiments, and well-tuned adaptive optimizers in the other evaluated settings. These findings connect the proposed update design with both theoretical convergence advantages and observed training performance. The convergence-condition comparison remains tied to the analyzed example, while the practical evidence comes from the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: ACProp combines centered second momentum with asynchronous scaling, achieving an optimal stated convergence rate and strong results across several training settings.

title: Momentum Centering and Asynchronous Update for Adaptive Gradient Methods

abstract: We introduce robust principal component analysis from a data matrix in which the entries of its columns have been corrupted by permutations, termed Unlabeled Principal Component Analysis (UPCA). Using algebraic geometry, we establish that UPCA is a well-defined algebraic problem in the sense that the only matrices of minimal rank that agree with the given data are row-permutations of the ground-truth matrix, arising as the unique solutions of a polynomial system of equations. Further, we propose an efficient two-stage algorithmic pipeline for UPCA suitable for the practically relevant case where only a fraction of the data have been permuted. Stage-I employs outlier-robust PCA methods to estimate the ground-truth column-space. Equipped with the column-space, Stage-II applies recent methods for unlabeled sensing to restore the permuted data. Experiments on synthetic data, face images, educational and medical records reveal the potential of UPCA for applications such as data privatization and record linkage.

paragraphs: Unlabeled Principal Component Analysis addresses a data matrix whose column entries have been shuffled by permutations. The problem is to recover its underlying low-rank structure despite those disrupted correspondences. Here, unlabeled refers to the missing alignment of entries caused by shuffling.

Using algebraic geometry, the authors establish that the minimum-rank matrices consistent with the observed data are row permutations of the ground-truth matrix. They characterize the solutions through polynomial equations. This gives the recovery problem a precise algebraic foundation while retaining the ambiguity associated with a common permutation of rows.

For the practically relevant case where only a fraction of the data is permuted, the paper proposes a two-stage pipeline. Outlier-robust PCA first estimates the original column space; unlabeled-sensing methods then use that space to restore permuted data. Experiments involving synthetic data, faces, and educational and medical records indicate potential applications in data privatization and record linkage. The work combines an algebraic characterization with a practical recovery procedure.
summary.tldr: UPCA studies low-rank recovery from column-wise shuffled data and proposes a two-stage recovery pipeline for partially permuted matrices.

title: Unlabeled Principal Component Analysis

abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a cornerstone of modern medical imaging. However, long image acquisition times, the need for qualitative expert analysis, and the lack of (and difficulty extracting) quantitative indicators that are sensitive to tissue health have curtailed widespread clinical and research studies. While recent machine learning methods for MRI reconstruction and analysis have shown promise for reducing this burden, these techniques are primarily validated with imperfect image quality metrics, which are discordant with clinically-relevant measures that ultimately hamper clinical deployment and clinician trust. To mitigate this challenge, we present the Stanford Knee MRI with Multi-Task Evaluation (SKM-TEA) dataset, a collection of quantitative knee MRI (qMRI) scans that enables end-to-end, clinically-relevant evaluation of MRI reconstruction and analysis tools. This 1.6TB dataset consists of raw-data measurements of ~25,000 slices (155 patients) of anonymized patient MRI scans, the corresponding scanner-generated DICOM images, manual segmentations of four tissues, and bounding box annotations for sixteen clinically relevant pathologies. We provide a framework for using qMRI parameter maps, along with image reconstructions and dense image labels, for measuring the quality of qMRI biomarker estimates extracted from MRI reconstruction, segmentation, and detection techniques. Finally, we use this framework to benchmark state-of-the-art baselines on this dataset. We hope our SKM-TEA dataset and code can enable a broad spectrum of research for modular image reconstruction and image analysis in a clinically informed manner. Dataset access, code, and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/skm-tea.

SKM-TEA addresses this evaluation gap with quantitative knee MRI data. The aim is to assess reconstruction and analysis through the quality of tissue-related biomarker estimates extracted from their outputs.

summary.tldr: SKM-TEA pairs knee MRI measurements and detailed labels with a framework for evaluating reconstruction and analysis through quantitative biomarker estimates.

title: SKM-TEA: A Dataset for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction with Dense Image Labels for Quantitative Clinical Evaluation

abstract: This paper introduces Timers and Such, a new open source dataset of spoken English commands for common voice control use cases involving numbers. We describe the gap in existing spoken language understanding datasets that Timers and Such fills, the design and creation of the dataset, and experiments with a number of ASR-based and end-to-end baseline models, the code for which has been made available as part of the SpeechBrain toolkit.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces Timers and Such, a new open source dataset of spoken English commands for common voice control use cases involving numbers. We describe the gap in existing spoken language understanding datasets that Timers and Such fills, the design and creation of the dataset, and experiments with a number of ASR-based and end-to-end baseline models, the code for which has been made available as part of the SpeechBrain toolkit.

paragraphs: Timers and Such is an open-source dataset of spoken English commands for everyday voice-control uses involving numbers. The paper identifies a gap in existing spoken-language-understanding datasets and builds a benchmark around this practical category of requests. Numerical content is central to the commands the resource is designed to represent.

The authors describe how the dataset was designed and created, then use it to experiment with several baseline models. These include approaches based on automatic speech recognition and end-to-end approaches. Including both families gives researchers a common dataset on which to investigate different ways of turning speech into an understood command.

The baseline code is available through the SpeechBrain toolkit, pairing the data contribution with reusable implementations. This makes the benchmark a concrete starting point for experiments on number-bearing voice commands. The paper's stated contribution is the dataset, its construction, and baseline experimentation, establishing a shared setting for studying this part of spoken-language understanding.
summary.tldr: Timers and Such benchmarks spoken English commands involving numbers and provides speech-recognition-based and end-to-end baseline implementations.

title: Timers and Such: A Practical Benchmark for Spoken Language Understanding with Numbers

abstract: ImageNet-1K serves as the primary dataset for pretraining deep learning models for computer vision tasks. ImageNet-21K dataset, which is bigger and more diverse, is used less frequently for pretraining, mainly due to its complexity, low accessibility, and underestimation of its added value.This paper aims to close this gap, and make high-quality efficient pretraining on ImageNet-21K available for everyone.Via a dedicated preprocessing stage, utilization of WordNet hierarchical structure, and a novel training scheme called semantic softmax, we show that various models significantly benefit from ImageNet-21K pretraining on numerous datasets and tasks, including small mobile-oriented models. We also show that we outperform previous ImageNet-21K pretraining schemes for prominent new models like ViT and Mixer.Our proposed pretraining pipeline is efficient, accessible, and leads to SoTA reproducible results, from a publicly available dataset. The training code and pretrained models are available at: https://github.com/Alibaba-MIIL/ImageNet21K
originalAbstract: ImageNet-1K serves as the primary dataset for pretraining deep learning models for computer vision tasks. ImageNet-21K dataset, which is bigger and more diverse, is used less frequently for pretraining, mainly due to its complexity, low accessibility, and underestimation of its added value.This paper aims to close this gap, and make high-quality efficient pretraining on ImageNet-21K available for everyone.Via a dedicated preprocessing stage, utilization of WordNet hierarchical structure, and a novel training scheme called semantic softmax, we show that various models significantly benefit from ImageNet-21K pretraining on numerous datasets and tasks, including small mobile-oriented models. We also show that we outperform previous ImageNet-21K pretraining schemes for prominent new models like ViT and Mixer.Our proposed pretraining pipeline is efficient, accessible, and leads to SoTA reproducible results, from a publicly available dataset. The training code and pretrained models are available at: https://github.com/Alibaba-MIIL/ImageNet21K

paragraphs: Pretraining gives a vision model a starting point before it is adapted to other tasks. Although ImageNet-21K is larger and more diverse than the commonly used ImageNet-1K, the authors argue that complexity, accessibility, and underappreciated benefits have limited its use. This paper develops a practical pipeline for making high-quality ImageNet-21K pretraining more widely usable.

The approach combines dedicated data preprocessing, the hierarchical organization provided by WordNet, and a training scheme called semantic softmax. These components make the dataset’s organization part of the training approach. The authors present the resulting pipeline as efficient, accessible, and capable of producing reproducible state-of-the-art results.

Across numerous evaluated datasets and tasks, several models benefit significantly from ImageNet-21K pretraining, including small models intended for mobile use. The method also outperforms previous ImageNet-21K pretraining schemes for models such as ViT and Mixer. Released training code and pretrained models make the reported approach available for reuse, supporting the paper’s goal of broadening access to this larger pretraining resource.
summary.tldr: A preprocessing and semantic-softmax training pipeline makes ImageNet-21K pretraining more accessible and improves results across the evaluated models and tasks.

title: ImageNet-21K Pretraining for the Masses

abstract: Graph classifiers are vulnerable to topological attacks. Although certificates of robustness have been recently developed, their threat model only counts local and global edge perturbations, which effectively ignores important graph structures such as isomorphism. To address this issue, we propose measuring the perturbation with the orthogonal Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy, and building its Fenchel biconjugate to facilitate convex optimization. Our key insight is drawn from the matching loss whose root connects two variables via a monotone operator, and it yields a tight outer convex approximation for resistance distance on graph nodes. When applied to graph classification by graph convolutional networks, both our certificate and attack algorithm are demonstrated effective.

paragraphs: Graph classifiers can be attacked by changing graph topology. Existing robustness certificates described in this paper measure such changes through local and global edge counts. The authors argue that counting edits misses important structural properties, including isomorphism: graphs can retain the same underlying structure despite differences in how their nodes are identified.

The proposed approach measures perturbations using the orthogonal Gromov-Wasserstein discrepancy. To make this structural measure usable in convex optimization, the authors construct its Fenchel biconjugate. Their mathematical development draws on a matching loss whose root relates two variables through a monotone operator. This yields a tight outer convex approximation for resistance distances between graph nodes.

The work develops both a robustness certificate and an attack algorithm within this framework. Applied to graph classification with graph convolutional networks, both are demonstrated to be effective. The contribution is therefore twofold: it changes how allowed graph perturbations are measured and supplies optimization machinery for evaluating robustness under that measure. Its central motivation is to account for structure that edge-edit totals alone overlook.
summary.tldr: The paper develops graph robustness certificates and attacks using a structural discrepancy that goes beyond counting edge changes.

title: Certifying Robust Graph Classification under Orthogonal Gromov-Wasserstein Threats

abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) has been shown to offer a principled way to regularize learning models. In this paper, we find that Tikhonov regularization is distributionally robust in an optimal transport sense (i.e. if an adversary chooses distributions in a suitable optimal transport neighborhood of the empirical measure), provided that suitable martingale constraints are also imposed. Further, we introduce a relaxation of the martingale constraints which not only provide a unified viewpoint to a class of existing robust methods but also lead to new regularization tools. To realize these novel tools, provably efficient computational algorithms are proposed. As a byproduct, the strong duality theorem proved in this paper can be potentially applied to other problems of independent interest.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization interprets learning as protection against adverse changes in the data distribution. This paper connects that viewpoint to Tikhonov regularization. It shows that the regularized objective has an optimal-transport robustness interpretation when an adversary chooses distributions within a suitable neighborhood of the empirical distribution and suitable martingale constraints are imposed.

Those constraints are essential to the stated connection. The paper then relaxes them, creating a broader framework that unifies a class of existing robust methods and yields new regularization tools. This turns the equivalence into a way to design methods: changing the permitted distributional shifts leads to additional forms of regularization within the framework.

The authors propose computational algorithms with provable efficiency to realize the new tools. They also prove a strong duality theorem that could potentially apply to other problems. The contribution links a familiar regularization method to a precisely constrained robustness problem, then uses that link to develop further methods. The possible broader use of the duality theorem remains a prospective application.
summary.tldr: Tikhonov regularization admits an optimal-transport robustness interpretation under suitable martingale constraints, whose relaxation yields new regularizers.

title: Tikhonov Regularization is Optimal Transport Robust under Martingale Constraints

abstract: Pre-training produces representations that are effective for a wide range of downstream tasks, but it is still unclear what properties of pre-training are necessary for effective gains. Notably, recent work shows that even pre-training on synthetic tasks can achieve significant gains in downstream tasks. In this work, we perform three experiments that iteratively simplify pre-training and show that the simplifications still retain much of its gains. First, building on prior work, we perform a systematic evaluation of three existing synthetic pre-training methods on six downstream tasks. We find the best synthetic pre-training method, LIME, attains an average of $67\%$ of the benefits of natural pre-training. Second, to our surprise, we find that pre-training on a simple and generic synthetic task defined by the set function achieves $65\%$ of the benefits, almost matching LIME. Third, we find that $39\%$ of the benefits can be attained by using merely the parameter statistics of synthetic pre-training. We release the source code at \url{https://github.com/felixzli/synthetic_pretraining}.
