paragraphs: Pre-training can make a model more effective on later tasks, but identifying which ingredients produce those gains is difficult. This paper investigates that question through three experiments that progressively simplify pre-training. The goal is to measure how much downstream benefit survives as the training setup becomes less elaborate.

First, the authors systematically compare three existing synthetic pre-training methods across six downstream tasks. The strongest, LIME, retains an average of 67% of the benefits of natural pre-training. Next, they use a simple, generic synthetic task defined by the set function. It retains 65% of the benefits, coming close to LIME despite the simpler construction.

The final experiment retains only parameter statistics from synthetic pre-training and still obtains 39% of the benefits. These percentages describe retained gains, not absolute task accuracy. Across the experiments, substantial benefits survive increasingly severe simplifications. The findings provide evidence that useful effects of pre-training can arise from simple synthetic structure and even from aspects of the resulting parameter statistics, without establishing that these capture every benefit of natural pre-training.
summary.tldr: Progressively simplified synthetic pre-training retains substantial downstream gains, with parameter statistics alone preserving 39% of the reported benefits.

title: Insights into Pre-training via Simpler Synthetic Tasks

abstract: Personalized PageRank (PPR) is a fundamental tool in unsupervised learning of graph representations such as node ranking, labeling, and graph embedding. However, while data privacy is one of the most important recent concerns, existing PPR algorithms are not designed to protect user privacy. PPR is highly sensitive to the input graph edges: the difference of only one edge may cause a big change in the PPR vector, potentially leaking private user data.In this work, we propose an algorithm which outputs an approximate PPR and has provably bounded sensitivity to input edges. In addition, we prove that our algorithm achieves similar accuracy to non-private algorithms when the input graph has large degrees. Our sensitivity-bounded PPR directly implies private algorithms for several tools of graph learning, such as, differentially private (DP) PPR ranking, DP node classification, and DP node embedding. To complement our theoretical analysis, we also empirically verify the practical performances of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Personalized PageRank supports graph tasks including ranking nodes, assigning labels, and constructing embeddings. However, its output can change substantially when just one edge changes. This sensitivity creates a privacy problem: a released representation may reveal information about a relationship in the graph. Existing PageRank algorithms were not designed to control that exposure.

The paper introduces an approximate Personalized PageRank algorithm with a provable bound on its sensitivity to input edges. Controlling this sensitivity supplies a foundation for differentially private graph tools. The authors derive private versions of PageRank ranking, node classification, and node embedding from the same underlying construction.

The accuracy guarantee has a stated condition: when the input graph has large degrees, the approximation achieves accuracy similar to non-private algorithms. The authors also evaluate practical performance empirically. The contribution therefore connects an edge-sensitivity guarantee to several downstream learning operations, while showing that the privacy-oriented approximation can retain useful accuracy in the graph setting covered by the theorem.
summary.tldr: A sensitivity-bounded approximation to Personalized PageRank enables private graph learning with comparable accuracy on graphs satisfying a large-degree condition.

title: Differentially Private Graph Learning via Sensitivity-Bounded Personalized PageRank

abstract: Evaluating robustness of machine-learning models to adversarial examples is a challenging problem. Many defenses have been shown to provide a false sense of robustness by causing gradient-based attacks to fail, and they have been broken under more rigorous evaluations.Although guidelines and best practices have been suggested to improve current adversarial robustness evaluations, the lack of automatic testing and debugging tools makes it difficult to apply these recommendations in a systematic manner.In this work, we overcome these limitations by: (i) categorizing attack failures based on how they affect the optimization of gradient-based attacks, while also unveiling two novel failures affecting many popular attack implementations and past evaluations; (ii) proposing six novel \emph{indicators of failure}, to automatically detect the presence of such failures in the attack optimization process; and (iii) suggesting a systematic protocol to apply the corresponding fixes. Our extensive experimental analysis, involving more than 15 models in 3 distinct application domains, shows that our indicators of failure can be used to debug and improve current adversarial robustness evaluations, thereby providing a first concrete step towards automatizing and systematizing them. Our open-source code is available at: https://github.com/pralab/IndicatorsOfAttackFailure.

paragraphs: An unsuccessful adversarial attack does not by itself establish that a model is robust. The attack's optimization procedure may have failed to find a weakness that exists. This paper addresses that evaluation problem by developing automatic diagnostics for gradient-based attacks, making robustness checks easier to debug systematically.

The authors categorize attack failures according to their effects on optimization. Their analysis identifies two previously unreported failures affecting popular implementations and earlier evaluations. They then propose six indicators that automatically detect signs of these problems during attack optimization, together with a protocol for applying the corresponding fixes.

Experiments involving more than fifteen models across three application domains show that these indicators can improve existing robustness evaluations. Their value is to reveal when an attack result may reflect a faulty search process and to help repair that process. The paper presents this as an initial concrete step toward automated, systematic evaluation, with evidence that diagnostic tools can make attack-based assessments more dependable.
summary.tldr: Six automatic indicators and a repair protocol help detect attack optimization failures that can make models appear falsely robust.

title: Indicators of Attack Failure: Debugging and Improving Optimization of Adversarial Examples

abstract: Current state-of-the-art document retrieval solutions mainly follow an index-retrieve paradigm, where the index is hard to be directly optimized for the final retrieval target. In this paper, we aim to show that an end-to-end deep neural network unifying training and indexing stages can significantly improve the recall performance of traditional methods. To this end, we propose Neural Corpus Indexer (NCI), a sequence-to-sequence network that generates relevant document identifiers directly for a designated query. To optimize the recall performance of NCI, we invent a prefix-aware weight-adaptive decoder architecture, and leverage tailored techniques including query generation, semantic document identifiers, and consistency-based regularization. Empirical studies demonstrated the superiority of NCI on two commonly used academic benchmarks, achieving +21.4% and +16.8% relative enhancement for Recall@1 on NQ320k dataset and R-Precision on TriviaQA dataset, respectively, compared to the best baseline method.

paragraphs: Document retrieval usually separates building an index from using that index to find relevant documents. This separation makes it difficult to optimize the index directly for retrieval quality. Neural Corpus Indexer brings the training and indexing stages into a single sequence-to-sequence neural network that generates relevant document identifiers from a query.

The model treats retrieval as identifier generation, so its decoder is central to selecting documents. The paper introduces a prefix-aware decoder with adaptive weights, together with query generation, document identifiers that carry semantic information, and consistency-based regularization. These components are tailored to improving recall within the unified retrieval system.

On two academic benchmarks, NCI improves over the best baseline reported in the study. The gains are 21.4% relative for Recall@1 on NQ320k and 16.8% relative for R-Precision on TriviaQA. These are relative improvements in distinct retrieval measures, rather than percentage-point gains. The results support the paper's central idea that learning to generate document identifiers can improve retrieval when indexing is trained toward the final task.
summary.tldr: Neural Corpus Indexer learns to generate document identifiers directly from queries and improves retrieval performance on two benchmarks.

title: A Neural Corpus Indexer for Document Retrieval

abstract: As a dominant paradigm, fine-tuning a pre-trained model on the target data is widely used in many deep learning applications, especially for small data sets. However, recent studies have empirically shown that training from scratch has the final performance that is no worse than this pre-training strategy once the number of training samples is increased in some vision tasks. In this work, we revisit this phenomenon from the perspective of generalization analysis by using excess risk bound which is popular in learning theory. The result reveals that the excess risk bound may have a weak dependency on the pre-trained model. The observation inspires us to leverage pre-training data for fine-tuning, since this data is also available for fine-tuning. The generalization result of using pre-training data shows that the excess risk bound on a target task can be improved when the appropriate pre-training data is included in fine-tuning. With the theoretical motivation, we propose a novel selection strategy to select a subset from pre-training data to help improve the generalization on the target task. Extensive experimental results for image classification tasks on 8 benchmark data sets verify the effectiveness of the proposed data selection based fine-tuning pipeline.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning starts from a pretrained model and adapts it to a target dataset. The paper revisits evidence that, in some vision tasks with more training examples, training from scratch can match this strategy. It analyzes the phenomenon using an excess-risk bound and finds that the bound may depend only weakly on the pretrained model.

That observation motivates using the pretraining examples themselves during fine-tuning, alongside the model they produced. The analysis shows that including appropriate pretraining data can improve the target task's excess-risk bound. The qualification matters: the result motivates choosing useful source examples, rather than assuming that any additional pretraining data will help.

The authors turn this motivation into a strategy for selecting a subset of the pretraining dataset to include during fine-tuning. Experiments on eight image classification benchmarks support the effectiveness of the resulting pipeline. The approach assumes access to pretraining data during adaptation and treats data selection as part of transfer learning, extending the usual emphasis on transferring a model's learned parameters.
summary.tldr: Selecting suitable pretraining examples for reuse during fine-tuning can improve target-task generalization, supported by analysis and image classification experiments.

title: Improved Fine-Tuning by Better Leveraging Pre-Training Data

abstract: Identifying the effects of new interventions from data is a significant challenge found across a wide range of the empirical sciences. A well-known strategy for identifying such effects is Pearl's front-door (FD) criterion. The definition of the FD criterion is declarative, only allowing one to decide whether a specific set satisfies the criterion. In this paper, we present algorithms for finding and enumerating possible sets satisfying the FD criterion in a given causal diagram. These results are useful in facilitating the practical applications of the FD criterion for causal effects estimation and helping scientists to select estimands with desired properties, e.g., based on cost, feasibility of measurement, or statistical power.

paragraphs: Estimating what would happen after an intervention is a central problem in causal inference. Pearl's front-door criterion offers one strategy for identifying such effects from data. Its definition tells researchers whether a proposed set of variables qualifies, but that leaves a practical search problem: which sets should they consider?

This paper provides algorithms that find and enumerate sets satisfying the front-door criterion in a supplied causal diagram. Finding a valid set makes the criterion actionable when researchers have not already selected one. Enumerating the alternatives goes further by exposing multiple possible ways to formulate an identifiable causal-effect estimation task.

Those alternatives matter because mathematically valid choices can differ in practical desirability. The authors highlight measurement cost, feasibility, and statistical power as considerations that can guide selection. The contribution therefore connects a graphical criterion to the decisions involved in applying it: researchers can search for qualifying sets and compare available options using properties relevant to their study, within the given causal diagram.
summary.tldr: New algorithms find and enumerate front-door adjustment sets, helping researchers choose practical options for causal-effect estimation.

title: Finding and Listing Front-door Adjustment Sets

abstract: Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to comprehend the intricate relationships between humans and objects, predicting <human, action, object> triplets, and serving as the foundation for numerous computer vision tasks. The complexity and diversity of human-object interactions in the real world, however, pose significant challenges for both annotation and recognition, particularly in recognizing interactions within an open world context. This study explores the universal interaction recognition in an open-world setting through the use of Vision-Language (VL) foundation models and large language models (LLMs). The proposed method is dubbed as UniHOI. We conduct a deep analysis of the three hierarchical features inherent in visual HOI detectors and propose a method for high-level relation extraction aimed at VL foundation models, which we call HO prompt-based learning. Our design includes an HO Prompt-guided Decoder (HOPD), facilitates the association of high-level relation representations in the foundation model with various HO pairs within the image. Furthermore, we utilize a LLM (i.e. GPT) for interaction interpretation, generating a richer linguistic understanding for complex HOIs. For open-category interaction recognition, our method supports either of two input types: interaction phrase or interpretive sentence. Our efficient architecture design and learning methods effectively unleash the potential of the VL foundation models and LLMs, allowing UniHOI to surpass all existing methods with a substantial margin, under both supervised and zero-shot settings. The code and pre-trained weights will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Human-object interaction detection identifies a person, an action, and an object together. The challenge extends beyond recognizing the separate entities: the system must understand their relationship. UniHOI explores this task in an open-world setting, where the diversity of possible interactions makes annotation and recognition especially difficult.

The method draws on vision-language foundation models and a large language model. Following an analysis of three levels of features in visual interaction detectors, the authors introduce human-object prompt learning to extract high-level relationships. GPT supplies richer linguistic interpretations of complex interactions. For open-category recognition, users can specify either an interaction phrase or an explanatory sentence. The authors report that UniHOI substantially surpasses existing methods in both supervised and zero-shot settings. The approach matters because it combines spatial association with linguistic interpretation, allowing the detector to use foundation-model knowledge when recognizing relationships between people and objects.
summary.tldr: UniHOI combines spatial prompts and language-model interpretations to improve supervised and zero-shot human-object interaction detection.

title: Detecting Any Human-Object Interaction Relationship: Universal HOI Detector with Spatial Prompt Learning on Foundation Models

abstract: In unsupervised causal representation learning for sequential data with time-delayed latent causal influences, strong identifiability results for the disentanglement of causally-related latent variables have been established in stationary settings by leveraging temporal structure.However, in nonstationary setting, existing work only partially addressed the problem by either utilizing observed auxiliary variables (e.g., class labels and/or domain indexes) as side information or assuming simplified latent causal dynamics. Both constrain the method to a limited range of scenarios.In this study, we further explored the Markov Assumption under time-delayed causally related process in nonstationary setting and showed that under mild conditions, the independent latent components can be recovered from their nonlinear mixture up to a permutation and a component-wise transformation, without the observation of auxiliary variables. We then introduce NCTRL, a principled estimation framework, to reconstruct time-delayed latent causal variables and identify their relations from measured sequential data only.Empirical evaluations demonstrated the reliable identification of time-delayed latent causal influences, with our methodology substantially outperforming existing baselines that fail to exploit the nonstationarity adequately and then, consequently, cannot distinguish distribution shifts.

Both constrain the method to a limited range of scenarios.In this study, we further explored the Markov Assumption under time-delayed causally related process in nonstationary setting and showed that under mild conditions, the independent latent components can be recovered from their nonlinear mixture up to a permutation and a component-wise transformation, without the observation of auxiliary variables. paragraphs: Sequential observations can mix together hidden variables whose causal influences unfold over time. Recovering those variables becomes harder when the data-generating process changes. Existing approaches to this nonstationary setting may rely on observed labels or domain indicators, or impose simplified hidden dynamics. This paper investigates recovery using the measured sequence without those auxiliary observations.

The theoretical analysis uses the Markov assumption for processes with time-delayed causal relationships. Under conditions described as mild, the authors show that independent latent components can be recovered from nonlinear mixtures up to permutation and component-wise transformation. That qualification defines the recovery guarantee: the components can be reordered and individually transformed, so exact recovery in their original coordinates is not claimed.

The proposed NCTRL framework estimates time-delayed latent variables and identifies their relationships from sequential data alone. Empirical evaluations show reliable identification of delayed causal influences and substantial improvements over compared methods that inadequately exploit nonstationarity and fail to distinguish distribution shifts. The contribution combines a conditional identifiability result with an estimation method that uses changing temporal structure.
summary.tldr: NCTRL recovers temporally related latent variables under unknown nonstationarity, supported by conditional identifiability guarantees and empirical results.

title: Temporally Disentangled Representation Learning under Unknown Nonstationarity

abstract: Mislabeled, duplicated, or biased data in real-world scenarios can lead to prolonged training and even hinder model convergence. Traditional solutions prioritizing easy or hard samples lack the flexibility to handle such a variety simultaneously. Recent work has proposed a more reasonable data selection principle by examining the data's impact on the model's generalization loss. However, its practical adoption relies on less principled approximations and additional holdout data. This work solves these problems by leveraging a lightweight Bayesian treatment and incorporating off-the-shelf zero-shot predictors built on large-scale pre-trained models. The resulting algorithm is efficient and easy to implement. We perform extensive empirical studies on challenging benchmarks with considerable data noise and imbalance in the online batch selection scenario, and observe superior training efficiency over competitive baselines. Notably, on the challenging WebVision benchmark, our method can achieve similar predictive performance with significantly fewer training iterations than leading data selection methods.

paragraphs: Real-world training sets can contain incorrect labels, duplicates, and biases that slow learning or interfere with convergence. Choosing samples solely because they appear easy or difficult may not handle all these issues together. This paper builds on the idea of choosing data according to its expected effect on generalization loss.

Earlier implementations of that principle relied on less principled approximations and additional holdout data. The proposed method addresses these obstacles through a lightweight Bayesian treatment combined with readily available zero-shot predictors built from large pretrained models. The resulting selection algorithm is described as efficient and straightforward to implement, making this generalization-oriented principle more practical.

The evaluation considers online batch selection on challenging benchmarks with substantial noise and imbalance. The method achieves better training efficiency than competitive baselines in these experiments. On WebVision, it reaches similar predictive performance with significantly fewer training iterations than leading data-selection methods. This finding supports more effective use of training updates, with the stated efficiency result specifically demonstrated through reduced iteration requirements.
summary.tldr: Bayesian data selection uses pretrained zero-shot predictors to choose useful training batches and reaches comparable WebVision performance in fewer iterations.

title: Towards Accelerated Model Training via Bayesian Data Selection

abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) focuses on training reward-maximizing agents subject to pre-defined safety constraints. Yet, learning versatile safe policies that can adapt to varying safety constraint requirements during deployment without retraining remains a largely unexplored and challenging area. In this work, we formulate the versatile safe RL problem and consider two primary requirements: training efficiency and zero-shot adaptation capability. To address them, we introduce the Conditioned Constrained Policy Optimization (CCPO) framework, consisting of two key modules: (1) Versatile Value Estimation (VVE) for approximating value functions under unseen threshold conditions, and (2) Conditioned Variational Inference (CVI) for encoding arbitrary constraint thresholds during policy optimization. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that CCPO outperforms the baselines in terms of safety and task performance while preserving zero-shot adaptation capabilities to different constraint thresholds data-efficiently. This makes our approach suitable for real-world dynamic applications.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning trains agents to pursue rewards while respecting specified constraints. The paper considers a further requirement: a deployed agent should adapt when the allowed constraint thresholds change, without needing to be trained again. It formulates this versatile setting around efficient training and zero-shot adaptation.

The proposed Conditioned Constrained Policy Optimization framework, or CCPO, contains two modules. Versatile Value Estimation approximates value functions under threshold conditions not previously seen. Conditioned Variational Inference incorporates constraint thresholds into policy optimization. Together, these components make the requested constraint level part of how the policy is learned and evaluated.

Experiments show that CCPO improves safety and task performance over the evaluated baselines while retaining data-efficient adaptation to different thresholds without retraining. The findings support policies that can respond to changing requirements rather than being tied to one fixed constraint setting. The reported safety advantage is an experimental result; the abstract does not claim a universal guarantee that every deployed action satisfies every possible threshold.
summary.tldr: CCPO trains constraint-conditioned policies that adapt to changing safety thresholds without retraining and improve safety and performance in experiments.

title: Constraint-Conditioned Policy Optimization for Versatile Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Pretrained transformers exhibit the remarkable ability of in-context learning (ICL): they can learn tasks from just a few examples provided in the prompt without updating any weights. This raises a foundational question: can ICL solve fundamentally _new_ tasks that are very different from those seen during pretraining? To probe this question, we examine ICL’s performance on linear regression while varying the diversity of tasks in the pretraining dataset. We empirically demonstrate a _task diversity threshold_ for the emergence of ICL. Below this threshold, the pretrained transformer cannot solve unseen regression tasks, instead behaving like a Bayesian estimator with the _non-diverse pretraining task distribution_ as the prior. Beyond this threshold, the transformer significantly outperforms this estimator; its behavior aligns with that of ridge regression, corresponding to a Gaussian prior over _all tasks_, including those not seen during pretraining. Thus, when pretrained on data with task diversity greater than the threshold, transformers _can_ optimally solve fundamentally new tasks in-context. Importantly, this capability hinges on it deviating from the Bayes optimal estimator with the pretraining distribution as the prior. This study also explores the effect of regularization, model capacity and task structure and underscores, in a concrete example, the critical role of task diversity, alongside data and model scale, in the emergence of ICL.

paragraphs: In-context learning allows a transformer to use examples in a prompt without changing its weights. This paper asks whether that ability can extend to fundamentally new tasks. The authors investigate linear regression while varying the diversity of tasks used during pretraining, making task variety a central experimental variable.

They observe a task-diversity threshold. Below it, the transformer fails to solve unseen regression tasks and behaves like a Bayesian estimator whose prior is the limited pretraining task distribution. Above it, the transformer substantially outperforms that estimator and behaves more like ridge regression, corresponding to a Gaussian prior that also covers tasks absent from pretraining.

In this regression setting, sufficiently diverse pretraining therefore enables optimal in-context solutions to fundamentally new tasks. The crucial departure is from the Bayes-optimal estimator tied specifically to the pretraining distribution; the ridge-like behavior still has a Bayesian interpretation under a broader prior. The study also examines regularization, capacity, and task structure, highlighting task diversity alongside data and model scale in this concrete example.
summary.tldr: In linear regression experiments, sufficient pretraining task diversity enables transformers to solve unseen tasks through ridge-like in-context learning.

title: Pretraining task diversity and the emergence of non-Bayesian in-context learning for regression

abstract: The video object segmentation (VOS) task involves the segmentation of an object over time based on a single initial mask. Current state-of-the-art approaches use a memory of previously processed frames and rely on matching to estimate segmentation masks of subsequent frames. Lacking any adaptation mechanism, such methods are prone to test-time distribution shifts. This work focuses on matching-based VOS under distribution shifts such as video corruptions, stylization, and sim-to-real transfer. We explore test-time training strategies that are agnostic to the specific task as well as strategies that are designed specifically for VOS. This includes a variant based on mask cycle consistency tailored to matching-based VOS methods. The experimental results on common benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed test-time training yields significant improvements in performance. In particular for the sim-to-real scenario and despite using only a single test video, our approach manages to recover a substantial portion of the performance gain achieved through training on real videos. Additionally, we introduce DAVIS-C, an augmented version of the popular DAVIS test set, featuring extreme distribution shifts like image-/video-level corruptions and stylizations. Our results illustrate that test-time training enhances performance even in these challenging cases.

paragraphs: Video object segmentation follows an object through a video using an initial mask. Matching-based methods compare new frames with a memory of previously processed frames, but without adaptation they can struggle when test videos differ from training data. This paper examines adaptation under corruption, stylization, and transfer from simulated to real videos.

The authors explore both general test-time training strategies and strategies designed for video object segmentation. These include a mask cycle-consistency variant tailored to matching-based methods. The central idea is to update the model using the test video itself so that matching can work better under the conditions currently being encountered.

Experiments on common benchmarks show significant improvements. In the simulation-to-real setting, adaptation using a single test video recovers a substantial portion of the gain available from training on real videos. The paper also introduces DAVIS-C, which adds severe corruptions and stylizations to DAVIS. Improvements on this test set support the usefulness of test-time training even under the challenging shifts included in the evaluation.
summary.tldr: Training on the test video improves matching-based object segmentation under corruptions, stylization, and simulation-to-real transfer.

title: Test-time Training for Matching-based Video Object Segmentation

abstract: Developing generalizable models that can effectively learn from limited data and with minimal reliance on human supervision is a significant objective within the machine learning community, particularly in the era of deep neural networks. Therefore, to achieve data-efficient learning, researchers typically explore approaches that can leverage more related or unlabeled data without necessitating additional manual labeling efforts, such as Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL), Transfer Learning (TL), and Data Augmentation (DA).SSL leverages unlabeled data in the training process, while TL enables the transfer of expertise from related data distributions. DA broadens the dataset by synthesizing new data from existing examples. However, the significance of additional knowledge contained within labels has been largely overlooked in research. In this paper, we propose a novel perspective on data efficiency that involves exploiting the semantic information contained in the labels of the available data. Specifically, we introduce a Language Semantic Graph (LSG) which is constructed from labels manifest as natural language descriptions. Upon this graph, an auxiliary graph neural network is trained to extract high-level semantic relations and then used to guide the training of the primary model, enabling more adequate utilization of label knowledge. Across image, video, and audio modalities, we utilize the LSG method in both TL and SSL scenarios and illustrate its versatility in significantly enhancing performance compared to other data-efficient learning approaches. Additionally, our in-depth analysis shows that the LSG method also expedites the training process.

paragraphs: Learning with limited labeled data often means adding unlabeled examples, transferring knowledge from another dataset, or creating augmented examples. This paper examines another source of information already present in the data: the meaning of labels expressed in natural language. Labels can carry relationships that are lost when they function only as category identifiers.

The proposed Language Semantic Graph represents those descriptions in graph form. An auxiliary graph neural network learns higher-level semantic relationships from the graph and uses them to guide the primary model's training. The approach therefore gives label meaning an explicit role in learning, aiming to make fuller use of the supervision that is already available.

The authors apply this method to transfer learning and semi-supervised learning across images, video, and audio. They report significant improvements over other approaches to data-efficient learning, and their analysis also finds faster training. These findings support the usefulness of semantic label relationships across the tested modalities and learning settings, with an auxiliary graph providing a shared mechanism for conveying that information.
summary.tldr: A graph built from natural-language labels guides model training, improving data efficiency and training speed in the evaluated settings.

title: Language Semantic Graph Guided Data-Efficient Learning

abstract: Unconstrained and natural behavior consists of dynamics that are complex and unpredictable, especially when trying to predict what will happen multiple steps into the future. While some success has been found in building representations of animal behavior under constrained or simplified task-based conditions, many of these models cannot be applied to free and naturalistic settings where behavior becomes increasingly hard to model. In this work, we develop a multi-task representation learning model for animal behavior that combines two novel components: (i) an action-prediction objective that aims to predict the distribution of actions over future timesteps, and (ii) a multi-scale architecture that builds separate latent spaces to accommodate short- and long-term dynamics. After demonstrating the ability of the method to build representations of both local and global dynamics in robots in varying environments and terrains, we apply our method to the MABe 2022 Multi-Agent Behavior challenge, where our model ranks first overall on both mice and fly benchmarks. In all of these cases, we show that our model can build representations that capture the many different factors that drive behavior and solve a wide range of downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Natural behavior becomes difficult to predict as one looks further into the future. Representations learned in constrained tasks may therefore fail to capture the dynamics of freely behaving animals. This paper develops a self-supervised, multi-task approach intended to represent behavior across both short and long timescales.

The method combines two components. An action-prediction objective targets the distribution of actions over future timesteps, accommodating the uncertainty in what comes next. A multi-scale architecture builds separate latent spaces for short-term and long-term dynamics. Together, these components give the representation distinct ways to capture local behavior and broader patterns without placing both timescales into a single undifferentiated space.

The authors first demonstrate representations of local and global dynamics in robots operating across different environments and terrains. They then apply the method to the MABe 2022 Multi-Agent Behavior challenge, placing first overall on both the mice and fly benchmarks. Across these settings, the reported representations capture multiple factors driving behavior and support a wide range of downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: Predicting future action distributions in separate short- and long-term latent spaces produces useful behavior representations and leads both MABe 2022 animal benchmarks.

title: Relax, it doesn’t matter how you get there: A new self-supervised approach for multi-timescale behavior analysis

abstract: Bayesian deep learning (BDL) is a promising approach to achieve well-calibrated predictions on distribution-shifted data. Nevertheless, there exists no large-scale survey that evaluates recent SOTA methods on diverse, realistic, and challenging benchmark tasks in a systematic manner. To provide a clear picture of the current state of BDL research, we evaluate modern BDL algorithms on real-world datasets from the WILDS collection containing challenging classification and regression tasks, with a focus on generalization capability and calibration under distribution shift. We compare the algorithms on a wide range of large, convolutional and transformer-based neural network architectures. In particular, we investigate a signed version of the expected calibration error that reveals whether the methods are over- or underconfident, providing further insight into the behavior of the methods. Further, we provide the first systematic evaluation of BDL for fine-tuning large pre-trained models, where training from scratch is prohibitively expensive. Finally, given the recent success of Deep Ensembles, we extend popular single-mode posterior approximations to multiple modes by the use of ensembles. While we find that ensembling single-mode approximations generally improves the generalization capability and calibration of the models by a significant margin, we also identify a failure mode of ensembles when finetuning large transformer-based language models. In this setting, variational inference based approaches such as last-layer Bayes By Backprop outperform other methods in terms of accuracy by a large margin, while modern approximate inference algorithms such as SWAG achieve the best calibration.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates how Bayesian deep learning methods behave when deployment data differ from training data. It examines both predictive performance and calibration, meaning how well reported confidence matches actual correctness. The evaluation uses classification and regression tasks from WILDS and covers large convolutional and transformer architectures.

The authors also investigate a signed calibration error that distinguishes overconfidence from underconfidence. This adds information that a calibration magnitude alone can hide. Their study includes fine-tuning large pretrained models, where training from scratch is prohibitively expensive, and extends posterior approximations focused on a single mode by combining them in ensembles.

Ensembling these approximations generally improves generalization and calibration substantially, but the findings are not uniform across settings. The authors identify an ensemble failure mode when fine-tuning large transformer language models. There, variational approaches such as last-layer Bayes By Backprop achieve substantially better accuracy, while methods such as SWAG provide the best calibration. The results make the training setting and the distinction between accuracy and confidence quality central to method selection.
summary.tldr: A large evaluation finds that Bayesian ensembles generally improve performance under distribution shift, with an important exception in language-model fine-tuning.

title: Beyond Deep Ensembles: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Bayesian Deep Learning under Distribution Shift

abstract: Therapeutic antibodies are an essential and rapidly flourishing drug modality. The binding specificity between antibodies and antigens is decided by complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) at the tips of these Y-shaped proteins. In this paper, we propose a \textbf{h}ierarchical \textbf{t}raining \textbf{p}aradigm (HTP) for the antibody sequence-structure co-design. HTP consists of four levels of training stages, each corresponding to a specific protein modality within a particular protein domain. Through carefully crafted tasks in different stages, HTP seamlessly and effectively integrates geometric graph neural networks (GNNs) with large-scale protein language models to excavate evolutionary information from not only geometric structures but also vast antibody and non-antibody sequence databases, which determines ligand binding pose and strength. Empirical experiments show HTP sets the new state-of-the-art performance in the co-design problem as well as the fix-backbone design. Our research offers a hopeful path to unleash the potential of deep generative architectures and seeks to illuminate the way forward for the antibody sequence and structure co-design challenge.

paragraphs: Designing an antibody involves choosing both its amino-acid sequence and its three-dimensional structure. These choices are closely connected in the complementarity-determining regions, or CDRs, at the antibody’s tips. Those regions determine binding specificity between an antibody and an antigen. This paper proposes a hierarchical training paradigm, HTP, to support the joint design of sequence and structure.

HTP organizes training into four stages, each associated with a particular protein modality and domain. Carefully chosen tasks connect geometric graph neural networks, which work with structural information, to large protein language models, which work with sequence information. This lets the approach draw on geometric structures alongside large databases of both antibody and non-antibody sequences, bringing several sources of evolutionary information into the design process.

The reported experiments establish new state-of-the-art performance for joint sequence–structure design and for design with a fixed backbone. The contribution is a training strategy for combining complementary protein information, with empirical evidence that this combination improves the evaluated design tasks.
summary.tldr: HTP combines structural and sequence models through four training stages to improve antibody sequence–structure co-design.

title: A Hierarchical Training Paradigm for Antibody Structure-sequence Co-design

abstract: The key to OOD detection has two aspects: generalized feature representation and precise category description. Recently, vision-language models such as CLIP provide significant advances in both two issues, but constructing precise category descriptions is still in its infancy due to the absence of unseen categories. This work introduces two hierarchical contexts, namely perceptual context and spurious context, to carefully describe the precise category boundary through automatic prompt tuning. Specifically, perceptual contexts perceive the inter-category difference (e.g., cats vs apples) for current classification tasks, while spurious contexts further identify spurious (similar but exactly not) OOD samples for every single category (e.g., cats vs panthers, apples vs peaches). The two contexts hierarchically construct the precise description for a certain category, which is, first roughly classifying a sample to the predicted category and then delicately identifying whether it is truly an ID sample or actually OOD. Moreover, the precise descriptions for those categories within the vision-language framework present a novel application: CATegory-EXtensible OOD detection (CATEX). One can efficiently extend the set of recognizable categories by simply merging the hierarchical contexts learned under different sub-task settings. And extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate CATEX’s effectiveness, robustness, and category-extensibility. For instance, CATEX consistently surpasses the rivals by a large margin with several protocols on the challenging ImageNet-1K dataset. In addition, we offer new insights on how to efficiently scale up the prompt engineering in vision-language models to recognize thousands of object categories, as well as how to incorporate large language models (like GPT-3) to boost zero-shot applications.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object category also requires knowing when a similar object falls outside that category. This paper addresses that boundary problem in out-of-distribution detection using vision-language models. It develops automatically tuned descriptions that distinguish both clearly different categories and unfamiliar examples that closely resemble a recognized category.

The method learns two levels of context. Perceptual context separates the categories involved in the current task, such as cats and apples. Spurious context distinguishes a category from similar outsiders, such as cats and panthers. Together, these support a two-stage decision: identify a likely category, then assess whether the example actually belongs inside its boundary.

The resulting CATEX framework can expand its recognizable category set by merging contexts learned for different subtasks. Experiments support its effectiveness, robustness, and extensibility, including consistently large improvements over rivals across several ImageNet-1K protocols. The paper also offers insights into scaling prompts to thousands of categories and incorporating large language models into zero-shot applications. Its contribution combines more precise rejection decisions with a practical mechanism for extending recognition.
summary.tldr: CATEX learns hierarchical category descriptions that reject similar outsiders and can be merged to recognize additional categories.

title: Category-Extensible Out-of-Distribution Detection via Hierarchical Context Descriptions

abstract: When domain knowledge is limited and experimentation is restricted by ethical, financial, or time constraints, practitioners turn to observational causal discovery methods to recover the causal structure, exploiting the statistical properties of their data. Because causal discovery without further assumptions is an ill-posed problem, each algorithm comes with its own set of usually untestable assumptions, some of which are hard to meet in real datasets. Motivated by these considerations, this paper extensively benchmarks the empirical performance of recent causal discovery methods on observational _iid_ data generated under different background conditions, allowing for violations of the critical assumptions required by each selected approach. Our experimental findings show that score matching-based methods demonstrate surprising performance in the false positive and false negative rate of the inferred graph in these challenging scenarios, and we provide theoretical insights into their performance. This work is also the first effort to benchmark the stability of causal discovery algorithms with respect to the values of their hyperparameters. Finally, we hope this paper will set a new standard for the evaluation of causal discovery methods and can serve as an accessible entry point for practitioners interested in the field, highlighting the empirical implications of different algorithm choices.

paragraphs: Causal discovery tries to recover cause-and-effect structure from data, which is especially useful when experiments are impractical. Observational data alone cannot generally determine that structure without additional assumptions. This paper examines what happens when the assumptions built into causal discovery methods fail, a concern when those assumptions are difficult to check or satisfy.

The authors benchmark recent methods using observational data whose samples are independent and identically distributed. They vary the conditions generating the data so that critical assumptions of the selected algorithms can be violated. The evaluation examines both incorrectly inferred causal connections and genuine connections that the methods miss. It also investigates how stable algorithms remain as their hyperparameters change.

Score matching methods show surprisingly strong empirical behavior on these graph error measures in the challenging settings studied. The paper supplies theoretical insights into that behavior, alongside the benchmark results. Its contribution is evidence about robustness under particular violations and tuning choices, helping practitioners assess methods beyond evaluations where each algorithm's assumptions are comfortably satisfied.
summary.tldr: Benchmarks under violated causal assumptions reveal encouraging robustness of score matching methods and examine sensitivity to hyperparameter choices.

title: Assumption violations in causal discovery and the robustness of score matching

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a powerful method for optimizing black-box functions with limited function evaluations. Recent works have shown that optimization in a latent space through deep generative models such as variational autoencoders leads to effective and efficient Bayesian optimization for structured or discrete data. However, as the optimization does not take place in the input space, it leads to an inherent gap that results in potentially suboptimal solutions. To alleviate the discrepancy, we propose Correlated latent space Bayesian Optimization (CoBO), which focuses on learning correlated latent spaces characterized by a strong correlation between the distances in the latent space and the distances within the objective function. Specifically, our method introduces Lipschitz regularization, loss weighting, and trust region recoordination to minimize the inherent gap around the promising areas. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several optimization tasks in discrete data, such as molecule design and arithmetic expression fitting, and achieve high performance within a small budget.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several optimization tasks in discrete data, such as molecule design and arithmetic expression fitting, and achieve high performance within a small budget.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks good solutions when evaluating a function is expensive and only a limited number of evaluations are available. For structured or discrete objects, generative models can provide a latent space in which to search. However, searching that representation introduces a mismatch with the original optimization problem, potentially leading to suboptimal solutions.

CoBO addresses this mismatch by learning a latent space whose distances strongly correlate with differences in objective values. The aim is to make the geometry used by the optimizer more informative about the quantity it actually wants to improve. The method combines Lipschitz regularization, loss weighting, and trust region recoordination, concentrating on reducing the gap around promising regions.

The authors evaluate the approach on discrete optimization tasks, including molecule design and arithmetic expression fitting, and report high performance with a small evaluation budget. These findings support learning representations specifically for optimization: a useful search space should reflect the objective, as well as represent the candidate objects.
summary.tldr: CoBO improves latent-space Bayesian optimization by learning distances that better reflect differences in objective values.

title: Advancing Bayesian Optimization via Learning Correlated Latent Space

abstract: Instruction tuning is an effective technique to align large language models (LLMs) with human intent. In this work, we investigate how an adversary can exploit instruction tuning by injecting specific instruction-following examples into the training data that intentionally changes the model's behavior. For example, an adversary can achieve content injection by injecting training examples that mention target content and eliciting such behavior from downstream models. To achieve this goal, we propose \textit{AutoPoison}, an automated data poisoning pipeline. It naturally and coherently incorporates versatile attack goals into poisoned data with the help of an oracle LLM. We showcase two example attacks: content injection and over-refusal attacks, each aiming to induce a specific exploitable behavior. We quantify and benchmark the strength and the stealthiness of our data poisoning scheme. Our results show that AutoPoison allows an adversary to change a model's behavior by poisoning only a small fraction of data while maintaining a high level of stealthiness in the poisoned examples. We hope our work sheds light on how data quality affects the behavior of instruction-tuned models and raises awareness of the importance of data quality for responsible deployments of LLMs.

This paper examines how that same learning process can be manipulated when an adversary inserts deliberately constructed examples into the training data. The focus is on changing downstream behavior through poisoned instruction-following data.

The authors introduce AutoPoison, an automated pipeline that uses an oracle language model to incorporate attack objectives into coherent training examples. These examples investigate different ways training-data contamination can redirect a model, while retaining the natural appearance of instruction-tuning examples.

The reported results show that changing only a small fraction of training examples can alter model behavior while keeping those examples difficult to distinguish as malicious. summary.tldr: AutoPoison shows that a small fraction of coherent poisoned instruction examples can induce targeted content or excessive refusals.

title: On the Exploitability of Instruction Tuning

abstract: Intelligent systems possess a crucial characteristic of breaking complicated problems into smaller reusable components or parts and adjusting to new tasks using these part representations. However, current part-learners encounter difficulties in dealing with incidental correlations resulting from the limited observations of objects that may appear only in specific arrangements or with specific backgrounds. These incidental correlations may have a detrimental impact on the generalization and interpretability of learned part representations. This study asserts that part-based representations could be more interpretable and generalize better with limited data, employing two innovative regularization methods. The first regularization separates foreground and background information's generative process via a unique mixture-of-parts formulation. Structural constraints are imposed on the parts using a weakly-supervised loss, guaranteeing that the mixture-of-parts for foreground and background entails soft, object-agnostic masks. The second regularization assumes the form of a distillation loss, ensuring the invariance of the learned parts to the incidental background correlations. Furthermore, we incorporate sparse and orthogonal constraints to facilitate learning high-quality part representations.By reducing the impact of incidental background correlations on the learned parts, we exhibit state-of-the-art (SoTA) performance on few-shot learning tasks on benchmark datasets, including MiniImagenet, TieredImageNet, and FC100. We also demonstrate that the part-based representations acquired through our approach generalize better than existing techniques, even under domain shifts of the background and common data corruption on the ImageNet-9 dataset.

paragraphs: Learning reusable object parts could help a model adapt from limited examples. The paper addresses this problem by regularizing how foreground, background, and part representations are learned.

The first regularizer separates the generative processes for foreground and background through a mixture-of-parts formulation. They also show better generalization than existing techniques when backgrounds shift or images undergo common corruptions on ImageNet-9. These findings support the approach's central claim: reducing the influence of coincidental backgrounds can make learned parts more useful beyond their original observations. The method connects structural separation during learning with improved performance under the evaluated changes.
summary.tldr: Foreground–background separation and distillation help part-based models resist incidental correlations and improve few-shot and shifted-data performance.

title: Mitigating the Effect of Incidental Correlations on Part-based Learning

abstract: We propose novel statistics which maximise the power of a two-sample test based on the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), byadapting over the set of kernels used in defining it.For finite sets, this reduces to combining (normalised) MMD values under each of these kernels via a weighted soft maximum.Exponential concentration bounds are proved for our proposed statistics under the null and alternative.We further show how these kernels can be chosen in a data-dependent but permutation-independent way, in a well-calibrated test, avoiding data splitting.This technique applies more broadly to general permutation-based MMD testing, and includes the use of deep kernels with features learnt using unsupervised models such as auto-encoders.We highlight the applicability of our MMD-Fuse tests on both synthetic low-dimensional and real-world high-dimensional data, and compare its performance in terms of power against current state-of-the-art kernel tests.

paragraphs: A two-sample test asks whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. Maximum Mean Discrepancy measures differences using a kernel, so the kernel choice influences which differences the test can detect. MMD-Fuse develops test statistics that adapt over multiple kernels to improve the ability to detect distributional differences.

For a finite collection of kernels, the method combines normalized MMD values through a weighted soft maximum. The authors prove exponential concentration bounds under both the null hypothesis and the alternative. They also show how kernels can depend on the observed data while remaining independent of the permutations used by the test, preserving calibration without splitting the data.

That kernel-selection technique extends to permutation-based MMD testing more broadly, including deep kernels built from features learned by unsupervised models such as autoencoders. The paper evaluates MMD-Fuse on synthetic low-dimensional and real high-dimensional data and compares test power with leading kernel tests. The stated contribution combines adaptive kernel use with statistical validity, without requiring a separate data subset for kernel selection.
summary.tldr: MMD-Fuse combines kernel-based discrepancy measures and permits data-dependent kernel selection without splitting data or losing test calibration.

title: MMD-Fuse: Learning and Combining Kernels for Two-Sample Testing Without Data Splitting

abstract: Autoregressive models for text sometimes generate repetitive and low-quality output because errors accumulate during the steps of generation. This issue is often attributed to exposure bias -- the difference between how a model is trained, and how it is used during inference. Denoising diffusion models provide an alternative approach in which a model can revisit and revise its output. However, they can be computationally expensive and prior efforts on text have led to models that produce less fluent output compared to autoregressive models, especially for longer text and paragraphs. In this paper, we propose PLANNER, a model that combines latent semantic diffusion with autoregressive generation, to generate fluent text while exercising global control over paragraphs. The model achieves this by combining an autoregressive "decoding" module with a "planning" module that uses latent diffusion to generate semantic paragraph embeddings in a coarse-to-fine manner. The proposed method is evaluated on various conditional generation tasks, and results on semantic generation, text completion and summarization show its effectiveness in generating high-quality long-form text in an efficient manner.

paragraphs: Text generators that write one token at a time can accumulate errors and produce repetitive or low-quality passages. Diffusion models offer the ability to revise outputs, but applying them to text can be expensive and can sacrifice fluency, particularly for paragraphs. PLANNER combines the two approaches to address these complementary difficulties.

Its planning module uses diffusion to generate semantic paragraph embeddings, refining a representation of the paragraph from coarse to fine. An autoregressive decoder then turns that representation into text. This division gives diffusion responsibility for paragraph-level semantic planning while retaining autoregressive generation for fluent wording. Global control is exercised through the latent plan rather than through direct diffusion over the final text.

The authors evaluate conditional generation tasks covering semantic generation, text completion, and summarization. The reported results support efficient generation of high-quality long-form text. The approach matters because it connects revision at the level of paragraph meaning with a decoder suited to producing readable sequences, offering a combined route to planning and fluency.
summary.tldr: PLANNER combines diffusion-based semantic paragraph planning with autoregressive decoding to generate fluent long-form text efficiently.

title: PLANNER: Generating Diversified Paragraph via Latent Language Diffusion Model

abstract: This study introduces the Federated Medical Knowledge Injection (FedMEKI) platform, a new benchmark designed to address the unique challenges of integrating medical knowledge into foundation models under privacy constraints. By leveraging a cross-silo federated learning approach, FedMEKI circumvents the issues associated with centralized data collection, which is often prohibited under health regulations like the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) in the USA. The platform is meticulously designed to handle multi-site, multi-modal, and multi-task medical data, which includes 7 medical modalities, including images, signals, texts, laboratory test results, vital signs, input variables, and output variables. The curated dataset to validate FedMEKI covers 8 medical tasks, including 6 classification tasks (lung opacity detection, COVID-19 detection, electrocardiogram (ECG) abnormal detection, mortality prediction, sepsis protection, and enlarged cardiomediastinum detection) and 2 generation tasks (medical visual question answering (MedVQA) and ECG noise clarification). This comprehensive dataset is partitioned across several clients to facilitate the decentralized training process under 16 benchmark approaches. FedMEKI not only preserves data privacy but also enhances the capability of medical foundation models by allowing them to learn from a broader spectrum of medical knowledge without direct data exposure, thereby setting a new benchmark in the application of foundation models within the healthcare sector.

It uses cross-silo federated learning, organizing training across separate data holders. This addresses the centralization difficulties that arise when medical information is subject to privacy constraints.

The platform covers multiple sites, data types, and tasks. Its seven modalities include images, signals, text, laboratory results, vital signs, and input and output variables. Data is partitioned among clients for decentralized training.

The benchmark includes 16 approaches, creating a shared setting for studying how medical knowledge can be incorporated across this varied collection. The authors present FedMEKI as enabling foundation models to learn from a broader range of medical information without directly exposing the underlying data. Its central value is bringing privacy-constrained, multi-modal medical learning into a common evaluation framework.
summary.tldr: FedMEKI benchmarks federated medical foundation-model adaptation across seven data modalities, eight tasks, and 16 approaches.

title: FEDMEKI: A Benchmark for Scaling Medical Foundation Models via Federated Knowledge Injection

abstract: Reconstructing a continuous surface from a raw 3D point cloud is a challenging task. Latest methods employ supervised learning or pretrained priors to learn a signed distance function (SDF). However, neural networks tend to smooth local details due to the lack of ground truth signed distnaces or normals, which limits the performance of learning-based methods in reconstruction tasks. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel method, named MultiPull, to learn multi-scale implicit fields from raw point clouds to optimize accurate SDFs from coarse to fine. We achieve this by mapping 3D query points into a set of frequency features, which makes it possible to leverage multi-level features during optimization. Meanwhile, we introduce optimization constraints from the perspective of spatial distance and normal consistency, which play a key role in point cloud reconstruction based on multi-scale optimization strategies. Our experiments on widely used object and scene benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in surface reconstruction.

paragraphs: MultiPull reconstructs continuous surfaces from raw 3D point clouds. The paper focuses on the loss of local detail when neural methods learn signed distance functions without ground-truth distances or surface normals. These functions represent a surface through a spatial field, but overly smooth learned fields can erase the fine structure needed for accurate reconstruction.

The method learns implicit fields at multiple scales and optimizes the signed distance function from coarse to fine. It maps 3D query points into frequency features so that different levels of detail are available during optimization. This provides a way to connect broad surface structure with finer geometric information during the same reconstruction process.

MultiPull also introduces constraints based on spatial distance and normal consistency. These guide the multiscale optimization toward geometrically consistent surfaces while supporting detail recovery. Experiments on commonly used object and scene benchmarks report better surface reconstruction than state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining multilevel representations with geometric constraints to improve reconstruction from raw points.
summary.tldr: MultiPull improves surface reconstruction from raw point clouds through coarse-to-fine implicit fields and geometric consistency constraints.

title: MultiPull: Detailing Signed Distance Functions by Pulling Multi-Level Queries at Multi-Step

abstract: In the realm of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), vision-language connector plays a crucial role to link the pre-trained vision encoders with Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite its importance, the vision-language connector has been relatively less explored. In this study, we aim to propose a strong vision-language connector that enables MLLM to simultaneously achieve high accuracy and low computation cost. We first reveal the existence of the visual anchors in Vision Transformer and propose a cost-effective search algorithm to progressively extract them. Building on these findings, we introduce the Anchor Former (AcFormer), a novel vision-language connector designed to leverage the rich prior knowledge obtained from these visual anchors during pretraining, guiding the aggregation of information. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs by nearly two-thirds, while simultaneously outperforming baseline methods. This highlights the effectiveness and efficiency of AcFormer.

paragraphs: A multimodal language model needs a connector that transfers information from its vision encoder to its language model. The quality and computational cost of this bridge affect the resulting system. This paper focuses on improving that connector so visual understanding can remain accurate while requiring less computation.

The authors identify visual anchors within a Vision Transformer and develop an inexpensive search procedure that extracts them progressively. They then introduce Anchor Former, or AcFormer, which uses the pretrained knowledge contained in these anchors to guide information aggregation. The connector therefore builds on informative visual structures already present in the vision encoder.

Extensive experiments show that the proposed method reduces computational costs by nearly two-thirds while outperforming baseline methods. The reported result is notable because improved efficiency accompanies improved performance in those evaluations, rather than a measured accuracy sacrifice. The contribution highlights the connector as a useful target for multimodal-model design and shows that visual anchors can provide effective guidance for gathering the information passed to the language model.
summary.tldr: AcFormer uses visual anchors to guide vision-language information aggregation, reducing computational costs by nearly two-thirds while outperforming baselines.

title: Visual Anchors Are Strong Information Aggregators For Multimodal Large Language Model

abstract: Object pose estimation plays a crucial role in robotic manipulation, however, its practical applicability still suffers from limited generalizability. This paper addresses the challenge of generalizable object pose estimation, particularly focusing on category-level object pose estimation for unseen object categories. Current methods either require impractical instance-level training or are confined to predefined categories, limiting their applicability. We propose VFM-6D, a novel framework that explores harnessing existing vision and language models, to elaborate object pose estimation into two stages: category-level object viewpoint estimation and object coordinate map estimation. Based on the two-stage framework, we introduce a 2D-to-3D feature lifting module and a shape-matching module, both of which leverage pre-trained vision foundation models to improve object representation and matching accuracy. VFM-6D is trained on cost-effective synthetic data and exhibits superior generalization capabilities. It can be applied to both instance-level unseen object pose estimation and category-level object pose estimation for novel categories. Evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of VFM-6D in various real-world scenarios.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation depends on estimating an object's pose, but practical methods often generalize poorly beyond the instances or categories used in training. VFM-6D targets this problem, particularly pose estimation for previously unseen object categories. It explores how existing vision and language models can support broader generalization.

The framework divides the task into category-level viewpoint estimation and object coordinate-map estimation. It introduces a module that lifts two-dimensional features into three dimensions and another that matches shapes. Both use pretrained vision foundation models to improve object representations and matching accuracy, connecting existing visual knowledge to the geometric requirements of pose estimation.

VFM-6D trains on cost-effective synthetic data and can be applied both to unseen individual objects and to objects from novel categories. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate its effectiveness and versatility across the reported real-world scenarios. The contribution is a framework for transferring pretrained representations into pose estimation, with evidence that synthetic training and the two-stage design can support generalization beyond a predefined set of object categories.
summary.tldr: VFM-6D uses pretrained foundation models and synthetic training to estimate poses for unseen objects and novel object categories.

title: Vision Foundation Model Enables Generalizable Object Pose Estimation

abstract: Diffusion-based image super-resolution (SR) models have attracted substantial interest due to their powerful image restoration capabilities. However, prevailing diffusion models often struggle to strike an optimal balance between efficiency and performance. Typically, they either neglect to exploit the potential of existing extensive pretrained models, limiting their generative capacity, or they necessitate a dozens of forward passes starting from random noises, compromising inference efficiency. In this paper, we present DoSSR, a $\textbf{Do}$main $\textbf{S}$hift diffusion-based SR model that capitalizes on the generative powers of pretrained diffusion models while significantly enhancing efficiency by initiating the diffusion process with low-resolution (LR) images. At the core of our approach is a domain shift equation that integrates seamlessly with existing diffusion models. This integration not only improves the use of diffusion prior but also boosts inference efficiency. Moreover, we advance our method by transitioning the discrete shift process to a continuous formulation, termed as DoS-SDEs. This advancement leads to the fast and customized solvers that further enhance sampling efficiency. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, while notably requiring $\textbf{\emph{only 5 sampling steps}}$. Compared to previous diffusion prior based methods, our approach achieves a remarkable speedup of 5-7 times, demonstrating its superior efficiency.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can restore detailed images, but super-resolution methods face a tension between image quality and inference cost. Some do not fully use large pretrained models, while others require many forward passes beginning from random noise. DoSSR aims to retain pretrained generative capabilities while making the restoration process substantially faster.

The method begins its diffusion process with the low-resolution image. A domain shift equation connects this starting point with existing diffusion models, providing a way to use their learned image prior. These findings suggest that changing the starting point and mathematical sampling process together can improve efficiency while preserving the benefits of a powerful pretrained model in the evaluated super-resolution settings.
summary.tldr: DoSSR starts diffusion from low-resolution images and uses domain-shift solvers to achieve strong super-resolution results in five sampling steps.

title: Taming Diffusion Prior for Image Super-Resolution with Domain Shift SDEs

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has already become the emerging research focus in the fields of 3D scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis. Given that training a 3DGS requires a significant amount of time and computational cost, it is crucial to protect the copyright, integrity, and privacy of such 3D assets. Steganography, as a crucial technique for encrypted transmission and copyright protection, has been extensively studied. However, it still lacks profound exploration targeted at 3DGS. Unlike its predecessor NeRF, 3DGS possesses two distinct features: 1) explicit 3D representation; and 2) real-time rendering speeds. These characteristics result in the 3DGS point cloud files being public and transparent, with each Gaussian point having a clear physical significance. Therefore, ensuring the security and fidelity of the original 3D scene while embedding information into the 3DGS point cloud files is an extremely challenging task. To solve the above-mentioned issue, we first propose a steganography framework for 3DGS, dubbed GS-Hider, which can embed 3D scenes and images into original GS point clouds in an invisible manner and accurately extract the hidden messages. Specifically, we design a coupled secured feature attribute to replace the original 3DGS's spherical harmonics coefficients and then use a scene decoder and a message decoder to disentangle the original RGB scene and the hidden message. Extensive experiments demonstrated that the proposed GS-Hider can effectively conceal multimodal messages without compromising rendering quality and possesses exceptional security, robustness, capacity, and flexibility. Our project is available at: https://xuanyuzhang21.github.io/project/gshider.
