paragraphs: Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting represents scenes explicitly and supports real-time rendering. Its accessible point-cloud representation creates a challenge for hiding information while preserving the visible scene. GS-Hider addresses this problem through steganography, embedding messages into Gaussian-splatting assets with the aim of supporting their protection and private information storage.

The framework replaces the original spherical-harmonic coefficients with a coupled secured feature attribute. A scene decoder and a message decoder then separate the visible RGB scene from the hidden content. This design allows images and three-dimensional scenes to be embedded within the original point cloud and extracted through the message-decoding pathway.

The authors report experiments in which multimodal messages are concealed effectively without compromising rendering quality. They also report strong security, robustness, capacity, and flexibility. The contribution is a representation-and-decoding scheme that accommodates visible scene reconstruction and hidden information within the same asset. Its findings show that this combination is achievable in the evaluated settings despite the explicit structure of Gaussian-splatting files.
summary.tldr: GS-Hider embeds recoverable images and 3D scenes into Gaussian-splatting assets while preserving rendering quality in reported experiments.

title: GS-Hider: Hiding Messages into 3D Gaussian Splatting

abstract: A single-index model (SIM) is a function of the form $\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\ast} \cdot \mathbf{x})$, where$\sigma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a known link function and $\mathbf{w}^{\ast}$ is a hidden unit vector. We study the task of learning SIMs in the agnostic (a.k.a. adversarial label noise) model with respect to the $L^2_2$-loss under the Gaussian distribution. Our main result is a sample and computationally efficient agnostic proper learner that attains $L^2_2$-error of $O(\mathrm{OPT})+\epsilon$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the optimal loss. The sample complexity of our algorithm is $\tilde{O}(d^{\lceil k^{\ast}/2\rceil}+d/\epsilon)$, where $k^{\ast}$ is the information-exponent of $\sigma$ corresponding to the degree of its first non-zero Hermite coefficient. This sample bound nearly matches known CSQ lower bounds, even in the realizable setting. Prior algorithmic work in this setting had focused on learning in the realizable case or in the presence of semi-random noise. Prior computationally efficient robust learners required significantly stronger assumptions on the link function.

paragraphs: A single-index model projects an input onto one hidden direction and applies a known link function to the result. This paper studies learning that direction when inputs follow a Gaussian distribution and labels may contain adversarial noise. The goal is a computationally efficient learner whose squared-error performance remains competitive with the best model in the specified class.

The authors provide a proper learner, meaning its output remains a single-index model using the given link function. Its error is bounded by a constant multiple of the optimal loss plus an adjustable accuracy term. Sample requirements depend on dimension, desired accuracy, and the link function's information exponent, defined through its first nonzero Hermite coefficient.

The sample bound nearly matches known lower bounds for correlational statistical-query methods, even when those bounds concern noiseless realizable learning. Earlier work either focused on realizable or semi-random-noise settings, or required stronger link-function assumptions for efficient robustness. The contribution is therefore an efficient guarantee under adversarial label noise within the stated Gaussian-input setting.
summary.tldr: The paper gives an efficient, noise-robust learner for Gaussian single-index models with error competitive with the best model in its class.

title: Sample and Computationally Efficient Robust Learning of Gaussian Single-Index Models

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is perhaps the most prevalent optimization method in modern machine learning. Contrary to the empirical practice of sampling from the datasets \emph{without replacement} and with (possible) reshuffling at each epoch, the theoretical counterpart of SGD usually relies on the assumption of \emph{sampling with replacement}. It is only very recently that SGD using sampling without replacement -- shuffled SGD -- has been analyzed with matching upper and lower bounds. However, we observe that those bounds are too pessimistic to explain often superior empirical performance of data permutations (sampling without replacement) over vanilla counterparts (sampling with replacement) on machine learning problems. Through fine-grained analysis in the lens of primal-dual cyclic coordinate methods and the introduction of novel smoothness parameters, we present several results for shuffled SGD on smooth and non-smooth convex losses, where our novel analysis framework provides tighter convergence bounds over all popular shuffling schemes (IG, SO, and RR). Notably, our new bounds predict faster convergence than existing bounds in the literature -- by up to a factor of $O(\sqrt{n})$, mirroring benefits from tighter convergence bounds using component smoothness parameters in randomized coordinate methods. Lastly, we numerically demonstrate on common machine learning datasets that our bounds are indeed much tighter, thus offering a bridge between theory and practice.

paragraphs: Practical stochastic gradient descent often processes examples without replacement, possibly reshuffling them each epoch. Traditional analysis more commonly assumes sampling with replacement. Although shuffled SGD has received theoretical treatment, this paper argues that existing bounds remain too pessimistic to account for the advantages often observed when training with data permutations.

The authors analyze shuffled SGD through its relationship to primal-dual cyclic coordinate methods. They introduce more detailed smoothness parameters to capture structure that earlier bounds miss. Their framework covers smooth and non-smooth convex losses and produces tighter convergence bounds for the shuffling schemes identified as IG, SO, and RR.

Numerical studies on common machine learning datasets show that the bounds are substantially tighter. The work helps reconcile existing shuffled optimization practice with a more informative theoretical account of its behavior.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual analysis yields tighter convergence bounds for shuffled SGD on convex losses, helping explain its observed practical advantages.

title: Tighter Convergence Bounds for Shuffled SGD via Primal-Dual Perspective

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is crucial for the safe deployment of neural networks. Existing CLIP-based approaches perform OOD detection by devising novel scoring functions or sophisticated fine-tuning methods. In this work, we propose SeTAR, a novel, training-free OOD detection method that leverages selective low-rank approximation of weight matrices in vision-language and vision-only models. SeTAR enhances OOD detection via post-hoc modification of the model's weight matrices using a simple greedy search algorithm. Based on SeTAR, we further propose SeTAR+FT, a fine-tuning extension optimizing model performance for OOD detection tasks. Extensive evaluations on ImageNet1K and Pascal-VOC benchmarks show SeTAR's superior performance, reducing the relatively false positive rate by up to 18.95\% and 36.80\% compared to zero-shot and fine-tuning baselines. Ablation studies further validate our approach's effectiveness, robustness, and generalizability across different model backbones. Our work offers a scalable, efficient solution for OOD detection, setting a new state-of-the-art in this area.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize inputs outside the distribution it is intended to handle. This paper approaches the problem by modifying an already trained model's weight matrices. SeTAR applies selective low-rank approximation to vision-language and vision-only models, offering a training-free way to improve detection.

A simple greedy search determines the post-hoc weight modifications. The approach makes the model's internal weights a direct target for improving detection, alongside existing approaches based on scoring functions or fine-tuning. The authors also introduce SeTAR+FT, an extension that adds fine-tuning to optimize performance for the detection task.

Evaluations on ImageNet1K and Pascal-VOC report superior performance, with relative false-positive-rate reductions of up to 18.95% and 36.80% compared with zero-shot and fine-tuning baselines. Ablation studies support effectiveness, robustness, and generalization across different backbones. The reported maxima describe improvements within these evaluations; the broader contribution is showing that selective weight approximation can be a useful detection intervention even without additional training.
summary.tldr: SeTAR improves out-of-distribution detection through training-free, selective low-rank changes to model weights.

title: SeTAR: Out-of-Distribution Detection with Selective Low-Rank Approximation

abstract: Large-scale diffusion models are adept at generating high-fidelity images and facilitating image editing and interpolation. However, they have limitations when tasked with generating images in dynamic, evolving domains. In this paper, we introduce Terra, a novel Time-varying low-rank adapter that offers a fine-tuning framework specifically tailored for domain flow generation. The key innovation of Terra lies in its construction of a continuous parameter manifold through a time variable, with its expressive power analyzed theoretically. This framework not only enables interpolation of image content and style but also offers a generation-based approach to address the domain shift problems in unsupervised domain adaptation and domain generalization. Specifically, Terra transforms images from the source domain to the target domain and generates interpolated domains with various styles to bridge the gap between domains and enhance the model generalization, respectively. We conduct extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of Terra. Our source code is publicly available on https://github.com/zwebzone/terra.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality images, but generating across changing domains poses additional challenges. Terra introduces a time-varying low-rank adapter for fine-tuning these models to represent a flow between domains. Its central construction uses a time variable to define a continuous manifold of parameters, allowing the adapted model to vary along that continuum.

This design supports interpolation of both image content and style. The authors also analyze its expressive power theoretically. Beyond image generation itself, they use the framework to address domain shift through generated data, connecting controllable movement between domains with the needs of models that must operate outside their original training distribution.

For unsupervised domain adaptation, Terra transforms source-domain images into the target domain. For domain generalization, it generates intermediate domains with varied styles to bridge differences and improve generalization. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets provide empirical support for the approach. The contribution is a continuous adaptation mechanism that serves both image interpolation and generation-based strategies for handling domain differences.
summary.tldr: Terra uses a time-varying low-rank adapter to generate continuous domain transitions and support adaptation and generalization through synthesized images.

title: Time-Varying LoRA: Towards Effective Cross-Domain Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models

abstract: In deep learning, model performance often deteriorates when trained on highly imbalanced datasets, especially when evaluation metrics require robust generalization across underrepresented classes. To address the challenges posed by imbalanced data distributions, this study introduces a novel method utilizing density ratio estimation for dynamic class weight adjustment, termed as Re-weighting with Density Ratio (RDR). Our method adaptively adjusts the importance of each class during training, mitigates overfitting on dominant classes and enhances model adaptability across diverse datasets. Extensive experiments conducted on various large scale benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of our method. Results demonstrate substantial improvements in generalization capabilities, particularly under severely imbalanced conditions.

Our method adaptively adjusts the importance of each class during training, mitigates overfitting on dominant classes and enhances model adaptability across diverse datasets. paragraphs: Re-weighting with Density Ratio, or RDR, addresses learning from datasets in which some classes have far more examples than others. Such imbalance can damage performance, especially when evaluation requires good generalization to underrepresented classes. The paper focuses on adjusting how much importance each class receives during training.

RDR uses density ratio estimation to make those class weights dynamic. Rather than treating class importance as a fixed setting throughout training, the method adapts it as training proceeds. The authors describe this adjustment as mitigating overfitting on dominant classes and improving adaptability across different datasets. Class re-weighting is therefore the mechanism through which the method addresses the uneven training distribution.

Experiments on several large-scale benchmark datasets validate the method's effectiveness, with substantial reported improvements in generalization, particularly under severe imbalance. These findings support adaptive class weighting as a useful response when dominant classes can disproportionately shape learning. The practical significance lies in improving generalization under the imbalanced conditions tested, especially where performance on underrepresented classes matters to the evaluation.
summary.tldr: RDR dynamically adjusts class weights using density ratio estimation and improves reported generalization, especially on severely imbalanced datasets.

title: Revive Re-weighting in Imbalanced Learning by Density Ratio Estimation

abstract: This work presents a novel approach to neural architecture search (NAS) that aims to increase carbon efficiency for the model design process. The proposed framework CE-NAS addresses the key challenge of high carbon cost associated with NAS by exploring the carbon emission variations of energy and energy differences of different NAS algorithms. At the high level, CE-NAS leverages a reinforcement-learning agent to dynamically adjust GPU resources based on carbon intensity, predicted by a time-series transformer, to balance energy-efficient sampling and energy-intensive evaluation tasks. Furthermore, CE-NAS leverages a recently proposed multi-objective optimizer to effectively reduce the NAS search space. We demonstrate the efficacy of CE-NAS in lowering carbon emissions while achieving SOTA results for both NAS datasets and open-domain NAS tasks. For example, on the HW-NasBench dataset, CE-NAS reduces carbon emissions by up to 7.22X while maintaining a search efficiency comparable to vanilla NAS. For open-domain NAS tasks, CE-NAS achieves SOTA results with 97.35% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 with only 1.68M parameters and a carbon consumption of 38.53 lbs of CO2. On ImageNet, our searched model achieves 80.6% top-1 accuracy with a 0.78 ms TensorRT latency using FP16 on NVIDIA V100, consuming only 909.86 lbs of CO2, making it comparable to other one-shot-based NAS baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/cake-lab/CE-NAS.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can consume substantial energy while exploring and evaluating candidate models. CE-NAS targets the carbon emissions of that design process. Its approach accounts for both differences in the energy demands of search operations and variation in the carbon intensity of the energy used to power them.

A time-series transformer predicts carbon intensity, and a reinforcement learning agent uses that information to adjust GPU resources dynamically. The controller balances relatively economical sampling against more energy-intensive evaluation. A multi-objective optimizer further reduces the search space, combining decisions about which architectures to explore with decisions about how to allocate computation.

They also report strong results for open-domain searches on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. These findings support treating resource allocation and carbon intensity as part of architecture search itself, alongside the performance of the model ultimately selected.
summary.tldr: CE-NAS combines carbon forecasts, adaptive GPU allocation, and search-space reduction to lower architecture-search emissions while retaining strong model performance.

title: CE-NAS: An End-to-End Carbon-Efficient Neural Architecture Search Framework

abstract: In safety-critical applications, machine learning models should generalize well under worst-case distribution shifts, that is, have a small robust risk. Invariance-based algorithms can provably take advantage of structural assumptions on the shifts when the training distributions are heterogeneous enough to identify the robust risk. However, in practice, such identifiability conditions are rarely satisfied – a scenario so far underexplored in the theoretical literature. In this paper, we aim to fill the gap and propose to study the more general setting of partially identifiable robustness. In particular, we define a new risk measure, the identifiable robust risk, and its corresponding (population) minimax quantity that is an algorithm-independent measure for the best achievable robustness under partial identifiability. We introduce these concepts broadly, and then study them within the framework of linear structural causal models for concreteness of the presentation. We use the introduced minimax quantity to show how previous approaches provably achieve suboptimal robustness in the partially identifiable case. We confirm our findings through empirical simulations and real-world experiments and demonstrate how the test error of existing robustness methods grows increasingly suboptimal as the proportion of previously unseen test directions increases.

paragraphs: Robust learning asks whether a model can perform well under unfavorable changes in its data distribution. Some methods use stable relationships across training environments to provide guarantees. Those guarantees can depend on having sufficiently varied environments to determine the relevant worst-case risk. This paper studies what robustness can mean when the available training distributions identify that risk only partially.

The authors introduce identifiable robust risk and a corresponding population minimax quantity. Together, these describe the best robustness achievable given the information available, independently of any particular learning algorithm. This changes the benchmark for evaluating methods: the comparison accounts for uncertainty that the training environments cannot resolve. The paper develops these concepts broadly and then examines them in linear structural causal models.

Using this benchmark, the authors prove that previous approaches can deliver suboptimal robustness under partial identifiability. Simulations and real-world experiments support the analysis. Existing methods become increasingly suboptimal as more test variation occurs in directions absent during training. The contribution is a framework for separating what robustness is achievable from what current methods actually achieve.
summary.tldr: The paper defines achievable robustness when training environments reveal only part of the worst-case risk and shows why existing methods can fall short.

title: Achievable distributional robustness when the robust risk is only partially identified

abstract: Unlike natural language processing and computer vision, the development of Foundation Models (FMs) for time series forecasting is blocked due to data scarcity. While recent efforts are focused on building such FMs by unlocking the potential of language models (LMs) for time series analysis, dedicated parameters for various downstream forecasting tasks need training, which hinders the common knowledge sharing across domains.Moreover, data owners may hesitate to share the access to local data due to privacy concerns and copyright protection, which makes it impossible to simply construct a FM on cross-domain training instances.To address these issues, we propose Time-FFM, a Federated Foundation Model for Time series forecasting by leveraging pretrained LMs.Specifically, we begin by transforming time series into the modality of text tokens.To bootstrap LMs for time series reasoning, we propose a prompt adaption module to determine domain-customized prompts dynamically instead of artificially.Given the data heterogeneity across domains, we design a personalized federated training strategy by learning global encoders and local prediction heads. Our comprehensive experiments indicate that Time-FFM outperforms state-of-the-arts and promises effective few-shot and zero-shot forecaster.The code is available at https://github.com/CityMind-Lab/NeurIPS24-Time-FFM/tree/main.

paragraphs: Building a broadly useful time-series forecasting model is difficult when data are scarce and distributed across owners who cannot readily share them. Separate task-specific parameters can also limit the knowledge shared between forecasting domains. Time-FFM addresses these issues by combining a pretrained language model with federated training, allowing domains to contribute to a shared forecasting approach.

The method transforms time series into a representation in the text-token modality. A prompt-adaptation module dynamically selects domain-customized prompts to support the language model's time-series reasoning. To accommodate differences between domains, training combines global encoders with local prediction heads. This structure shares representations while retaining domain-specific prediction components.

The experiments report performance above the compared state-of-the-art approaches and promising few-shot and zero-shot forecasting ability. These results suggest that the shared language-model foundation and domain adaptation can work together despite heterogeneous data. The contribution is a coordinated design for representation conversion, learned prompting, and personalized federated training, addressing both cross-domain knowledge sharing and the practical difficulty of centralizing time-series datasets.
summary.tldr: Time-FFM combines pretrained language models, adaptive prompts, and personalized federated training for cross-domain time-series forecasting.

title: Time-FFM: Towards LM-Empowered Federated Foundation Model for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: We study the density estimation problem defined as follows: given $k$ distributions $p_1, \ldots, p_k$ over a discrete domain $[n]$, as well as a collection of samples chosen from a "query" distribution $q$ over $[n]$, output $p_i$ that is "close" to $q$. Recently Aamand et al. gave the first and only known result that achieves sublinear bounds in both the sampling complexity and the query time while preserving polynomial data structure space. However, their improvement over linear samples and time is only by subpolynomial factors.Our main result is a lower bound showing that, for a broad class of data structures, their bounds cannot be significantly improved. In particular, if an algorithm uses $O(n/\log^c k)$ samples for some constant $c>0$ and polynomial space, then the query time of the data structure must be at least $k^{1-O(1)/\log \log k}$, i.e., close to linear in the number of distributions $k$. This is a novel statistical-computational trade-off for density estimation, demonstrating that any data structure must use close to a linear number of samples or take close to linear query time. The lower bound holds even in the realizable case where $q=p_i$ for some $i$, and when the distributions are flat (specifically, all distributions are uniform over half of the domain $[n]$). We also give a simple data structure for our lower bound instance with asymptotically matching upper bounds. Experiments show that the data structure is quite efficient in practice.

paragraphs: The paper studies selecting a distribution close to an unknown query distribution from a collection of k known distributions over n outcomes. A data structure must balance how many query samples it needs, how long selection takes, and how much information it stores.

For a broad class of polynomial-space data structures, using O(n/log^c(k)) samples forces query time at least k^(1-O(1)/log log(k)). This is close to linear in the number of candidates. The lower bound holds even when the query exactly equals a candidate and every candidate is uniform on half the domain.

The authors also construct a simple data structure matching the lower-bound instance asymptotically and show practical efficiency experimentally. The result limits the analyzed data-structure class; it should not be read as excluding every specialized method under additional assumptions about a particular distribution collection.
summary.tldr: Density-estimation data structures face a near-linear tradeoff between query samples and search time.

title: Statistical-Computational Trade-offs for Density Estimation

abstract: Concept-based learning, a promising approach in machine learning, emphasizes the value of high-level representations called concepts. However, despite growing interest in concept-bottleneck models (CBMs), there is a lack of clear understanding regarding the properties of concept sets and their impact on model performance. In this work, we define concepts within the machine learning context, highlighting their core properties: 'expressiveness' and 'model-aware inductive bias', and we make explicit the underlying assumption of CBMs. We establish theoretical results for concept-bottleneck models (CBMs), revealing how these properties guide the design of concept sets that optimize model performance. Specifically, we demonstrate that well-chosen concept sets can improve sample efficiency and out-of-distribution robustness in the appropriate regimes. Based on these insights, we propose a method to effectively identify informative and non-redundant concepts. We validate our approach with experiments on CIFAR-10 and MetaShift, showing that concept-bottleneck models outperform the foundational embedding counterpart, particularly in low-data regimes and under distribution shifts. We also examine failure modes and discuss how they can be tackled.

We also examine failure modes and discuss how they can be tackled.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through an intermediate set of high-level concepts. Their usefulness therefore depends on which concepts are available, yet the paper argues that the properties of a good concept set have not been clearly understood. It develops a theoretical account of concepts organized around expressiveness and model-aware inductive bias, while making the underlying assumption of these models explicit.

The theory connects these properties to predictive performance. In appropriate regimes, a well-designed concept set can reduce the amount of training data needed and improve robustness when the data distribution changes. These are conditional benefits of suitable concept choices, rather than a claim that introducing a concept bottleneck always improves a model.

The authors turn these insights into a method for selecting informative concepts that avoid redundancy. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and MetaShift show improvements over the foundational embedding counterpart, especially with little training data and under distribution shifts. The paper also examines failure modes, making concept selection itself a central part of designing effective models.
summary.tldr: A theory of concept-set design guides concept selection that can improve data efficiency and robustness in suitable regimes.

title: A theoretical design of concept sets: improving the predictability of concept bottleneck models

abstract: The adversarial robustness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has been questioned due to the false sense of security uncovered by strong adaptive attacks despite the existence of numerous defenses.In this work, we delve into the robustness analysis of representative robust GNNs and provide a unified robust estimation point of view tounderstand their robustness and limitations.Our novel analysis of estimation bias motivates the design of a robust and unbiased graph signal estimator. We then develop an efficient Quasi-Newton Iterative Reweighted Least Squares algorithm to solve the estimation problem, which is unfolded as robust unbiased aggregation layers in GNNs with theoretical guarantees.Our comprehensive experiments confirm the strong robustness of our proposed model under various scenarios, and the ablation study provides a deep understanding of its advantages.

paragraphs: Graph neural network defenses can appear secure until strong adaptive attacks expose weaknesses. This paper examines representative robust graph neural networks through a shared statistical lens: robust estimation. That perspective is used to explain both the robustness these methods achieve and the limitations that remain in their estimation behavior.

The analysis focuses on estimation bias and motivates a graph signal estimator designed to be both robust and unbiased. The authors develop an efficient algorithm combining Quasi-Newton optimization with iterative reweighted least squares to solve the estimation problem. They then unfold its computational steps into aggregation layers for graph neural networks.

This construction connects the network's aggregation operation directly to the proposed estimation procedure and comes with theoretical guarantees. Comprehensive experiments report strong robustness across multiple scenarios, while an ablation study investigates the sources of the method's advantages. The contribution is a linked analysis-and-design approach: diagnose bias in existing robust aggregation, formulate an estimator that addresses it, and translate the solver into a usable neural architecture.
summary.tldr: A robust, unbiased graph signal estimator becomes neural aggregation layers with theoretical guarantees and strong reported adversarial robustness.

title: Robust Graph Neural Networks via Unbiased Aggregation

abstract: The proliferation of abundant electricity time series (ETS) data presents numerous opportunities for various applications within power systems, including demand-side management, grid stability, and consumer behavior analysis. Deep learning models have advanced ETS modeling by effectively capturing sequence dependence. However, learning a generic representation of ETS data for various applications is challenging due to the inherently complex hierarchical structure of ETS data. Moreover, ETS data exhibits intricate temporal dependencies and is susceptible to the influence of exogenous variables. Furthermore, different instances exhibit diverse electricity consumption behavior. In this paper, we propose a foundation model PowerPM for ETS data, providing a large-scale, off-the-shelf model for power systems. PowerPM consists of a temporal encoder and a hierarchical encoder. The temporal encoder captures temporal dependencies within ETS data, taking into account exogenous variables. The hierarchical encoder models correlations between different levels of hierarchy. Furthermore, PowerPM leverages a novel self-supervised pre-training framework consisting of masked ETS modeling and dual-view contrastive learning. This framework enables PowerPM to capture temporal dependency within ETS windows and aware the discrepancy across ETS windows, providing two different perspectives to learn generic representation. Our experiments span five real-world scenario datasets, including both private and public data. Through pre-training on massive ETS data, PowerPM achieves SOTAperformance on diverse downstream tasks within the private dataset. Notably, when transferred to public datasets, PowerPM retains its edge, showcasing its remarkable generalization ability across various tasks and domains. Moreover, ablation studies and few-shot experiments further substantiate the effectiveness of our model.

The paper addresses that combination with a foundation model intended to provide an off-the-shelf starting point for downstream tasks.

Pretraining combines masked electricity-series modeling with dual-view contrastive learning. Together, these objectives address dependencies within individual time windows and differences across windows, giving the representation two complementary perspectives on electricity behavior.

Experiments span five real-world scenario datasets containing private and public data. After large-scale pretraining, PowerPM achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse downstream tasks in the private dataset and retains an advantage when transferred to public datasets. summary.tldr: PowerPM combines temporal and hierarchical encoders with self-supervised pretraining to learn transferable electricity time series representations.

title: PowerPM: Foundation Model for Power Systems

abstract: We propose a novel unsupervised method to learn pose and part-segmentation of articulated objects with rigid parts. Given two observations of an object in different articulation states, our method learns the geometry and appearance of object parts by using an implicit model from the first observation, distills the part segmentation and articulation from the second observation while rendering the latter observation. Additionally, to tackle the complexities in the joint optimization of part segmentation and articulation, we propose a voxel grid based initialization strategy and a decoupled optimization procedure. Compared to the prior unsupervised work, our model obtains significantly better performance, generalizes to objects with multiple parts while it can be efficiently from few views for the latter observation.

paragraphs: This paper learns the parts and poses of articulated objects from two observations showing different articulation states. Its setting assumes that the individual parts are rigid, while their arrangement can change. The goal is to recover both what those parts look like and how their movement explains the difference between observations, without supervised part annotations.

The method uses an implicit model from the first observation to learn object geometry and appearance. It then renders the second observation while extracting part segmentation and articulation. Rendering provides a connection between the proposed object decomposition and the observed images: the learned parts and their poses must account for the second state.

Learning segmentation and articulation together creates an optimization challenge. The authors address it with initialization based on a voxel grid and a procedure that separates the optimization. Relative to prior unsupervised work, they report significantly better performance, support for objects with multiple parts, and efficient learning when the second observation has few views. These findings make the two-state formulation useful for recovering movable structure from limited visual evidence.
summary.tldr: The method learns rigid object parts and their articulation without supervision by explaining two observed states through view synthesis.

title: Articulate your NeRF: Unsupervised articulated object modeling via conditional view synthesis

abstract: Urban knowledge graph has recently worked as an emerging building block to distill critical knowledge from multi-sourced urban data for diverse urban application scenarios. Despite its promising benefits, urban knowledge graph construction (UrbanKGC) still heavily relies on manual effort, hindering its potential advancement. This paper presents UrbanKGent, a unified large language model agent framework, for urban knowledge graph construction. Specifically, we first construct the knowledgeable instruction set for UrbanKGC tasks (such as relational triplet extraction and knowledge graph completion) via heterogeneity-aware and geospatial-infused instruction generation. Moreover, we propose a tool-augmented iterative trajectory refinement module to enhance and refine the trajectories distilled from GPT-4. Through hybrid instruction fine-tuning with augmented trajectories on Llama 2 and Llama 3 family, we obtain UrbanKGC agent family, consisting of UrbanKGent-7/8/13B version. We perform a comprehensive evaluation on two real-world datasets using both human and GPT-4 self-evaluation. The experimental results demonstrate that UrbanKGent family can not only significantly outperform 31 baselines in UrbanKGC tasks, but also surpass the state-of-the-art LLM, GPT-4, by more than 10% with approximately 20 times lower cost. Compared with the existing benchmark, the UrbanKGent family could help construct an UrbanKG with hundreds of times richer relationships using only one-fifth of the data. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/UrbanKGent.

UrbanKGent develops language-model agents for tasks such as extracting relational triplets and completing missing graph knowledge. Its training instructions explicitly account for heterogeneous data and geospatial information relevant to urban settings.

The framework refines action trajectories distilled from GPT-4 through an iterative, tool-augmented module. It then combines these augmented trajectories with instructions to fine-tune models from the Llama 2 and Llama 3 families. The resulting agent family includes versions with 7, 8, and 13 billion parameters.

Evaluation on two real-world datasets uses both human assessment and GPT-4 self-evaluation. The authors report outperforming 31 baselines and exceeding GPT-4 by more than 10% at approximately twenty times lower cost. They also report potential to construct graphs with hundreds of times richer relationships using one-fifth of the existing benchmark's data. These findings support specialized instruction and trajectory training for more efficient urban graph construction.
summary.tldr: UrbanKGent trains specialized language-model agents with urban instructions and refined tool-use trajectories to improve knowledge-graph construction.

title: UrbanKGent: A Unified Large Language Model Agent Framework for Urban Knowledge Graph Construction

abstract: The application of reinforcement learning in traffic signal control (TSC) has been extensively researched and yielded notable achievements. However, most existing works for TSC assume that traffic data from all surrounding intersections is fully and continuously available through sensors. In real-world applications, this assumption often fails due to sensor malfunctions or data loss, making TSC with missing data a critical challenge. To meet the needs of practical applications, we introduce DiffLight, a novel conditional diffusion model for TSC under data-missing scenarios in the offline setting. Specifically, we integrate two essential sub-tasks, i.e., traffic data imputation and decision-making, by leveraging a Partial Rewards Conditioned Diffusion (PRCD) model to prevent missing rewards from interfering with the learning process. Meanwhile, to effectively capture the spatial-temporal dependencies among intersections, we design a Spatial-Temporal transFormer (STFormer) architecture. In addition, we propose a Diffusion Communication Mechanism (DCM) to promote better communication and control performance under data-missing scenarios. Extensive experiments on five datasets with various data-missing scenarios demonstrate that DiffLight is an effective controller to address TSC with missing data. The code of DiffLight is released at https://github.com/lokol5579/DiffLight-release.

paragraphs: Traffic-signal controllers often assume continuous access to sensor data from surrounding intersections. Sensor failures and lost data can break that assumption, leaving the controller with incomplete information. DiffLight studies this problem in an offline setting and uses a conditional diffusion model to connect filling in missing traffic data with choosing control actions.

Its Partial Rewards Conditioned Diffusion model combines data imputation and decision-making while preventing missing rewards from interfering with learning. A Spatial-Temporal Transformer captures relationships between intersections and their evolution over time. A separate Diffusion Communication Mechanism supports communication and control when parts of the traffic information are unavailable.

Experiments on five datasets, covering multiple missing-data scenarios, demonstrate that DiffLight can effectively control traffic signals under these conditions. The approach matters because missing observations affect both the description of traffic and the decisions made from it. By treating reconstruction and control as connected tasks, the framework addresses that dependence within a single modeling approach.
summary.tldr: DiffLight combines missing-data reconstruction and traffic-signal decisions in a diffusion model conditioned on partially available rewards.

title: DiffLight: A Partial Rewards Conditioned Diffusion Model for Traffic Signal Control with Missing Data

abstract: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) object detection has gained significant attention recently due to its irreplaceable all-weather imaging capabilities. However, this research field suffers from both limited public datasets (mostly comprising <2K images with only mono-category objects) and inaccessible source code. To tackle these challenges, we establish a new benchmark dataset and an open-source method for large-scale SAR object detection. Our dataset, SARDet-100K, is a result of intense surveying, collecting, and standardizing 10 existing SAR detection datasets, providing a large-scale and diverse dataset for research purposes. To the best of our knowledge, SARDet-100K is the first COCO-level large-scale multi-class SAR object detection dataset ever created. With this high-quality dataset, we conducted comprehensive experiments and uncovered a crucial challenge in SAR object detection: the substantial disparities between the pretraining on RGB datasets and finetuning on SAR datasets in terms of both data domain and model structure. To bridge these gaps, we propose a novel Multi-Stage with Filter Augmentation (MSFA) pretraining framework that tackles the problems from the perspective of data input, domain transition, and model migration. The proposed MSFA method significantly enhances the performance of SAR object detection models while demonstrating exceptional generalizability and flexibility across diverse models. This work aims to pave the way for further advancements in SAR object detection. The dataset and code is available at \url{https://github.com/zcablii/SARDet_100K}.

Releasing both data and code also makes the proposed research setup accessible to other researchers.
summary.tldr: SARDet-100K standardizes ten radar detection datasets and introduces a pretraining framework that improves transfer from RGB images to SAR detection.

title: SARDet-100K: Towards Open-Source Benchmark and ToolKit for Large-Scale SAR Object Detection

abstract: Prophet inequality concerns a basic optimal stopping problem and states that simple threshold stopping policies --- i.e., accepting the first reward larger than a certain threshold --- can achieve tight $\frac{1}{2}$-approximation to the optimal prophet value. Motivated by its economic applications, this paper studies the robustness of this approximation to natural strategic manipulations in which each random reward is associated with a self-interested player who may selectively reveal his realized reward to the searcher in order to maximize his probability of being selected. We say a threshold policy is $\alpha$(-strategically)-robust if it (a) achieves the $\alpha$-approximation to the prophet value for strategic players; and (b) meanwhile remains a $\frac{1}{2}$-approximation in the standard non-strategic setting.Starting with a characterization of each player's optimal information revealing strategy, we demonstrate the intrinsic robustness of prophet inequalities to strategic reward signaling through the following results:(1) for arbitrary reward distributions, there is a threshold policy that is $\frac{1-\frac{1}{e}}{2}$-robust, and this ratio is tight;(2) for i.i.d. reward distributions, there is a threshold policy that is $\frac{1}{2}$-robust, which is tight for the setting; and (3) for log-concave (but non-identical) reward distributions, the $\frac{1}{2}$-robustness can also be achieved under certain regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: The prophet inequality studies when to accept a reward encountered in sequence. In the standard setting, a suitable threshold policy guarantees half the value available to an ideal prophet. This paper asks how much of that guarantee survives when each reward belongs to a player who selectively reveals information to improve their chance of selection.

The authors first characterize each player's optimal disclosure strategy. They define strategic robustness to require two guarantees: an approximation under strategic behavior and preservation of the usual one-half approximation when players are non-strategic. This definition evaluates protection against manipulation without giving up the standard guarantee in its absence.

For arbitrary reward distributions, they establish a tight robustness ratio of (1 − 1/e)/2. For independent, identically distributed rewards, a tight one-half robustness guarantee is achievable. One-half robustness is also achievable for non-identical log-concave distributions under certain regularity assumptions. Thus, the amount of protection available depends on distributional structure, with the final result explicitly conditional on those assumptions.
summary.tldr: Threshold stopping policies retain provable approximation guarantees under strategic reward disclosure, with stronger guarantees for specified distribution classes.

title: Intrinsic Robustness of Prophet Inequality to Strategic Reward Signaling

abstract: While existing query-based 3D end-to-end visual trackers integrate detection and tracking via the *tracking-by-attention* paradigm, these two chicken-and-egg tasks encounter optimization difficulties when sharing the same parameters. Our findings reveal that these difficulties arise due to two inherent constraints on the self-attention mechanism, i.e., over-deduplication for object queries and self-centric attention for track queries. In contrast, removing self-attention mechanism not only minimally impacts regression predictions of the tracker, but also tends to generate more latent candidate boxes. Based on these analyses, we present SynCL, a novel plug-and-play synergistic training strategy designed to co-facilitate multi-task learning for detection and tracking. Specifically, we propose a Task-specific Hybrid Matching module for a weight-shared cross-attention-based decoder that matches the targets of track queries with multiple object queries to exploit promising candidates overlooked by the self-attention mechanism and the bipartite matching. To flexibly select optimal candidates for the one-to-many matching, we also design a Dynamic Query Filtering module controlled by model training status. Moreover, we introduce Instance-aware Contrastive Learning to break through the barrier of self-centric attention for track queries, effectively bridging the gap between detection and tracking. Without additional inference costs, SynCL consistently delivers improvements in various benchmarks and achieves state-of-the-art performance with $58.9\%$ AMOTA on the nuScenes dataset. Code and raw results are available at .

paragraphs: Multi-camera 3D trackers must both detect objects and maintain their identities over time. Sharing parameters between these tasks can create optimization difficulties. The authors trace problems to self-attention that removes too many object-query candidates and keeps track queries overly focused on themselves. They find that removing self-attention barely affects regression predictions and tends to expose more candidate boxes.

SynCL builds on this analysis with a shared cross-attention decoder and task-specific hybrid matching. Track targets can match multiple object queries, allowing training to use promising candidates that self-attention and one-to-one matching might overlook. A dynamic filtering module adjusts candidate selection according to training status. Instance-aware contrastive learning further connects detection and tracking representations.

These changes form a plug-and-play training strategy without additional inference cost. SynCL consistently improves results across the evaluated benchmarks and reaches a reported state-of-the-art 58.9% AMOTA on nuScenes. The findings suggest that coordinating candidate matching and representation learning during training can improve the cooperation between detection and tracking within a shared model.
summary.tldr: SynCL improves joint 3D detection and tracking through adaptive candidate matching and instance-aware contrastive training without extra inference cost.

title: SynCL: A Synergistic Training Strategy with Instance-Aware Contrastive Learning for End-to-End Multi-Camera 3D Tracking

abstract: Textual claims are often accompanied by images to enhance their credibility and spread on social media, but this also raises concerns about the spread of misinformation.Existing datasets for automated verification of image-text claims remain limited, as they often consist of synthetic claims and lack evidence annotations to capture the reasoning behind the verdict.In this work, we introduce AVerImaTeC, a dataset consisting of 1,297 real-world image-text claims. Each claim is annotated with question-answer (QA) pairs containing evidence from the web, reflecting a decomposed reasoning regarding the verdict.We mitigate common challenges in fact-checking datasets such as contextual dependence, temporal leakage, and evidence insufficiency, via claim normalization, temporally constrained evidence annotation, and a two-stage sufficiency check. We assess the consistency of the annotation in AVerImaTeC via inter-annotator studies, achieving a $\kappa=0.742$ on verdicts and $74.7\%$ consistency on QA pairs. We also propose a novel evaluation method for evidence retrieval and conduct extensive experiments to establish baselines for verifying image-text claims using open-web evidence.

paragraphs: AVerImaTeC addresses fact-checking claims that combine text and images. Such combinations can make information appear more credible, so verification needs to examine the evidence supporting the overall claim. The authors identify two weaknesses in existing datasets: reliance on synthetic claims and limited annotation of the reasoning behind a verdict.

Their dataset contains 1,297 real-world image-text claims. Each is accompanied by question-answer pairs grounded in web evidence, breaking the verification process into smaller questions. The construction process normalizes claims to reduce dependence on surrounding context, constrains evidence temporally to mitigate leakage, and checks evidence sufficiency in two stages. These choices make the evidence trail a central part of the dataset.

Annotation studies report a verdict agreement score of κ = 0.742 and 74.7% consistency for question-answer pairs. The authors also introduce an evaluation method for evidence retrieval and establish verification baselines using open-web evidence. Together, these contributions support evaluating both the final judgment and the evidence gathered to justify it.
summary.tldr: AVerImaTeC pairs real image-text claims with structured web evidence to evaluate evidence-based automated fact-checking.

title: AVerImaTeC: A Dataset for Automatic Verification of Image-Text Claims with Evidence from the Web

abstract: The distribution of data changes over time; models operating in dynamic environments need retraining. But knowing when to retrain, without access to labels, is an open challenge since some, but not all shifts degrade model performance. This paper formalizes and addresses the problem of post-deployment deterioration (PDD) monitoring. We propose D3M, a practical and efficient monitoring algorithm based on the disagreement of predictive models, achieving low false positive rates under non-deteriorating shifts and provides sample complexity bounds for high true positive rates under deteriorating shifts. Empirical results on both standard benchmark and a real-world large-scale internal medicine dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework and highlight its viability as an alert mechanism for high-stakes machine learning pipelines.

But knowing when to retrain, without access to labels, is an open challenge since some, but not all shifts degrade model performance. This paper formalizes and addresses the problem of post-deployment deterioration (PDD) monitoring. We propose D3M, a practical and efficient monitoring algorithm based on the disagreement of predictive models, achieving low false positive rates under non-deteriorating shifts and provides sample complexity bounds for high true positive rates under deteriorating shifts. Empirical results on both standard benchmark and a real-world large-scale internal medicine dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework and highlight its viability as an alert mechanism for high-stakes machine learning pipelines.

paragraphs: A deployed model may encounter changing data without having access to new outcome labels. Detecting a shift alone does not establish that performance has worsened, because some changes are harmless. This paper formalizes post-deployment deterioration monitoring: identifying changes that damage predictive performance so that retraining alerts are more meaningful.

The proposed D3M algorithm uses disagreement among predictive models as its monitoring signal. The framework achieves low false positive rates for shifts that do not cause deterioration and provides sample complexity bounds for obtaining high true positive rates when deterioration occurs. These bounds address how much evidence is needed for effective detection.

Experiments on standard benchmarks and a large-scale internal medicine dataset demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The stated practical role is an alert mechanism for machine learning pipelines, including high-stakes applications. Its contribution is to focus unlabeled monitoring on performance deterioration rather than treating every distribution change as equally concerning. This connects the monitoring signal more closely to the operational question of when a deployed model may need attention.
summary.tldr: D3M uses predictive disagreement to detect deployment deterioration without labels while limiting alarms for harmless distribution shifts.

title: Reliably detecting model failures in deployment without labels

abstract: Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) are commonly considered *interpretable* within the ML community, as their structure makes the relationship between inputs and outputs relatively understandable. Therefore, it may seem natural to hypothesize that obtaining meaningful explanations for GAMs could be performed efficiently and would not be computationally infeasible. In this work, we challenge this hypothesis by analyzing the *computational complexity* of generating different explanations for various forms of GAMs across multiple contexts. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly diverse landscape of both positive and negative complexity outcomes. Particularly, under standard complexity assumptions such as P$\neq$NP, we establish several key findings: (1) in stark contrast to many other common ML models, the complexity of generating explanations for GAMs is heavily influenced by the structure of the input space; (2) the complexity of explaining GAMs varies significantly with the types of component models used - but interestingly, these differences only emerge under specific input domain settings; (3) significant complexity distinctions appear for obtaining explanations in regression tasks versus classification tasks in GAMs; and (4) expressing complex models like neural networks additively (e.g., as neural additive models) can make them easier to explain, though interestingly, this benefit appears only for certain explanation methods and input domains. Collectively, these results shed light on the feasibility of computing diverse explanations for GAMs, offering a rigorous theoretical picture of the conditions under which such computations are possible or provably hard.

paragraphs: Generalized additive models combine component contributions in a structure that is often considered understandable. That reputation raises a separate computational question: can meaningful explanations always be obtained efficiently? This paper investigates the computational difficulty of producing different explanations for several forms of additive models, rather than treating structural interpretability as an assurance of easy explanation.

The analysis finds that the answer depends strongly on the allowed input space. Component model choices also matter, but their effects emerge only in particular input domains. Regression and classification introduce further differences. Together, these findings show why an explanation method that is feasible in one additive-model setting may become computationally difficult in another.

Under standard complexity assumptions, including P not equaling NP, the paper establishes both tractable and hard cases. It also finds that expressing complex models such as neural networks additively can simplify explanation, but only for certain explanation methods and domains. The contribution is a conditional map of feasibility: understanding the model's structure is only part of determining whether a requested explanation can be computed efficiently.
summary.tldr: Explaining additive models can be computationally easy or hard depending on the input domain, component models, task, and explanation method.

title: Additive Models Explained: A Computational Complexity Approach

abstract: Differentiable vector graphics (VGs) are widely used in image vectorization and vector synthesis, while existing representations are costly to optimize and struggle to achieve high-quality rendering results for high-resolution images. This work introduces a new differentiable VG representation, dubbed Bézier Splatting, that enables fast yet high-fidelity VG rasterization. Bézier Splatting samples 2D Gaussians along Bézier curves, which naturally provide positional gradients at object boundaries. Thanks to the efficient splatting-based differentiable rasterizer, Bézier Splatting achieves 30× and 150× faster per forward and backward rasterization step for open curves compared to DiffVG. Additionally, we introduce an adaptive pruning and densification strategy that dynamically adjusts the spatial distribution of curves to escape local minima, further improving VG quality. Furthermore, our new VG representation supports conversion to standard XML-based SVG format, enhancing interoperability with existing VG tools and pipelines. Experimental results show that Bézier Splatting significantly outperforms existing methods with better visual fidelity and significant optimization speedup.

paragraphs: Differentiable vector graphics allow a system to adjust curves using feedback from a rendered image. Existing representations can be expensive to optimize, particularly when seeking detailed results at high resolution. Bézier Splatting introduces a representation intended to make both rendering and the computation of optimization gradients faster while preserving visual quality.

The method places two-dimensional Gaussians along Bézier curves and renders them through splatting. These Gaussian samples naturally provide positional gradients at object boundaries, helping optimization determine how curve positions should change. An adaptive pruning and densification procedure also changes the spatial distribution of curves to help escape local minima and improve the resulting graphics.

For open curves, the authors report forward rasterization steps that are 30 times faster and backward steps that are 150 times faster than DiffVG. Experiments also show improved visual fidelity and optimization speed. Conversion to standard SVG connects the representation to existing vector graphics tools, making the proposed rendering approach useful beyond its own optimization pipeline.
summary.tldr: Bézier Splatting renders Gaussian samples along curves to accelerate differentiable vector graphics optimization while improving visual fidelity.

title: Bézier Splatting for Fast and Differentiable Vector Graphics Rendering

abstract: Current 3D scene understanding methods are limited by offline-collected multi-view data or pre-constructed 3D geometry. In this paper, we present ExtractAnything3D (EA3D), a unified online framework for open-world 3D object extraction that enables simultaneous geometric reconstruction and holistic scene understanding. Given a streaming video, EA3D dynamically interprets each frame using vision-language and 2D vision foundation encoders to extract object-level knowledge. This knowledge is integrated and embedded into a Gaussian feature map via a feed-forward online update strategy. We then iteratively estimate visual odometry from historical frames and incrementally update online Gaussian features with new observations. A recurrent joint optimization module directs the model's attention to regions of interest, simultaneously enhancing both geometric reconstruction and semantic understanding. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and tasks, including photo-realistic rendering, semantic and instance segmentation, 3D bounding box and semantic occupancy estimation, and 3D mesh generation, demonstrate the effectiveness of EA3D. Our method establishes a unified and efficient framework for joint online 3D reconstruction and holistic scene understanding, enabling a broad range of downstream tasks. The project webpage is available at \url{https://github.com/VDIGPKU/EA3D}.

paragraphs: EA3D builds a geometric and semantic understanding of a scene as video frames arrive. This addresses a restriction of approaches that depend on previously collected views or an already constructed 3D representation. The framework combines object extraction with reconstruction, so information about what objects are and how they occupy space develops within the same online process.

For each frame, vision-language and 2D vision encoders extract object-level information. EA3D incorporates this information into a Gaussian feature map through feed-forward updates. It also estimates camera motion from historical frames and adds new observations incrementally. A recurrent joint optimization module focuses on regions of interest while improving geometry and semantic understanding together.

Experiments cover photorealistic rendering, semantic and instance segmentation, 3D bounding boxes, semantic occupancy estimation, and mesh generation. The reported effectiveness across these tasks supports the value of a shared representation for several scene-understanding outputs. The central contribution is a unified, efficient online framework in which streaming observations continuously refine both the reconstructed scene and its object-level interpretation.
summary.tldr: EA3D incrementally combines streaming video observations into a shared representation for 3D reconstruction and object-level scene understanding.

title: EA3D: Online Open-World 3D Object Extraction from Streaming Videos

abstract: Recent rehearsal-free continual learning (CL) methods guided by prompts achieve strong performance on vision tasks with non-stationary data but remain resource-intensive, hindering real-world deployment. We introduce resource-efficient prompting (REP), which improves the computational and memory efficiency of prompt-based rehearsal-free methods while minimizing accuracy trade-offs. Our approach employs swift prompt selection to refine input data using a carefully provisioned model and introduces adaptive token merging AToM and adaptive layer dropping ALD for efficient prompt updates. AToM and ALD selectively skip data and model layers while preserving task-specific features during the learning of new tasks. Extensive experiments on multiple image classification datasets demonstrate REP’s superior resource efficiency over state-of-the-art rehearsal-free CL methods.

paragraphs: REP targets the resource cost of prompt-based continual learning for vision. These methods learn from changing data without rehearsing earlier examples, but strong predictive performance can still come with substantial computation and memory requirements. The paper aims to reduce those requirements while keeping accuracy trade-offs small.

The framework combines swift prompt selection with adaptive token merging and adaptive layer dropping. Prompt selection refines input data using a carefully provisioned model. During prompt updates, token merging reduces the data processed, while layer dropping selectively skips model layers. These adaptive mechanisms seek to retain features relevant to the current task as new tasks are learned.

Experiments across multiple image classification datasets show better resource efficiency than state-of-the-art rehearsal-free continual learning methods. The contribution addresses more than the size of the learned prompts: it also changes how much data and model computation each update uses. The reported findings support selective processing as a practical way to reduce the cost of adapting vision models to changing tasks.
summary.tldr: REP reduces the resource demands of rehearsal-free continual learning through efficient prompt selection, adaptive token merging, and layer dropping.

title: REP: Resource-Efficient Prompting for Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning

abstract: 3D Semantic Scene Graph Prediction aims to detect objects and their semantic relationships in 3D scenes, and has emerged as a crucial technology for robotics and AR/VR applications. While previous research has addressed dataset limitations and explored various approaches including Open-Vocabulary settings, they frequently fail to optimize the representational capacity of object and relationship features, showing excessive reliance on Graph Neural Networks despite insufficient discriminative capability. In this work, we demonstrate through extensive analysis that the quality of object features plays a critical role in determining overall scene graph accuracy. To address this challenge, we design a highly discriminative object feature encoder and employ a contrastive pretraining strategy that decouples object representation learning from the scene graph prediction. This design not only enhances object classification accuracy but also yields direct improvements in relationship prediction. Notably, when plugging in our pretrained encoder into existing frameworks, we observe substantial performance improvements across all evaluation metrics. Additionally, whereas existing approaches have not fully exploited the integration of relationship information, we effectively combine both geometric and semantic features to achieve superior relationship prediction. Comprehensive experiments on the 3DSSG dataset demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/VisualScienceLab-KHU/OCRL-3DSSG-Codes.

paragraphs: A 3D semantic scene graph represents both the objects in a scene and the relationships between them. This paper investigates the quality of the object features feeding that prediction process. Its analysis finds that these features strongly influence overall accuracy, highlighting a weakness in approaches that rely heavily on graph neural networks despite insufficiently discriminative inputs.

The authors develop an object encoder and pretrain it contrastively, separating object representation learning from scene graph prediction. The goal is to make object features more informative before they enter the larger prediction system. They find that this improves object classification and directly benefits relationship prediction. Inserting the pretrained encoder into existing frameworks improves all evaluated metrics.

The method additionally combines geometric and semantic information when predicting relationships, making fuller use of both kinds of evidence. Experiments on the 3DSSG dataset report significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods. The results connect stronger object representations to better scene-level understanding and show that improving an input component can benefit existing prediction frameworks.
summary.tldr: Contrastively pretrained object features improve both object and relationship prediction in 3D scene graphs, including when inserted into existing frameworks.

title: Object-Centric Representation Learning for Enhanced 3D Semantic Scene Graph Prediction

abstract: World models have recently gained prominence for action-conditioned visual prediction in complex environments. However, relying on only a few recent observations causes them to lose long-term context. Consequently, within a few steps, the generated scenes drift from what was previously observed, undermining temporal coherence. This limitation, common in state-of-the-art world models, which are diffusion-based, stems from the lack of a lasting environment state. To address this problem, we introduce StateSpaceDiffuser, where a diffusion model is enabled to perform long-context tasks by integrating features from a state-space model, representing the entire interaction history. This design restores long-term memory while preserving the high-fidelity synthesis of diffusion models. To rigorously measure temporal consistency, we develop an evaluation protocol that probes a model’s ability to reinstantiate seen content in extended rollouts. Comprehensive experiments show that StateSpaceDiffuser significantly outperforms a strong diffusion-only baseline, maintaining a coherent visual context for an order of magnitude more steps. It delivers consistent views in both a 2D maze navigation and a complex 3D environment. These results establish that bringing state-space representations into diffusion models is highly effective in demonstrating both visual details and long-term memory. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/StateSpaceDiffuser/

paragraphs: A visual world model predicts what an environment will look like as actions are taken. Diffusion-based world models can synthesize detailed images, but using only a few recent observations leaves them without lasting context. Generated scenes can then drift away from previously observed content, weakening consistency over an extended interaction.

StateSpaceDiffuser adds features from a state-space model that represents the full interaction history. The diffusion model uses these features to retain long-term context while preserving detailed image synthesis. The authors also introduce an evaluation protocol that asks whether a model can recreate previously seen content during long rollouts, directly testing the memory problem the architecture targets.

Experiments compare the method with a strong diffusion-only baseline in a two-dimensional navigation maze and a complex three-dimensional environment. StateSpaceDiffuser maintains coherent visual context for an order of magnitude more steps and produces consistent views in both settings. The finding supports combining persistent state representations with diffusion generation: visual quality and memory can be addressed together, rather than expecting recent observations alone to preserve an environment's history.
summary.tldr: StateSpaceDiffuser adds state-space memory to diffusion world models, maintaining coherent visual context for an order of magnitude more steps than a strong baseline.

title: StateSpaceDiffuser: Bringing Long Context to Diffusion World Models

abstract: Proprietary large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong generalization capabilities across diverse tasks and are increasingly deployed on edge devices for efficiency and privacy reasons. However, deploying proprietary LLMs at the edge without adequate protection introduces critical security threats. Attackers can extract model weights and architectures, enabling unauthorized copying and misuse. Even when protective measures prevent full extraction of model weights, attackers may still perform advanced attacks, such as fine-tuning, to further exploit the model. Existing defenses against these threats typically incur significant computational and communication overhead, making them impractical for edge deployment. To safeguard the edge-deployed LLMs, we introduce CoreGuard, a computation- and communication-efficient protection method. CoreGuard employs an efficient protection protocol to reduce computational overhead and minimize communication overhead via a propagation protocol. Extensive experiments show that CoreGuard achieves upper-bound security protection with negligible overhead.

paragraphs: Deploying proprietary language models on edge devices brings their capabilities closer to users, supporting efficiency and privacy. It also creates opportunities for attackers to extract model weights and architecture, enabling unauthorized copies. The paper further considers exploitation through techniques such as fine-tuning, even when a defense prevents complete extraction of the weights.

CoreGuard targets the cost of protecting these deployments. Existing defenses can require substantial computation and communication, undermining their practicality on edge devices. The proposed method combines a protection protocol designed to reduce computational overhead with a propagation protocol designed to minimize communication overhead. Both costs are part of the protection problem because an expensive defense can weaken the motivation for deploying locally.

The authors report extensive experiments in which CoreGuard achieves what they describe as upper-bound security protection with negligible overhead. This is the stated experimental finding, rather than an unrestricted promise against every attack. The contribution is a protection approach intended to preserve foundational model capabilities while keeping the computational and communication burden small enough for edge deployment.
summary.tldr: CoreGuard protects edge-deployed language models against stealing and exploitation while reporting negligible computational and communication overhead.

title: CoreGuard: Safeguarding Foundational Capabilities of LLMs Against Model Stealing in Edge Deployment

abstract: Modern language‑model deployments must often balance competing objectives—for example, helpfulness versus harmlessness, cost versus accuracy, and reward versus safety. We introduce Conformal Arbitrage, a post‑hoc framework that learns a data‑driven threshold to mediate between a Primary model optimized for a primary objective and a more conservative Guardian—which could be another model or a human domain expert—aligned with a guardrail objective. The threshold is calibrated with conformal risk control, yielding finite‑sample, distribution‑free guarantees that the long‑run frequency of undesirable events (such as factual errors or safety violations) does not exceed a user‑specified quota. Because Conformal Arbitrage operates wholly at the API level—without requiring access to model logits or updating model weights—it complements weight‑based alignment techniques and integrates seamlessly with existing cost‑aware cascades. Empirically, Conformal Arbitrage traces an efficient frontier, allowing users to define an acceptable performance level for one objective while maximizing utility in another. We observe that our method outperforms (in terms of accuracy) cost-matched random routing between models. These properties make Conformal Arbitrage a practical, theoretically grounded tool for trustworthy and economical deployment of large language models across a broad range of potentially competing objectives.

paragraphs: Language-model deployments often need to balance goals that pull in different directions, such as accuracy and cost or helpfulness and safety. Conformal Arbitrage manages this trade-off between a Primary model serving the main objective and a more conservative Guardian serving a guardrail objective. The Guardian can be another model or a human expert.

The framework learns a threshold from data and calibrates it using conformal risk control. The stated guarantee is finite-sample and distribution-free: the long-run frequency of undesirable events stays within a user-specified quota. Their method also achieves higher accuracy than random routing with matched costs. These findings support calibrated routing as a practical addition to existing model cascades and weight-based alignment methods when deployments must manage competing objectives.
summary.tldr: Conformal Arbitrage calibrates routing between a Primary model and a Guardian to balance utility against a specified undesirable-event quota.

title: Conformal Arbitrage: Risk-Controlled Balancing of Competing Objectives in Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in multimodal models have raised questions about whether vision-and-language models (VLMs) integrate cross-modal information in ways that reflect human cognition. One well-studied test case in this domain is the bouba-kiki effect, where humans reliably associate pseudowords like ‘bouba’ with round shapes and ‘kiki’ with jagged ones. Given the mixed evidence found in prior studies for this effect in VLMs, we present a comprehensive re-evaluation focused on two variants of CLIP, ResNet and Vision Transformer (ViT), given their centrality in many state-of-the-art VLMs. We apply two complementary methods closely modelled after human experiments: a prompt-based evaluation that uses probabilities as a measure of model preference, and we use Grad-CAM as a novel approach to interpret visual attention in shape-word matching tasks. Our findings show that these model variants do not consistently exhibit the bouba-kiki effect. While ResNet shows a preference for round shapes, overall performance across both model variants lacks the expected associations. Moreover, direct comparison with prior human data on the same task shows that the models’ responses fall markedly short of the robust, modality-integrated behaviour characteristic of human cognition. These results contribute to the ongoing debate about the extent to which VLMs truly understand cross-modal concepts, highlighting limitations in their internal representations and alignment with human intuitions.
