paragraphs: People commonly associate the invented word bouba with rounded shapes and kiki with jagged shapes. This provides a concrete test of associations between language and vision. The paper revisits whether vision-and-language models show this pattern, focusing on two CLIP variants with different visual architectures: ResNet and Vision Transformer.

The researchers use two complementary evaluations modeled closely on human experiments. A prompt-based test measures model preferences through probabilities. Together, the methods examine both the models' choices and the image regions involved in those choices, allowing more than a single overall preference measurement.

Comparisons with existing human results on the same task show markedly weaker associations in the models. The findings identify a specific gap between these CLIP variants and human cross-modal behavior, informing questions about how their internal representations connect visual and linguistic information.
summary.tldr: Tests of two CLIP variants find that their shape-word associations do not consistently reproduce the human bouba-kiki effect.

title: Cross-modal Associations in Vision and Language Models: Revisiting the Bouba-Kiki Effect

abstract: We introduce IntrinsiX, a novel method that generates high-quality intrinsic images from text description. In contrast to existing text-to-image models whose outputs contain baked-in scene lighting, our approach predicts physically-based rendering (PBR) maps. This enables the generated outputs to be used for content creation scenarios in core graphics applications that facilitate re-lighting, editing, and texture generation tasks. In order to train our generator, we exploit strong image priors, and pre-train separate models for each PBR material component (albedo, roughness, metallic, normals). We then align these models with a new cross-intrinsic attention formulation that concatenates key and value features in a consistent fashion. This allows us to exchange information between each output modality and to obtain semantically coherent PBR predictions. To ground each intrinsic component, we propose a rendering loss which provides image-space signals to constrain the model, thus facilitating sharp details also in the output BRDF properties. Our results demonstrate detailed intrinsic generation with strong generalization capabilities that outperforms existing intrinsic image decomposition methods used with generated images by a significant margin. Finally, we show a series of applications, including re-lighting, editing, and for the first time text-conditioned room-scale PBR texture generation. We will release the code and the pre-trained model weights.

We then align these models with a new cross-intrinsic attention formulation that concatenates key and value features in a consistent fashion. To ground each intrinsic component, we propose a rendering loss which provides image-space signals to constrain the model, thus facilitating sharp details also in the output BRDF properties. Our results demonstrate detailed intrinsic generation with strong generalization capabilities that outperforms existing intrinsic image decomposition methods used with generated images by a significant margin. Finally, we show a series of applications, including re-lighting, editing, and for the first time text-conditioned room-scale PBR texture generation. We will release the code and the pre-trained model weights.

paragraphs: IntrinsiX generates material-property maps from text descriptions, producing assets that graphics applications can relight and edit. Ordinary generated images already contain a particular scene's lighting. By predicting physically based rendering maps instead, the method supplies separate information about surface color, roughness, metallic properties, and normals that a renderer can use under different lighting.

The system starts with separately pretrained models for each material component, drawing on strong image priors. A cross-intrinsic attention mechanism then connects their key and value features so the components exchange information and describe a coherent scene. A rendering loss adds constraints in image space, helping ground the individual maps and preserve fine detail in the predicted surface-reflection properties.

The authors report detailed outputs, strong generalization, and a significant advantage over decomposing generated images into intrinsic components using existing methods. They demonstrate relighting, editing, and text-conditioned room-scale PBR texture generation. The approach matters because it directly generates coordinated rendering inputs, making the text-driven outputs usable for graphics workflows that need control over materials and illumination.
summary.tldr: IntrinsiX turns text into coordinated material maps for detailed, editable, and relightable graphics assets.

title: IntrinsiX: High-Quality PBR Generation using Image Priors

abstract: We present Perceive Anything Model (PAM), a conceptually straightforward and efficient framework for comprehensive region-level visual understanding in images and videos. Our approach extends the powerful segmentation model SAM 2 by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs), enabling simultaneous object segmentation with the generation of diverse, region-specific semantic outputs, including categories, label definition, functional explanations, and detailed captions. A key component, Semantic Perceiver, is introduced to efficiently transform SAM 2's rich visual features, which inherently carry general vision, localization, and semantic priors into multi-modal tokens for LLM comprehension. To support robust multi-granularity understanding, we also develop a dedicated data refinement and augmentation pipeline, yielding a high-quality dataset of 1.5M image and 0.6M video region-semantic annotations, including novel region-level streaming video caption data. PAM is designed for lightweightness and efficiency, while also demonstrates strong performance across a diverse range of region understanding tasks. It runs 1.2$-$2.4$\times$ faster and consumes less GPU memory than prior approaches, offering a practical solution for real-world applications. We believe that our effective approach will serve as a strong baseline for future research in region-level visual understanding.

title: Perceive Anything: Recognize, Explain, Caption, and Segment Anything in Images and Videos

abstract: As we scale to more massive machine learning models, the frequent synchronization demands inherent in data-parallel approaches create significant slowdowns, posing a critical challenge to further scaling. Recent work develops an approach (DiLoCo) that relaxes synchronization demands without compromising model quality. However, these works do not carefully analyze how DiLoCo's behavior changes with model size. In this work, we study the scaling law behavior of DiLoCo when training LLMs under a fixed compute budget. We focus on how algorithmic factors, including number of model replicas, hyperparameters, and token budget affect training in ways that can be accurately predicted via scaling laws. We find that DiLoCo scales both predictably and robustly with model size. When well-tuned, DiLoCo scales better than data-parallel training with model size, and can outperform data-parallel training even at small model sizes. Our results showcase a more general set of benefits of DiLoCo than previously documented, including increased optimal batch sizes, improved downstream generalization with scale, and improved evaluation loss for a fixed token budget.

paragraphs: Distributed language-model training can slow down when parallel workers must synchronize frequently. DiLoCo reduces this communication requirement. This paper examines how its behavior changes as models grow, asking whether its training outcomes can be predicted under a fixed compute budget.

The study considers the number of model replicas, training hyperparameters, and the token budget. It uses scaling laws to describe how these choices interact with model size. The authors find that DiLoCo's behavior scales predictably and robustly. When appropriately tuned, it scales more favorably with model size than conventional data-parallel training and can outperform that approach even for smaller models.

The reported benefits extend beyond reduced synchronization. The authors find larger optimal batch sizes, better downstream generalization as scale increases, and lower evaluation loss for a fixed token budget. These findings make tuning central to the interpretation: DiLoCo offers quality and scaling benefits in the studied conditions, with the strongest comparison explicitly depending on good settings. The work supplies evidence for planning training configurations as well as reducing communication costs.
summary.tldr: DiLoCo scales predictably and, when well tuned, can improve language-model training quality while reducing synchronization demands.

title: Communication-Efficient Language Model Training Scales Reliably and Robustly: Scaling Laws for DiLoCo

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new method called \textit{Self-Training with Dynamic Weighting} (STDW), which aims to enhance robustness in Gradual Domain Adaptation (GDA) by addressing the challenge of smooth knowledge migration from the source to the target domain. Traditional GDA methods mitigate domain shift through intermediate domains and self-training but often suffer from inefficient knowledge migration or incomplete intermediate data. Our approach introduces a dynamic weighting mechanism that adaptively balances the loss contributions of the source and target domains during training. Specifically, we design an optimization framework governed by a time-varying hyperparameter $\varrho$ (progressing from 0 to 1), which controls the strength of domain-specific learning and ensures stable adaptation. The method leverages self-training to generate pseudo-labels and optimizes a weighted objective function for iterative model updates, maintaining robustness across intermediate domains. Experiments on rotated MNIST, color-shifted MNIST, portrait datasets, and the Cover Type dataset demonstrate that STDW outperforms existing baselines. Ablation studies further validate the critical role of $\varrho$'s dynamic scheduling in achieving progressive adaptation, confirming its effectiveness in reducing domain bias and improving generalization. This work provides both theoretical insights and a practical framework for robust gradual domain adaptation, with potential applications in dynamic real-world scenarios.

paragraphs: Gradual domain adaptation moves a model from a source distribution toward a different target distribution through intermediate domains. Existing methods often use self-training, but knowledge transfer can be inefficient or intermediate data incomplete. Self-Training with Dynamic Weighting addresses the transition by changing how strongly source and target objectives influence training.

The method generates pseudo-labels from the model’s own predictions and uses them for iterative updates. A time-varying parameter progresses from zero to one, controlling the balance of domain-specific loss contributions. This scheduled weighting is intended to make the movement toward the target domain stable while maintaining robustness across the intermediate domains.

Experiments on rotated MNIST, color-shifted MNIST, portraits, and Cover Type show improvements over existing baselines. Ablation studies support the importance of the dynamic schedule in reducing domain bias and improving generalization. The contribution is a training framework that manages the strength of adaptation over time, with theoretical insights and empirical evidence supporting its use for gradual distribution changes.
summary.tldr: STDW progressively reweights source and target training losses during self-training, improving gradual domain adaptation on the reported datasets.

title: Self-Training with Dynamic Weighting for Robust Gradual Domain Adaptation

abstract: We consider a common case of the combinatorial semi-bandit problem, the $m$-set semi-bandit, where the learner exactly selects $m$ arms from the total $d$ arms. In the adversarial setting, the best regret bound, known to be $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{nmd})$ for time horizon $n$, is achieved by the well-known Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) policy. However, this requires to explicitly compute the arm-selection probabilities via optimizing problems at each time step and sample according to them. This problem can be avoided by the Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) policy, which simply pulls the $m$ arms that rank among the $m$ smallest (estimated) loss with random perturbation. In this paper, we show that FTPL with a Fr\'echet perturbation also enjoys the near optimal regret bound $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{nm}(\sqrt{d\log(d)}+m^{5/6}))$ in the adversarial setting and approaches best-of-both-world regret bounds, i.e., achieves a logarithmic regret for the stochastic setting. Moreover, our lower bounds show that the extra factors are unavoidable with our approach; any improvement would require a fundamentally different and more challenging method.

paragraphs: The m-set semi-bandit problem requires a learner to select exactly m options from d possibilities at every round. The goal is to limit regret, the accumulated disadvantage relative to the comparison strategy. A known optimal adversarial regret bound is achieved by Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, but that policy must repeatedly solve optimization problems to obtain selection probabilities.

This paper analyzes Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader as a simpler selection procedure. It adds random perturbations to estimated losses and chooses the m options with the smallest resulting values. With Fréchet perturbations, the authors prove an adversarial regret bound of order √(nm)(√(d log d) + m^(5/6)), where n is the number of rounds. This approaches the known optimal order of √(nmd).

The same approach achieves logarithmic regret in the stochastic setting, bringing it close to desirable guarantees in both environments. The paper also proves lower bounds showing that the additional factors cannot be removed within the authors' approach. Its contribution therefore combines a simpler decision rule with strong guarantees while identifying a specific theoretical barrier to further improvement.
summary.tldr: Fréchet-perturbed leader selection achieves near-optimal adversarial regret and logarithmic stochastic regret for m-set semi-bandits, with approach-specific lower bounds.

title: Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader Nearly Achieves Best-of-Both-Worlds for the m-Set Semi-Bandit Problems

abstract: Sampling from unnormalised discrete distributions is a fundamental problem across various domains. While Markov chain Monte Carlo offers a principled approach, it often suffers from slow mixing and poor convergence. In this paper, we propose Discrete Neural Flow Samplers (DNFS), a trainable and efficient framework for discrete sampling. DNFS learns the rate matrix of a continuous-time Markov chain such that the resulting dynamics satisfy the Kolmogorov equation. As this objective involves the intractable partition function, we then employ control variates to reduce the variance of its Monte Carlo estimation, leading to a coordinate descent learning algorithm. To further facilitate computational efficiency, we propose locally equivaraint Transformer, a novel parameterisation of the rate matrix that significantly improves training efficiency while preserving powerful network expressiveness. Empirically, we demonstrate the efficacy of DNFS in a wide range of applications, including sampling from unnormalised distributions, training discrete energy-based models, and solving combinatorial optimisation problems.

paragraphs: Sampling a discrete distribution is difficult when only unnormalized scores are available. Markov chain Monte Carlo provides a principled approach, but its transitions can explore the possibilities slowly. Discrete Neural Flow Samplers instead learn a sampling process, aiming to make movement through the discrete space more efficient.

DNFS learns the rate matrix of a continuous-time Markov chain, which controls transitions between states. Training seeks dynamics that satisfy the Kolmogorov equation describing how probabilities evolve. The objective involves an intractable partition function, so the authors use control variates to reduce noise in its Monte Carlo estimation. This leads to a coordinate-descent learning algorithm.

A locally equivariant transformer provides the rate-matrix parameterization. The authors report that this design improves training efficiency while retaining expressive modeling capacity. Empirical evaluations cover sampling unnormalized distributions, training discrete energy-based models, and solving combinatorial optimization problems. Together, these applications demonstrate the usefulness of learning discrete sampling dynamics, with both the estimation procedure and network design contributing to computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: DNFS learns continuous-time transitions for efficient discrete sampling, combining variance-reduced training with a locally equivariant transformer.

title: Discrete Neural Flow Samplers with Locally Equivariant Transformer

abstract: Drone Visual Active Tracking aims to autonomously follow a target object by controlling the motion system based on visual observations, providing a more practical solution for effective tracking in dynamic environments. However, accurate Drone Visual Active Tracking using reinforcement learning remains challenging due to the absence of a unified benchmark and the complexity of open-world environments with frequent interference. To address these issues, we pioneer a systematic solution. First, we propose DAT, the first open-world drone active air-to-ground tracking benchmark. It encompasses 24 city-scale scenes, featuring targets with human-like behaviors and high-fidelity dynamics simulation. DAT also provides a digital twin tool for unlimited scene generation. Additionally, we propose a novel reinforcement learning method called GC-VAT, which aims to improve the performance of drone tracking targets in complex scenarios. Specifically, we design a Goal-Centered Reward to provide precise feedback across viewpoints to the agent, enabling it to expand perception and movement range through unrestricted perspectives. Inspired by curriculum learning, we introduce a Curriculum-Based Training strategy that progressively enhances the tracking performance in complex environments. Besides, experiments on simulator and real-world images demonstrate the superior performance of GC-VAT, achieving a Tracking Success Rate of approximately 72% on the simulator. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/SHWplus/DAT_Benchmark.

paragraphs: Drone active tracking requires a drone to move in response to visual observations so that it can keep following a target. Complex surroundings and frequent interference make this difficult for reinforcement learning. The paper contributes both a benchmark for evaluating the task and a learning method intended to improve tracking in such environments.

The DAT benchmark includes 24 city-scale scenes, targets with human-like behavior, and high-fidelity dynamics simulation. A digital twin tool supports additional scene generation. The proposed method, GC-VAT, uses a goal-centered reward to give the agent feedback across viewpoints, supporting a wider range of perception and movement. Curriculum-based training progressively develops tracking performance in complex environments.

Experiments using simulation and real-world images report superior performance for GC-VAT, including approximately 72% tracking success in the simulator. That number specifically describes the simulated evaluation. The benchmark and method together provide a framework for studying how visual feedback, reward design, and progressive training affect active tracking amid varied scenes and interference.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces the DAT drone-tracking benchmark and GC-VAT, whose goal-centered rewards and curriculum achieve about 72% simulated tracking success.

title: Open-World Drone Active Tracking with Goal-Centered Rewards

abstract: Existing NAS methods for semantic segmentation typically apply uniform optimization to all candidate networks (paths) within a one-shot supernet. However, the concurrent existence of both promising and suboptimal paths often results in inefficient weight updates and gradient conflicts. This issue is particularly severe in semantic segmentation due to its complex multi-branch architectures and large search space, which further degrade the supernet's ability to accurately evaluate individual paths and identify high-quality candidates. To address this issue, we propose Dynamic Path Selection (DPS), a selective training strategy that leverages multiple performance proxies to guide path optimization. DPS follows a stage-wise paradigm, where each phase emphasizes a different objective: early stages prioritize convergence, the middle stage focuses on expressiveness, and the final stage emphasizes a balanced combination of expressiveness and generalization. At each stage, paths are selected based on these criteria, concentrating optimization efforts on promising paths, thus facilitating targeted and efficient model updates. Additionally, DPS integrates a dynamic stage scheduler and a diversity-driven exploration strategy, which jointly enable adaptive stage transitions and maintain structural diversity among selected paths. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, under the same search space, DPS can discover efficient models with strong generalization and superior performance.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search for semantic segmentation often trains many candidate networks as paths through one shared supernet. Treating every path uniformly can waste updates and create conflicting gradients between promising and poor candidates. The problem is especially pronounced in segmentation, where multi-branch designs create a large search space and make candidate evaluation difficult.

Dynamic Path Selection changes which paths receive training attention over time. Early stages favor convergence, the middle stage emphasizes expressiveness, and the final stage balances expressiveness with generalization. Multiple performance proxies guide selection at each stage, concentrating updates on candidates that fit the current objective. A dynamic scheduler adapts stage transitions, while diversity-driven exploration preserves variety among selected structures.

Experiments show that, within the same search space, this strategy can identify efficient models with strong generalization and superior performance. The result suggests that the quality of architecture search depends partly on how shared training effort is distributed. Selecting paths according to changing training needs can make the supernet more useful for discovering strong candidates.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Path Selection improves segmentation architecture search by adapting which candidate networks are trained as optimization priorities change.

title: Searching Efficient Semantic Segmentation Architectures via Dynamic Path Selection

abstract: Curriculum learning is a class of training strategies that organizes the data being exposed to a model by difficulty, gradually from simpler to more complex examples. This research explores a reverse curriculum generation approach that recursively decomposes complex datasets into simpler, more learnable components. We propose a teacher-student framework where the teacher is equipped with the ability to reason step-by-step, which is used to recursively generate easier versions of examples, enabling the student model to progressively master difficult tasks. We propose a novel scoring system to measure data difficulty based on its structural complexity and conceptual depth, allowing curriculum construction over decomposed data. Experiments on math datasets (MATH and AIME) and code generation datasets demonstrate that models trained with curricula generated by our approach exhibit superior performance compared to standard training on original datasets.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning organizes training examples so that a model encounters simpler material before harder material. This paper constructs that progression by starting with difficult examples and recursively generating easier versions. The reversal concerns how the curriculum is created: the student still learns through a progression intended to help it master increasingly difficult tasks.

A teacher model capable of step-by-step reasoning performs the decomposition. Its role is to turn complex dataset examples into simpler, more learnable components that can support student training. The authors also introduce a difficulty score based on structural complexity and conceptual depth. This score provides a basis for organizing the decomposed examples into a curriculum.

Experiments cover mathematical problems from MATH and AIME, along with code-generation datasets. Students trained with the generated curricula outperform models trained conventionally on the original datasets in these evaluations. The findings support using a reasoning-capable teacher to shape the learning sequence itself. They connect problem decomposition, difficulty assessment, and curriculum construction as parts of one training approach.
summary.tldr: A reasoning-capable teacher builds learning curricula by recursively simplifying difficult examples, improving student performance on tested math and code tasks.

title: Learning to Solve Complex Problems via Dataset Decomposition

abstract: The information exponent (Ben Arous et al. [2021]) and its extensions --- which are equivalent to the lowest degree in the Hermite expansion of the link function (after a potential label transform) for Gaussian single-index models --- have played an important role in predicting the sample complexity of online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in various learning tasks. In this work, we demonstrate that, for multi-index models, focusing solely on the lowest degree can miss key structural details of the model and result in suboptimal rates. Specifically, we consider the task of learning target functions of form $f_*(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{P} \phi(v_k^* \cdot x)$, where $P \le d$, the ground-truth directions $\\{ v_k^* \\}_{k=1}^P$ are orthonormal, and the information exponent of $\phi$ is $L$. Based on the theory of information exponent, when $L = 2$, only the relevant subspace (not the exact directions) can be recovered due to the rotational invariance of the second-order terms, and when $L > 2$, recovering the directions using online SGD require $\tilde{O}(P d^{L-1})$ samples. In this work, we show that by considering both second- and higher-order terms, we can first learn the relevant space using the second-order terms, and then the exact directions using the higher-order terms, and the overall sample and complexity of online SGD is $\tilde{O}( d P^{L-1} )$.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning functions built by applying the same link function along several unknown, mutually orthogonal directions and summing the results. A common way to predict learning difficulty is the information exponent, which tracks the lowest relevant degree in a Hermite expansion. The authors argue that this summary can miss useful structure when several directions are involved.

The key distinction is between finding the subspace containing the directions and identifying each direction within it. Second-order information can reveal the subspace, but its rotational symmetry prevents it from distinguishing the exact directions. Higher-order information can supply that distinction. The proposed analysis combines these roles in a two-stage learning strategy.

For P orthonormal directions in dimension d, with P no larger than d, the authors give an online-SGD sample and computational complexity of roughly d times P to the power L−1, suppressing logarithmic factors. They contrast this with the earlier P times d to the power L−1 scaling for L greater than two. The improvement comes from exploiting both subspace structure and higher-order directional information.
summary.tldr: Combining second-order subspace information with higher-order directional information improves learning bounds for orthogonal multi-index models.

title: Learning Orthogonal Multi-Index Models: A Fine-Grained Information Exponent Analysis

abstract: We study the ability of language models to reason about appropriate information disclosure - a central aspect of the evolving field of agentic privacy. Whereas previous works have focused on evaluating a model's ability to align with human decisions, we examine the role of ambiguity and missing context on model performance when making information-sharing decisions. We identify context ambiguity as a crucial barrier for high performance in privacy assessments. By designing Camber, a framework for context disambiguation, we show that model-generated decision rationales can reveal ambiguities and that systematically disambiguating context based on these rationales leads to significant accuracy improvements (up to 13.3% in precision and up to 22.3% in recall) as well as reductions in prompt sensitivity. Overall, our results indicate that approaches for context disambiguation are a promising way forward to enhance agentic privacy reasoning.

paragraphs: Deciding whether to share information depends on the circumstances around a disclosure. This paper studies how language models make those decisions when context is ambiguous or incomplete. It identifies ambiguity as an important obstacle to accurate privacy assessments, extending evaluation beyond whether a model’s decision agrees with a human judgment.

The proposed framework, Camber, uses model-generated explanations of decisions to uncover unclear aspects of the context. It then systematically disambiguates the context based on those rationales. The explanation therefore serves as a source of evidence about what needs clarification, connecting the model’s reasoning about a decision to the information supplied for assessing it.

The authors report improvements of up to 13.3 percent in precision and 22.3 percent in recall, alongside reduced sensitivity to prompt wording. These results suggest that clarifying the decision context can improve both accuracy and consistency in information-sharing assessments. The paper presents context disambiguation as a promising direction for agentic privacy reasoning, rather than treating the observed gains as a complete solution.
summary.tldr: Camber uses models’ decision rationales to clarify ambiguous contexts and improve privacy-related information-sharing judgments.

title: Privacy Reasoning in Ambiguous Contexts

abstract: Biclustering is a major tool of data mining in many domains and many algorithms have emerged in recent years. All these algorithms aim to obtain coherent biclusters and it is crucial to have a reliable procedure for their validation. We point out the problem of size bias in biclustering evaluation and show how it can lead to wrong conclusions in a comparative study. We present the theoretical corrections for all of the most popular measures in order to remove this bias. We introduce the corrected precision-recall space that combines the advantages of corrected measures, the ease of interpretation and visualization of uncorrected measures. Numerical experiments demonstrate the interest of our approach.

paragraphs: Biclustering algorithms seek coherent groups within data, but comparing their outputs requires trustworthy evaluation measures. This paper identifies size bias as a problem in that evaluation. A score can favor certain sizes of biclusters in ways that distort a comparison, potentially leading researchers to draw the wrong conclusion about which algorithm performs better.

The authors derive theoretical corrections for all of the most popular measures considered in the paper. The purpose is to remove the identified size bias so that evaluation more faithfully reflects the quality being assessed. This addresses the measurement procedure used to compare algorithms, rather than proposing another algorithm for discovering biclusters.

The paper also introduces a corrected precision-recall space. It combines the benefits of corrected measures with the interpretability and visualization advantages of their uncorrected counterparts. Numerical experiments demonstrate the usefulness of the approach. Together, these contributions make the case that a reliable comparison needs both bias correction and a presentation that allows the resulting quality differences to be understood.
summary.tldr: The paper corrects size bias in biclustering evaluation and introduces an interpretable corrected precision-recall space.

title: Precision-recall space to correct external indices for biclustering

abstract: A consistent loss function for multiclass classification is one such that for any source of labeled examples, any tuple of scoring functions that minimizes the expected loss will have classification accuracy close to that of the Bayes optimal classifier. While consistency has been proposed as a desirable property for multiclass loss functions, we give experimental and theoretical results exhibiting a sequence of linearly separable data sources with the following property: a multiclass classification algorithm which optimizes a loss function due to Crammer and Singer (which is known not to be consistent) produces classifiers whose expected error goes to 0, while the expected error of an algorithm which optimizes a generalization of the loss function used by LogitBoost (a loss function which is known to be consistent) is bounded below by a positive constant. We identify a property of a loss function, realizable consistency with respect to a restricted class of scoring functions, that accounts for this difference. As our main technical results we show that the Crammer–Singer loss function is realizable consistent for the class of linear scoring functions, while the generalization of LogitBoost is not. Our result for LogitBoost is a special case of a more general theorem that applies to several other loss functions that have been proposed for multiclass classification.

paragraphs: A consistent classification loss connects minimizing expected loss with achieving accuracy close to the Bayes optimum. This paper shows why that desirable property can be insufficient for comparing losses when the learner uses a restricted class of scoring functions. Its focus is multiclass prediction with linear scoring functions and data that are linearly separable.

The authors construct a sequence of data sources where optimizing the Crammer–Singer loss produces expected error tending to zero. On the same sequence, optimizing a generalized LogitBoost loss leaves error bounded below by a positive constant. This is striking because the former loss is known to lack ordinary consistency, while the latter possesses it. Both theoretical and experimental results exhibit the difference.

The explanation is realizable consistency relative to the restricted scoring class. The paper proves that Crammer–Singer has this property for linear scoring functions, whereas generalized LogitBoost does not. The LogitBoost result follows from a broader theorem covering other multiclass losses. The lesson concerns matching guarantees to the scoring class, rather than universally ranking these losses.
summary.tldr: For restricted linear scoring functions, realizable consistency can explain performance differences that ordinary multiclass loss consistency does not.

title: Consistency versus Realizable H-Consistency for Multiclass Classification

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of active learning for cost-sensitive multiclass classification. We propose selective sampling algorithms, which process the data in a streaming fashion, querying only a subset of the labels. For these algorithms, we analyze the regret and label complexity when the labels are generated according to a generalized linear model. We establish that the gains of active learning over passive learning can range from none to exponentially large, based on a natural notion of margin. We also present a safety guarantee to guard against model mismatch. Numerical simulations show that our algorithms indeed obtain a low regret with a small number of queries.

For these algorithms, we analyze the regret and label complexity when the labels are generated according to a generalized linear model. paragraphs: In cost-sensitive multiclass classification, prediction mistakes can have different costs. Obtaining labels can also be expensive, motivating algorithms that choose which examples need annotation. This paper develops selective sampling methods that process a stream of data and request labels for only a subset of the examples.

The analysis studies regret and label complexity under a generalized linear model for label generation. These quantities capture prediction performance and the number of requested labels. A margin condition determines how much active learning helps: the advantage over passive learning can range from no gain to an exponentially large gain.

This range is a central finding because selective querying does not provide the same benefit in every setting. The paper also supplies a safety guarantee intended to guard against mismatch between the assumed model and the data. Numerical simulations report low regret with few label requests, supporting the methods' ability to combine selective annotation with effective cost-sensitive prediction in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Streaming selective-sampling algorithms achieve margin-dependent labeling gains for cost-sensitive prediction, with a safeguard against model mismatch.

title: Selective sampling algorithms for cost-sensitive multiclass prediction

abstract: Support Vector Machines (SVM) is among the most popular classification techniques in machine learning, hence designing fast primal SVM algorithms for large-scale datasets is a hot topic in recent years. This paper presents a new L2-norm regularized primal SVM solver using Augmented Lagrange Multipliers, with linear-time computational cost for Lp-norm loss functions. The most computationally intensive steps (that determine the algorithmic complexity) of the proposed algorithm is purely and simply matrix-by-vector multiplication, which can be easily parallelized on a multi-core server for parallel computing. We implement and integrate our algorithm into the interfaces and framework of the well-known LibLinear software toolbox. Experiments show that our algorithm is with stable performance and on average faster than the state-of-the-art solvers such as SVMperf , Pegasos and the LibLinear that integrates the TRON, PCD and DCD algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper presents a solver intended to make support vector machine training more practical on large datasets. It works with the primal SVM formulation, uses L2 regularization, and supports Lp loss functions. The optimization method is based on augmented Lagrange multipliers and is presented with a linear-time computational cost.

A central computational feature is that matrix-vector multiplication accounts for the most intensive steps determining the algorithm's complexity. These operations are straightforward to parallelize on a multicore server. The approach therefore connects its optimization formulation to a concrete kind of computation that can take advantage of parallel hardware.

The authors implement the solver within the interfaces and framework of LibLinear. Experiments report stable performance and faster average execution than evaluated solvers, including SVMperf, Pegasos, and LibLinear's TRON, PCD, and DCD implementations. The average qualification matters: the stated finding is a comparative empirical result, not a claim of winning every individual case. The contribution combines an SVM optimization method, a parallelizable computational core, and integration into an established software framework.
summary.tldr: An augmented-Lagrangian primal SVM solver uses parallelizable matrix-vector operations and reports faster average performance than evaluated alternatives.

title: Linear Time Solver for Primal SVM

abstract: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is a widely used spectral technique for finding correlation structures in multi-view datasets. In this paper, we tackle the problem of large scale CCA, where classical algorithms, usually requiring computing the product of two huge matrices and huge matrix decomposition, are computationally and storage expensive. We recast CCA from a novel perspective and propose a scalable and memory efficient \textitAugmented Approximate Gradient (AppGrad) scheme for finding top k dimensional canonical subspace which only involves large matrix multiplying a thin matrix of width k and small matrix decomposition of dimension k\times k. Further, \textitAppGrad achieves optimal storage complexity O(k(p_1+p_2)), compared with classical algorithms which usually require O(p_1^2+p_2^2) space to store two dense whitening matrices. The proposed scheme naturally generalizes to stochastic optimization regime, especially efficient for huge datasets where batch algorithms are prohibitive. The online property of stochastic \textitAppGrad is also well suited to the streaming scenario, where data comes sequentially. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first stochastic algorithm for CCA. Experiments on four real data sets are provided to show the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis, or CCA, finds correlated linear structure across different views of the same data. Classical algorithms can become costly because they require large matrix products and decompositions, along with substantial storage. This paper focuses on recovering the leading k-dimensional canonical subspace without paying the full computational and memory costs of those operations.

The proposed Augmented Approximate Gradient method, AppGrad, reformulates the computation around multiplying large matrices by thin matrices with only k columns. Its matrix decompositions are restricted to k-by-k matrices. The stated storage requirement is O(k(p1+p2)), where p1 and p2 are the view dimensions, compared with the quadratic storage commonly needed for dense whitening matrices in classical methods.

AppGrad also extends naturally to stochastic optimization. This makes it suitable for datasets where full-batch processing is prohibitive and for streams whose observations arrive sequentially. Experiments on four real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The central benefit is that the desired subspace dimension, rather than full dense transformations of both views, drives the main storage requirement.
summary.tldr: AppGrad makes CCA more scalable through thin-matrix operations, small decompositions, and stochastic updates with storage proportional to the desired subspace dimension.

title: Finding Linear Structure in Large Datasets with Scalable Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: There has been significant recent work on the theory and application of randomized coordinate descent algorithms, beginning with the work of Nesterov [SIAM J. Optim., 22(2), 2012], who showed that a random-coordinate selection rule achieves the same convergence rate as the Gauss-Southwell selection rule. This result suggests that we should never use the Gauss-Southwell rule, as it is typically much more expensive than random selection. However, the empirical behaviours of these algorithms contradict this theoretical result: in applications where the computational costs of the selection rules are comparable, the Gauss-Southwell selection rule tends to perform substantially better than random coordinate selection. We give a simple analysis of the Gauss-Southwell rule showing that—except in extreme cases—it’s convergence rate is faster than choosing random coordinates. Further, in this work we (i) show that exact coordinate optimization improves the convergence rate for certain sparse problems, (ii) propose a Gauss-Southwell-Lipschitz rule that gives an even faster convergence rate given knowledge of the Lipschitz constants of the partial derivatives, (iii) analyze the effect of approximate Gauss-Southwell rules, and (iv) analyze proximal-gradient variants of the Gauss-Southwell rule.

However, the empirical behaviours of these algorithms contradict this theoretical result: in applications where the computational costs of the selection rules are comparable, the Gauss-Southwell selection rule tends to perform substantially better than random coordinate selection. Further, in this work we (i) show that exact coordinate optimization improves the convergence rate for certain sparse problems, (ii) propose a Gauss-Southwell-Lipschitz rule that gives an even faster convergence rate given knowledge of the Lipschitz constants of the partial derivatives, (iii) analyze the effect of approximate Gauss-Southwell rules, and (iv) analyze proximal-gradient variants of the Gauss-Southwell rule.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent improves a solution by updating one coordinate at a time, making the selection rule an important design choice. Earlier theory assigned the same convergence rate to random selection and the Gauss-Southwell rule, despite the latter typically costing more to apply. Experiments nevertheless often favored Gauss-Southwell when selection costs were comparable.

This paper gives an analysis showing a faster convergence rate for Gauss-Southwell except in extreme cases. It therefore helps explain the gap between the earlier theoretical comparison and observed behavior. The distinction between convergence rate and selection cost remains important: an improvement in the former does not by itself settle total computational expense.

The authors also show that exact coordinate optimization improves rates for certain sparse problems. A proposed Gauss-Southwell-Lipschitz rule achieves a further rate improvement when the partial derivatives' Lipschitz constants are known. Analyses of approximate selection rules and proximal-gradient variants extend the discussion to additional ways of implementing coordinate updates.
summary.tldr: A sharper analysis explains why Gauss-Southwell coordinate selection usually converges faster than random selection, while retaining computational-cost considerations.

title: Coordinate Descent Converges Faster with the Gauss-Southwell Rule Than Random Selection

abstract: While classic machine learning paradigms assume training and test data are generated from the same process, domain adaptation addresses the more realistic setting in which the learner has large quantities of labeled data from some source task but limited or no labeled data from the target task it is attempting to learn. In this work, we give the first formal analysis showing that using active learning for domain adaptation yields a way to address the statistical challenges inherent in this setting. We propose a novel nonparametric algorithm, ANDA, that combines an active nearest neighbor querying strategy with nearest neighbor prediction. We provide analyses of its querying behavior and of finite sample convergence rates of the resulting classifier under covariate shift. Our experiments show that ANDA successfully corrects for dataset bias in multi-class image categorization.

In this work, we give the first formal analysis showing that using active learning for domain adaptation yields a way to address the statistical challenges inherent in this setting. We propose a novel nonparametric algorithm, ANDA, that combines an active nearest neighbor querying strategy with nearest neighbor prediction. We provide analyses of its querying behavior and of finite sample convergence rates of the resulting classifier under covariate shift. paragraphs: A classifier may have abundant labeled examples from one task but few labels from the task where it must actually operate. This mismatch is the domain adaptation problem. The paper investigates how actively choosing which examples to label can address its statistical challenges, rather than relying only on the available source labels.

The proposed algorithm, ANDA, combines an active nearest neighbor querying strategy with nearest neighbor prediction. Querying determines where to obtain additional label information, while prediction uses neighboring examples to assign a class. Bringing these two operations together makes label acquisition part of adapting the classifier to its target task.

The authors analyze both the algorithm's querying behavior and its convergence with finite samples under covariate shift, a setting where input distributions change. Experiments in multiclass image categorization show that ANDA successfully corrects dataset bias. The theoretical claims are tied to the stated shift setting, while the image experiments demonstrate the approach's usefulness in a concrete adaptation problem.
summary.tldr: ANDA combines active label queries with nearest neighbor prediction to adapt classifiers under covariate shift.

title: Active Nearest Neighbors in Changing Environments

abstract: We show that a generative random field model, which we call generative ConvNet, can be derived from the commonly used discriminative ConvNet, by assuming a ConvNet for multi-category classification and assuming one of the category is a base category generated by a reference distribution. If we further assume that the non-linearity in the ConvNet is Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and the reference distribution is Gaussian white noise, then we obtain a generative ConvNet model that is unique among energy-based models: The model is piecewise Gaussian, and the means of the Gaussian pieces are defined by an auto-encoder, where the filters in the bottom-up encoding become the basis functions in the top-down decoding, and the binary activation variables detected by the filters in the bottom-up convolution process become the coefficients of the basis functions in the top-down deconvolution process. The Langevin dynamics for sampling the generative ConvNet is driven by the reconstruction error of this auto-encoder. The contrastive divergence learning of the generative ConvNet reconstructs the training images by the auto-encoder. The maximum likelihood learning algorithm can synthesize realistic natural image patterns.

paragraphs: This paper connects a convolutional network used for classification with a model that generates images. The derivation assumes a multicategory classifier in which one category comes from a reference distribution. That reference category provides the starting point for constructing a generative random field from the discriminative network.

With the additional assumptions of ReLU nonlinearities and Gaussian white noise as the reference distribution, the resulting model is piecewise Gaussian. Its Gaussian means are specified by an autoencoder. Filters used to encode an image from the bottom up also serve as basis functions for decoding from the top down, while binary activation variables supply the decoding coefficients.

The connection extends to sampling and learning. Langevin sampling is driven by the autoencoder’s reconstruction error, and contrastive divergence learning reconstructs training images through that same autoencoder. The authors also report that maximum likelihood learning can synthesize realistic natural image patterns. The contribution is therefore a conditional theoretical account tying classification, reconstruction, and generation together within one convolutional model.
summary.tldr: Under specified classifier, activation, and reference-distribution assumptions, a generative ConvNet links image generation to autoencoder reconstruction.

title: A Theory of Generative ConvNet

abstract: A variety of large-scale machine learning problems can be cast as instances of constrained submodular maximization. Existing approaches for distributed submodular maximization have a critical drawback: The capacity - number of instances that can fit in memory - must grow with the data set size. In practice, while one can provision many machines, the capacity of each machine is limited by physical constraints. We propose a truly scalable approach for distributed submodular maximization under fixed capacity. The proposed framework applies to a broad class of algorithms and constraints and provides theoretical guarantees on the approximation factor for any available capacity. We empirically evaluate the proposed algorithm on a variety of data sets and demonstrate that it achieves performance competitive with the centralized greedy solution.

paragraphs: Many large machine-learning problems can be expressed as constrained submodular maximization. Distributing these problems across machines seems attractive, but the paper identifies a limitation in existing approaches: the number of instances that must fit in a machine's memory grows with the dataset. Adding machines does not remove that per-machine capacity requirement.

The authors propose a distributed framework that works with fixed capacity. Its goal is to accommodate larger datasets while respecting the physical memory limit of each machine. The framework covers a broad class of algorithms and constraints, and it provides theoretical approximation-factor guarantees for any available capacity. This explicitly connects the quality guarantee to the resources available for the computation.

Experiments on a variety of datasets show performance competitive with a centralized greedy solution. That comparison indicates that distributing the computation under fixed capacity can still produce strong solutions in the evaluated settings. The main contribution is the combination of a practical memory constraint, broad algorithmic applicability, and theoretical control over approximation quality.
summary.tldr: A distributed submodular maximization framework supports fixed per-machine capacity while providing approximation guarantees.

title: Horizontally Scalable Submodular Maximization

abstract: We propose in this paper a differentiable learning loss between time series, building upon the celebrated dynamic time warping (DTW) discrepancy. Unlike the Euclidean distance, DTW can compare time series of variable size and is robust to shifts or dilatations across the time dimension. To compute DTW, one typically solves a minimal-cost alignment problem between two time series using dynamic programming. Our work takes advantage of a smoothed formulation of DTW, called soft-DTW, that computes the soft-minimum of all alignment costs. We show in this paper that soft-DTW is a differentiable loss function, and that both its value and gradient can be computed with quadratic time/space complexity (DTW has quadratic time but linear space complexity). We show that this regularization is particularly well suited to average and cluster time series under the DTW geometry, a task for which our proposal significantly outperforms existing baselines (Petitjean et al., 2011). Next, we propose to tune the parameters of a machine that outputs time series by minimizing its fit with ground-truth labels in a soft-DTW sense. Source code is available at https://github.com/mblondel/soft-dtw

paragraphs: Time series can describe similar behavior while differing in length or in when particular changes occur. Dynamic time warping addresses this by finding a low-cost alignment between sequences, accommodating shifts and stretching along the time axis. This paper develops soft-DTW, a smoothed version suitable for use as a differentiable learning loss.

Soft-DTW replaces the minimum alignment cost with a soft minimum over all alignment costs. The authors show that both its value and its gradient can be computed in quadratic time and space. The space requirement is a stated computational tradeoff: ordinary DTW takes quadratic time but can use linear space.

The paper demonstrates that this smoothing works particularly well for averaging and clustering time series according to DTW geometry, substantially outperforming the existing baselines considered. It also proposes training a model that outputs time series by minimizing soft-DTW against target sequences. The contribution makes alignment-sensitive comparison directly usable in gradient-based learning, while retaining explicit computational costs.
summary.tldr: Soft-DTW smooths time-series alignment into a differentiable loss, improving the reported averaging and clustering results and enabling gradient-based sequence fitting.

title: Soft-DTW: a Differentiable Loss Function for Time-Series

abstract: Stochastic gradient MCMC (SG-MCMC) algorithms have proven useful in scaling Bayesian inference to large datasets under an assumption of i.i.d data. We instead develop an SG-MCMC algorithm to learn the parameters of hidden Markov models (HMMs) for time-dependent data. There are two challenges to applying SG-MCMC in this setting: The latent discrete states, and needing to break dependencies when considering minibatches. We consider a marginal likelihood representation of the HMM and propose an algorithm that harnesses the inherent memory decay of the process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm on synthetic experiments and an ion channel recording data, with runtimes significantly outperforming batch MCMC.

We instead develop an SG-MCMC algorithm to learn the parameters of hidden Markov models (HMMs) for time-dependent data. There are two challenges to applying SG-MCMC in this setting: The latent discrete states, and needing to break dependencies when considering minibatches. We consider a marginal likelihood representation of the HMM and propose an algorithm that harnesses the inherent memory decay of the process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm on synthetic experiments and an ion channel recording data, with runtimes significantly outperforming batch MCMC.

paragraphs: Stochastic-gradient MCMC can make Bayesian inference more scalable by working with smaller portions of a dataset. Its usual independent-data assumption is problematic for time series, where observations are linked across time. This paper develops an algorithm for learning hidden Markov model parameters while addressing those temporal dependencies.

Two obstacles motivate the design: the model contains discrete hidden states, and constructing minibatches requires breaking dependencies within the sequence. The authors use a marginal-likelihood representation of the hidden Markov model and exploit the process’s inherent memory decay. The approach therefore uses a property of temporal dependence to make smaller-scale computation possible.

The method is evaluated in synthetic experiments and on ion-channel recording data. The results demonstrate effectiveness, with runtimes significantly better than batch MCMC. This supports the practical value of adapting stochastic-gradient sampling to sequential models rather than relying on an independent-observation formulation. The contribution joins a representation that handles hidden states with a strategy informed by how dependence fades over time.
summary.tldr: An SG-MCMC algorithm exploits memory decay in hidden Markov models to accelerate Bayesian parameter learning from time-dependent data.

title: Stochastic Gradient MCMC Methods for Hidden Markov Models

abstract: Online optimization has been a successful framework for solving large-scale problems under computational constraints and partial information. Current methods for online convex optimization require either a projection or exact gradient computation at each step, both of which can be prohibitively expensive for large-scale applications. At the same time, there is a growing trend of non-convex optimization in machine learning community and a need for online methods. Continuous DR-submodular functions, which exhibit a natural diminishing returns condition, have recently been proposed as a broad class of non-convex functions which may be efficiently optimized. Although online methods have been introduced, they suffer from similar problems. In this work, we propose Meta-Frank-Wolfe, the first online projection-free algorithm that uses stochastic gradient estimates. The algorithm relies on a careful sampling of gradients in each round and achieves the optimal $O( \sqrt{T})$ adversarial regret bounds for convex and continuous submodular optimization. We also propose One-Shot Frank-Wolfe, a simpler algorithm which requires only a single stochastic gradient estimate in each round and achieves an $O(T^{2/3})$ stochastic regret bound for convex and continuous submodular optimization. We apply our methods to develop a novel "lifting" framework for the online discrete submodular maximization and also see that they outperform current state-of-the-art techniques on various experiments.

At the same time, there is a growing trend of non-convex optimization in machine learning community and a need for online methods. Continuous DR-submodular functions, which exhibit a natural diminishing returns condition, have recently been proposed as a broad class of non-convex functions which may be efficiently optimized. Although online methods have been introduced, they suffer from similar problems. In this work, we propose Meta-Frank-Wolfe, the first online projection-free algorithm that uses stochastic gradient estimates. The algorithm relies on a careful sampling of gradients in each round and achieves the optimal $O( \sqrt{T})$ adversarial regret bounds for convex and continuous submodular optimization. We also propose One-Shot Frank-Wolfe, a simpler algorithm which requires only a single stochastic gradient estimate in each round and achieves an $O(T^{2/3})$ stochastic regret bound for convex and continuous submodular optimization. We apply our methods to develop a novel "lifting" framework for the online discrete submodular maximization and also see that they outperform current state-of-the-art techniques on various experiments.

paragraphs: Online optimization makes decisions over successive rounds using limited information. For large problems, projecting each update onto the feasible set or computing exact gradients can be expensive. This paper develops methods that avoid projections and use stochastic gradient estimates, covering convex objectives and continuous submodular objectives with a diminishing-returns structure.

Meta-Frank-Wolfe carefully samples gradients during each round and achieves the optimal O(sqrt(T)) adversarial regret bound for the stated optimization settings. The authors also introduce One-Shot Frank-Wolfe, which uses just one stochastic gradient estimate per round. Its guarantee is an O(T^(2/3)) stochastic regret bound. These results describe different tradeoffs and retain distinct adversarial and stochastic settings.

The methods also support a new lifting framework for online discrete submodular maximization, extending the work beyond continuous decision spaces. Experiments show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art techniques. The contribution connects reduced per-round computational requirements with formal regret guarantees, while offering a simpler single-estimate option for the stochastic setting.
summary.tldr: Two projection-free online algorithms use stochastic gradients with regret guarantees for convex and continuous submodular optimization.

title: Projection-Free Online Optimization with Stochastic Gradient: From Convexity to Submodularity

abstract: We revisit convex relaxation based methods for stochastic optimization of principal component analysis (PCA). While methods that directly solve the nonconvex problem have been shown to be optimal in terms of statistical and computational efficiency, the methods based on convex relaxation have been shown to enjoy comparable, or even superior, empirical performance – this motivates the need for a deeper formal understanding of the latter. Therefore, in this paper, we study variants of stochastic gradient descent for a convex relaxation of PCA with (a) $\ell_2$, (b) $\ell_1$, and (c) elastic net ($\ell_1+\ell_2)$ regularization in the hope that these variants yield (a) better iteration complexity, (b) better control on the rank of the intermediate iterates, and (c) both, respectively. We show, theoretically and empirically, that compared to previous work on convex relaxation based methods, the proposed variants yield faster convergence and improve overall runtime to achieve a certain user-specified $\epsilon$-suboptimality on the PCA objective. Furthermore, the proposed methods are shown to converge both in terms of the PCA objective as well as the distance between subspaces. However, there still remains a gap in computational requirements for the proposed methods when compared with existing nonconvex approaches.

Although direct nonconvex methods have strong efficiency results, convex approaches have shown competitive or better empirical behavior. This motivates a closer theoretical study of how to improve stochastic optimization within the convex formulation.

The authors investigate stochastic gradient methods with three forms of regularization. The ℓ2 variant targets better iteration complexity, the ℓ1 variant targets control over the rank of intermediate iterates, and elastic net combines the two motivations. These choices address both progress toward the objective and the structure of the objects maintained during optimization.

Theory and experiments show faster convergence and lower runtime to reach a user-specified objective accuracy compared with earlier convex-relaxation methods. summary.tldr: Regularized stochastic methods accelerate convex-relaxation PCA, although their computational requirements still lag existing nonconvex approaches.

title: Stochastic PCA with $\ell_2$ and $\ell_1$ Regularization

abstract: Data that is gathered adaptively — via bandit algorithms, for example — exhibits bias. This is true both when gathering simple numeric valued data — the empirical means kept track of by stochastic bandit algorithms are biased downwards — and when gathering more complicated data — running hypothesis tests on complex data gathered via contextual bandit algorithms leads to false discovery. In this paper, we show that this problem is mitigated if the data collection procedure is differentially private. This lets us both bound the bias of simple numeric valued quantities (like the empirical means of stochastic bandit algorithms), and correct the p-values of hypothesis tests run on the adaptively gathered data. Moreover, there exist differentially private bandit algorithms with near optimal regret bounds: we apply existing theorems in the simple stochastic case, and give a new analysis for linear contextual bandits. We complement our theoretical results with experiments validating our theory.

paragraphs: When a data collection algorithm uses earlier observations to decide what to collect next, the resulting data can be biased. The paper describes downward bias in empirical means maintained by stochastic bandit algorithms and false discoveries from hypothesis tests on contextual-bandit data. These problems affect what researchers can infer from adaptively gathered observations.

The authors show that making the collection procedure differentially private mitigates this issue. Their results bound bias in numerical summaries such as empirical means and provide a way to correct hypothesis-test p-values. Differential privacy therefore serves here as a tool for controlling statistical consequences of adaptive collection, as well as a property of the collection procedure.

The paper also addresses the performance of the collecting algorithm. It uses existing results for stochastic bandits and supplies a new analysis for linear contextual bandits to establish the availability of private algorithms with near-optimal regret bounds. Experiments validate the theory, supporting the possibility of reducing inferential bias while retaining strong data-collection performance.
summary.tldr: Differentially private adaptive collection enables bias bounds and corrected hypothesis tests while allowing bandit algorithms with near-optimal regret.

title: Mitigating Bias in Adaptive Data Gathering via Differential Privacy

abstract: In recent years, Deep Reinforcement Learning has made impressive advances in solving several important benchmark problems for sequential decision making. Many control applications use a generic multilayer perceptron (MLP) for non-vision parts of the policy network. In this work, we propose a new neural network architecture for the policy network representation that is simple yet effective. The proposed Structured Control Net (SCN) splits the generic MLP into two separate sub-modules: a nonlinear control module and a linear control module. Intuitively, the nonlinear control is for forward-looking and global control, while the linear control stabilizes the local dynamics around the residual of global control. We hypothesize that this will bring together the benefits of both linear and nonlinear policies: improve training sample efficiency, final episodic reward, and generalization of learned policy, while requiring a smaller network and being generally applicable to different training methods. We validated our hypothesis with competitive results on simulations from OpenAI MuJoCo, Roboschool, Atari, and a custom urban driving environment, with various ablation and generalization tests, trained with multiple black-box and policy gradient training methods. The proposed architecture has the potential to improve upon broader control tasks by incorporating problem specific priors into the architecture. As a case study, we demonstrate much improved performance for locomotion tasks by emulating the biological central pattern generators (CPGs) as the nonlinear part of the architecture.

Structured Control Nets introduce a simple architectural division: one module is nonlinear and the other is linear. A locomotion case study further shapes the nonlinear module to emulate biological central pattern generators and achieves much improved performance. This illustrates how control-specific prior knowledge can be built into the architecture. Broader improvements from such priors are presented as potential, rather than an established result for every control task.
summary.tldr: Structured Control Nets combine linear and nonlinear policy modules, with competitive control results and gains from locomotion-specific structure.

title: Structured Control Nets for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce block descent algorithms for projecting onto Minkowski sums of sets. Projection onto such sets is a crucial step in many statistical learning problems, and may regularize complexity of solutions to an optimization problem or arise in dual formulations of penalty methods. We show that projecting onto the Minkowski sum admits simple, efficient algorithms when complications such as overlapping constraints pose challenges to existing methods. We prove that our algorithm converges linearly when sets are strongly convex or satisfy an error bound condition, and extend the theory and methods to encompass non-convex sets as well. We demonstrate empirical advantages in runtime and accuracy over competitors in applications to $\ell_{1,p}$-regularized learning, constrained lasso, and overlapping group lasso.

We prove that our algorithm converges linearly when sets are strongly convex or satisfy an error bound condition, and extend the theory and methods to encompass non-convex sets as well. We demonstrate empirical advantages in runtime and accuracy over competitors in applications to $\ell_{1,p}$-regularized learning, constrained lasso, and overlapping group lasso.

paragraphs: This paper develops algorithms for projecting onto Minkowski sums, sets formed by adding together elements from component sets. Such projections occur in statistical learning when controlling solution complexity or working with dual formulations of penalty methods. The challenge becomes particularly relevant when constraints overlap and existing methods become difficult to use.

The authors propose block descent algorithms that make these projection problems simple and efficient to solve. They prove linear convergence when the component sets are strongly convex or satisfy an error bound condition. This is a conditional speed guarantee: the stated geometric or error-bound properties are sufficient for the convergence result.

The theory and methods are also extended to non-convex sets. Empirical evaluations cover l1,p-regularized learning, constrained lasso, and overlapping group lasso, with reported advantages over competitors in runtime and accuracy. These applications show why the projection problem matters beyond geometry: improving this computational step can benefit learning procedures whose regularization or constraints create precisely this structure.
summary.tldr: Block descent efficiently projects onto Minkowski sums, with conditional linear convergence and empirical gains in constrained and regularized learning.

title: Projection onto Minkowski Sums with Application to Constrained Learning

abstract: Though deep neural networks have achieved significant progress on various tasks, often enhanced by model ensemble, existing high-performance models can be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Many efforts have been devoted to enhancing the robustness of individual networks and then constructing a straightforward ensemble, e.g., by directly averaging the outputs, which ignores the interaction among networks. This paper presents a new method that explores the interaction among individual networks to improve robustness for ensemble models. Technically, we define a new notion of ensemble diversity in the adversarial setting as the diversity among non-maximal predictions of individual members, and present an adaptive diversity promoting (ADP) regularizer to encourage the diversity, which leads to globally better robustness for the ensemble by making adversarial examples difficult to transfer among individual members. Our method is computationally efficient and compatible with the defense methods acting on individual networks. Empirical results on various datasets verify that our method can improve adversarial robustness while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy on normal examples.

paragraphs: Combining several accurate neural networks does not automatically address how adversarial attacks move between them. This paper examines interactions among ensemble members as a way to improve robustness. Its motivation is that strengthening individual models and then simply averaging their outputs leaves those interactions out of the training objective.

The authors define diversity through the members' non-maximal predictions: the predictions below each member's highest-scoring choice. An adaptive diversity promoting regularizer encourages differences among those predictions. The intended effect is to make an adversarial example that affects one network harder to transfer to other members, improving robustness at the ensemble level.

The method is described as computationally efficient and compatible with defenses applied to individual networks. Experiments across multiple datasets show improved adversarial robustness while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy on normal examples. The findings support training the relationships among ensemble members as part of the defense strategy, with diversity serving a specific purpose in reducing attack transfer rather than merely increasing disagreement.
summary.tldr: Encouraging diversity among ensemble members' non-maximal predictions improves adversarial robustness by making attacks harder to transfer between members.

title: Improving Adversarial Robustness via Promoting Ensemble Diversity

abstract: Recent advances in neural architecture search (NAS) demand tremendous computational resources, which makes it difficult to reproduce experiments and imposes a barrier-to-entry to researchers without access to large-scale computation. We aim to ameliorate these problems by introducing NAS-Bench-101, the first public architecture dataset for NAS research. To build NAS-Bench-101, we carefully constructed a compact, yet expressive, search space, exploiting graph isomorphisms to identify 423k unique convolutional architectures. We trained and evaluated all of these architectures multiple times on CIFAR-10 and compiled the results into a large dataset of over 5 million trained models. This allows researchers to evaluate the quality of a diverse range of models in milliseconds by querying the pre-computed dataset. We demonstrate its utility by analyzing the dataset as a whole and by benchmarking a range of architecture optimization algorithms.
