paragraphs: Neural architecture search can demand enough computation to make experiments difficult to reproduce and inaccessible to researchers with limited resources. NAS-Bench-101 addresses this problem by making previously computed architecture evaluations available as a public dataset. Researchers can use those stored results to assess search methods without repeatedly performing the underlying training.

The authors construct a compact but expressive search space containing 423,000 unique convolutional architectures. They identify equivalent graph structures so that architectural duplicates do not count as distinct designs. Each architecture is trained and evaluated multiple times on CIFAR-10, producing a collection of more than five million trained models.

Querying the dataset returns model evaluations in milliseconds, substantially changing the computational requirements of experiments within this search space. The authors demonstrate its usefulness by analyzing the collection and benchmarking architecture optimization algorithms. The contribution is a reusable experimental resource that supports comparisons on a shared set of measured outcomes, with the stated coverage defined by its convolutional architectures and CIFAR-10 evaluations.
summary.tldr: NAS-Bench-101 makes precomputed evaluations of 423,000 convolutional architectures available for fast, reproducible architecture-search experiments.

title: NAS-Bench-101: Towards Reproducible Neural Architecture Search

abstract: we consider the problem of sequential change-point detection where both the change-points and the distributions before and after the change are assumed to be unknown. For this problem of primary importance in statistical and sequential learning theory, we derive a variant of the Bayesian Online Change Point Detector proposed by \cite{fearnhead2007line} which is easier to analyze than the original version while keeping its powerful message-passing algorithm. We provide a non-asymptotic analysis of the false-alarm rate and the detection delay that matches the existing lower-bound. We further provide the first explicit high-probability control of the detection delay for such approach. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that this proposal outperforms the state-of-art change-point detection strategy, namely the Improved Generalized Likelihood Ratio (Improved GLR) while compares favorably with the original Bayesian Online Change Point Detection strategy.

paragraphs: Sequential change-point detection aims to recognize when the distribution generating an incoming data stream changes. Here, neither the change times nor the distributions before and after a change are known. A useful detector must respond quickly while controlling false alarms, making the relationship between these two properties central to the problem.

The authors develop a restarted variant of the Bayesian Online Change Point Detector that retains its message-passing algorithm while being easier to analyze. They provide finite-sample analysis of false alarms and detection delay, with a delay result matching an existing lower bound. They also give explicit high-probability control of detection delay for this type of approach.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show the proposed detector outperforming Improved Generalized Likelihood Ratio detection and comparing favorably with the original Bayesian detector. The contribution combines an analyzable algorithm with strong delay guarantees and empirical support, addressing both the statistical reliability of alarms and the speed with which changes are recognized.
summary.tldr: A restarted Bayesian change-point detector gains finite-sample false-alarm and detection-delay guarantees while performing well on synthetic and real data.

title: Restarted Bayesian Online Change-point Detector achieves Optimal Detection Delay

abstract: Instance- and Label-dependent label Noise (ILN) widely exists in real-world datasets but has been rarely studied. In this paper, we focus on Bounded Instance- and Label-dependent label Noise (BILN), a particular case of ILN where the label noise rates—the probabilities that the true labels of examples flip into the corrupted ones—have upper bound less than $1$. Specifically, we introduce the concept of distilled examples, i.e. examples whose labels are identical with the labels assigned for them by the Bayes optimal classifier, and prove that under certain conditions classifiers learnt on distilled examples will converge to the Bayes optimal classifier. Inspired by the idea of learning with distilled examples, we then propose a learning algorithm with theoretical guarantees for its robustness to BILN. At last, empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets show effectiveness of our algorithm in learning with BILN.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can depend on both the individual example and its true label. This makes label noise more complicated than a single uniform corruption rate. The paper studies a bounded version of this setting, where the probabilities of labels being flipped have an upper bound strictly below one.

The authors introduce distilled examples: examples whose labels agree with the labels assigned by the Bayes optimal classifier. This definition ties the useful training examples to the best classification decision under the underlying distribution. They prove that, under certain conditions, classifiers trained on distilled examples converge to that optimal classifier.

The distilled-example idea then motivates an algorithm with theoretical guarantees of robustness to the bounded noise setting. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. The significance is the connection between a precisely defined kind of trustworthy example and a learning procedure for corrupted labels. Both the bounded-noise assumption and the conditions behind the convergence result are part of the stated theoretical scope.
summary.tldr: Distilled examples motivate a theoretically supported algorithm for learning when label corruption depends on the example and label but remains bounded.

title: Learning with Bounded Instance and Label-dependent Label Noise

abstract: Classical linear metric learning methods have recently been extended along two distinct lines: deep metric learning methods for learning embeddings of the data using neural networks, and Bregman divergence learning approaches for extending learning Euclidean distances to more general divergence measures such as divergences over distributions. In this paper, we introduce deep Bregman divergences, which are based on learning and parameterizing functional Bregman divergences using neural networks, and which unify and extend these existing lines of work. We show in particular how deep metric learning formulations, kernel metric learning, Mahalanobis metric learning, and moment-matching functions for comparing distributions arise as special cases of these divergences in the symmetric setting. We then describe a deep learning framework for learning general functional Bregman divergences, and show in experiments that this method yields superior performance on benchmark datasets as compared to existing deep metric learning approaches. We also discuss novel applications, including a semi-supervised distributional clustering problem, and a new loss function for unsupervised data generation.

In this paper, we introduce deep Bregman divergences, which are based on learning and parameterizing functional Bregman divergences using neural networks, and which unify and extend these existing lines of work. We show in particular how deep metric learning formulations, kernel metric learning, Mahalanobis metric learning, and moment-matching functions for comparing distributions arise as special cases of these divergences in the symmetric setting. We then describe a deep learning framework for learning general functional Bregman divergences, and show in experiments that this method yields superior performance on benchmark datasets as compared to existing deep metric learning approaches. We also discuss novel applications, including a semi-supervised distributional clustering problem, and a new loss function for unsupervised data generation.

paragraphs: Learning how to compare examples can mean learning a neural representation or learning a more general measure of difference. Deep metric learning develops the representation, while Bregman divergence learning broadens the comparison beyond ordinary Euclidean distance. This paper brings these directions together by using neural networks to parameterize and learn functional Bregman divergences.

The resulting framework covers several established approaches within one mathematical construction. In the symmetric setting, the authors show that deep metric learning formulations, kernel metric learning, Mahalanobis metric learning, and moment-based comparisons between distributions arise as special cases. This connection matters because it relates methods for comparing individual representations to methods for comparing distributions.

The authors also provide a deep learning framework for learning general functional divergences. On the benchmark datasets they evaluate, it outperforms existing deep metric learning approaches. They discuss additional uses in semi-supervised clustering of distributions and an unsupervised generation loss. These applications illustrate the broader scope of learning the comparison function itself.
summary.tldr: Deep Bregman divergences unify several representation and distribution comparison methods and outperform existing deep metric learning approaches on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Deep Divergence Learning

abstract: Policy gradient methods in reinforcement learning update policy parameters by taking steps in the direction of an estimated gradient of policy value. In this paper, we consider the efficient estimation of policy gradients from off-policy data, where the estimation is particularly non-trivial. We derive the asymptotic lower bound on the feasible mean-squared error in both Markov and non-Markov decision processes and show that existing estimators fail to achieve it in general settings. We propose a meta-algorithm that achieves the lower bound without any parametric assumptions and exhibits a unique 4-way double robustness property. We discuss how to estimate nuisances that the algorithm relies on. Finally, we establish guarantees at the rate at which we approach a stationary point when we take steps in the direction of our new estimated policy gradient.
originalAbstract: Policy gradient methods in reinforcement learning update policy parameters by taking steps in the direction of an estimated gradient of policy value. In this paper, we consider the efficient estimation of policy gradients from off-policy data, where the estimation is particularly non-trivial. We derive the asymptotic lower bound on the feasible mean-squared error in both Markov and non-Markov decision processes and show that existing estimators fail to achieve it in general settings. We propose a meta-algorithm that achieves the lower bound without any parametric assumptions and exhibits a unique 4-way double robustness property. We discuss how to estimate nuisances that the algorithm relies on. Finally, we establish guarantees at the rate at which we approach a stationary point when we take steps in the direction of our new estimated policy gradient.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a decision policy by estimating which parameter changes increase its value. Estimating that direction from off-policy data is particularly difficult because the data come from a different policy. This paper asks how accurately such gradients can be estimated and how that accuracy affects optimization.

The authors derive asymptotic lower bounds on achievable mean-squared error for both Markov and non-Markov decision processes. They show that existing estimators generally fail to attain those bounds. A proposed meta-algorithm reaches the lower bound without parametric assumptions and has a four-way double robustness property, providing several forms of protection involving its auxiliary estimates.

The paper also discusses how to estimate the nuisance quantities required by the meta-algorithm. It then connects gradient estimation to learning by establishing rates for approaching a stationary point when updates use the proposed estimated gradient. This links a statistical optimality result to an optimization guarantee, with stationarity being the stated endpoint of the learning analysis.
summary.tldr: An off-policy gradient meta-algorithm attains asymptotic error lower bounds, offers four-way double robustness, and supports convergence-to-stationarity guarantees.

title: Statistically Efficient Off-Policy Policy Gradients

abstract: We seek to learn models that we can interact with using high-level concepts: if the model did not think there was a bone spur in the x-ray, would it still predict severe arthritis? State-of-the-art models today do not typically support the manipulation of concepts like "the existence of bone spurs", as they are trained end-to-end to go directly from raw input (e.g., pixels) to output (e.g., arthritis severity). We revisit the classic idea of first predicting concepts that are provided at training time, and then using these concepts to predict the label. By construction, we can intervene on these concept bottleneck models by editing their predicted concept values and propagating these changes to the final prediction. On x-ray grading and bird identification, concept bottleneck models achieve competitive accuracy with standard end-to-end models, while enabling interpretation in terms of high-level clinical concepts ("bone spurs") or bird attributes ("wing color"). These models also allow for richer human-model interaction: accuracy improves significantly if we can correct model mistakes on concepts at test time.

paragraphs: A conventional prediction model often maps raw inputs directly to an answer, leaving users little opportunity to change an intermediate interpretation. This paper revisits models that first predict understandable concepts and then use those concepts to predict the final label. The concepts must be supplied during training.

This intermediate concept layer creates a direct point of interaction. For an x-ray model, a user can edit whether the model predicts a bone spur and observe how that changes its arthritis prediction. For bird identification, the intermediate information can include attributes such as wing color. Changes to predicted concepts propagate through the model to its final answer.

On x-ray grading and bird identification, the authors find accuracy competitive with standard end-to-end models. They also report significant accuracy improvements when concept mistakes can be corrected at test time. The contribution therefore combines understandable intermediate predictions with a concrete mechanism for human correction, and the improvement from intervention depends on being able to provide those corrections.
summary.tldr: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through editable human-understandable concepts, enabling useful corrections while retaining competitive accuracy on two tasks.

title: Concept Bottleneck Models

abstract: Optimizing convolutional neural networks for fast inference has recently become an extremely active area of research. One of the go-to solutions in this context is weight pruning, which aims to reduce computational and memory footprint by removing large subsets of the connections in a neural network. Surprisingly, much less attention has been given to exploiting sparsity in the activation maps, which tend to be naturally sparse in many settings thanks to the structure of rectified linear (ReLU) activation functions. In this paper, we present an in-depth analysis of methods for maximizing the sparsity of the activations in a trained neural network, and show that, when coupled with an efficient sparse-input convolution algorithm, we can leverage this sparsity for significant performance gains. To induce highly sparse activation maps without accuracy loss, we introduce a new regularization technique, coupled with a new threshold-based sparsification method based on a parameterized activation function called Forced-Activation-Threshold Rectified Linear Unit (FATReLU). We examine the impact of our methods on popular image classification models, showing that most architectures can adapt to significantly sparser activation maps without any accuracy loss. Our second contribution is showing that these these compression gains can be translated into inference speedups: we provide a new algorithm to enable fast convolution operations over networks with sparse activations, and show that it can enable significant speedups for end-to-end inference on a range of popular models on the large-scale ImageNet image classification task on modern Intel CPUs, with little or no retraining cost.

paragraphs: This paper studies faster neural-network inference through sparse activation maps. ReLU activations naturally produce zeros in many settings, creating an opportunity to reduce computation. The authors investigate both how to increase this sparsity in a trained network and how to turn it into actual execution speed.

To make activation maps sparser, they introduce a regularization technique together with threshold-based sparsification using a parameterized activation called FATReLU. Their image-classification experiments show that most architectures examined can accommodate substantially sparser activations without losing accuracy. This finding concerns the tested architectures rather than an unconditional property of every network.

Sparse activations only yield practical benefits if the computation can exploit them. The paper therefore also introduces an algorithm for fast convolution with sparse inputs. On a range of popular ImageNet models running on modern Intel CPUs, the authors report substantial end-to-end inference speedups with little or no retraining cost. The contribution connects learned sparsity to an implementation that can realize its computational value.
summary.tldr: Regularization, thresholded activations, and sparse-input convolution jointly enable faster CNN inference while preserving accuracy in most tested architectures.

title: Inducing and Exploiting Activation Sparsity for Fast Inference on Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Designing stable and efficient algorithms for model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) with function approximation has remained challenging despite growing interest in the field. To help expose the practical challenges in MBRL and simplify algorithm design from the lens of abstraction, we develop a new framework that casts MBRL as a game between: (1) a policy player, which attempts to maximize rewards under the learned model; (2) a model player, which attempts to fit the real-world data collected by the policy player. We show that a near-optimal policy for the environment can be obtained by finding an approximate equilibrium for aforementioned game, and we develop two families of algorithms to find the game equilibrium by drawing upon ideas from Stackelberg games. Experimental studies suggest that the proposed algorithms achieve state of the art sample efficiency, match the asymptotic performance of model-free policy gradient, and scale gracefully to high-dimensional tasks like dexterous hand manipulation. Project page: \url{https://sites.google.com/view/mbrl-game}.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning involves learning how an environment behaves and choosing actions using that learned model. These two activities depend on each other: a policy determines which experiences are collected, while the model influences which policy looks promising. This paper organizes that interaction as a game to make algorithm design easier to reason about.

The game has two players. The policy player seeks high rewards according to the current model, and the model player tries to explain real observations collected by the policy. The authors show that finding an approximate equilibrium of this game can yield a near-optimal policy for the actual environment. They develop two algorithm families using ideas from Stackelberg games.

Experiments suggest that these algorithms achieve leading sample efficiency while matching the eventual performance of model-free policy gradient methods. They also handle high-dimensional tasks such as dexterous hand manipulation. The contribution connects a theoretical solution concept with practical ways to coordinate model fitting and policy improvement.
summary.tldr: A game between policy learning and model fitting yields algorithms with theoretical support and promising empirical sample efficiency.

title: A Game Theoretic Framework for Model Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Node classification in attributed graphs is an important task in multiple practical settings, but it can often be difficult or expensive to obtain labels. Active learning can improve the achieved classification performance for a given budget on the number of queried labels. The best existing methods are based on graph neural networks, but they often perform poorly unless a sizeable validation set of labelled nodes is available in order to choose good hyperparameters. We propose a novel graph-based active learning algorithm for the task of node classification in attributed graphs; our algorithm uses graph cognizant logistic regression, equivalent to a linearized graph-convolutional neural network (GCN), for the prediction phase and maximizes the expected error reduction in the query phase. To reduce the delay experienced by a labeller interacting with the system, we derive a preemptive querying system that calculates a new query during the labelling process, and to address the setting where learning starts with almost no labelled data, we also develop a hybrid algorithm that performs adaptive model averaging of label propagation and linearized GCN inference. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets, demonstrating a significant improvement over state-of-the-art approaches and illustrate the practical value of the method by applying it to a private microwave link network dataset.

paragraphs: Classifying nodes in a graph can require labels that are expensive to collect. Active learning addresses this by choosing which nodes a person should label next. The paper targets graphs with node attributes, where existing graph neural network approaches can struggle without a substantial labeled validation set for selecting their settings.

The proposed method predicts labels with graph cognizant logistic regression, which is equivalent to a linearized graph convolutional network. It chooses queries by maximizing the expected reduction in prediction error. To shorten the wait between labeling requests, it computes the next query while the person is still labeling the current one.

For situations starting with almost no labels, the authors also combine label propagation and linearized graph network predictions through adaptive model averaging. Experiments on five public benchmarks show significant improvements over the compared leading approaches, and an application to a private microwave link network illustrates practical use. Together, the components address both label efficiency and the pace of human interaction.
summary.tldr: A graph-based active learner combines targeted label requests, adaptive predictions, and advance query computation to improve classification with limited labels.

title: Active Learning on Attributed Graphs via Graph Cognizant Logistic Regression and Preemptive Query Generation

abstract: Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRFs) are probabilistic graphical models widely used in spatial statistics and related fields to model dependencies over spatial structures. We establish a formal connection between GMRFs and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Common GMRFs are special cases of a generative model where the inverse mapping from data to latent variables is given by a 1-layer linear CNN. This connection allows us to generalize GMRFs to multi-layer CNN architectures, effectively increasing the order of the corresponding GMRF in a way which has favorable computational scaling. We describe how well-established tools, such as autodiff and variational inference, can be used for simple and efficient inference and learning of the deep GMRF. We demonstrate the flexibility of the proposed model and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art on a dataset of satellite temperatures, in terms of prediction and predictive uncertainty.

paragraphs: Gaussian Markov random fields model dependencies across spatial structures and are widely used in spatial statistics. This paper establishes a formal connection between those probabilistic models and convolutional neural networks. Specifically, common GMRFs can be expressed as special cases of a generative model whose mapping from observed data back to latent variables is a single-layer linear CNN.

That connection provides a route to richer models: replace the single convolutional layer with a multilayer architecture. The resulting deep GMRF increases the order of the spatial model while retaining favorable computational scaling. The contribution therefore joins a probabilistic approach to spatial dependence with the compositional structure of convolutional networks.

The authors describe how automatic differentiation and variational inference support efficient learning and inference in the resulting model. On a satellite temperature dataset, they report better prediction and predictive uncertainty than the state of the art. These findings show the practical value of the connection for both estimating spatial quantities and expressing uncertainty about those estimates.
summary.tldr: A formal connection to convolutional networks enables deeper Gaussian Markov random fields with efficient inference and improved satellite temperature predictions.

title: Deep Gaussian Markov Random Fields

abstract: Automating molecular design using deep reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of accelerating the discovery of new chemical compounds. Existing approaches work with molecular graphs and thus ignore the location of atoms in space, which restricts them to 1) generating single organic molecules and 2) heuristic reward functions. To address this, we present a novel RL formulation for molecular design in Cartesian coordinates, thereby extending the class of molecules that can be built. Our reward function is directly based on fundamental physical properties such as the energy, which we approximate via fast quantum-chemical methods. To enable progress towards de-novo molecular design, we introduce MolGym, an RL environment comprising several challenging molecular design tasks along with baselines. In our experiments, we show that our agent can efficiently learn to solve these tasks from scratch by working in a translation and rotation invariant state-action space.

paragraphs: This paper reformulates molecular design as reinforcement learning in three-dimensional Cartesian coordinates. The authors identify a restriction of existing graph-based approaches: ignoring atoms' spatial locations limits the molecules they can construct and leads to heuristic rewards. Including coordinates extends the class of molecules the agent can build and makes spatial configuration part of the design problem.

The reward is based directly on fundamental physical properties, such as energy, estimated using fast quantum-chemical methods. This connects the learning signal to physical characteristics of the proposed structures. The authors also introduce MolGym, an environment containing several challenging molecular design tasks and baselines intended to support progress toward designing molecules from scratch.

Their agent operates in a state-action space that is invariant to translation and rotation. Moving or rotating the overall configuration therefore does not change that representation of the problem. Experiments show that the agent can efficiently learn the included tasks from scratch. The findings demonstrate a workable route to spatially explicit, physically guided molecular construction, with the physical rewards supplied through quantum-chemical approximations.
summary.tldr: MolGym enables reinforcement learning to construct molecules in 3D using rewards derived from approximate quantum-chemical properties.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Molecular Design Guided by Quantum Mechanics

abstract: Extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC) is a task for tagging a given text with the most relevant labels from an extremely large label set. We propose a novel deep learning method called APLC-XLNet. Our approach fine-tunes the recently released generalized autoregressive pretrained model (XLNet) to learn a dense representation for the input text. We propose Adaptive Probabilistic Label Clusters (APLC) to approximate the cross entropy loss by exploiting the unbalanced label distribution to form clusters that explicitly reduce the computational time. Our experiments, carried out on five benchmark datasets, show that our approach has achieved new state-of-the-art results on four benchmark datasets. Our source code is available publicly at https://github.com/huiyegit/APLC_XLNet.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label text classification assigns relevant labels to a text from a very large collection of possibilities. A useful system must represent the text effectively while handling the computational burden of that label collection. This paper introduces APLC-XLNet, combining a pretrained language model with a method for organizing labels during training.

The approach fine-tunes XLNet to produce a dense representation of the input text. Adaptive Probabilistic Label Clusters then approximate the cross-entropy loss by exploiting the imbalance in label frequencies. Forming these clusters explicitly reduces computation time. The method therefore addresses both the representation of the document and the expense of learning predictions across an extremely large label space.

Experiments cover five benchmark datasets, with new state-of-the-art results reported on four of them. These findings support combining pretrained text representations with a loss approximation designed around uneven label distributions. The contribution is a specific integration of language-model fine-tuning and efficient label handling, evaluated in the setting where texts may need multiple labels drawn from a very large vocabulary.
summary.tldr: APLC-XLNet combines XLNet fine-tuning with probabilistic label clusters to reduce computation and improve extreme multi-label text classification.

title: Pretrained Generalized Autoregressive Model with Adaptive Probabilistic Label Clusters for Extreme Multi-label Text Classification

abstract: Detecting the Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS) between two input graphs is fundamental for applications in drug synthesis, malware detection, cloud computing, etc. However, MCS computation is NP-hard, and state-of-the-art MCS solvers rely on heuristic search algorithms which in practice cannot find good solution for large graph pairs given a limited computation budget. We propose GLSearch, a Graph Neural Network (GNN) based learning to search model. Our model is built upon the branch and bound algorithm, which selects one pair of nodes from the two input graphs to expand at a time. We propose a novel GNN-based Deep Q-Network (DQN) to select the node pair, making the search process much faster. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph pairs demonstrate that our model learns a search strategy that is able to detect significantly larger common subgraphs than existing MCS solvers given the same computation budget. GLSearch can be potentially extended to solve many other combinatorial problems with constraints on graphs.

paragraphs: Finding the largest subgraph shared by two graphs is useful in applications such as drug synthesis and malware detection. The computation is NP-hard, and heuristic solvers can struggle to find good matches for large graph pairs within a limited budget. GLSearch addresses how a solver should spend that search effort.

The method builds on branch and bound, which expands the search by choosing a pair of nodes, one from each input graph. A graph-neural-network-based Deep Q-Network learns which pair to select next. This places learning inside the search procedure, where each decision influences which candidate common subgraphs the algorithm explores.

Experiments on synthetic and real graph pairs show that the learned strategy finds significantly larger common subgraphs than existing solvers given the same computation budget. The practical result is better use of limited search time. The authors also identify potential extensions to other constrained graph-combinatorial problems, presenting that broader applicability as a possibility.
summary.tldr: GLSearch learns node-pair choices inside branch and bound to find larger common subgraphs within the same computation budget.

title: GLSearch: Maximum Common Subgraph Detection via Learning to Search

abstract: Recently there has been increased interest in semi-supervised classification in the presence of graphical information. A new class of learning models has emerged that relies, at its most basic level, on classifying the data after first applying a graph convolution. To understand the merits of this approach, we study the classification of a mixture of Gaussians, where the data corresponds to the node attributes of a stochastic block model. We show that graph convolution extends the regime in which the data is linearly separable by a factor of roughly $1/\sqrt{D}$, where $D$ is the expected degree of a node, as compared to the mixture model data on its own. Furthermore, we find that the linear classifier obtained by minimizing the cross-entropy loss after the graph convolution generalizes to out-of-distribution data where the unseen data can have different intra- and inter-class edge probabilities from the training data.

paragraphs: This paper asks why applying a graph convolution before classification can help when examples have both attributes and graph connections. It studies a specific probabilistic setting: node attributes come from a mixture of Gaussian distributions, and the graph follows a stochastic block model. This setup makes it possible to analyze the contribution of graph information mathematically.

The authors show that graph convolution enlarges the regime in which a linear classifier can separate the data. The improvement has a scaling factor of roughly 1/√D, where D is the expected node degree, relative to using the Gaussian-mixture attributes alone. The result describes how connectivity changes the conditions under which simple classification succeeds.

They also study a linear classifier trained by minimizing cross-entropy after convolution. It generalizes to unseen data with different probabilities of edges within and between classes. This provides a theoretical account of robustness to that particular distribution shift, within the modeled relationship between node attributes and graph structure.
summary.tldr: In a Gaussian-mixture graph model, graph convolution improves linear separability and supports generalization when class-dependent edge probabilities change.

title: Graph Convolution for Semi-Supervised Classification: Improved Linear Separability and Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: Machine learning approached through supervised learning requires expensive annotation of data. This motivates weakly supervised learning, where data are annotated with incomplete yet discriminative information. In this paper, we focus on partial labelling, an instance of weak supervision where, from a given input, we are given a set of potential targets. We review a disambiguation principle to recover full supervision from weak supervision, and propose an empirical disambiguation algorithm. We prove exponential convergence rates of our algorithm under classical learnability assumptions, and we illustrate the usefulness of our method on practical examples.

paragraphs: Fully supervised learning requires annotations that can be expensive to obtain. Partial labeling offers weaker information: each input comes with a set of possible targets rather than one identified answer. The challenge is to use these candidate sets to learn despite the unresolved ambiguity in individual training examples.

The paper revisits a disambiguation principle for recovering full supervision from weak supervision and turns it into an empirical algorithm. The key task is to resolve which targets the incomplete annotations support, making the information useful for learning. This connects the practical appeal of cheaper annotations with a procedure intended to recover the guidance that complete labels would provide.

Under classical learnability assumptions, the authors prove exponential convergence rates for their algorithm. This is a conditional guarantee about how rapidly the method converges, rather than a claim that arbitrary ambiguous labels can always be resolved. Practical examples illustrate its usefulness. Together, the algorithm and analysis explain how partial labels can support effective learning when the assumed learnability conditions hold.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes an algorithm for disambiguating partial labels and proves exponential convergence under classical learnability assumptions.

title: Disambiguation of Weak Supervision leading to Exponential Convergence rates

abstract: This paper prescribes a distance between learning tasks modeled as joint distributions on data and labels. Using tools in information geometry, the distance is defined to be the length of the shortest weight trajectory on a Riemannian manifold as a classifier is fitted on an interpolated task. The interpolated task evolves from the source to the target task using an optimal transport formulation. This distance, which we call the "coupled transfer distance" can be compared across different classifier architectures. We develop an algorithm to compute the distance which iteratively transports the marginal on the data of the source task to that of the target task while updating the weights of the classifier to track this evolving data distribution. We develop theory to show that our distance captures the intuitive idea that a good transfer trajectory is the one that keeps the generalization gap small during transfer, in particular at the end on the target task. We perform thorough empirical validation and analysis across diverse image classification datasets to show that the coupled transfer distance correlates strongly with the difficulty of fine-tuning.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to measure the distance between learning tasks in a way that reflects the difficulty of transferring a classifier. Each task is represented by a joint distribution of inputs and labels. The proposed coupled transfer distance connects changes in that distribution with changes in the classifier’s weights during adaptation.

An optimal-transport formulation creates an evolving task between the source and target. As the classifier follows this evolution, information geometry supplies a way to measure the length of its weight trajectory on a Riemannian manifold. The distance uses the shortest such trajectory. The authors also develop a computational algorithm that alternates transporting the input distribution and updating classifier weights.

The resulting distance can be compared across classifier architectures. The theory connects favorable transfer trajectories with keeping the generalization gap small throughout adaptation, including on the final target task. Experiments across image-classification datasets find a strong correlation with fine-tuning difficulty, supporting the distance as a meaningful description of transfer behavior in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: Coupled transfer distance measures task separation through distribution transport and classifier adaptation, and empirically correlates with fine-tuning difficulty.

title: An Information-Geometric Distance on the Space of Tasks

abstract: The great success of modern machine learning models on large datasets is contingent on extensive computational resources with high financial and environmental costs. One way to address this is by extracting subsets that generalize on par with the full data. In this work, we propose a general framework, GRAD-MATCH, which finds subsets that closely match the gradient of the \emph{training or validation} set. We find such subsets effectively using an orthogonal matching pursuit algorithm. We show rigorous theoretical and convergence guarantees of the proposed algorithm and, through our extensive experiments on real-world datasets, show the effectiveness of our proposed framework. We show that GRAD-MATCH significantly and consistently outperforms several recent data-selection algorithms and achieves the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off. GRAD-MATCH is available as a part of the CORDS toolkit: \url{https://github.com/decile-team/cords}.

paragraphs: Training on large datasets can demand substantial computation, with financial and environmental costs. GRAD-MATCH addresses this by selecting smaller subsets intended to preserve useful learning behavior. The guiding question is which examples can collectively provide a training signal close to the signal obtained from a larger training or validation set.

The framework selects subsets by matching gradients. A gradient describes how the model's parameters should change to improve an objective, so matching it makes subset selection directly relevant to optimization. The authors use an orthogonal matching pursuit algorithm to find suitable subsets effectively and provide theoretical and convergence guarantees for their approach.

Experiments on real-world datasets show significant and consistent improvements over several recent data-selection algorithms, with the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off among those compared. These findings support gradient matching as a useful criterion for reducing training work while retaining predictive performance. The reported advantage concerns the evaluated comparisons; the broader aim is to make subset choice reflect the learning task rather than treating all examples as equally useful.
summary.tldr: GRAD-MATCH selects training subsets whose gradients resemble those of a larger dataset, improving the observed accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

title: GRAD-MATCH: Gradient Matching based Data Subset Selection for Efficient Deep Model Training

abstract: Machine learning algorithms with empirical risk minimization usually suffer from poor generalization performance due to the greedy exploitation of correlations among the training data, which are not stable under distributional shifts. Recently, some invariant learning methods for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization have been proposed by leveraging multiple training environments to find invariant relationships. However, modern datasets are frequently assembled by merging data from multiple sources without explicit source labels. The resultant unobserved heterogeneity renders many invariant learning methods inapplicable. In this paper, we propose Heterogeneous Risk Minimization (HRM) framework to achieve joint learning of latent heterogeneity among the data and invariant relationship, which leads to stable prediction despite distributional shifts. We theoretically characterize the roles of the environment labels in invariant learning and justify our newly proposed HRM framework. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness of our HRM framework.

Recently, some invariant learning methods for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization have been proposed by leveraging multiple training environments to find invariant relationships. However, modern datasets are frequently assembled by merging data from multiple sources without explicit source labels. paragraphs: A predictor can fit its training data well by using correlations that change when the data distribution changes. Invariant learning addresses this by searching for relationships that persist across training environments. However, datasets often combine several sources without recording which source produced each example, leaving the environments unavailable to methods that require them.

Heterogeneous Risk Minimization, or HRM, jointly learns the hidden heterogeneity in the data and the invariant predictive relationship. These are connected learning problems: the method seeks useful distinctions among the underlying data environments while also seeking a relationship that remains stable across them. This targets the practical setting where environment labels are missing.

The authors theoretically characterize the role of environment labels in invariant learning and provide justification for HRM. Extensive experiments support the framework’s effectiveness for prediction under distribution shifts. The contribution is a way to pursue invariant learning using inferred heterogeneity, extending the approach to merged datasets whose source structure is not explicitly supplied.
summary.tldr: HRM jointly learns hidden data environments and invariant predictive relationships to improve generalization under distribution shifts.

title: Heterogeneous Risk Minimization

abstract: Model-based algorithms—algorithms that explore the environment through building and utilizing an estimated model—are widely used in reinforcement learning practice and theoretically shown to achieve optimal sample efficiency for single-agent reinforcement learning in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). However, for multi-agent reinforcement learning in Markov games, the current best known sample complexity for model-based algorithms is rather suboptimal and compares unfavorably against recent model-free approaches. In this paper, we present a sharp analysis of model-based self-play algorithms for multi-agent Markov games. We design an algorithm \emph{Optimistic Nash Value Iteration} (Nash-VI) for two-player zero-sum Markov games that is able to output an $\epsilon$-approximate Nash policy in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(H^3SAB/\epsilon^2)$ episodes of game playing, where $S$ is the number of states, $A,B$ are the number of actions for the two players respectively, and $H$ is the horizon length. This significantly improves over the best known model-based guarantee of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(H^4S^2AB/\epsilon^2)$, and is the first that matches the information-theoretic lower bound $\Omega(H^3S(A+B)/\epsilon^2)$ except for a $\min\{A,B\}$ factor. In addition, our guarantee compares favorably against the best known model-free algorithm if $\min\{A,B\}=o(H^3)$, and outputs a single Markov policy while existing sample-efficient model-free algorithms output a nested mixture of Markov policies that is in general non-Markov and rather inconvenient to store and execute. We further adapt our analysis to designing a provably efficient task-agnostic algorithm for zero-sum Markov games, and designing the first line of provably sample-efficient algorithms for multi-player general-sum Markov games.

paragraphs: This paper studies how efficiently agents can learn competitive behavior by building an estimated model of a game and playing against themselves. summary.tldr: Nash-VI substantially tightens model-based self-play guarantees while producing a single Markov policy.

title: A Sharp Analysis of Model-based Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play

abstract: Measures of similarity (or dissimilarity) are a key ingredient to many machine learning algorithms. We introduce DID, a pairwise dissimilarity measure applicable to a wide range of data spaces, which leverages the data’s internal structure to be invariant to diffeomorphisms. We prove that DID enjoys properties which make it relevant for theoretical study and practical use. By representing each datum as a function, DID is defined as the solution to an optimization problem in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space and can be expressed in closed-form. In practice, it can be efficiently approximated via Nystr{ö}m sampling. Empirical experiments support the merits of DID.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms depend on a rule for deciding how different two examples are. This paper introduces DID, a pairwise dissimilarity measure designed to use the internal structure of data. Its defining property is invariance to diffeomorphisms: smooth, invertible changes in the way that structure is represented.

The construction represents each datum as a function. It then defines the comparison through an optimization problem in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a mathematical setting for working with functions using kernels. The resulting measure has a closed-form expression, connecting its optimization-based definition to a direct mathematical form.

For practical computation, DID can be approximated efficiently using Nyström sampling. The authors prove properties supporting theoretical study and practical use, and report empirical experiments supporting the measure’s merits. The contribution brings together structural invariance, a function-based formulation, and an efficient approximation route. Its intended reach spans a wide range of data spaces, making it a proposed general comparison tool rather than a measure restricted to one stated application.
summary.tldr: DID compares data through a kernel-based construction that is invariant to smooth invertible transformations.

title: Measuring dissimilarity with diffeomorphism invariance

abstract: Recent work highlights the role of causality in designing equitable decision-making algorithms. It is not immediately clear, however, how existing causal conceptions of fairness relate to one another, or what the consequences are of using these definitions as design principles. Here, we first assemble and categorize popular causal definitions of algorithmic fairness into two broad families: (1) those that constrain the effects of decisions on counterfactual disparities; and (2) those that constrain the effects of legally protected characteristics, like race and gender, on decisions. We then show, analytically and empirically, that both families of definitions almost always —in a measure theoretic sense—result in strongly Pareto dominated decision policies, meaning there is an alternative, unconstrained policy favored by every stakeholder with preferences drawn from a large, natural class. For example, in the case of college admissions decisions, policies constrained to satisfy causal fairness definitions would be disfavored by every stakeholder with neutral or positive preferences for both academic preparedness and diversity. Indeed, under a prominent definition of causal fairness, we prove the resulting policies require admitting all students with the same probability, regardless of academic qualifications or group membership. Our results highlight formal limitations and potential adverse consequences of common mathematical notions of causal fairness.

paragraphs: Causal definitions of fairness specify which cause-and-effect relationships a decision system should constrain. This paper organizes popular definitions into two families: those restricting how decisions affect counterfactual disparities, and those restricting how protected characteristics affect decisions. It then asks what happens when these definitions become requirements for choosing a policy.

The authors find analytically and empirically that both families almost always produce strongly Pareto dominated policies, in a measure-theoretic sense. Here, domination means that an unconstrained alternative is preferred by every stakeholder whose preferences belong to a specified broad, natural class. The qualification about preferences matters: the result is framed around that class, rather than every imaginable view of fairness.

For college admissions, the relevant stakeholders have neutral or positive preferences for academic preparedness and diversity. Under one prominent fairness definition, the authors prove that admissions must assign every student the same probability, regardless of qualifications or group. These findings identify formal limitations and potentially adverse consequences of the studied causal constraints, showing why a mathematically defined fairness requirement needs scrutiny of its resulting decisions.
summary.tldr: Common causal fairness constraints can yield policies that every stakeholder within a broad specified preference class would prefer to replace.

title: Causal Conceptions of Fairness and their Consequences

abstract: Teaching dimension (TD) is a fundamental theoretical property for understanding machine teaching algorithms. It measures the sample complexity of teaching a target hypothesis to a learner. The TD of linear learners has been studied extensively, whereas the results of teaching non-linear learners are rare. A recent result investigates the TD of polynomial and Gaussian kernel learners. Unfortunately, the theoretical bounds therein show that the TD is high when teaching those non-linear learners. Inspired by the fact that regularization can reduce the learning complexity in machine learning, a natural question is whether the similar fact happens in machine teaching. To answer this essential question, this paper proposes a unified theoretical framework termed STARKE to analyze the TD of regularized kernel learners. On the basis of STARKE, we derive a generic result of any type of kernels. Furthermore, we disclose that the TD of regularized linear and regularized polynomial kernel learners can be strictly reduced. For regularized Gaussian kernel learners, we reveal that, although their TD is infinite, their epsilon-approximate TD can be exponentially reduced compared with that of the unregularized learners. The extensive experimental results of teaching the optimization-based learners verify the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Machine teaching asks how to choose examples that lead a learner to a target hypothesis. Teaching dimension measures how many examples that requires. This paper examines whether regularization can make teaching easier for kernel learners, extending a question beyond the better-studied linear setting to nonlinear learners whose known teaching bounds can be large.

The authors introduce STARKE, a unified theoretical framework for analyzing regularized kernel learners. It yields a general result applicable across kernel types and more specific findings for linear, polynomial, and Gaussian kernels. For regularized linear and polynomial kernel learners, the analysis shows that teaching dimension can be strictly smaller.

Gaussian kernels expose an important distinction between exact and approximate teaching. Their regularized learners still have infinite teaching dimension, but allowing an epsilon-level approximation can reduce the required teaching dimension exponentially relative to unregularized learners. Experiments with optimization-based learners support the theoretical findings. The result shows how regularization can reduce teaching requirements while preserving the difference between reaching a target exactly and reaching it within a permitted tolerance.
summary.tldr: STARKE shows how regularization can reduce kernel learners’ teaching requirements, including exponential reductions for approximate teaching with Gaussian kernels.

title: The Teaching Dimension of Regularized Kernel Learners

abstract: Dynamic topic models explore the time evolution of topics in temporally accumulative corpora. While existing topic models focus on the dynamics of individual documents, we propose two neural topic models aimed at learning unified topic distributions that incorporate both document dynamics and network structure. For the first model, by adding a time dimension, we propose Time-Aware Optimal Transport, which measures the probability of a link between two differently timestamped documents using their semantic distance. Since the gradually evolving topological structure of network may also influence the establishment of a new link, for the second model, we further design a Temporal Point Process to capture the impact of historical neighbors on the current link formation at the network level. Experiments on four dynamic document networks demonstrate the advantage of our models in jointly modeling document dynamics and network adjacency.

paragraphs: A growing document collection contains both changing subject matter and connections between documents. This paper develops two neural topic models that learn topic distributions using both sources of information. The aim is to represent how document content evolves while also accounting for the network in which those documents are linked.

The first model introduces Time-Aware Optimal Transport. It incorporates timestamps into a method that uses semantic distance to estimate the probability of a link between two documents from different times. This connects the topic representation to relationships across the document network, rather than treating temporal changes in individual documents as the only modeling target.

The second model adds a Temporal Point Process to represent how historical neighbors affect the formation of current links. It therefore also accounts for the influence of the network’s evolving structure. Experiments on four dynamic document networks show an advantage for the proposed models in jointly representing document dynamics and network adjacency, supporting the value of modeling content and connections together.
summary.tldr: Two neural topic models combine changing document content with temporal links and network history to model evolving document networks.

title: Dynamic Topic Models for Temporal Document Networks

abstract: Recent work have demonstrated that robustness (to "corruption") can be at odds with generalization. Adversarial training, for instance, aims to reduce the problematic susceptibility of modern neural networks to small data perturbations. Surprisingly, overfitting is a major concern in adversarial training despite being mostly absent in standard training. We provide here theoretical evidence for this peculiar “robust overfitting” phenomenon. Subsequently, we advance a novel distributionally robust loss function bridging robustness and generalization. We demonstrate both theoretically as well as empirically the loss to enjoy a certified level of robustness against two common types of corruption|data evasion and poisoning attacks|while ensuring guaranteed generalization. We show through careful numerical experiments that our resulting holistic robust (HR) training procedure yields SOTA performance. Finally, we indicate that HR training can be interpreted as a direct extension of adversarial training and comes with a negligible additional computational burden. A ready-to-use python library implementing our algorithm is available at https://github.com/RyanLucas3/HR_Neural_Networks.

paragraphs: Training a neural network to resist small perturbations can introduce a surprising problem: robust performance may overfit even when ordinary training shows little overfitting. This paper provides theoretical evidence for that phenomenon. It treats resistance to corrupted data and generalization to new data as connected requirements that a training objective should address together.

The authors introduce a distributionally robust loss and use it to construct holistic robust training, abbreviated HR. They establish a certified level of robustness against two kinds of corruption, data evasion and poisoning attacks, alongside a generalization guarantee. The stated certification concerns a level of protection against these attacks, rather than an unrestricted promise that corruption cannot affect the model.

The paper supports its approach with theory and numerical experiments, reporting state-of-the-art performance in the experiments. It also interprets HR as a direct extension of adversarial training with negligible additional computational burden. The contribution is therefore both an explanation of robust overfitting and a training method intended to reconcile robustness with generalization without substantially increasing computation.
summary.tldr: HR training uses a distributionally robust loss to combine certified corruption resistance with generalization guarantees and little additional computation.

title: Certified Robust Neural Networks: Generalization and Corruption Resistance

abstract: We consider online learning in multi-player smooth monotone games. Existing algorithms have limitations such as (1) being only applicable to strongly monotone games; (2) lacking the no-regret guarantee; (3) having only asymptotic or slow $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ last-iterate convergence rate to a Nash equilibrium. While the $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ rate is tight for a large class of algorithms including the well-studied extragradient algorithm and optimistic gradient algorithm, it is not optimal for all gradient-based algorithms. We propose the accelerated optimistic gradient (AOG) algorithm, the first doubly optimal no-regret learning algorithm for smooth monotone games. Namely, our algorithm achieves both (i) the optimal $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret in the adversarial setting under smooth and convex loss functions and (ii) the optimal $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{T})$ last-iterate convergence rate to a Nash equilibrium in multi-player smooth monotone games. As a byproduct of the accelerated last-iterate convergence rate, we further show that each player suffers only an $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ individual worst-case dynamic regret , providing an exponential improvement over the previous state-of-the-art $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ bound.

paragraphs: Learning in a multiplayer game raises two related questions: how well does each player perform while learning, and how quickly do the players approach equilibrium? Algorithms can have strong guarantees for one question without resolving the other. This paper introduces accelerated optimistic gradient, or AOG, to address both in smooth monotone games.

Under smooth, convex losses in an adversarial setting, AOG achieves the optimal O(√T) regret bound. In multiplayer smooth monotone games, its latest iterate approaches a Nash equilibrium at the optimal O(1/T) rate. The focus on the latest iterate matters because the guarantee describes the current strategies themselves. It improves on the O(1/√T) rate that is tight for several established algorithm families.

The authors also derive an O(log T) bound on each player's individual worst-case dynamic regret, compared with the previous O(√T) bound. These results connect accelerated equilibrium convergence with stronger guarantees during learning. Their scope is the stated smoothness, convexity, and monotonicity settings; the paper does not claim the same behavior for arbitrary games.
summary.tldr: Accelerated optimistic gradient combines optimal adversarial regret with optimal last-iterate equilibrium convergence in smooth monotone games.

title: Doubly Optimal No-Regret Learning in Monotone Games

abstract: Gaussianization is a simple generative model that can be trained without backpropagation. It has shown compelling performance on low dimensional data. As the dimension increases, however, it has been observed that the convergence speed slows down. We show analytically that the number of required layers scales linearly with the dimension for Gaussian input. We argue that this is because the model is unable to capture dependencies between dimensions. Empirically, we find the same linear increase in cost for arbitrary input $p(x)$, but observe favorable scaling for some distributions. We explore potential speed-ups and formulate challenges for further research.

paragraphs: Gaussianization is a generative modeling approach that can be trained without backpropagation. It has performed well on low-dimensional data, but its convergence has been observed to slow as dimensionality grows. This paper investigates that scaling behavior for Gaussianization with random rotations, focusing on how many layers the method requires.

For Gaussian input, the authors analytically show that the required number of layers grows linearly with dimension. They argue that the slowdown arises because the model cannot adequately capture dependencies between dimensions. This explanation directs attention to relationships among coordinates as a source of difficulty when the input becomes larger.

Experiments with more general input distributions show the same linear increase in cost, although some distributions exhibit more favorable scaling. The analytical result therefore has a specific Gaussian-input scope, while the broader pattern is empirical and admits exceptions. The authors also investigate possible speedups and identify research challenges. Their contribution clarifies why success in low dimensions does not by itself settle how efficiently Gaussianization will scale.
summary.tldr: Gaussianization with random rotations requires layers growing linearly with dimension for Gaussian input, with similar but nonuniform empirical scaling more broadly.

title: On the Convergence Rate of Gaussianization with Random Rotations

abstract: Graphs are omnipresent and GNNs are a powerful family of neural networks for learning over graphs. Despite their popularity, scaling GNNs either by deepening or widening suffers from prevalent issues of $\textit{unhealthy gradients, over-smoothening, information squashing}$, which often lead to sub-standard performance. In this work, we are interested in exploring a principled way to scale GNNs capacity without deepening or widening, which can improve its performance across multiple small and large graphs. Motivated by the recent intriguing phenomenon of model soups, which suggest that fine-tuned weights of multiple large-language pre-trained models can be merged to a better minima, we argue to exploit the fundamentals of model soups to mitigate the aforementioned issues of memory bottleneck and trainability during GNNs scaling. More specifically, we propose not to deepen or widen current GNNs, but instead present $\textbf{first data-centric perspective}$ of model soups to build powerful GNNs by dividing giant graph data to build independently and parallelly trained multiple comparatively weaker GNNs without any intermediate communication, and $\textit{combining their strength}$ using a greedy interpolation soup procedure to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, we provide a wide variety of model soup preparation techniques by leveraging state-of-the-art graph sampling and graph partitioning approaches that can handle large graph data structures. Our extensive experiments across many real-world small and large graphs, illustrate the effectiveness of our approach and point towards a promising orthogonal direction for GNN scaling. Codes are available at: https://github.com/VITA-Group/graph_ladling

paragraphs: Increasing a graph neural network’s depth or width can worsen gradient problems, over-smoothing, and information compression, alongside memory demands. Graph Ladling investigates another way to increase the capacity of graph learning systems: divide the graph data, train several smaller models independently, and then combine what they have learned.

The approach adapts the idea of model soups, which merge trained model weights. Graph sampling and partitioning create data portions for comparatively weaker GNNs that can train in parallel without intermediate communication. A greedy interpolation procedure then combines their weights. This makes data division and subsequent model combination the central mechanisms for scaling, without requiring deeper or wider individual networks.

The paper presents several ways to prepare these model combinations using graph sampling and partitioning techniques suited to large graph structures. Experiments across real-world graphs of different sizes report state-of-the-art performance and demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The findings support independent training followed by weight combination as an additional direction for GNN scaling, addressing trainability and memory bottlenecks through how training is organized.
summary.tldr: Graph Ladling trains GNNs independently on divided graph data and greedily combines their weights, reporting strong performance without intermediate communication.

title: Graph Ladling: Shockingly Simple Parallel GNN Training without Intermediate Communication

abstract: Potential harms of large language models can be mitigated by watermarking model output, i.e., embedding signals into generated text that are invisible to humans but algorithmically detectable from a short span of tokens. We propose a watermarking framework for proprietary language models. The watermark can be embedded with negligible impact on text quality, and can be detected using an efficient open-source algorithm without access to the language model API or parameters. The watermark works by selecting a randomized set of "green" tokens before a word is generated, and then softly promoting use of green tokens during sampling. We propose a statistical test for detecting the watermark with interpretable p-values, and derive an information-theoretic framework for analyzing the sensitivity of the watermark. We test the watermark using a multi-billion parameter model from the Open Pretrained Transformer (OPT) family, and discuss robustness and security.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way to mark language-model output so that an algorithm can recognize the mark even when a person reading the text cannot. The framework targets proprietary language models and separates the ability to generate marked text from the ability to detect it. Detection does not require access to the model’s parameters or API.

Before generating a word, the method randomly selects a set of preferred, or green, tokens. It then gently increases the chance of selecting those tokens during sampling. Rather than inserting an explicit label into the text, this process creates a statistical pattern across the generated tokens. The authors describe a statistical detection test that reports interpretable p-values.

The paper also develops an information-theoretic analysis of detection sensitivity and tests the framework with a multi-billion-parameter OPT model. It reports that the watermark can have negligible impact on text quality and can be detected efficiently from a short token span. Robustness and security are discussed, without a claim that detection is guaranteed under every modification.
summary.tldr: Softly favoring randomized token sets creates a statistical watermark that can be detected without access to the generating language model.

title: A Watermark for Large Language Models

abstract: Recently, denoising diffusion models have led to significant breakthroughs in the generation of images, audio and text. However, it is still an open question on how to adapt their strong modeling ability to model time series. In this paper, we propose TimeDiff, a non-autoregressive diffusion model that achieves high-quality time series prediction with the introduction of two novel conditioning mechanisms: future mixup and autoregressive initialization. Similar to teacher forcing, future mixup allows parts of the ground-truth future predictions for conditioning, while autoregressive initialization helps better initialize the model with basic time series patterns such as short-term trends. Extensive experiments are performed on nine real-world datasets. Results show that TimeDiff consistently outperforms existing time series diffusion models, and also achieves the best overall performance across a variety of the existing strong baselines (including transformers and FiLM).

Results show that TimeDiff consistently outperforms existing time series diffusion models, and also achieves the best overall performance across a variety of the existing strong baselines (including transformers and FiLM).

paragraphs: TimeDiff adapts denoising diffusion to time-series prediction using a non-autoregressive forecasting model. The paper focuses on how to condition the model effectively, introducing two mechanisms that connect diffusion-based prediction to the structure of time-series data. These mechanisms are future mixup and autoregressive initialization.

Future mixup uses parts of the ground-truth future as conditioning information during learning, in a manner similar to teacher forcing. Autoregressive initialization supplies an initial prediction containing basic time-series patterns, such as short-term trends. The two mechanisms serve different purposes: one enriches the learning signal, while the other provides a more informed starting point for prediction.

The authors evaluate TimeDiff on nine real-world datasets. They report consistent improvements over existing time-series diffusion models and the best overall performance across a wider group of strong baselines, including transformers and FiLM. These results support the value of the proposed conditioning design for the evaluated forecasting tasks. The model remains non-autoregressive despite using an autoregressive component for initialization, so that component’s role is specifically to help establish the starting forecast.
summary.tldr: TimeDiff improves diffusion-based forecasting with future mixup and autoregressive initialization, achieving strong results across nine datasets.

title: Non-autoregressive Conditional Diffusion Models for Time Series Prediction

abstract: Temporal point processes (TPP) are a natural tool for modeling event-based data. Among all TPP models, Hawkes processes have proven to be the most widely used, mainly due to their adequate modeling for various applications, particularly when considering exponential or non-parametric kernels. Although non-parametric kernels are an option, such models require large datasets. While exponential kernels are more data efficient and relevant for specific applications where events immediately trigger more events, they are ill-suited for applications where latencies need to be estimated, such as in neuroscience. This work aims to offer an efficient solution to TPP inference using general parametric kernels with finite support. The developed solution consists of a fast $\ell_2$ gradient-based solver leveraging a discretized version of the events. After theoretically supporting the use of discretization, the statistical and computational efficiency of the novel approach is demonstrated through various numerical experiments. Finally, the method’s effectiveness is evaluated by modeling the occurrence of stimuli-induced patterns from brain signals recorded with magnetoencephalography (MEG). Given the use of general parametric kernels, results show that the proposed approach leads to an improved estimation of pattern latency than the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Hawkes processes model event sequences in which earlier events influence the occurrence of later ones. The influence is described by a kernel. Exponential kernels are data efficient but poorly suited to estimating delayed responses, while nonparametric kernels can require large datasets. FaDIn targets a more flexible parametric alternative for applications where timing delays matter.

The method fits general parametric kernels with finite support using a fast gradient-based solver for an ℓ₂ objective. It operates on a discretized representation of event times, and the paper provides theoretical support for that discretization. This connects the computational simplification to the inference problem rather than relying solely on its practical speed.

Numerical experiments demonstrate statistical and computational efficiency. The authors also apply the method to stimulus-related patterns in magnetoencephalography brain recordings. In that application, the flexibility of the parametric kernels produces better estimates of pattern latency than the state of the art described in the abstract. The result highlights the value of modeling delayed event influence explicitly.
summary.tldr: FaDIn efficiently fits flexible Hawkes-process kernels and improves latency estimation for stimulus-related brain-signal patterns.

title: FaDIn: Fast Discretized Inference for Hawkes Processes with General Parametric Kernels

abstract: Graph neural networks aim to learn representations for graph-structured data and show impressive performance in node classification. Recently, many methods have studied the representations of GNNs from the perspective of optimization goals and spectral graph theory. However, the feature space that dominates representation learning has not been systematically studied in graph neural networks. In this paper, we propose to fill this gap by analyzing the feature space of both spatial and spectral models. We decompose graph neural networks into determined feature spaces and trainable weights, providing the convenience of studying the feature space explicitly using matrix space analysis. In particular, we find theoretically that the feature space tends to be linearly correlated due to repeated aggregations. In this case, the feature space is bounded by the poor representation of shared weights or the limited dimensionality of node attributes in existing models, leading to poor performance. Motivated by these findings, we propose 1) feature subspaces flattening and 2) structural principal components to expand the feature space. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of our proposed more comprehensive feature space, with comparable inference time to the baseline, and demonstrate its efficient convergence capability.

paragraphs: This paper examines the feature space available to graph neural networks: the collection of information their learned representations can draw on. Earlier studies had emphasized optimization objectives and spectral graph theory. Here, the authors separate spatial and spectral models into determined feature spaces and trainable weights, making the feature space itself accessible to matrix-based analysis.
