When this happens, shared weights or the limited dimensionality of node attributes can restrict the resulting representations. The analysis identifies a reason that repeated processing may leave a model with a constrained set of useful features.

The authors introduce feature-subspace flattening and structural principal components to expand this space. Experiments support the effectiveness of the expanded representations, show efficient convergence, and report inference time comparable to the baseline. The findings connect a specific representational restriction with architectural remedies, suggesting that improving what features are available can benefit graph learning without a substantial inference-time increase in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: Analyzing and expanding graph neural networks' feature spaces improves representations while retaining comparable inference time in experiments.

title: Feature Expansion for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The article proposes and theoretically analyses a computationally efficient multi-task learning (MTL) extension of popular principal component analysis (PCA)-based supervised learning schemes. The analysis reveals that (i) by default, learning may dramatically fail by suffering from negative transfer , but that (ii) simple counter-measures on data labels avert negative transfer and necessarily result in improved performances. Supporting experiments on synthetic and real data benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves comparable performance with state-of-the-art MTL methods but at a significantly reduced computational cost .
originalAbstract: The article proposes and theoretically analyses a computationally efficient multi-task learning (MTL) extension of popular principal component analysis (PCA)-based supervised learning schemes. The analysis reveals that (i) by default, learning may dramatically fail by suffering from negative transfer , but that (ii) simple counter-measures on data labels avert negative transfer and necessarily result in improved performances. Supporting experiments on synthetic and real data benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves comparable performance with state-of-the-art MTL methods but at a significantly reduced computational cost .

paragraphs: Multi-task learning tries to improve prediction by learning related tasks together. Sharing information can also backfire when one task harms another, a failure known as negative transfer. This paper develops a computationally efficient multi-task extension of supervised learning methods based on principal component analysis and analyzes when that sharing helps or hurts.

The analysis shows that the default learning procedure can suffer dramatic failure through negative transfer. It also identifies simple adjustments to data labels that prevent this problem and necessarily improve performance within the analyzed framework. The label treatment is therefore a substantive part of the method: the theoretical benefit comes from correcting how the tasks enter the learning procedure.

Experiments on synthetic and real-data benchmarks show performance comparable to state-of-the-art multi-task methods at substantially lower computational cost. The contribution pairs an efficient learning construction with an explanation of a central failure mode. It also provides a theoretically supported correction, giving the empirical efficiency results a connection to how information is shared across tasks.
summary.tldr: A PCA-based multi-task method uses theoretically motivated label adjustments to avert negative transfer while achieving competitive performance at lower computational cost.

title: PCA-based Multi-Task Learning: a Random Matrix Approach

abstract: Accurate prediction of the out-of-distribution data is desired for a learning algorithm. In domain generalization, training data from source domains tend to have different distributions from that of the target domain, while the target data are absence in the training process. We propose a Distribution Free Domain Generalization (DFDG) procedure for classification by conducting standardization to avoid the dominance of a few domains in the training process. The essence of the DFDG is its reformulating the cross domain/class discrepancy by pairwise two sample test statistics, and equally weights their importance or the covariance structures to avoid dominant domain/class. A theoretical generalization bound is established for the multi-class classification problem. The DFDG is shown to offer a superior performance in empirical studies with fewer hyperparameters, which means faster and easier implementation.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a classifier to work on a new distribution without seeing target-domain data during training. When training examples come from several source domains, a few domains or classes can dominate the learning process. This paper proposes Distribution Free Domain Generalization, or DFDG, to counter that imbalance through standardization.

The method expresses discrepancies across domains and classes using pairwise two-sample test statistics. These statistics provide a way to compare distributions within the training data. DFDG then balances their importance or covariance structures so that a dominant domain or class does not disproportionately determine the training objective. The key idea is therefore to change how cross-domain differences are measured and weighted.

The authors establish a generalization bound for multiclass classification and report superior performance in empirical studies. They also emphasize that the procedure uses fewer hyperparameters, making implementation and tuning easier and faster. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: how the procedure’s generalization can be analyzed, and whether its balancing strategy helps on the evaluated prediction problems.
summary.tldr: DFDG standardizes pairwise domain and class discrepancies to reduce dominance during training and improve generalization to unseen domains.

title: Distribution Free Domain Generalization

abstract: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (HTE) is crucial for identifying the variation of treatment effects across individuals or subgroups. Most existing methods estimate HTE by removing the confounding bias from imbalanced treatment assignments. However, these methods may produce unreliable estimates of treatment effects and potentially allocate suboptimal treatment arms for underrepresented populations. To improve the estimation accuracy of HTE for underrepresented populations, we propose a novel Stable CounterFactual Regression (StableCFR) to smooth the population distribution and upsample the underrepresented subpopulations, while balancing confounders between treatment and control groups. Specifically, StableCFR upsamples the underrepresented data using uniform sampling, where each disjoint subpopulation is weighted proportional to the Lebesgue measure of its support. Moreover, StableCFR balances covariates by using an epsilon-greedy matching approach. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our StableCFR on estimating HTE for underrepresented populations.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation asks how a treatment's effect varies across people or groups. Existing approaches often focus on removing confounding caused by imbalanced treatment assignment. The paper highlights another concern: underrepresented populations can still receive unreliable effect estimates, potentially leading to suboptimal treatment choices even when confounding is addressed.

Stable CounterFactual Regression, or StableCFR, combines population rebalancing with confounder balancing. It smooths the population distribution and upsamples underrepresented subpopulations using uniform sampling. Each disjoint subpopulation receives a weight proportional to the Lebesgue measure of its support, tying the weighting to the size of the region it occupies.

StableCFR also uses epsilon-greedy matching to balance covariates between treatment and control groups. These mechanisms address representation within the population and comparability across treatment assignments together. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior treatment-effect estimation for underrepresented populations. The findings support treating insufficient population representation as an explicit part of the estimation problem alongside the usual concern about confounding.
summary.tldr: StableCFR combines upsampling of underrepresented populations with covariate matching to improve heterogeneous treatment-effect estimates.

title: Stable Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

abstract: We propose $\textsf{ScaledGD($\lambda$)}$, a preconditioned gradient descent method to tackle the low-rank matrix sensing problem when the true rank is unknown, and when the matrix is possibly ill-conditioned. Using overparametrized factor representations, $\textsf{ScaledGD($\lambda$)}$ starts from a small random initialization, and proceeds by gradient descent with a specific form of preconditioning with a fixed damping term to combat overparameterization. At the expense of light computational overhead incurred by preconditioners, $\textsf{ScaledGD($\lambda$)}$ is remarkably robust to ill-conditioning compared to vanilla gradient descent ($\mathsf{GD}$). Specifically, we show that, under the Gaussian design, $\textsf{ScaledGD($\lambda$)}$ converges to the true low-rank matrix at a constant linear rate that is independent of the condition number (apart from a short nearly dimension-free burdening period), with near-optimal sample complexity. This significantly improves upon the convergence rate of vanilla $\mathsf{GD}$ which suffers from a polynomial dependency with the condition number. Our work provides evidence on the power of preconditioning in accelerating the convergence without hurting generalization in overparameterized learning.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix sensing seeks to recover a matrix from measurements, even when its true rank is unknown. Recovery becomes harder when the matrix is ill-conditioned. This paper proposes ScaledGD(λ), a gradient method that uses overparameterized factors, allowing the representation to have more capacity than the unknown rank requires.

Starting from a small random initialization, the algorithm rescales gradient updates through preconditioning and uses a fixed damping term to handle overparameterization. The preconditioners add a small computational overhead. Under Gaussian measurement design, the authors prove convergence to the true matrix at a constant linear rate independent of its condition number, after a short, nearly dimension-free initial period.

The result also has near-optimal sample complexity. It improves the condition-number dependence of ordinary gradient descent, whose convergence rate has polynomial dependence on that quantity. Within this matrix-sensing setting, the analysis provides evidence that preconditioning can accelerate overparameterized learning without damaging generalization. The Gaussian-design assumption and the qualification about the initial period are part of the stated convergence result.
summary.tldr: Damped preconditioning accelerates overparameterized matrix recovery, with condition-number-independent linear convergence after an initial period under Gaussian design.

title: The Power of Preconditioning in Overparameterized Low-Rank Matrix Sensing

abstract: Offline data are both valuable and practical resources for teaching robots complex behaviors. Ideally, learning agents should not be constrained by the scarcity of available demonstrations, but rather generalize beyond the training distribution. However, the complexity of real-world scenarios typically requires huge amounts of data to prevent neural network policies from picking up on spurious correlations and learning non-causal relationships. We propose CAIAC, a data augmentation method that can create feasible synthetic transitions from a fixed dataset without having access to online environment interactions. By utilizing principled methods for quantifying causal influence, we are able to perform counterfactual reasoning by swapping $\textit{action}$-unaffected parts of the state-space between independent trajectories in the dataset. We empirically show that this leads to a substantial increase in robustness of offline learning algorithms against distributional shift.

paragraphs: Offline robot learning must extract useful behavior from a fixed collection of demonstrations or transitions. When those data are scarce, a policy can rely on accidental correlations rather than relationships that remain useful in new situations. Collecting additional interactions is not always available as a way to repair that problem.

The paper introduces CAIAC, a method for creating feasible synthetic transitions from the existing dataset. It quantifies the causal influence of actions to identify parts of the state that an action does not affect. Those action-unaffected parts can then be swapped between independent trajectories, producing counterfactual examples grounded in the available data.

The causal distinction guides which components are exchanged, making the augmentation more structured than arbitrary mixing of observations. It also allows the method to operate without online interaction with the environment. Experiments show a substantial increase in the robustness of offline learning algorithms under distributional shift. The result supports using action influence to expand training experience in ways that help policies cope with changed conditions, rather than relying solely on collecting more demonstrations.
summary.tldr: CAIAC improves offline learning robustness by creating counterfactual transitions through swaps of action-unaffected state components.

title: Causal Action Influence Aware Counterfactual Data Augmentation

abstract: In previous literature, backward error analysis was used to find ordinary differential equations (ODEs) approximating the gradient descent trajectory. It was found that finite step sizes implicitly regularize solutions because terms appearing in the ODEs penalize the two-norm of the loss gradients. We prove that the existence of similar implicit regularization in RMSProp and Adam depends on their hyperparameters and the training stage, but with a different "norm" involved: the corresponding ODE terms either penalize the (perturbed) one-norm of the loss gradients or, conversely, impede its reduction (the latter case being typical). We also conduct numerical experiments and discuss how the proven facts can influence generalization.
originalAbstract: In previous literature, backward error analysis was used to find ordinary differential equations (ODEs) approximating the gradient descent trajectory. It was found that finite step sizes implicitly regularize solutions because terms appearing in the ODEs penalize the two-norm of the loss gradients. We prove that the existence of similar implicit regularization in RMSProp and Adam depends on their hyperparameters and the training stage, but with a different "norm" involved: the corresponding ODE terms either penalize the (perturbed) one-norm of the loss gradients or, conversely, impede its reduction (the latter case being typical). We also conduct numerical experiments and discuss how the proven facts can influence generalization.

paragraphs: An optimizer can influence the solutions reached during training beyond what is explicitly specified by the loss. Earlier analyses of gradient descent used ordinary differential equations to approximate its trajectory and found that finite step sizes introduce terms penalizing the gradient’s two-norm. This paper asks how that implicit effect changes for RMSProp and Adam.

The authors prove that analogous regularization effects depend on the optimizer’s hyperparameters and the stage of training. The relevant quantity is also different: the differential-equation terms involve a perturbed one-norm of the loss gradients. Depending on the conditions, these terms can penalize that quantity or impede its reduction, with the latter behavior described as typical.

This means that the regularization interpretation established for gradient descent does not transfer uniformly to these adaptive optimizers. The direction of their implicit influence matters, as well as the quantity being affected. The paper supplements the theory with numerical experiments and discusses possible consequences for generalization, without claiming a universal generalization improvement from the derived effects.
summary.tldr: Adam and RMSProp have implicit gradient effects whose direction depends on hyperparameters and training stage.

title: On the Implicit Bias of Adam

abstract: Federated Prompt Learning (FPL) incorporates large pre-trained Vision-Language models (VLM) into federated learning through prompt tuning. The transferable representations and remarkable generalization capacity of VLM make them highly compatible with the integration of federated learning. Addressing data heterogeneity in federated learning requires personalization, but excessive focus on it across clients could compromise the model’s ability to generalize effectively. To preserve the impressive generalization capability of VLM, it is crucial to strike a balance between personalization and generalization in FPL. To tackle this challenge, we proposed Federated Prompt Learning with CLIP Generalization and low-rank Personalization (FedPGP), which employs pre-trained CLIP to provide knowledge-guidance on the global prompt for improved generalization and incorporates a low-rank adaptation term to personalize the global prompt. Further, FedPGP integrates a prompt-wise contrastive loss to achieve knowledge guidance and personalized adaptation simultaneously, enabling a harmonious balance between personalization and generalization in FPL. We conduct extensive experiments on various datasets to explore base-to-novel generalization in both category-level and domain-level scenarios with heterogeneous data, showing the superiority of FedPGP in balancing generalization and personalization.

paragraphs: Federated prompt learning adapts pretrained vision-language models through prompts across clients with different data. Personalization helps accommodate those differences, but emphasizing it too much can weaken the model’s ability to generalize. This paper focuses on preserving transferable knowledge while still allowing prompts to reflect individual clients’ needs.

The proposed FedPGP method uses pretrained CLIP to guide a shared global prompt. It then introduces a low-rank adaptation term to personalize that prompt. A prompt-wise contrastive loss brings the knowledge guidance and personalized adaptation together. The method therefore assigns explicit roles to preserving general knowledge and adjusting to client-specific data within the same learning process.

The authors evaluate generalization from base to novel categories and domains across multiple datasets with heterogeneous data. They report that FedPGP achieves a superior balance between personalization and generalization in these experiments. The findings support the idea that retaining guidance from the pretrained model can complement local adaptation, rather than requiring the shared prompt to absorb every client difference on its own.
summary.tldr: FedPGP combines CLIP-guided global prompts with low-rank personalization to balance client adaptation and generalization.

title: Harmonizing Generalization and Personalization in Federated Prompt Learning

abstract: Offline safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to train a constraint satisfaction policy from a fixed dataset. Current state-of-the-art approaches are based on supervised learning with a conditioned policy. However, these approaches fall short in real-world applications that involve complex tasks with rich temporal and logical structures. In this paper, we propose temporal logic Specification-conditioned Decision Transformer (SDT), a novel framework that harnesses the expressive power of signal temporal logic (STL) to specify complex temporal rules that an agent should follow and the sequential modeling capability of Decision Transformer (DT). Empirical evaluations on the DSRL benchmarks demonstrate the better capacity of SDT in learning safe and high-reward policies compared with existing approaches. In addition, SDT shows good alignment with respect to different desired degrees of satisfaction of the STL specification that it is conditioned on.

paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning aims to learn a policy from a fixed dataset while satisfying constraints. Some tasks involve rules about how behavior unfolds over time, together with logical relationships between requirements. The paper argues that existing supervised approaches with conditioned policies do not adequately handle this richer structure in complex tasks.

The proposed Specification-conditioned Decision Transformer, or SDT, combines signal temporal logic with the sequence-modeling capabilities of a Decision Transformer. Temporal logic expresses the rules an agent should follow, and the policy is conditioned on those specifications. This gives the model a way to connect its sequential decisions to requirements that describe behavior across time.

On DSRL benchmarks, the authors report better learning of safe, high-reward policies than existing approaches. SDT also shows good alignment with different requested degrees of specification satisfaction. That result suggests the conditioning signal can meaningfully influence how closely behavior follows the temporal rules. The evidence is empirical and supports controllability across requested satisfaction levels within the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: SDT conditions an offline decision-making model on temporal-logic specifications, improving empirical safety, reward, and alignment with requested satisfaction levels.

title: Temporal Logic Specification-Conditioned Decision Transformer for Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) is the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform new tasks when conditioned on prompts comprising a few task examples. However, ICL performance can be critically sensitive to the choice of examples. To dynamically select the best examples for every test input, we propose Example Gisting, a novel approach for training example encoders through supervised finetuning with an attention bottleneck between the inputs and outputs. These gist models form the basis for GistScore, a novel metric for scoring and selecting informative examples. Further, we experiment with two variations: (1) finetuning gist models for each dataset and (2) multi-task training a single model on a large collection of datasets. The latter can be used for new tasks out-of-the-box, enabling a training-free ICL pipeline. Evaluations with 21 datasets spanning 9 tasks and 8 diverse LLMs show that our fine-tuned models get state-of-the-art ICL performance with over 20% absolute gain over off-the-shelf retrievers and 5% over the best prior methods. Further, our multi-task model generalizes well to new tasks, datasets, and prompt templates. Selection using this model matches or outperforms prior methods while being three orders of magnitude faster than the strongest training-free baseline.

paragraphs: Language models can learn a task from examples included in a prompt, but performance depends strongly on which examples are chosen. This paper develops Example Gisting to learn representations useful for selecting examples for each new input. Supervised fine-tuning places an attention bottleneck between inputs and outputs, creating gist representations that support a selection metric called GistScore.

The authors explore two ways to train these representations. One fine-tunes a gist model for each dataset. The other trains one model across many datasets so that it can select examples for new tasks without additional task-specific training. This second option makes the resulting in-context learning pipeline training-free at deployment to a new task, despite the selector having been trained previously.

Evaluation spans 21 datasets, nine tasks, and eight language models. Dataset-specific models deliver reported absolute gains exceeding 20% over off-the-shelf retrievers and 5% over the best prior methods. The multi-task selector generalizes across tasks, datasets, and prompt templates, matching or outperforming prior selection methods while running three orders of magnitude faster than the strongest training-free baseline.
summary.tldr: GistScore learns compact representations for choosing informative prompt examples, improving in-context learning with both dataset-specific and reusable selectors.

title: GistScore: Learning Better Representations for In-Context Example Selection with Gist Bottlenecks

abstract: In this paper, we derive an upper bound of the difference between a kernel matrix and its expectation under a mild assumption. Specifically, we assume that the true distribution of the training data is an unknown isotropic Gaussian distribution. When the kernel function is a Gaussian kernel, and the mean of each cluster is sufficiently separated, we find that the expectation of a kernel matrix can be close to a rank-$k$ matrix, where $k$ is the cluster number. Moreover, we prove that the normalized kernel matrix of the training set deviates (w.r.t. Frobenius norm) from its expectation in the order of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\sqrt{d})$, where $d$ is the dimension of samples. Based on the above theoretical results, we propose a novel multiple kernel clustering framework which attempts to learn the information of the expectation kernel matrices. First, we aim to minimize the distance between each base kernel and a rank-$k$ matrix, which is a proxy of the expectation kernel. Then, we fuse these rank-$k$ matrices into a consensus rank-$k$ matrix to find the clustering structure. Using an anchor-based method, the proposed framework is flexible with the sizes of input kernel matrices and able to handle large-scale datasets. We also provide the approximation guarantee by deriving two non-asymptotic bounds for the consensus kernel and clustering indicator matrices. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments to verify the clustering performance of the proposed method and the correctness of the proposed theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper builds a scalable clustering method around the expected structure of kernel matrices. Its theory assumes an unknown isotropic Gaussian data distribution. For a Gaussian kernel with sufficiently separated cluster means, the expected kernel matrix can be close to a rank-k matrix, where k is the number of clusters.

The authors also bound the normalized kernel matrix’s deviation from its expectation in Frobenius norm. The deviation scales approximately as the inverse square root of sample dimension, up to logarithmic factors. These results motivate fitting each base kernel with a rank-k matrix that serves as a proxy for its expectation, then combining the proxies into a consensus rank-k representation.

An anchor-based construction makes the framework flexible about input matrix sizes and suitable for large datasets. The authors provide two non-asymptotic approximation bounds covering the consensus kernel and clustering indicator matrices. Experiments examine both clustering performance and the proposed theory. The approach links its low-rank clustering design to explicit distributional and separation conditions rather than assuming such structure without justification.
summary.tldr: The method combines low-rank approximations of expected kernel structure into a scalable clustering framework supported by conditional theoretical bounds.

title: Scalable Multiple Kernel Clustering: Learning Clustering Structure from Expectation

abstract: Aligning language models with human preferences is crucial for reducing errors and biases in these models. Alignment techniques, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), are typically cast as optimizing a tradeoff between human preference rewards and a proximity regularization term that encourages staying close to the unaligned model. Selecting an appropriate level of regularization is critical: insufficient regularization can lead to reduced model capabilities due to reward hacking, whereas excessive regularization hinders alignment. Traditional methods for finding the optimal regularization level require retraining multiple models with varying regularization strengths. This process, however, is resource-intensive, especially for large models. To address this challenge, we propose decoding-time realignment (DeRa), a simple method to explore and evaluate different regularization strengths in aligned models without retraining. DeRa enables control over the degree of alignment, allowing users to smoothly transition between unaligned and aligned models. It also enhances the efficiency of hyperparameter tuning by enabling the identification of effective regularization strengths using a validation dataset.

paragraphs: Aligning a language model with human preferences involves balancing two goals: increasing its preference reward and keeping its behavior close to the unaligned model. The second goal acts as a restraint on how far alignment can change the model. Choosing the strength of that restraint is an important part of the alignment process.

Too little restraint can allow reward hacking, where the model pursues reward in ways that can reduce its capabilities. Too much restraint can prevent useful alignment changes. Traditionally, exploring this balance requires training multiple models with different regularization strengths, which consumes substantial resources for large models.

The paper introduces decoding-time realignment, or DeRa, to explore different regularization strengths without retraining. It provides control while the model generates text, allowing users to move smoothly between unaligned and aligned behavior. This makes the degree of alignment adjustable during generation rather than requiring a new training run for each strength being evaluated.

DeRa also supports selecting effective regularization strengths with a validation dataset. Its stated contribution is a more efficient way to investigate the alignment tradeoff and tune that choice. The practical significance is the ability to evaluate different degrees of alignment while avoiding the repeated training that traditional tuning requires.
summary.tldr: DeRa lets users adjust and evaluate a language model’s degree of alignment during decoding, making regularization tuning possible without retraining.

title: Decoding-time Realignment of Language Models

abstract: Neural networks typically generalize well when fitting the data perfectly, even though they are heavily overparameterized. Many factors have been pointed out as the reason for this phenomenon, including an implicit bias of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and a possible simplicity bias arising from the neural network architecture. The goal of this paper is to disentangle the factors that influence generalization stemming from optimization and architectural choices by studying random and SGD-optimized networks that achieve zero training error. We experimentally show, in the low sample regime, that overparameterization in terms of increasing width is beneficial for generalization, and this benefit is due to the bias of SGD and not due to an architectural bias. In contrast, for increasing depth, overparameterization is detrimental for generalization, but random and SGD-optimized networks behave similarly, so this can be attributed to an architectural bias.

paragraphs: Neural networks can fit every training example and still predict well on unseen data, even when they have many more parameters than seem necessary. This paper examines two explanations: the network architecture may favor useful solutions, or stochastic gradient descent may preferentially find them. Separating these effects requires looking beyond training accuracy alone.

The authors compare random networks and networks optimized by stochastic gradient descent, considering networks that achieve zero training error. They vary width and depth to distinguish different forms of overparameterization. Because both groups fit the training data, differences in generalization help reveal whether the optimization procedure or the architecture accounts for the observed behavior.

In experiments with few training samples, increasing width improves generalization through the bias of stochastic gradient descent, rather than an architectural bias. Increasing depth instead hurts generalization, with random and optimized networks behaving similarly; the authors attribute this effect to architecture. These findings make the low-sample setting and the distinction between width and depth central to interpreting overparameterization.
summary.tldr: In low-sample experiments, wider networks benefit from SGD’s bias, while greater depth harms generalization through an architectural effect.

title: Bias of Stochastic Gradient Descent or the Architecture: Disentangling the Effects of Overparameterization of Neural Networks

abstract: Graph representation learning aims to represent graphs as vectors that can be utilized in downstream tasks such as graph classification. In this work, we focus on learning diverse representations that can capture the graph information as much as possible. We propose quantifying graph information using graph entropy, where we define a probability distribution of a graph based on its nodes’ representations and global-graph representation. However, the computation of graph entropy is NP-hard due to the complex vertex-packing polytope involved in its definition. To address this challenge, we provide an approximation method leveraging orthonormal representations for graph entropy maximization. The proposed method is implemented via graph neural networks, resulting in informative node-level and graph-level representations. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in comparison to many baselines in unsupervised learning and semi-supervised learning tasks. The code of our method is available at https://github.com/MathAdventurer/GeMax.

paragraphs: Graph representation learning converts graphs into vectors that can support tasks such as classification. This paper focuses on making those representations diverse and informative. It introduces graph entropy as the quantity to maximize, defining a probability distribution using both the representations of individual nodes and a representation of the whole graph.

Directly computing this entropy is NP-hard because its definition involves a difficult vertex-packing polytope. The authors address that obstacle with an approximation based on orthonormal representations. This makes entropy maximization usable as a learning approach without requiring direct solution of the original hard computation.

The method is implemented with graph neural networks and produces representations at both node and graph levels. Experiments compare it with many baselines in unsupervised and semi-supervised tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness. The significance is the connection between an explicit information-based objective and practical representation learning. The approximation is central to that connection: it makes a theoretically motivated but computationally difficult measure useful for training models in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: An approximation to graph entropy maximization trains graph neural networks to produce informative node and graph representations.

title: Learning Graph Representation via Graph Entropy Maximization

abstract: Learning from preference labels plays a crucial role in fine-tuning large language models — this is done via supervised learning, on-policy reinforcement learning (RL), or contrastive learning. Different methods come with different implementation tradeoffs, and existing empirical findings present different conclusions, for instance, some results show that online RL is quite important to attain good fine-tuning results, while others find offline methods sufficient. This raises a question: what kind of approaches are important for fine-tuning with preference data and why? In this paper, we answer this question by performing a rigorous analysis of a number of fine-tuning techniques on didactic and full-scale LLM problems. Our main finding is that approaches that use on-policy sampling and attempt to push down the likelihood on certain responses (i.e., employ a ”negative gradient”) outperform offline and maximum likelihood objectives. We conceptualize our insights and unify methods that use on-policy sampling or negative gradient under a notion of mode-seeking objectives for categorical distributions. Mode-seeking objectives are able to alter probability mass on specific bins of a categorical distribution at a fast rate compared to maximum likelihood, allowing them to relocate masses across bins more effectively. Our analysis prescribes actionable insights for preference fine-tuning of LLMs and informs how data should be collected for maximal improvement.

paragraphs: This paper examines why different approaches to preference-based language-model fine-tuning can produce conflicting results. It compares techniques through rigorous analysis on simplified problems and full-scale language-model tasks. The aim is to identify which properties of a training procedure matter, including where its responses come from and how it changes their probabilities.

The main finding favors approaches that sample from the current policy and reduce the likelihood of certain responses. Sampling from the current policy supplies on-policy data; explicitly pushing probabilities downward supplies a negative gradient. In the studied problems, approaches using these properties outperform offline methods and maximum-likelihood objectives.

The authors explain the results using mode-seeking objectives for categorical distributions. These objectives can change probability mass on particular categories faster than maximum likelihood, enabling more effective redistribution among responses. This connects the value of suboptimal responses to the learning update: such responses can supply useful evidence about what to suppress. The analysis offers guidance for both preference-training objectives and data collection, grounded in the settings examined.
summary.tldr: The analysis favors preference fine-tuning that samples current-model responses and actively lowers the probability of undesirable ones.

title: Preference Fine-Tuning of LLMs Should Leverage Suboptimal, On-Policy Data

abstract: Pretraining auto-regressive large language models (LLMs) with retrieval demonstrates better perplexity and factual accuracy by leveraging external databases. However, the size of existing pretrained retrieval-augmented LLM is still limited (e.g., Retro has 7.5B parameters), which limits the effectiveness of instruction tuning and zero-shot generalization. In this work, we introduce Retro 48B, the largest LLM pretrained with retrieval. Specifically, we continue to pretrain a 43B GPT model on additional 100 billion tokens using the Retro augmentation method by retrieving from 1.2 trillion tokens. Notably, the obtained foundation model, Retro 48B, largely outperforms the counterpart GPT 43B trained on 1.2T tokens in terms of perplexity with only 2.58% additional GPU hours, demonstrating the significant scaling potential of the method. After instruction tuning on Retro, InstructRetro demonstrates significant improvement over the instruction-tuned GPT on a wide range of zero-shot tasks. Specifically, the average improvement of InstructRetro is 7% over its GPT counterpart across 8 short-form QA and reading comprehension tasks, 10% over GPT across 4 challenging long-form QA tasks, and 16% over GPT across 3 summarization tasks. Surprisingly, we find that one can ablate the encoder from InstructRetro architecture and directly use its decoder backbone, while achieving comparable results. Our results highlight the promising direction to obtain a better GPT decoder through continued pretraining with retrieval before instruction tuning. Our code and checkpoints are publicly available at: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/retro-48b-instruct-4k.

paragraphs: InstructRetro investigates whether retrieval-augmented pretraining can strengthen a language model before instruction tuning. The authors build Retro 48B by continuing the pretraining of a 43B GPT model on 100 billion additional tokens, using retrieval from 1.2 trillion tokens. This expands the scale of the retrieval-pretrained models discussed in the paper.

Retro 48B substantially improves perplexity over the GPT 43B counterpart trained on 1.2 trillion tokens, with 2.58% additional GPU hours. After instruction tuning, InstructRetro also improves zero-shot task performance. The reported average gains over the instruction-tuned GPT counterpart are 7% across eight short-form question-answering and reading-comprehension tasks, 10% across four long-form question-answering tasks, and 16% across three summarization tasks.

A notable finding is that removing InstructRetro's encoder and using its decoder backbone yields comparable results. This suggests that retrieval during continued pretraining can improve the decoder in a way that remains useful after the encoder is removed. The paper therefore supports retrieval-augmented pretraining as a promising route to stronger instruction-tuned decoders.
summary.tldr: InstructRetro improves zero-shot performance through retrieval-augmented pretraining before instruction tuning, with comparable results after removing its encoder.

title: InstructRetro: Instruction Tuning post Retrieval-Augmented Pretraining

abstract: Foundation models have brought changes to the landscape of machine learning, demonstrating sparks of human-level intelligence across a diverse array of tasks. However, a gap persists in complex tasks such as causal inference, primarily due to challenges associated with intricate reasoning steps and high numerical precision requirements. In this work, we take a first step towards building causally-aware foundation models for treatment effect estimations. We propose a novel, theoretically justified method called Causal Inference with Attention (CInA), which utilizes multiple unlabeled datasets to perform self-supervised causal learning, and subsequently enables zero-shot causal inference on unseen tasks with new data. This is based on our theoretical results that demonstrate the primal-dual connection between optimal covariate balancing and self-attention, facilitating zero-shot causal inference through the final layer of a trained transformer-type architecture. We demonstrate empirically that CInA effectively generalizes to out-of-distribution datasets and various real-world datasets, matching or even surpassing traditional per-dataset methodologies. These results provide compelling evidence that our method has the potential to serve as a stepping stone for the development of causal foundation models.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects is a demanding target for foundation models because causal inference involves intricate reasoning and numerical precision. This paper introduces Causal Inference with Attention, or CInA, as a step toward models that can handle such tasks across datasets. It learns from multiple unlabeled datasets through a self-supervised procedure.

The method rests on a theoretical primal-dual connection between optimal covariate balancing and self-attention. Covariate balancing provides the causal-estimation side of this connection, while attention supplies a mechanism available in transformer-type architectures. The authors use the relationship to enable zero-shot causal inference through the final layer of a trained model on new tasks with new data.

Experiments show that CInA generalizes to out-of-distribution and real-world datasets, matching or surpassing traditional methods fitted separately to each dataset. These results support transferring learned causal-estimation behavior across datasets. The paper presents this as evidence of potential for causal foundation models, with treatment-effect estimation providing the concrete task on which that potential is demonstrated.
summary.tldr: CInA connects covariate balancing with self-attention to learn across unlabeled datasets and perform zero-shot treatment-effect estimation.

title: Towards Causal Foundation Model: on Duality between Optimal Balancing and Attention

abstract: Recently, extensive studies in Reinforcement Learning have been carried out on the ability of transformers to adapt in-context to various environments and tasks. Current in-context RL methods are limited by their strict requirements for data, which needs to be generated by RL agents or labeled with actions from an optimal policy. In order to address this prevalent problem, we propose AD$^\varepsilon$, a new data acquisition approach that enables in-context Reinforcement Learning from noise-induced curriculum. We show that it is viable to construct a synthetic noise injection curriculum which helps to obtain learning histories. Moreover, we experimentally demonstrate that it is possible to alleviate the need for generation using optimal policies, with in-context RL still able to outperform the best suboptimal policy in a learning dataset by a 2x margin.

paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning studies whether transformers can adapt to tasks and environments through the histories provided in their context. Existing approaches impose demanding data requirements: histories may need to come from reinforcement learning agents, or actions must be labeled by an optimal policy. This paper investigates whether a different data acquisition process can relax those requirements.

The proposed approach, ADε, constructs a curriculum through synthetic noise injection. The authors show that such a curriculum can produce learning histories suitable for in-context reinforcement learning. The key change is in how the training experience is assembled: noise supplies a means of constructing the curriculum without relying on the same optimal-policy data requirements.

Experiments demonstrate that the need for generation using optimal policies can be reduced. The resulting in-context learner outperforms the best suboptimal policy in its learning dataset by a reported factor of two. This finding is significant because the learned behavior can exceed the strongest suboptimal policy supplying the data. It supports noise-based curricula as a viable route to acquiring useful learning histories under the studied conditions.
summary.tldr: ADε uses synthetic noise curricula to enable in-context reinforcement learning while reducing reliance on optimal-policy training data.

title: Emergence of In-Context Reinforcement Learning from Noise Distillation

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the most common way of adapting large language models (LLMs) to a new domain. In this paper, we improve the efficiency of SFT by selecting an informative subset of training examples. Specifically, for a fixed budget of training examples, which determines the computational cost of fine-tuning, we select those that maximize information gain, as measured by the Fisher information matrix of the SFT objective. We approximate it efficiently by linearization at the last layer of the LLM. Our approach is computationally efficient, analyzable, and performs well empirically. We demonstrate this on several problems, with both quantitative results and LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning adapts a language model using training examples from a target domain. When only a fixed number of examples can be used, choosing the subset becomes part of the efficiency problem. FisherSFT addresses this choice by seeking examples that maximize information gain under a mathematical criterion tied to the fine-tuning objective.

The criterion uses the Fisher information matrix, which supplies the paper’s measure of informativeness. To make selection efficient, the authors approximate this quantity through a linearization at the model’s last layer. This approximation connects a theoretically analyzable selection rule to a computation intended to be practical for language-model fine-tuning.

The authors report favorable empirical performance on several problems, using both quantitative measurements and language-model judgments. The contribution is therefore a method for allocating a fixed training-example budget more effectively, supported by analysis and experiments. Its stated findings suggest that selecting examples by their information contribution can improve the efficiency of adaptation without requiring the selection procedure to handle the full model in the same way.
summary.tldr: FisherSFT selects informative fine-tuning examples using an efficient last-layer approximation to a Fisher-information-based selection criterion.

title: FisherSFT: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-Tuning of Language Models Using Information Gain

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models face deployment challenges due to their large parameter counts and computational demands. We explore quantization for MoE models and highlight two key insights: 1) linear blocks exhibit varying quantization sensitivity, and 2) divergent expert activation frequencies create heterogeneous computational characteristics. Based on these observations, we introduce MxMoE, a mixed-precision optimization framework for MoE models that considers both algorithmic and system perspectives. MxMoE navigates the design space defined by parameter sensitivity, expert activation dynamics, and hardware resources to derive efficient mixed-precision configurations. Additionally, MxMoE automatically generates optimized mixed-precision GroupGEMM kernels, enabling parallel execution of GEMMs with different precisions. Evaluations show that MxMoE outperforms existing methods, achieving 2.4 lower Wikitext-2 perplexity than GPTQ at 2.25-bit and delivering up to 3.4x speedup over full precision, as well as up to 29.4% speedup over uniform quantization at equivalent accuracy with 5-bit weight-activation quantization. Our code is available at https://github.com/cat538/MxMoE.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models are difficult to deploy because of their parameter counts and computational demands. MxMoE starts from two observations: different linear blocks tolerate quantization differently, and experts are activated at different frequencies. These differences mean that choosing numerical precision involves both prediction quality and the way computation is distributed across experts.

The framework selects mixed-precision configurations by considering parameter sensitivity, expert activation patterns, and hardware resources together. It also generates optimized GroupGEMM kernels that run matrix multiplications with different precisions in parallel. This connects the numerical choices made for accuracy with the implementation needed to realize their performance benefits.

Evaluations report Wikitext-2 perplexity 2.4 lower than GPTQ at 2.25-bit precision. They also report speedups of up to 3.4 times over full precision and up to 29.4% over uniform quantization at equivalent accuracy with five-bit weight-activation quantization. These are distinct reported comparisons, supporting the value of coordinating precision selection with hardware execution rather than treating quantization solely as weight compression.
summary.tldr: MxMoE jointly optimizes mixed precision and GPU execution for Mixture-of-Experts models, improving reported accuracy and inference speed.

title: MxMoE: Mixed-precision Quantization for MoE with Accuracy and Performance Co-Design

abstract: The alignment of large language models (LLMs) often assumes that using more clean data yields better outcomes, overlooking the match between model capacity and example difficulty. Challenging this, we propose a new principle: Preference data vary in difficulty, and overly difficult examples hinder alignment, by exceeding the model’s capacity. Through systematic experimentation, we validate this principle with three key findings: (1) preference examples vary in difficulty, as evidenced by consistent learning orders across alignment runs; (2) overly difficult examples significantly degrade performance across four LLMs and two datasets; and (3) the capacity of a model dictates its threshold for handling difficult examples, underscoring a critical relationship between data selection and model capacity. Building on this principle, we introduce Selective DPO, which filters out overly difficult examples. This simple adjustment improves alignment performance by 9-16% in win rates on the AlpacaEval 2 benchmark compared to the DPO baseline, surpassing a series of DPO variants with different algorithmic adjustments. These results together illuminate the importance of aligning data difficulty with model capacity, offering a transformative perspective for improving alignment strategies in LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/glorgao/SelectiveDPO
originalAbstract: The alignment of large language models (LLMs) often assumes that using more clean data yields better outcomes, overlooking the match between model capacity and example difficulty. Challenging this, we propose a new principle: Preference data vary in difficulty, and overly difficult examples hinder alignment, by exceeding the model’s capacity. Through systematic experimentation, we validate this principle with three key findings: (1) preference examples vary in difficulty, as evidenced by consistent learning orders across alignment runs; (2) overly difficult examples significantly degrade performance across four LLMs and two datasets; and (3) the capacity of a model dictates its threshold for handling difficult examples, underscoring a critical relationship between data selection and model capacity. Building on this principle, we introduce Selective DPO, which filters out overly difficult examples. This simple adjustment improves alignment performance by 9-16% in win rates on the AlpacaEval 2 benchmark compared to the DPO baseline, surpassing a series of DPO variants with different algorithmic adjustments. These results together illuminate the importance of aligning data difficulty with model capacity, offering a transformative perspective for improving alignment strategies in LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/glorgao/SelectiveDPO

paragraphs: This paper examines whether adding more clean preference data always helps align a large language model. Its central proposal is that the usefulness of an example depends on whether the model has enough capacity to learn from it. Examples that are too difficult can hinder alignment, making the match between data and model an important consideration in selecting training data.

The authors investigate this idea through systematic experiments. They find consistent orders in which preference examples are learned across alignment runs, providing evidence that examples differ in difficulty. They also report that overly difficult examples significantly reduce performance across four language models and two datasets. The difficulty threshold a model can handle depends on its capacity, so an example’s suitability is tied to the model being trained.

Using these findings, the authors introduce Selective DPO, which filters out overly difficult preference examples. They report improvements of 9–16% in win rates on AlpacaEval 2 compared with the DPO baseline, along with better results than several DPO variants that change the algorithm. These results support selecting preference data according to model capacity: in the reported experiments, removing examples beyond that capacity improved alignment performance.
summary.tldr: Selective DPO improves alignment in the reported experiments by filtering out preference examples that are too difficult for a model’s capacity.

title: Principled Data Selection for Alignment: The Hidden Risks of Difficult Examples

abstract: To circumvent the alignment of large language models (LLMs), current optimization-based adversarial attacks usually craft adversarial prompts by maximizing the likelihood of a so-called affirmative response. An affirmative response is a manually designed start of a harmful answer to an inappropriate request. While it is often easy to craft prompts that yield a substantial likelihood for the affirmative response, the attacked model frequently does not complete the response in a harmful manner. Moreover, the affirmative objective is usually not adapted to model-specific preferences and essentially ignores the fact that LLMs output a distribution over responses. If low attack success under such an objective is taken as a measure of robustness, the true robustness might be grossly overestimated. To alleviate these flaws, we propose an adaptive and semantic optimization problem over the population of responses. We derive a generally applicable objective via the REINFORCE policy-gradient formalism and demonstrate its efficacy with the state-of-the-art jailbreak algorithms Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD). For example, our objective doubles the attack success rate (ASR) on Llama3 and increases the ASR from 2% to 50% with circuit breaker defense.

paragraphs: Many optimization-based attacks on language models try to make a predefined affirmative opening likely. The paper identifies a mismatch in that objective: a model can produce a seemingly compliant beginning and still avoid completing a harmful answer. The objective also neglects model-specific preferences and the fact that a prompt induces a distribution of possible responses.

The authors formulate an adaptive objective that evaluates response meaning across that distribution. They derive it using the REINFORCE policy-gradient framework and demonstrate it within the existing GCG and PGD attack algorithms. The conceptual change is to align optimization more closely with the harmful-response outcome being measured, rather than relying on a manually chosen opening as its proxy.

Reported examples include doubling attack success on Llama3 and raising success from 2% to 50% against a circuit breaker defense. These results show that the choice of attack objective can substantially change an evaluation. Consequently, low success from the affirmative-response objective may overstate robustness when a better-aligned objective finds more failures.
summary.tldr: A distribution-aware semantic attack objective exposes failures that affirmative-response objectives can miss, changing assessments of model robustness.

title: REINFORCE Adversarial Attacks on Large Language Models: An Adaptive, Distributional, and Semantic Objective

abstract: While numerous frameworks have been developed to enhance the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), there is a scarcity of methods that effectively balance the trade-off between cost and quality. In this paper, we introduce Fleet of Agents (FoA), a novel and intuitive yet principled framework utilizing LLMs as agents to navigate through dynamic tree searches, employing a genetic-type particle filtering approach. FoA spawns a multitude of agents, each exploring the search space autonomously, followed by a selection phase where resampling based on a heuristic value function optimizes the balance between exploration and exploitation. This mechanism enables dynamic branching, adapting the exploration strategy based on discovered solutions. We conduct extensive experiments on four benchmark tasks, ‘G̀ame of 24’\’, ‘M̀ini-Crosswords’\’, ‘ẀebShop’\’{and} ‘S̀ciBench’\’, utilizing four different LLMs, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA3.2-11B, and LLaMA3.2-90B. On average across all tasks and LLMs, FoA obtains an absolute quality improvement of $\simeq 5%$ while requiring only $\simeq 35%$ of the cost of previous SOTA methods. Notably, our analyses reveal that (1) FoA achieves the best cost-quality trade-off among all benchmarked methods, and (2) FoA+ LLaMA3.2-11B surpasses the Llama3.2-90B model. FoA is publicly available at https://github.com/au-clan/FoA.

paragraphs: Using more language-model reasoning can improve answers, but the extra computation must justify its cost. Fleet of Agents addresses this trade-off by organizing multiple LLM agents into a dynamic tree search. Agents initially explore independently, giving the system multiple candidate paths through a problem.

A selection phase then resamples agents according to a heuristic value function using a genetic-type particle-filtering approach. This steers effort toward promising paths while retaining exploration across alternatives. Branching adapts to the solutions encountered, so the search can change how it distributes effort as evidence accumulates.

The authors evaluate four language models on Game of 24, Mini-Crosswords, WebShop, and SciBench. Averaged across these tasks and models, they report roughly five percentage points of absolute quality improvement at approximately 35% of the cost of previous leading methods. Fleet of Agents has the best cost–quality trade-off among the tested methods, and its combination with LLaMA3.2-11B surpasses the evaluated Llama3.2-90B model. These findings show how coordinated search can improve the value obtained from model computation.
summary.tldr: Fleet of Agents adaptively resamples LLM search paths, reporting better average solution quality at about 35% of previous leading methods’ cost.

title: Fleet of Agents: Coordinated Problem Solving with Large Language Models

abstract: We propose Electrostatic Field Matching (EFM), a novel method that is suitable for both generative modelling and distribution transfer tasks. Our approach is inspired by the physics of an electrical capacitor. We place source and target distributions on the capacitor plates and assign them positive and negative charges, respectively. We then learn the capacitor’s electrostatic field using a neural network approximator. To map the distributions to each other, we start at one plate of the capacitor and move the samples along the learned electrostatic field lines until they reach the other plate. We theoretically justify that this approach provably yields the distribution transfer. In practice, we demonstrate the performance of our EFM in toy and image data experiments.

paragraphs: Electrostatic Field Matching treats data generation and distribution transfer as a problem of moving samples between two distributions. Its organizing idea comes from a capacitor: the source distribution occupies one plate with positive charge, and the target distribution occupies the other with negative charge. This supplies a physical picture for the transformation the model should learn.

A neural network approximates the electrostatic field associated with this arrangement. To transfer samples, the method starts them on one plate and follows the learned field lines toward the other. The field therefore determines a continuous route from source samples to their transformed counterparts, making sample movement the central mechanism of generation and transfer.

The authors provide a theoretical justification that the electrostatic construction yields the desired distribution transfer. They also demonstrate the method on toy data and image data. The contribution brings both tasks into one field-based framework: learning the field defines how samples travel, while the theoretical result explains why the construction can connect the intended distributions.
summary.tldr: Electrostatic Field Matching learns a capacitor-inspired field whose trajectories transport samples between distributions for generation and transfer.

title: Field Matching: an Electrostatic Paradigm to Generate and Transfer Data

abstract: We introduce Orthus, a unified multimodal model that excels in generating interleaved images and text from mixed-modality inputs by simultaneously handling discrete text tokens and continuous image features under the AR modeling principle. The continuous treatment of visual signals minimizes the information loss while the fully AR formulation renders the characterization of the correlation between modalities straightforward. Orthus leverages these advantages through its modality-specific heads—one regular language modeling (LM) head predicts discrete text tokens and one diffusion head generates continuous image features. We devise an efficient strategy for building Orthus—by substituting the Vector Quantization (VQ) operation in the existing unified AR model with a soft alternative, introducing a diffusion head, and tuning the added modules to reconstruct images, we can create an Orthus-base model effortlessly (e.g., within 72 A100 GPU hours). Orthus-base can further embrace post-training to craft lengthy interleaved image-text, reflecting the potential for handling intricate real-world tasks. For visual understanding and generation, Orthus achieves a GenEval score of 0.58 and an MME-P score of 1265.8 using 7B parameters, outperforming competing baselines including Show-o and Chameleon.

paragraphs: Orthus generates sequences that interleave images and text from inputs that can also mix these modalities. Its central design combines discrete text tokens with continuous image features within an autoregressive framework. Keeping visual features continuous minimizes information loss, while the sequential formulation makes relationships between image and text content straightforward to model.

The model uses two output heads: a language-modeling head predicts text tokens, and a diffusion head generates image features. To construct a base model, the authors replace hard vector quantization in an existing unified autoregressive model with a soft alternative, add the diffusion head, and tune the new modules for image reconstruction. They report an example requiring 72 A100 GPU hours.

With seven billion parameters, Orthus achieves a GenEval score of 0.58 and an MME-P score of 1265.8, outperforming compared baselines including Show-o and Chameleon. These results support the architecture's combination of visual understanding and generation, while the extended outputs indicate potential for more intricate multimodal tasks.
summary.tldr: Orthus combines autoregressive text prediction with a diffusion image head to generate interleaved image-text sequences using continuous visual features.

title: Orthus: Autoregressive Interleaved Image-Text Generation with Modality-Specific Heads

abstract: We study convergence properties of the discrete-time Mean-Field Langevin Stochastic Gradient Descent-Ascent (MFL-SGDA) algorithm for solving distributional minimax optimization. These problems arise in various applications, such as zero-sum games, generative adversarial networks and distributionally robust learning. Despite the significance of MFL-SGDA in these contexts, the discrete-time convergence rate remains underexplored. To address this gap, we establish a last-iterate convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ for MFL-SGDA. This rate is nearly optimal when compared to the complexity lower bound of its Euclidean counterpart. This rate also matches the complexity of mean-field Langevin stochastic gradient descent for distributional minimization and the outer-loop iteration complexity of an existing double-loop algorithm for distributional minimax problems. By leveraging an elementary analysis framework that avoids PDE-based techniques, we overcome previous limitations and achieve a faster convergence rate.

paragraphs: Distributional minimax optimization involves opposing optimization objectives over distributions. Such problems arise in zero-sum games, generative adversarial networks, and distributionally robust learning. This paper studies the discrete-time Mean-Field Langevin Stochastic Gradient Descent-Ascent algorithm, addressing a gap in understanding how quickly its actual sequence of updates converges.

The main result is a last-iterate convergence rate of O((1/ε) log(1/ε)). Here, ε represents the target accuracy, and last-iterate convergence concerns the final iterate produced by the algorithm. The authors describe the rate as nearly optimal relative to the complexity lower bound for the corresponding Euclidean problem. That comparison gives a specific reference point for assessing the strength of the result.

The rate also matches the complexity of mean-field Langevin stochastic gradient descent for distributional minimization and the outer-loop iteration complexity of an existing double-loop minimax algorithm. The proof uses an elementary analysis framework that avoids techniques based on partial differential equations. Together, the rate and analysis improve the theoretical account of discrete-time distributional minimax optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a nearly optimal last-iterate convergence rate for discrete-time mean-field Langevin stochastic descent-ascent.

title: Convergence of Mean-Field Langevin Stochastic Descent-Ascent for Distributional Minimax Optimization

abstract: Kernel-based hypothesis tests offer a flexible, non-parametric tool to detect high-order interactions in multivariate data, beyond pairwise relationships. Yet the scalability of such tests is limited by the computationally demanding permutation schemes used to generate null approximations. Here we introduce a family of permutation-free high-order tests for joint independence and partial factorisations of $d$ variables. Our tests eliminate the need for permutation-based approximations by leveraging V-statistics and a novel cross-centring technique to yield test statistics with a standard normal limiting distribution under the null. We present implementations of the tests and showcase their efficacy and scalability through synthetic datasets. We also show applications inspired by causal discovery and feature selection, which highlight both the importance of high-order interactions in data and the need for efficient computational methods.

paragraphs: Relationships involving several variables can contain structure that pairwise comparisons do not capture. Kernel-based hypothesis tests offer a flexible way to investigate these higher-order relationships without choosing a fixed parametric model. Their computational bottleneck is often the repeated permutations used to approximate how a statistic behaves when the tested relationship is absent.

The paper introduces tests for joint independence and partial factorizations among multiple variables that avoid those permutations. It combines V-statistics with a new cross-centring technique. Under the null hypothesis, the resulting statistics have a standard normal limiting distribution, providing an asymptotic reference for testing without constructing a permutation-based approximation.

Implementations are evaluated on synthetic datasets to demonstrate effectiveness and scalability. The authors also present applications motivated by causal discovery and feature selection, where relationships among groups of variables can matter. The contribution is a computationally more scalable testing framework whose justification rests on a limiting distribution under the null. It makes higher-order statistical structure more accessible without the repeated reshuffling used by conventional permutation procedures.
summary.tldr: New kernel tests detect higher-order dependence using an asymptotic normal reference instead of costly permutation approximations.

title: Permutation-Free High-Order Interaction Tests

abstract: Collaborative training methods like Federated Learning (FL) and Split Learning (SL) enable distributed machine learning without sharing raw data. However, FL assumes clients can train entire models, which is infeasible for large-scale models. In contrast, while SL alleviates the client memory constraint in FL by offloading most training to the server, it increases network latency due to its sequential nature. Other methods address the conundrum by using local loss functions for parallel client-side training to improve efficiency, but they lack server feedback and potentially suffer poor accuracy. We propose FSL-SAGE (Federated Split Learning via Smashed Activation Gradient Estimation), a new federated split learning algorithm that estimates server-side gradient feedback via auxiliary models. These auxiliary models periodically adapt to emulate server behavior on local datasets. We show that FSL-SAGE achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ is the number of communication rounds. This result matches FedAvg, while significantly reducing communication costs and client memory requirements. Our empirical results also verify that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art FSL methods, offering both communication efficiency and accuracy.

paragraphs: FSL-SAGE addresses a tension in collaborative training without sharing raw data. Federated learning requires clients to train complete models, which can exceed their memory capacity. Split learning moves much of that work to a server, but its sequential exchanges introduce network delays. Training clients with local losses enables parallel work, yet can sacrifice useful server feedback.

The proposed method uses auxiliary models to estimate the server-side gradient feedback that clients need. These auxiliary models periodically adapt to emulate server behavior on local datasets. This creates a way to retain a connection to server training while reducing dependence on sequential feedback exchanges.

The authors establish a convergence rate proportional to one over the square root of the number of communication rounds. This matches the stated FedAvg rate while reducing communication costs and client memory requirements. Experiments also show better accuracy and communication efficiency than existing state-of-the-art federated split learning methods. Together, the theory and empirical results support gradient estimation as a way to address both client resource limits and communication overhead.
summary.tldr: FSL-SAGE estimates server gradients locally to improve federated split learning efficiency while retaining convergence and accuracy benefits.

title: FSL-SAGE: Accelerating Federated Split Learning via Smashed Activation Gradient Estimation

abstract: In this paper, we consider a recommender system that elicits user feedback through pairwise comparisons instead of ratings. We study the problem of learning personalised preferences from such comparison data via collaborative filtering. Similar to the classical matrix completion setting, we assume that users and items are endowed with low-dimensional latent features. These features give rise to user-item utilities, and the comparison outcomes are governed by a discrete choice model over these utilities. The task of learning these features is then formulated as a maximum likelihood problem over the comparison dataset. Despite the resulting optimization problem being nonconvex, we show that gradient-based methods converge exponentially to the latent features, given a warm start. Importantly, this result holds in a sparse data regime, where each user compares only a few pairs of items. Our main technical contribution is to extend key concentration results commonly used in matrix completion to our model. Simulations reveal that the empirical performance of the method exceeds theoretical predictions, even when some assumptions are relaxed. Our work demonstrates that learning personalised recommendations from comparison data is both computationally and statistically efficient.

paragraphs: This paper studies personalized recommendations learned from users choosing between pairs of items. Such feedback supplies relative preferences rather than numerical ratings. The model assumes that users and items have low-dimensional latent features, which determine user-item utilities. A discrete choice model then describes how those utilities produce observed comparison outcomes.

Learning the hidden features becomes a maximum-likelihood problem whose objective is nonconvex. Despite this difficulty, the authors prove that gradient-based methods converge exponentially to the latent features when given a warm start. The initialization condition is part of the guarantee. The result also covers sparse data, where each user compares only a few item pairs.

The technical contribution extends concentration results from matrix completion to this comparison-based model. Simulations show performance better than the theoretical predictions, including when some assumptions are relaxed. Those experiments complement the conditional convergence result. Together, they support the computational and statistical efficiency of learning personalized preferences from a limited number of comparisons.
summary.tldr: Under a latent-feature choice model and warm-start condition, gradient methods rapidly learn personalized preferences from sparse pairwise comparisons.

title: Recommendations with Sparse Comparison Data: Provably Fast Convergence for Nonconvex Matrix Factorization

abstract: Collecting gold-standard phenotype data via manual extraction is typically labor-intensive and slow, whereas automated computational phenotypes (ACPs) offer a systematic and much faster alternative. However, simply replacing the gold-standard with ACPs, without acknowledging their differences, could lead to biased results and misleading conclusions. Motivated by the complexity of incorporating ACPs while maintaining the validity of downstream analyses, in this paper, we consider a semi-supervised learning setting that consists of both labeled data (with gold-standard) and unlabeled data (without gold-standard), under the covariate shift framework. We develop doubly robust and semiparametrically efficient estimators that leverage ACPs for general target parameters in the unlabeled and combined populations. In addition, we carefully analyze the efficiency gains achieved by incorporating ACPs, comparing scenarios with and without their inclusion. Notably, we identify that ACPs for the unlabeled data, instead of for the labeled data, drive the enhanced efficiency gains. To validate our theoretical findings, we conduct comprehensive synthetic experiments and apply our method to multiple real-world datasets, confirming the practical advantages of our approach.
