paragraphs: Automated computational phenotypes can be obtained much faster than manually extracted gold-standard phenotype labels. However, substituting automated outputs directly for those labels can bias downstream analyses. This paper studies how to use the automated information while preserving valid statistical inference when gold-standard labels are available for only part of the data.

The setting is semi-supervised and allows covariate shift between populations. The authors develop doubly robust, semiparametrically efficient estimators for general target parameters in the unlabeled population and in the combined population. These properties concern robustness and statistical efficiency within the stated framework, making the automated phenotypes inputs to a principled estimation procedure rather than unquestioned replacement labels.

The analysis compares estimation efficiency with and without automated phenotypes and identifies a specific source of benefit: automated phenotypes for the unlabeled data drive the additional efficiency gains. Synthetic experiments and applications to several real-world datasets support the theoretical findings. The result clarifies both how to incorporate automated phenotypes and which part of the data supplies their statistical value.
summary.tldr: The paper develops efficient estimators under covariate shift and identifies automated phenotypes on unlabeled data as the source of added efficiency.

title: Towards the Efficient Inference by Incorporating Automated Computational Phenotypes under Covariate Shift

abstract: Commonly used evaluation metrics in multi-label learning all involve base loss functions, and the theoretical guarantees of multi-label learning often rely on the properties of base loss functions. Some recent theoretical works have used the Lipschitz continuity of base loss functions to prove the generalization bounds for multi-label learning, but the impact of the smoothness of base loss functions on the generalization bounds is completely unknown. In an attempt to make up for this gap in the generalization theory of multi-label learning, we develop some novel vector-contraction inequalities for smooth base loss functions and derive tight generalization bounds with no dependency on the number of labels, up to logarithmic terms. We then exploit local Rademacher complexity to develop some novel local vector-contraction inequalities for smooth base loss functions, which induce generalization bounds with a tighter dependency on the number of labels and a faster convergence rate with respect to the number of examples. In addition, we derive tight generalization bounds with no dependency on the number of labels, up to logarithmic terms, for Macro-Averaged AUC by exploiting the Lipschitz continuity and smoothness of base loss functions, respectively. Our state-of-the-art theoretical results provide general theoretical guarantees for the generalization of multi-label learning.

paragraphs: Multi-label learning assigns multiple labels to an example, and its evaluation metrics depend on underlying loss functions. Earlier generalization analyses used the Lipschitz continuity of those losses, which controls how much loss values can change. This paper investigates what additional guarantees follow from smoothness, another property of the loss function.

The authors develop vector-contraction inequalities for smooth base losses and derive tight generalization bounds that are independent of the number of labels apart from logarithmic terms. They then use local Rademacher complexity to build local versions of these inequalities. The resulting bounds have tighter label dependence and converge faster as the number of training examples increases.

The analysis also covers Macro-Averaged AUC, deriving bounds with only logarithmic label dependence through Lipschitz continuity and smoothness, respectively. These results show how properties of base losses shape theoretical guarantees for multi-label prediction. The contribution is a set of sharper guarantees, including faster sample-size convergence, with smoothness providing an analytical ingredient that previous work had left unexplored.
summary.tldr: New inequalities exploit smooth losses to give tighter and faster multi-label generalization bounds, including bounds with only logarithmic label dependence.

title: Tight and Fast Bounds for Multi-Label Learning

abstract: This position paper argues for a fundamental shift in how Large Language Models (LLMs) are integrated into the mental health care domain. We advocate for their role as co-creators rather than mere assistive tools. While LLMs have the potential to enhance accessibility, personalization, and crisis intervention, their adoption remains limited due to concerns about bias, evaluation, over-reliance, dehumanization, and regulatory uncertainties. To address these challenges, we propose two structured pathways: SAFE-i (Supportive, Adaptive, Fair, and Ethical Implementation) Guidelines for ethical and responsible deployment, and HAAS-e (Human-AI Alignment and Safety Evaluation) Framework for multidimensional, human-centered assessment. SAFE-i provides a blueprint for data governance, adaptive model engineering, and real-world integration, ensuring LLMs align with clinical and ethical standards. HAAS-e introduces evaluation metrics that go beyond technical accuracy to measure trustworthiness, empathy, cultural sensitivity, and actionability. We call for the adoption of these structured approaches to establish a responsible and scalable model for LLM-driven mental health support, ensuring that AI complements—rather than replaces—human expertise.

title: Position: Beyond Assistance – Reimagining LLMs as Ethical and Adaptive Co-Creators in Mental Health Care

abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled deep research systems that synthesize comprehensive, report-style answers to open-ended queries by combining retrieval, reasoning, and generation. Yet, most frameworks rely on rigid workflows with one-shot scoping and long autonomous runs, offering little room for course correction if user intent shifts mid-process. We present SteER, a framework for steerable deep research that introduces interpretable, mid-process control into long-horizon research workflows. At each decision point, SteER uses a cost–benefit formulation to determine whether to pause for user input or proceed autonomously. It combines diversity-aware planning with utility signals that reward alignment, novelty, and coverage, and maintains a live persona model that evolves throughout the session. SteER outperforms state-of-the-art open-source and proprietary baselines by up to 22.80% on alignment, leads on quality metrics such as breadth and balance, and is preferred by human readers in 85%+ of pairwise alignment judgments. We also introduce a persona–query benchmark and data-generation pipeline. To our knowledge, this is the first work to advance deep research with an interactive, interpretable control paradigm, paving the way for controllable, user-aligned agents in long-form tasks.

At decision points, the framework weighs the costs and benefits of asking for input against continuing independently. Its planning encourages diverse research directions, while utility signals favor alignment with the user, new information, and coverage. A live persona model changes during the session, giving later decisions an updated representation of the user rather than relying entirely on the opening query.

They also introduce a persona–query benchmark and a data-generation pipeline. These findings support selective, interpretable interaction as a useful component of long research workflows.
summary.tldr: SteER decides when research agents should seek user input, improving reported alignment and report quality through mid-process steering.

title: An Interactive Paradigm for Deep Research

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) enhance performance by generating explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectories, yet enabling them to self-evaluate correctness without external supervision remains a critical challenge. Existing methods often rely on ground-truth labels or shallow output probabilities, neglecting the layerwise evolution of the reasoning trajectory. In this work, we introduce GeoR (Geometry of Reasoning), a white-box self-evaluation framework based on layerwise trajectory evolution. GeoR decomposes reasoning fidelity into two complementary dimensions: (1) Geometric Evolution, which synthesizes the first- and second-order evolution of layerwise hidden-state trajectories to quantify geometric progress in reasoning; and (2) Difficulty-Aware Calibration, which utilizes cross-entropy of reasoning progress to normalize the Geometric Evolution against intrinsic query uncertainty. By jointly modeling these factors, GeoR effectively distinguishes the coherent evolution of correct reasoning from the chaotic trajectories of errors. Extensive experiments across eight LRMs and seven benchmarks demonstrate that GeoR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in AUROC, AUPR, and FPR@95.

title: The Geometry of Reasoning: Self-Evaluation via Layerwise Trajectory Evolution

abstract: Remote change detection in LLMs is a difficult problem. Existing methods are either too expensive for deployment at scale, or require initial white-box access to model weights or grey-box access to log probabilities. We aim to achieve both low cost and strict black-box operation, observing only output tokens. Our approach hinges on specific inputs we call Border Inputs, for which there exists more than one output top token. From a statistical perspective, optimal change detection depends on the model’s Jacobian and the Fisher information of the output distribution, whose analysis at low temperature regimes shows that border inputs enable powerful change detection tests. Building on this insight, we propose the Black-Box Border Input Tracking (B3IT) scheme. Extensive in-vivo and in-vitro experiments show that border inputs are easily found for non-reasoning tested endpoints, and present on-par performance with the best available grey-box approaches. B3IT reduces costs by $30\times$ compared to existing methods, while operating in a strict black-box setting.

paragraphs: Detecting whether a remote language model has changed is difficult when an API exposes only generated tokens. Existing approaches can be expensive or depend on access to model weights or output probabilities. This paper develops a method for monitoring changes under strict black-box access while reducing the cost of repeated testing.

The key is to find Border Inputs, prompts for which more than one output token shares the top position. The authors analyze change detection using the model’s Jacobian and the Fisher information of its output distribution. At low temperatures, that analysis shows why border inputs can support powerful statistical tests. Black-Box Border Input Tracking, or B3IT, builds a monitoring scheme around this insight.

Experiments find border inputs readily for the tested non-reasoning endpoints. B3IT matches the performance of the best available grey-box approaches while reducing costs by 30 times relative to existing methods. The findings support concentrating monitoring on sensitive inputs, with the reported ease of finding them specifically established for the non-reasoning endpoints tested.
summary.tldr: B3IT detects remote language-model changes using only output tokens from carefully selected inputs, with reported costs reduced by 30 times.

title: Token-Efficient Change Detection in LLM APIs

abstract: Despite rapid progress on coding agents, progress on their multimodal counterparts has lagged behind. A key challenge is the scarcity of evaluation testbeds that combine the complexity of software development with the need for deep multimodal understanding. In game development, agents must navigate large, dense codebases while manipulating intrinsically multimodal assets such as shaders, sprites, and animations within a visual game scene. We present GameDevBench, the first benchmark for evaluating agents on game development tasks. GameDevBench consists of 333 tasks derived from web and video tutorials. Tasks require significant multimodal understanding and are complex—the average solution requires over three times the lines of code and file changes compared to prior software development benchmarks. Agents struggle with game development, with the best agent and method solving only $53.8%$ of tasks. We find a strong correlation between perceived task difficulty and multimodal complexity, with average success rate dropping from $51.4%$ on gameplay-oriented tasks to $33.0%$ on 2D graphics tasks. To improve multimodal capability, we introduce two simple image and video-based feedback mechanisms for agents. Despite their simplicity, these methods consistently improve performance, increasing GPT-5.4’s performance from $41.1%$ to $52.0%$ when given visual feedback.

title: GameDevBench: Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Through Game Development

abstract: We present SWE-Bench Pro, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate software engineering capabilities through complex, realistic programming challenges. This benchmark extends beyond traditional algorithmic problems to encompass the full spectrum of professional software development tasks. The dataset comprises 1,865 problems sourced from 41 active software engineering repositories, spanning 123 unique programming languages and various application domains. The benchmark is structured into public and private components, with public access to problems from 11 repositories and private evaluation sets from 12 repositories across 4 distinct problem categories. SWE-Bench Pro addresses limitations of existing evaluation frameworks by incorporating problems that reflect real-world software engineering scenarios, including substantial codebases, complex enterprise applications, and multi-file projects requiring sophisticated reasoning and code modification skills. Problems range from early-stage startup environments to enterprise-level applications, with the private commercial set remaining inaccessible to maintain evaluation integrity while enabling public access to representative problems for professional development. Our evaluation methodology employs diverse coding approaches and models under controlled conditions, ensuring robust performance assessment across multiple programming paradigms. Results demonstrate significant performance variations across different problem categories, with traditional algorithmic challenges showing notably higher success rates compared to complex, multi-file engineering tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial gaps in current capabilities for handling real-world software engineering scenarios, particularly in areas requiring deep contextual understanding, cross-file reasoning, and integration with existing large-scale systems. This work contributes a more comprehensive and realistic evaluation framework for assessing software engineering capabilities, providing insights into current limitations and establishing a foundation for future development in automated software engineering tools and methodologies.

summary.tldr: SWE-Bench Pro tests realistic repository-scale engineering and reveals substantial capability gaps on complex, multi-file tasks.

title: SWE-Bench Pro: Can AI Agents Solve Long-Horizon Software Engineering Tasks?

abstract: Continual Learning (CL) requires models to sequentially adapt to new tasks without forgetting old knowledge. Recently, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a representative Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, has gained increasing attention in CL. Several LoRA-based CL methods reduce interference across tasks by separating their update spaces, typically building the new space from the estimated null space of past tasks. However, they (i) overlook task-shared directions, which suppresses knowledge transfer, and (ii) fail to capture truly effective task-specific directions since these “null bases" of old tasks can remain nearly inactive for new task under correlated tasks. To address this, we study LoRA learning capability from a projection energy perspective, and propose Low-rank Decomposition and Adaptation (LoDA). It performs a task-driven decomposition to build general and truly task-specific LoRA subspaces by solving two energy-based objectives, decoupling directions for knowledge sharing and isolation. LoDA fixes LoRA down-projections on two subspaces and learns robust up-projections via a Gradient-Aligned Optimization (GAO) approach. After each task, before integrating the LoRA updates into the backbone, LoDA derives a closed-form recalibration for the general update, approximating a feature-level joint optimum along this task-shared direction. Experiments indicate that LoDA outperforms existing CL methods.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires adapting to new tasks while retaining previous knowledge. LoRA-based methods often separate update spaces to reduce interference, using estimated null spaces of older tasks. This paper argues that such separation can overlook shared knowledge and select directions that remain nearly inactive for a new task, particularly when tasks are correlated.

Low-rank Decomposition and Adaptation, or LoDA, uses projection energy to construct two kinds of subspace: one for general, shared knowledge and another for genuinely task-specific updates. It solves separate energy-based objectives to distinguish sharing from isolation. LoRA down-projections are fixed on these subspaces, while up-projections are learned through Gradient-Aligned Optimization.

After each task, LoDA recalibrates the general update with a closed-form expression before incorporating the adapter updates into the backbone. This approximates a feature-level joint optimum along the shared direction. Experiments indicate better performance than existing continual-learning methods. The contribution makes useful transfer and interference control separate design objectives, rather than assuming that avoiding old-task directions alone produces effective new-task learning.
summary.tldr: LoDA separates shared and task-specific LoRA directions to support knowledge transfer while controlling interference during continual learning.

title: Task-Driven Subspace Decomposition for Knowledge Sharing and Isolation in LoRA-based Continual Learning

abstract: Recent studies have shown that semantic watermarks, which embed information into the initial noise of latent diffusion models (LDMs), are vulnerable to black-box forgery attacks. However, existing methods primarily rely on empirical evidence and lack a rigorous theoretical understanding of the conditions under which such attacks succeed or fail. To bridge this gap, we rethink the nature of such attacks through the lens of rate-distortion in the latent space. Our analysis identifies an irreducible distortion floor due to structural mismatches between proxy and target models, which fundamentally limits the fidelity of forged watermarks. We further characterize this distortion as structured geometric deviations on the latent manifold, in the form of global drift and local deformation rather than stochastic noise. Leveraging these insights, we propose a scheme-agnostic detection method that distinguishes forged samples before watermark verification. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across diverse black-box scenarios, while preserving robustness to common distortions.

paragraphs: Semantic watermarks place information in the initial noise used by latent diffusion models. Previous work has demonstrated black-box forgery attacks, but the conditions governing their success have lacked a clear theoretical explanation. This paper examines the problem through rate-distortion analysis in latent space, focusing on what prevents a forgery from reproducing the target watermark faithfully.

The analysis identifies an irreducible distortion floor arising from structural differences between proxy and target models. It further describes the resulting errors as organized geometric deviations: global drift and local deformation of the latent manifold. Treating these errors as structured changes, rather than ordinary random noise, provides the basis for a different way to recognize forged samples.

The authors use that insight to develop a detection method that operates before watermark verification and does not depend on a particular watermark scheme. Experiments report effectiveness across diverse black-box scenarios while retaining robustness to common distortions. The contribution connects an analyzed fidelity limit to a practical detection signal, rather than interpreting the distortion floor as proof that all forgery attempts must fail.
summary.tldr: The paper links black-box watermark forgery to structured latent-space distortion and uses that structure to detect forged samples.

title: Rethinking Forgery Attacks on Semantic Watermarks in Black-Box Settings: A Geometric Distortion Perspective

abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) can boost LLM reasoning through long chain-of-thought (CoT), but the linear KV-cache growth amplifies the memory-bound bottleneck of LLM decoding. Query-aware sparse decoding methods can achieve state-of-the-art performance under constrained FLOP budget, but are mainly constrained by both sequential-dependent page filtering and coarse-grained token selection, hampering the serving efficiency and model performance on TTS tasks under high concurrency and long CoT scenarios, where token selection can even occupy higher runtime than the forward pipeline itself. In this paper, we first find that the query state of the current decoding token can be approximated in a unified manner from a short sliding window of recent queries, enabling training-free query-aware sparsity without sequential dependency in the decoding loop. Based on the findings, we propose $\texttt{\textbf{AsyncSpade}}$, an asynchronous framework for efficient TTS, built on two core components: $\textbf{(1) a novel light-weight temporal-regressive module}$ that predicts the next-token query state, and $\textbf{(2) an asynchronous disaggregated framework}$ that decouples the KV cache selection from the auto-regressive decoding loop, overlapping the token-level KV selection with the forward inference computation through asynchronism, thereby eliminating the sequential dependency without sacrificing model performance. We validate the effectiveness of $\texttt{AsyncSpade}$ on common LLM serving setups with an A100 node, where $\texttt{AsyncSpade}$ can fully overlap KV-cache operations with the inference pipeline within a certain workload range, $\textbf{achieving theoretical optimal time-per-output-token (TPOT)}$. Specifically, $\texttt{AsyncSpade}$ delivers over 20% reduction on TPOT compared to SoTA baseline ($\textit{i.e.}$ Quest) and at least 50% TPOT reduction compared to full attention on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B models, while matching or surpassing their accuracy on various TTS benchmarks (AIME-24/25, GPQA-Diamond, MATH-500). Our code is available through https://github.com/UNITES-Lab/AsyncSpade.

paragraphs: Long reasoning sequences can improve language-model answers, but they also enlarge the cache of attention keys and values. Sparse decoding reduces how much of that cache the model reads. Selecting the relevant entries can itself become expensive, especially with many concurrent requests, because selection normally waits for information from the current decoding step.

AsyncSpade uses the observation that a short window of recent attention queries can approximate the query needed next. A lightweight temporal prediction module supplies that estimate without additional training. The system then separates cache selection from the main decoding loop, allowing token-level selection to run alongside forward computation instead of delaying it.

On an A100 serving setup, the method reduces time per output token by over 20% against Quest and at least 50% against full attention for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, while matching or exceeding their tested reasoning accuracy. Within a particular workload range, cache operations overlap completely with inference, reaching the paper’s theoretical optimum for token latency. That optimum is explicitly workload-dependent.
summary.tldr: AsyncSpade predicts upcoming attention queries so cache selection can overlap with decoding, reducing reasoning latency while preserving tested accuracy.

title: AsyncSpade: Efficient Test-Time Scaling with Asynchronous Sparse Decoding

abstract: In streaming Reinforcement Learning (RL), transitions are observed and discarded immediately after a single update. While this minimizes resource usage for on-device applications, it makes agents notoriously sample-inefficient, since value-based losses alone struggle to extract meaningful representations from transient data. We propose extending Self-Predictive Representations (SPR) to the streaming pipeline to maximize the utility of every observed frame. However, due to the highly correlated samples induced by the streaming regime, naively applying this auxiliary loss results in training instabilities. Thus, we introduce orthogonal gradient updates relative to the momentum target and resolve gradient conflicts arising from streaming-specific optimizers. Validated across the Atari, MinAtar, and Octax suites, our approach systematically outperforms existing streaming baselines. Latent-space analysis, including t-SNE visualizations and effective-rank measurements, confirms that our method learns significantly richer representations, bridging the performance gap caused by the absence of a replay buffer, while remaining efficient enough to train on just a few CPU cores.

We propose extending Self-Predictive Representations (SPR) to the streaming pipeline to maximize the utility of every observed frame. However, due to the highly correlated samples induced by the streaming regime, naively applying this auxiliary loss results in training instabilities. Thus, we introduce orthogonal gradient updates relative to the momentum target and resolve gradient conflicts arising from streaming-specific optimizers. Validated across the Atari, MinAtar, and Octax suites, our approach systematically outperforms existing streaming baselines. Latent-space analysis, including t-SNE visualizations and effective-rank measurements, confirms that our method learns significantly richer representations, bridging the performance gap caused by the absence of a replay buffer, while remaining efficient enough to train on just a few CPU cores.

The proposed solution uses gradient updates orthogonal to the momentum target and addresses conflicts introduced by optimizers designed for streaming learning.

The contribution is therefore both a way to extract more learning from transient observations and a set of changes that make the auxiliary objective workable in the streaming regime.
summary.tldr: Streaming-compatible self-predictive learning improves representations and reinforcement learning performance while retaining low resource requirements.

title: Squeezing More from the Stream : Learning Representation Online for Streaming Reinforcement Learning

abstract: While the shift toward unified foundation models has revolutionized many deep learning domains, sleep medicine remains largely restricted to task-specific models that focus on localized micro-structure features. These approaches often neglect the rich, multi-modal context of Polysomnography (PSG) and fail to capture the global macro-structure of a full night’s sleep. To address this, we introduce SleepMaMi, a Sleep Foundation Model engineered to master both hour-long sleep architectures and fine-grained signal morphologies. Our framework utilizes a hierarchical dual-encoder design: a Macro-Encoder to model full-night temporal dependencies and a Micro-Encoder to capture short-term characteristics from biosignals. Macro-Encoder is trained via Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning, which aligns overnight sleep patterns with objective subject metadata, such as age and sex, to refine global representations. Micro-Encoder is optimized via a hybrid Masked Autoencoder (MAE) and multi-modal contrastive objective. Pre-trained on a massive corpus of $>$20,000 PSG recordings (158K hours), SleepMaMi outperforms or matches existing foundation models across a diverse suite of downstream tasks, demonstrating superior generalizability and label-efficient adaptation for clinical sleep analysis.

title: SleepMaMi: A Universal Sleep Foundation Model for Integrating Macro- and Micro-structures

abstract: Transformers have shown inconsistent success in AI planning tasks, and theoretical understanding of when generalization should be expected has been limited. We take important steps towards addressing this gap by analyzing the ability of decoder-only models to verify whether a given plan correctly solves a given planning instance. To analyse the general setting where the number of objects – and thus the effective input alphabet – grows at test time, we introduce C*-RASP, an extension of C-RASP designed to establish length generalization guarantees for transformers under the simultaneous growth in sequence length and vocabulary size. Our results identify a large class of classical planning domains for which transformers can provably learn to verify long plans, and structural properties that significantly affects the learnability of length generalizable solutions. Empirical experiments corroborate our theory.

Empirical experiments corroborate our theory.

paragraphs: A planning verifier checks whether a proposed sequence of actions solves a given problem. This paper studies when decoder-only transformers can learn that task and generalize to longer plans. The motivation is the inconsistent performance of transformers on planning tasks and the limited theoretical understanding of when successful generalization should be expected.

The analysis addresses a setting where test problems contain more objects than training problems. This expands both the sequence length and the effective vocabulary, so a guarantee about longer inputs alone would not capture the full challenge. The authors introduce C*-RASP, an extension of C-RASP designed to reason about these two kinds of growth together.

Using this framework, the paper identifies a large class of classical planning domains in which transformers can provably learn to verify long plans. It also identifies structural properties that substantially affect whether length-generalizing solutions are learnable. Experiments support the theoretical account. The results clarify conditions for successful verification across planning domains, rather than asserting that every planning task admits the same generalization behavior.
summary.tldr: C*-RASP provides a framework for proving transformer plan-verification generalization as both plan length and object vocabulary grow.

title: On the Ability of Transformers to Verify Plans

abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) shape classification plays a central role in computer vision and computer-aided design (CAD), underpinning applications in intelligent manufacturing, automated inspection, and digital engineering. Despite recent progress with 3D CNNs and graph-based approaches, existing methods often overlook the geometric-topological regularities and symmetry principles intrinsic to CAD boundary representations (B-reps). To address this challenge, we introduce EquiCAD, a symmetry-aware learning framework that integrates equivariant representations with graph-based reasoning. By leveraging group-theoretic decomposition of curve and surface descriptors, EquiCAD preserves symmetry-consistent feature transformations while retaining rich geometric details. The model further exploits hierarchical message passing to capture interactions between local features and global structure. Experimental results across multiple datasets, including SolidLetters, Parts, the Machining Feature benchmark, and our newly constructed Features dataset, demonstrate substantial improvements over prior state-of-the-art approaches, particularly on industrially relevant shapes with fine-grained attributes. These findings highlight the value of symmetry-aware modeling for robust and generalizable 3D shape analysis.

paragraphs: CAD shapes contain geometric detail and structured relationships among their boundary elements. The paper argues that existing 3D classification methods often underuse these regularities and the symmetry principles inherent in boundary representations. EquiCAD is designed to incorporate both into how a model represents and reasons about a shape.

The method uses a group-theoretic decomposition of curve and surface descriptors to construct equivariant representations. In plain terms, its features transform consistently with the symmetries being modeled while retaining detailed geometry. Hierarchical message passing then links information at different levels, allowing local features and broader shape structure to influence one another.

Experiments on SolidLetters, Parts, the Machining Feature benchmark, and the authors' new Features dataset show substantial improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods. The gains are particularly pronounced for industrially relevant shapes distinguished by fine-grained attributes. These findings support combining symmetry-aware representations with graph reasoning when classification depends on subtle geometric features and their arrangement within a complete CAD object.
summary.tldr: EquiCAD combines symmetry-consistent geometric features and hierarchical graph reasoning to improve classification of detailed CAD shapes.

title: EquiCAD: A Geometric Equivariant Neural Network for 3D Shape Classification

abstract: Understanding gradient descent dynamics is key to explaining the success of over-parameterized models, where implicit bias manifests through conservation laws in gradient flow. While such laws are well understood for linear and ReLU networks, they remain largely unexplored for modern architectures. This work develops a unified framework to characterize conservation laws for contemporary models, including feedforward networks with GELU, SiLU, and SwiGLU activations, multihead attention with sinusoidal and rotary positional encodings, and Mixture-of-Experts architectures under diverse gating designs. Our theoretical findings are supported by experiments that validate the predicted invariants.

paragraphs: Training changes a neural network’s parameters, but some relationships among those parameters can remain constant along gradient flow, the continuous-time description of gradient-based learning. These conserved quantities help describe implicit bias: the ways an optimization process favors particular solutions even when a large model has many possible ways to fit its data.

This paper develops a unified framework for characterizing such conservation laws in modern architectures. Its scope includes feedforward networks using GELU, SiLU, and SwiGLU activations, multihead attention using sinusoidal or rotary positional encodings, and mixtures of experts with different gating designs. This extends the analysis beyond linear and ReLU networks, where conservation laws are already better understood.

The authors also report experiments supporting the invariants predicted by their theory. The contribution is a way to connect concrete architectural choices with quantities preserved during training dynamics. That makes conservation laws available as a tool for studying contemporary models, while keeping the theoretical focus on gradient flow rather than asserting that every discrete training procedure preserves identical quantities.
summary.tldr: A unified framework characterizes conserved quantities in gradient flow for modern activations, positional encodings, and mixture-of-experts architectures.

title: Conservation Laws for Modern Neural Architectures

abstract: The progressive scaling of large language models (LLMs) has consistently enhanced multimodal understanding and advanced reasoning capabilities, but has substantially increased computational and hardware execution overhead. In this paper, we present S-Quant, a novel post-method that compresses only model weights. We partition each weight tensor into fixed-size blocks and assign a single seed to each block. The seed drives a hardware-friendly Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) generator that dynamically produces multiple basis matrices. Each block is then reconstructed as a linear combination of these basis matrices, with block-specific coefficients, which substantially reduces the amount of stored data, increases the data-transfer efficiency between memory and compute units, and consequently speeds up memory-bound inference for large language models. Experimental results on different LLM models ranging from 7B–70B parameters show that S-Quant attains state-of-the-art performance when weights are compressed to approximately 3-bit or 4-bit. We also design a dedicated ASIC accelerator that achieves a 4$\times$ speed-up for memory-bound LLM inference.

paragraphs: Large language models require substantial storage and movement of model weights. When inference is limited by memory access, reducing the information transferred to compute units can improve speed. S-Quant tackles this by compressing weights through a representation that regenerates parts of each weight block from a compact seed.

The method partitions weight tensors into fixed-size blocks. Each block receives a seed that drives a hardware-friendly Linear Feedback Shift Register generator, producing several basis matrices. Block-specific coefficients combine these matrices to reconstruct the weights. Storing seeds and coefficients substantially reduces the stored data and improves transfer efficiency between memory and computation.

Experiments on language models ranging from seven to 70 billion parameters report state-of-the-art performance at approximately three-bit and four-bit weight compression. The authors also design a dedicated ASIC accelerator and report a fourfold speedup for memory-bound inference. The contribution joins a compact weight representation with hardware designed to regenerate it efficiently; the stated acceleration applies to the memory-bound setting.
summary.tldr: S-Quant reconstructs weight blocks from seeded basis matrices and coefficients, delivering strong low-bit results and a fourfold memory-bound inference speedup on its ASIC.

title: S-Quant: Rethinking Weight Quantization with Seed-Based Generation

abstract: While Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) excel at predictive tasks on satellite imagery, their performance can arise from visual correlations rather than underlying structural invariants, making certain perception-based out-of-distribution accuracy a poor proxy for scientific utility. As a result, models may look correct without reasoning correctly—a discrepancy we term the Perception–Physics Paradox. To address this gap, we introduce Scientific Alignment as an implicit objective for representation learning in scientific domains. We study a principled, testable aspect of scientific alignment through Structural Isomorphism, which requires latent representations to uniquely identify physical systems up to a linear reparameterization. This perspective induces a hierarchy of necessary conditions and yields a systematic probing protocol for physical and causal interpretability. To operationalize this framework, we release TC-Bench, a foundational global dataset and automated construction pipeline for tropical cyclone research, and show that current VFMs rely on visual shortcuts that collapse in extreme regimes, indicating that scientific alignment does not arise as a natural byproduct of visual scaling alone.

title: The Perception–Physics Paradox: Probing Scientific Alignment with TC-Bench

abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of carrying out long-running, real-world tasks. However, as the amount of context grows, their reliability often deteriorate, a phenomenon known as "context rot". Existing long-context benchmarks primarily focus on single-step settings that evaluate a model’s ability to retrieve information from a long snippet. In realistic scenarios, however, LLMs often need to act as agents that explore environments, follow instructions and plans, extract useful information, and predict correct actions under a dynamically growing context. To assess language agents in such settings, we introduce LOCA-bench (a benchmark for LOng-Context Agents). Given a task prompt, LOCA-bench leverages automated and scalable control of environment states to regulate the agent’s context length. This design enables LOCA-bench to extend the context length potentially to infinity in a controlled way while keeping the underlying task semantics fixed. LOCA-bench evaluates language agents as a combination of models and scaffolds, including various context management strategies. While agent performance generally degrades as the environment states grow more complex, advanced context management techniques can substantially improve the overall success rate. We will open-source LOCA-bench to provide a platform for evaluating models and scaffolds in long-context, agentic scenarios.

summary.tldr: LOCA-bench measures agent reliability under controlled context growth while keeping the underlying task semantics fixed.

title: LOCA-bench: Benchmarking Language Agents Under Controllable and Extreme Context Growth

abstract: Zeroth-order optimizers have recently emerged as an attractive approach for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), as they avoid backpropagation and can substantially reduce memory overhead relative to standard first-order training. However, existing zeroth-order methods rely on hand-crafted, static sampling strategies that are not adaptable to model-specific structures. To address this, we propose ZO-Finetuner, a learning-based zeroth-order optimizer for LLMs that automatically learns efficient perturbation strategies through a compact and memory-efficient design. Motivated by the fact that a small set of base LLMs is repeatedly fine-tuned across tasks, ZO-Finetuner supports one-time per-model training and reuse across downstream tasks with minimal overhead. Therefore, learning the optimizer once for a given LLM and reusing it across diverse downstream tasks is both feasible and highly desirable. Accordingly, ZO-Finetuner is designed to scale learning to learn (L2L) to the foundation-model era by supporting one-time per-model training with minimal overhead. Experiments on 4 LLMs and 7 datasets show that ZO-Finetuner outperforms prior zeroth-order baselines in 82.1% of task-model combinations, thereby demonstrating strong performance and scalability for efficient LLM fine-tuning.

Its effectiveness depends on how it perturbs model parameters to guide updates. This paper targets a weakness of existing approaches: their sampling strategies are hand-designed and static, rather than adapted to a particular model’s structure.

ZO-Finetuner learns the perturbation strategy using a compact, memory-efficient optimizer. summary.tldr: ZO-Finetuner learns reusable, model-specific perturbation strategies for memory-efficient language-model fine-tuning without backpropagation.

title: Learning a Zeroth-Order Optimizer for Fine-Tuning LLMs

abstract: Training 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) at billion-primitive scale is fundamentally memory-bound: each Gaussian primitive carries a large attribute vector, and the aggregate parameter table quickly exceeds GPU capacity, limiting prior systems to tens of millions of Gaussians on commodity single-GPU hardware. We observe that 3DGS training is inherently sparse and trajectory-conditioned: each iteration activates only the Gaussians visible from the current camera batch, so GPU memory can serve as a working-set cache rather than a persistent parameter store. Building on this insight, we introduce TideGS, an out-of-core training framework that manages parameters across an SSD-CPU-GPU hierarchy via three synergistic techniques: block-virtualized geometry for SSD-aligned spatial locality, a hierarchical asynchronous pipeline to overlap I/O with computation, and trajectory-adaptive differential streaming that transfers only incremental working-set deltas between iterations. Experiments show that TideGS enables training with over one billion Gaussians on a single 24-GB GPU while achieving the best reconstruction quality among evaluated single-GPU baselines on large-scale scenes, scaling beyond prior out-of-core baselines (e.g., 100M Gaussians) and standard in-memory training (e.g., 11M Gaussians). Project page: https://sponge-lab.github.io/TideGS/

TideGS exploits the observation that each training iteration uses only primitives visible from its current camera batch. GPU memory can therefore hold the active working set while the larger parameter collection resides elsewhere.

The framework manages parameters across SSD storage, CPU memory, and GPU memory. It groups geometry into blocks suited to SSD access, overlaps data movement with computation through an asynchronous hierarchy, and adapts streaming to the camera trajectory. The results show how exploiting visibility and camera-dependent reuse can make storage capacity outside the GPU useful for substantially larger training problems.
summary.tldr: TideGS streams active Gaussian parameters across SSD, CPU, and GPU memory to train billion-primitive scenes on one 24-GB GPU.

title: TideGS: Scalable Training of Over One Billion 3D Gaussian Splatting Primitives via Out-of-Core Optimization

abstract: Red teaming is critical for uncovering vulnerabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs). While automated methods have improved scalability, existing approaches often rely on static heuristics or stochastic search, rendering them brittle against advanced safety alignment. To address this, we introduce Metis, a framework that reformulates jailbreaking as inference-time policy optimization within an adversarial Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Metis employs a self-evolving metacognitive loop to perform causal diagnosis of a target’s defense logic and leverages structured feedback as a semantic gradient to refine its policy, offering enhanced interpretability through transparent reasoning traces. Extensive evaluations across 10 diverse models demonstrate that Metis achieves the strongest average Attack Success Rate (ASR) among compared methods at 89.2%, maintaining high efficacy on resilient frontier models (e.g., 76.0% on O1 and 78.0% on GPT-5-chat) where traditional baselines exhibit substantial performance degradation. By replacing redundant exploration with directed optimization, Metis reduces token costs by an average of 8.2$\times$ (and up to 11.4$\times$). Our analysis reveals that current defenses remain vulnerable to internally-steered, closed-loop reasoning trajectories under the tested settings, highlighting a critical need for next-generation defenses capable of reasoning about safety dynamically during inference.

The paper argues that static heuristics and stochastic search can become brittle against stronger alignment. Metis instead treats the process as policy optimization at inference time, using an adversarial partially observable decision model to represent uncertainty about the target’s defenses.

Its central mechanism is a feedback loop that diagnoses the target’s defense behavior and updates its policy. Structured feedback acts as a semantic optimization signal, while reasoning traces make the adaptation process more interpretable. The intended advantage is more directed exploration: information from previous interactions informs subsequent decisions instead of repeatedly searching without that structure.

Across ten models, Metis reports the strongest average attack success rate among compared methods, at 89.2%, including 76.0% on O1 and 78.0% on GPT-5-chat. Reported token costs fall by an average factor of 8.2, reaching 11.4 in some cases. The findings identify vulnerability to adaptive, closed-loop reasoning in the tested settings and motivate defenses that reason dynamically about safety during inference.
summary.tldr: Metis uses feedback-driven policy optimization for red teaming, reporting high attack success and lower token costs across ten tested models.

title: Metis: Learning to Jailbreak LLMs via Self-Evolving Metacognitive Policy Optimization

abstract: Engineering problem solving is central to real-world decision-making, requiring mathematical formulations that not only represent complex problems but also produce feasible solutions under data and physical constraints. Unlike mathematical problem solving, which operates on predefined formulations, engineering tasks demand open-ended analysis, feasibility-driven modeling, and iterative refinement. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in reasoning and code generation, they often fail to ensure feasibility, which limits their applicability to engineering problem solving. To address this challenge, we propose EngiAgent, a multi-agent system with a fully connected coordinator that simulates expert workflows through specialized agents for problem analysis, modeling, verification, solving, and solution evaluation. The fully connected coordinator enables flexible feedback routing, overcoming the rigidity of prior pipeline-based reflection methods and ensuring feasibility at every stage of the process. This design not only improves robustness to diverse failure cases such as data extraction errors, constraint inconsistencies, and solver failures, but also enhances the overall quality of problem solving. Empirical results across four representative domains demonstrate that EngiAgent achieves substantial improvements in feasibility compared to prior approaches, establishing a new paradigm for feasibility-oriented engineering problem solving with LLMs. Our source code and data are available at https://github.com/AI4Engi/EngiAgent.

paragraphs: Engineering problems require more than solving a supplied equation. A system must interpret the situation, construct a mathematical formulation, and produce a solution compatible with available data and physical constraints. Language models can reason and write code, yet failures to satisfy those constraints can make their proposed engineering solutions unusable.

EngiAgent organizes specialized agents around problem analysis, modeling, verification, solving, and solution evaluation. A fully connected coordinator routes feedback flexibly among these roles. This supports iterative correction throughout the workflow instead of restricting reflection to a fixed sequence. The design targets several distinct failure sources, including incorrectly extracted data, inconsistent constraints, and unsuccessful solver runs.

Across four representative domains, the authors report substantial improvements in solution feasibility compared with prior approaches. The central contribution is coordination organized around whether a proposed solution can actually work under the problem’s constraints. Flexible feedback matters because different failures originate at different stages, and improving the final answer may require revisiting the formulation or underlying data rather than only repeating the solving step.
summary.tldr: EngiAgent uses flexible coordination among specialized agents to improve the feasibility of solutions to open-ended engineering problems.

title: EngiAgent: Fully Connected Coordination of LLM Agents for Solving Open-ended Engineering Problems with Feasible Solutions

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents trained using reinforcement learning has achieved superhuman performance in low-cost environments like games, mathematics, and coding. However, these successes have not translated to complex domains where the cost of interaction is high, such as the physical cost of running robots, the time cost of ML engineering, and the resource cost of scientific experiments. The true bottleneck for achieving the next level of agent performance for these complex and high-cost domains lies in the expense of executing actions to acquire reward signals. To address this gap, this paper argues that we should use world models as an intermediary between agents and the real world. We discuss how world models, viewed as models of dynamics, rewards, and task distributions, can overcome fundamental barriers of high-cost actions such as extreme off-policy learning and sample inefficiency in long-horizon tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate how world models can provide critical and rich learning signals to agents across a broad set of domains, including machine learning engineering, computer use, robotics, and AI for science. Lastly, we identify the challenges of building these world models and propose actionable items along dataset curation, architecture design, scaling, and evaluation of world models.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that the cost of obtaining feedback limits agents in complex domains. Reinforcement-learning successes in relatively inexpensive environments have not readily transferred to robotics, machine-learning engineering, or scientific experimentation. In these settings, taking an action to learn whether it was useful can consume substantial physical resources, time, or experimental capacity.

The authors propose placing world models between agents and the real world. They define these models broadly to include environment dynamics, rewards, and task distributions. Such models could supply learning signals while addressing difficulties associated with learning from actions generated by different policies and with obtaining useful feedback across long sequences of actions.

The paper demonstrates how world models can provide rich learning signals across machine-learning engineering, computer use, robotics, and AI for science. It also identifies challenges in building them and proposes work on dataset curation, architectures, scaling, and evaluation. The central research direction is to improve the intermediary that supplies experience and feedback when direct interaction is expensive.
summary.tldr: The authors propose world models as intermediaries that provide learning signals for agents when real-world actions are costly.

abstract: The hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model (HDP-HMM) is a flexible, nonparametric model which allows state spaces of unknown size to be learned from data. We demonstrate some limitations of the original HDP-HMM formulation, and propose a sticky extension which allows more robust learning of smoothly varying dynamics. Using DP mixtures, this formulation also allows learning of more complex, multimodal emission distributions. We further develop a sampling algorithm that employs a truncated approximation of the DP to jointly resample the full state sequence, greatly improving mixing rates. Via extensive experiments with synthetic data and the NIST speaker diarization database, we demonstrate the advantages of our sticky extension, and the utility of the HDP-HMM in real-world applications.

We demonstrate some limitations of the original HDP-HMM formulation, and propose a sticky extension which allows more robust learning of smoothly varying dynamics. Using DP mixtures, this formulation also allows learning of more complex, multimodal emission distributions. We further develop a sampling algorithm that employs a truncated approximation of the DP to jointly resample the full state sequence, greatly improving mixing rates. paragraphs: The paper studies a hidden-state model for sequences in which the number of underlying states is unknown. The hierarchical Dirichlet process hidden Markov model can learn the size of its state space from data. The authors identify limitations in its original formulation when modeling dynamics that should persist smoothly over time.

They introduce a sticky extension that supports state persistence and more robust learning of such dynamics. The formulation also uses Dirichlet process mixtures to represent more complex emission distributions, including distributions with several modes. This allows observations associated with a state to have richer patterns without giving up the model's flexible treatment of hidden states.

The authors additionally develop a sampling procedure that jointly redraws the entire state sequence using a truncated approximation of the Dirichlet process. They report greatly improved mixing rates, meaning the sampler moves more effectively through possible explanations of the data. Experiments on synthetic sequences and a speaker diarization database demonstrate advantages of the sticky extension and support its usefulness for real-world sequence modeling.
summary.tldr: A sticky HDP-HMM improves modeling of persistent states and combines richer observations with more effective sequence sampling.

title: An HDP-HMM for systems with state persistence

abstract: We propose an analytic moment-based filter for nonlinear stochastic dynamical systems modeled by Gaussian processes. Exact expressions for the expected value and the covariance matrix are provided for both the prediction and the filter step, where an additional Gaussian assumption is exploited in the latter case. The new filter does not require further approximations. In particular, it avoids sample approximations. We compare the filter to a variety of available Gaussian filters, such as the EKF, the UKF, and the GP-UKF recently proposed by Ko et al. (2007).
originalAbstract: We propose an analytic moment-based filter for nonlinear stochastic dynamical systems modeled by Gaussian processes. Exact expressions for the expected value and the covariance matrix are provided for both the prediction and the filter step, where an additional Gaussian assumption is exploited in the latter case. The new filter does not require further approximations. In particular, it avoids sample approximations. We compare the filter to a variety of available Gaussian filters, such as the EKF, the UKF, and the GP-UKF recently proposed by Ko et al. (2007).

paragraphs: Filtering estimates the evolving state of a system from uncertain observations. This paper considers nonlinear stochastic dynamical systems modeled with Gaussian processes. Its focus is on computing the expected state and its covariance, which describe the estimate and the uncertainty associated with it during the filtering process.

The proposed filter derives analytic expressions for these quantities in both the prediction step and the filtering step. Prediction carries the estimate forward, while filtering incorporates observations. The expressions for the filtering step exploit an additional Gaussian assumption. Within this formulation, the method requires no further approximations and specifically avoids approximating the moments through samples.

The significance is that the required uncertainty summaries can be calculated analytically under the stated modeling assumptions. This should not be read as an unrestricted claim of exact inference for every nonlinear system. The paper compares the method with several Gaussian filters, including the extended Kalman filter, unscented Kalman filter, and Gaussian-process unscented Kalman filter, placing its analytic approach alongside established alternatives.
summary.tldr: The paper derives analytic filtering moments for Gaussian-process dynamical models, using an additional Gaussian assumption in the filtering step.

title: Analytic moment-based Gaussian process filtering

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of approximate singular value decomposition of large dense matrices that arises naturally in many machine learning applications. We discuss two recently introduced sampling-based spectral decomposition techniques: the Nystrom and the Column-sampling methods. We present a theoretical comparison between the two methods and provide novel insights regarding their suitability for various applications. We then provide experimental results motivated by this theory. Finally, we propose an efficient adaptive sampling technique to select informative columns from the original matrix. This novel technique outperforms standard sampling methods on a variety of datasets.

We discuss two recently introduced sampling-based spectral decomposition techniques: the Nystrom and the Column-sampling methods. We present a theoretical comparison between the two methods and provide novel insights regarding their suitability for various applications. paragraphs: Large dense matrices appear in many machine-learning problems, and computing their singular value decomposition can be demanding. This paper examines sampling-based ways to approximate that decomposition. Sampling offers a route to a smaller computational problem, but the choice of approximation method and the information retained from the original matrix both matter.

The authors theoretically compare the Nystrom and Column-sampling methods. Their analysis provides insights into which applications suit each technique, and they follow it with experiments motivated by that theory. This makes the comparison more than a performance contest: it aims to explain differences that can guide the choice of approximation approach.

The paper also proposes an efficient adaptive sampling procedure for choosing informative columns from the original matrix. That procedure outperforms standard sampling methods across a variety of evaluated datasets. The result highlights column selection as a meaningful part of approximation quality. Together, the comparison and adaptive method address both how to construct an approximate decomposition and how to select the data used in it.
summary.tldr: A theoretical comparison of sampling-based decompositions motivates experiments and an adaptive column-selection method that improves on standard sampling across tested datasets.

title: On sampling-based approximate spectral decomposition

abstract: In this paper we introduce the first algorithms for efficiently learning a simulation policy for Monte-Carlo search. Our main idea is to optimise the balance of a simulation policy, so that an accurate spread of simulation outcomes is maintained, rather than optimising the direct strength of the simulation policy. We develop two algorithms for balancing a simulation policy by gradient descent. The first algorithm optimises the balance of complete simulations, using a policy gradient algorithm; whereas the second algorithm optimises the balance over every two steps of simulation. We compare our algorithms to reinforcement learning and supervised learning algorithms for maximising the strength of the simulation policy. We test each algorithm in the domain of 5x5 Computer Go, using a softmax policy that is parameterised by weights for a hundred simple patterns. When used in a simple Monte-Carlo search, the policies learnt by simulation balancing achieved significantly better performance, with half the mean squared error of a uniform random policy, and equal overall performance to a sophisticated Go engine.

The first algorithm optimises the balance of complete simulations, using a policy gradient algorithm; whereas the second algorithm optimises the balance over every two steps of simulation. We compare our algorithms to reinforcement learning and supervised learning algorithms for maximising the strength of the simulation policy. We test each algorithm in the domain of 5x5 Computer Go, using a softmax policy that is parameterised by weights for a hundred simple patterns. paragraphs: Monte-Carlo search uses simulated outcomes to guide decisions, making the policy that generates simulations an important part of the search. This paper learns that policy by optimizing its balance: the objective is to maintain an accurate spread of outcomes. That goal differs from optimizing how strongly the simulation policy plays on its own.

The authors develop two gradient-based balancing algorithms. One uses policy gradients to optimize complete simulations, while the other targets balance over every two simulation steps. They compare these approaches with reinforcement and supervised learning methods designed to strengthen the simulation policy. Tests use 5x5 Go and a softmax policy with weights for one hundred simple patterns.

Within a simple Monte-Carlo search, the balanced policies achieve significantly better performance. Their mean squared error is half that of a uniform random policy, and overall performance matches a sophisticated Go engine. These findings support learning simulation policies specifically for the quality of their search estimates, with the reported results grounded in the tested Go setting.
summary.tldr: Learning balanced simulation outcomes improves Monte-Carlo search in 5x5 Go, supporting a training objective distinct from simulation-policy playing strength.

title: Monte-Carlo simulation balancing

abstract: We present an online learning framework tailored towards real-time learning from observed user behavior in search engines and other information retrieval systems. In particular, we only require pairwise comparisons, which were shown to be reliably inferred from implicit feedback. We will present an algorithm with theoretical guarantees as well as simulation results.
originalAbstract: We present an online learning framework tailored towards real-time learning from observed user behavior in search engines and other information retrieval systems. In particular, we only require pairwise comparisons, which were shown to be reliably inferred from implicit feedback. We will present an algorithm with theoretical guarantees as well as simulation results.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an online learning framework for improving search engines and other information retrieval systems from observed user behavior. The intended setting is real-time learning, where the system can use feedback as interaction occurs. Its central design choice is to require only comparisons between pairs of alternatives.

A pairwise comparison supplies a relative judgment about two alternatives. That makes the form of feedback central to the learning problem: the framework works with these comparisons rather than requiring a richer assessment from each interaction. The abstract points to evidence that such comparisons can be inferred reliably from implicit feedback, connecting the framework to behavior users already exhibit while using a retrieval system.

The authors present an algorithm with theoretical guarantees and report simulation results. Together, these address the formal behavior of the proposed learning procedure and its behavior in simulated settings. The contribution is a framework tailored to comparative feedback, making pairwise preference information the basis for interactive optimization of information retrieval.
summary.tldr: The paper frames real-time retrieval optimization as online learning from pairwise comparisons inferred from user behavior.
